crops.name: Angelica
varieties: Angelica gigas (ornamental, purple flowers, not for eating)

info: Angelica is a majestic, architectural plant with huge, ribbed, hollow stems, lacy leaves and globe-shaped greenish-white flowerheads loved by hoverflies. It is the source of the green candied stems used in cake decoration.
It thrives in moist, partial shade, and is biennial: it grows leaves in year one, and flowers in year two, then dies, though it self-seeds freely. Allow space for a huge plant.
sow: Sow fresh seed as soon as it is ripe, in August or September, as it loses viability quickly. Scatter on the surface of moist compost or soil and press in lightly; germination takes 3–6 weeks. Alternatively, buy young plants.
Plant in moist, rich soil in partial shade, 90 cm apart. Thin seedlings, or pot on and move before the long taproot develops.
grow: Water in dry weather and mulch with compost. To prolong the plant’s life, remove flower stalks as they appear in the second year, though the plant may then live a few more years. Allow a plant to seed to keep a supply.
Leaf miner and aphids may affect the foliage. Support tall flowering stems in windy sites. Plants die after seeding if allowed.

Angelica grows best in cool, moist soil, and suffers in hot, dry sites, where the leaves scorch. Give it room: a mature plant covers a square metre or more. Keep the base mulched, and if you want it to persist, cut the flower stalks before seeds form, which can turn it into a short-lived perennial for several more years.
grow_tips: Remove flower stalks to prolong life.
harvest: Cut young stems in April to June of the second year, before the plant flowers, while still tender and about 1 cm thick. Leaves can be picked from the first year, and the roots and seeds can also be used.
Use stems immediately to candy them. Collect seeds in late summer when ripe.
use: Candy the stems by simmering in sugar syrup over several days, then drying; the result is bright green and used in cake decoration. Add chopped leaves to stewed fruit such as rhubarb to reduce acidity. Stems can be added to jams. Seeds flavour liqueurs, such as Chartreuse.
Candied angelica keeps for months in an airtight jar. Do not eat if you are pregnant, take blood thinners or have diabetes, and avoid confusing angelica with poisonous lookalikes such as hemlock.

care.job: Mulch with compost in spring and give plants plenty of room, as angelica grows into a large, statuesque plant.
Water in dry weather, as angelica likes moist soil and partial shade, and cut off flower heads if you want to extend the life of the plant.
Cut young stems for candying in late spring or early summer, before they become tough.
Cut dead stems to the ground after the foliage dies back and mulch the crown.

preserving.how: Simmer young stems in sugar syrup over several days until translucent, then dry on a rack and store in an airtight tin.
Hang bunches in a warm, airy place, then crumble the leaves or shake out the seeds into jars for teas and flavouring.
Chop young leaves and stems and freeze in bags to add to stewed rhubarb or fruit.

safety: Do not eat if you are pregnant, take blood thinners or have diabetes, and avoid confusing angelica with poisonous lookalikes such as hemlock.

crops.name: Apple
crops.sun_text: Full sun; sheltered from strong wind

facts.Spacing: 1.2–5 m apart, depending on form and rootstock

varieties: Cox’s Orange Pippin (classic flavour, needs care)

types.name: Early (August to September)
types.when: Eat straight from the tree · Do not store
types.note: Juicy, refreshing, and short-lived. Pick as they ripen and eat within days.

types.name: Mid-season (September to October)
types.when: Eat within a few weeks
types.note: Good all-rounders that keep for a month or so in a cool place.

types.name: Late (October onwards)
types.when: Pick in October · Store until spring
types.note: Hard and sharp when picked, mellowing in store. Keep in a cool, dark, frost-free place.

info: Apples are the great British fruit tree, with thousands of varieties adapted to our climate and a wide range of flavours, from crisp sweet eaters to sharp cookers. A single tree on a dwarf rootstock gives bumper crops in a small garden or a large pot.

Most apples need a pollination partner flowering at the same time, so choose compatible varieties, or take advantage of neighbours’ trees and crab apples. Trees can be trained as cordons, espaliers or fans to save space, making them suitable even for small gardens.
sow: Plant bare-root trees from November to March, when the soil is not frozen or waterlogged, in a sunny, sheltered site with fertile, well-drained soil. Container-grown trees can be planted year round if watered well. Choose rootstock for the space: M27 (very dwarf, pots), M9 (dwarf), M26 (semi-dwarf), MM106 (medium).

Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots, drive in a stake, plant so the graft union is 5 cm above ground, and firm in. Tie to the stake with a tree tie and water well. Mulch around the base, leaving the trunk clear. In grass, keep a 1 m circle weed-free.
sow_tips: Choose a rootstock to suit your space.
Keep the graft union above soil.
grow: Water newly planted trees regularly for the first two years, particularly in dry spells. Mulch each spring and feed with a general fertiliser. Prune in winter (November to March) to an open framework, removing dead, diseased or crossing branches and shortening new growth; spur-bearing types are pruned on a regular, light basis. Summer-prune trained forms in August.

Thin fruitlets in June to one per cluster, 10–15 cm apart, for larger apples and to prevent biennial cropping. Codling moth (maggots in fruit), apple scab, canker and aphids are the common problems. Pheromone traps catch codling moths, and clearing fallen leaves reduces scab.
grow_tips: Clear fallen leaves to reduce scab.
harvest: Apples are ready when they come away easily with a gentle lift and twist; the pips turn brown and the fruit has full colour. Early varieties ripen in August and September and should be eaten soon, while late varieties are picked in October and stored. Don’t pull, as it will damage spurs.

Pick carefully to avoid bruising and handle each apple like an egg. Windfalls are good for immediate cooking but won’t store. Late-season apples often improve in flavour during storage and are best left on the tree as long as frost allows.
harvest_tips: Lift and twist: ripe fruit comes away easily.
use: Eat dessert apples fresh, in salads and slaws, or slice them for baking. Cookers such as Bramley collapse into a fluffy purée for pies, crumbles, sauces and chutneys. Apples can be juiced and made into cider, jelly, and dried rings. They pair well with cheese, pork, cinnamon and blackberries.

Store sound, unbruised late apples in a cool (3–5°C), dark, frost-free place such as a garage or shed, wrapped in newspaper or in trays with space between. Check weekly and remove any that rot. Many varieties keep until February to March. Cooked apple purée freezes well.
use_tips: Wrap late apples individually for storage.

care.job: Prune established trees in the dormant season, removing dead, diseased and crossing branches and opening up the centre.
Feed with a general fertiliser and mulch around the base, keeping the mulch clear of the trunk.
Protect blossom with fleece on frosty nights if the tree is small enough, and encourage pollinators by planting nearby flowers.
Thin heavy crops of fruitlets in June, leaving one apple per cluster, to get bigger fruit and reduce biennial bearing.
Summer prune trained forms (cordons, espaliers) and water young trees in dry spells.
Put grease bands around trunks in October to catch winter moth, and clear fallen fruit to reduce disease.
Plant new bare-root trees from November while the soil is workable and stake them well.

preserving.how: Wrap sound, unbruised late apples individually in paper and store in a single layer in trays in a cool, frost-free shed or garage.
Keep in the salad drawer, loosely bagged, away from strongly flavoured foods.
Peel, core and slice, then freeze on a tray before bagging. Or freeze cooked apple purée in tubs.
Press into juice and freeze, or pasteurise in clean bottles. Windfalls and bruised fruit are ideal for this.
Make apple sauce, chutney, jelly or dried apple rings from the surplus.

crops.name: Apricot
crops.sun_text: Full sun; a warm, south-facing wall

info: Apricots can succeed in the UK against a warm, sheltered, south-facing wall, where they are sheltered from frost and ripen in the heat reflected from the brickwork. Self-fertile varieties such as Moorpark give delicious fruit in a good summer.
The key challenge is frost protection of the early blossom in February to March, so be prepared to cover with fleece on cold nights. A fan-trained tree is the best form.
sow: Plant a young tree in a sunny, sheltered spot against a south-facing wall, in fertile, free-draining soil, ideally with lime. Dig a large hole and add compost. Plant with graft 5 cm above soil, and tie into wires as a fan.
Apricots on St Julien A rootstock are most common. Mulch around the base. Container-grown trees can go in a large pot in a greenhouse.
grow: Protect blossom with a double layer of fleece on frosty nights, removing during the day for pollinators. Hand-pollinate flowers with a soft brush if few insects are about. Thin fruitlets in June to 8 cm apart.
Prune in summer only to avoid silver leaf and bacterial canker. Water regularly in dry weather, especially when fruit swells. Feed with a general fertiliser in spring.
harvest: Pick apricots when fully coloured, slightly soft, and they come away from the tree easily, in August. Ripen fully on the tree for the best flavour, but pick before they split. Pick over several visits.
Handle gently; they bruise easily. Eat soon after picking.

Test ripeness by gently cupping the fruit and giving it a slight twist; ripe apricots come away easily, and the flesh gives a little near the stalk. Apricots picked underripe never develop their full sweetness, so be patient even if wasps and birds are interested, and net or cover the tree with a fine mesh bag to protect it.
use: Eat fresh, bake in tarts, cakes, and crumbles, poach, or make jam, chutney and dried apricots. Their flavour concentrates when cooked. Pair with almonds, honey and vanilla.
Fresh fruit lasts 3–5 days. Halve, stone and freeze on trays, or dry in a low oven.

Apricots make an outstanding jam, particularly when a few of the kernels are cracked and added for an almond-like flavour. Halve and roast them with honey and thyme, serve poached with vanilla ice cream, or dry them in a very low oven (70°C) for several hours for chewy, intensely flavoured snacks.

care.job: Protect blossom on wall-trained trees with fleece on frosty nights, as apricots flower very early. Hand-pollinate with a soft brush on warm days.
Thin fruitlets to about 8 to 10 cm apart, and tie in new shoots on fan-trained trees.
Water consistently in dry spells and feed with a high-potash feed once the fruit is swelling.
Prune only in summer, never in winter, to avoid silver leaf and bacterial canker. Cut out dead wood and crossing branches.

preserving.how: Keep ripe fruit in a single layer in the fridge and eat quickly.
Halve and stone, then freeze on a tray before bagging. Best used cooked or in smoothies once thawed.
Apricots set well with a little added lemon juice. Pot into sterilised jars.
Halve and dry in a very low oven or dehydrator until leathery but still pliable.

facts.Spacing: 30–45 cm apart in rows 1 m apart
facts.Time to harvest: Light picking from year 3; full crop from year 4

info: Asparagus is a luxury crop that needs patience: plants take three years to establish before cropping, but a well-kept bed will produce tender spears every spring for 20 years or more. Freshly cut asparagus is far sweeter than any in the shops.

The British season is short, around late April to mid-June, and part of its pleasure. It needs a sunny, free-draining, weed-free bed, and it is best suited to medium or large plots. Choose all-male varieties for higher yields.
sow: Buy one-year-old crowns and plant them in March or April, in a bed prepared months in advance by removing every weed, especially perennial ones, and digging in plenty of compost. Dig a trench about 30 cm wide and 20 cm deep, with a ridge down the middle, and drape the crown over the ridge with its roots spread out.

Space crowns 30–45 cm apart, cover with 5 cm of soil, then fill the trench gradually as the shoots grow. Water in well. Raised beds help in heavy soil. Keep weeds out in the first years and mark the rows.
sow_tips: Use raised beds in heavy soil.
grow: Keep the bed weed-free, hand-weeding gently as roots are shallow. Mulch with compost or well-rotted manure each spring. Do not cut any spears in the first two years. In autumn, when the ferny foliage turns yellow, cut it down to 5 cm and clear it away.

Asparagus beetle and slugs damage spears, so pick off the beetles by hand. Support the tall ferns with canes and string in windy spots. Feed with a general fertiliser in late winter, and apply a mulch of seaweed or salt-free compost in spring.
harvest: Do not harvest in the first two years. In year 3, cut spears for about 3–4 weeks, and from year 4 for six weeks, from late April to mid-June (ending by about 21 June). Cut spears when they are 12–18 cm tall, with a sharp knife 2.5 cm below the surface.

Stop cutting by midsummer to let the ferns grow and build up the crown for next year’s crop. Cut spears every day or two in warm weather, as they grow fast. Fresh spears are best eaten within hours of cutting.
harvest_tips: Cut every day or two in warm weather.
use: Steam or boil spears for 3–4 minutes, or roast or grill them with olive oil and sea salt. Serve with butter, hollandaise, a poached egg or parmesan, or add to risottos, quiches and salads. The thicker spears are the most prized. Snap off the tough ends before cooking.

Fresh spears keep for 2–3 days in the fridge, standing upright in a jar of water or wrapped in damp paper. To freeze, blanch for 2 minutes (thin spears) or 4 (thick), cool quickly and freeze on a tray, then bag. Frozen spears are best used cooked.
use_tips: Stand spears in water in the fridge.
Roast with olive oil for a nutty taste.

care.job: Weed carefully by hand and feed with a general fertiliser in spring, then mulch with well-rotted compost.
Cut spears when they reach 15 to 20 cm, but never harvest in the first year after planting, and only lightly in the second.
Stop cutting by the end of June and let the ferny growth develop to build up energy for next year.
Support tall ferns with stakes and string to stop wind damage, and water in dry weather.
Cut ferns down to 2 to 3 cm when they turn yellow, then mulch the bed with compost.

preserving.how: Stand the spears upright in a glass with 2 cm of water, loosely covered, or wrap the ends in damp kitchen paper.
Blanch for 2 minutes (thin spears) or 4 (thick), cool in iced water, dry and freeze on a tray before bagging.
Pack blanched spears upright into jars and cover with hot spiced vinegar brine.

crops.name: Aubergine
crops.sun_text: Full sun; needs warmth, best under glass

facts.Type: Tender perennial, grown as an annual

info: Aubergines are the most demanding of the fruiting vegetables for UK gardeners, needing a long season and plenty of warmth, but a greenhouse, polytunnel or warm conservatory makes them achievable. The glossy fruits and lilac flowers are attractive.

Choose early, compact varieties bred for northern climates and aim for just three to five fruits per plant, which gives larger and better-quality aubergines. Smaller, rounder types often do best outdoors in warm summers.
sow: Sow early, in February to March, 5 mm deep in seed compost at 22–25°C in a heated propagator. They germinate in two to three weeks, and warmth is crucial. Prick out into individual 7–9 cm pots and keep them warm and bright.

Pot on into 12 cm pots and then into final 25–30 cm pots by late May. Keep them in a heated or frost-free greenhouse, or on a sunny windowsill, and move outdoors only after the frost, in June, if the weather is warm and the position sheltered. Even then, a greenhouse is more reliable.
sow_tips: Sow in February–March with strong heat.
Grow under glass for reliable results.
grow: Keep plants warm and out of draughts. Water consistently, keeping the compost moist but not soggy, and feed weekly with tomato fertiliser once the first flowers set. Pinch out the growing tip when plants are 30 cm tall, and limit each plant to four to six fruits.

Mist the flowers in the morning to help setting, and support heavy plants with a cane. Red spider mite and whitefly are common under glass; keep humidity up and check the leaf undersides regularly. Cold nights stop growth and drop flowers.
grow_tips: Mist the flowers to aid setting.
harvest: Pick aubergines in August to October when the skin is glossy, firm and fully coloured, and springs back when gently pressed. If the skin has lost its shine or the flesh is spongy, they are overripe. Cut off with a sharp knife or secateurs, leaving a short stalk.
Picking regularly encourages more fruits. Before the first frost, pick all the remaining fruit, even if small. Aubergines are best used on the day or within a few days of picking.
harvest_tips: Cut, don’t pull, off the plant.
use: Roast, grill, fry or bake aubergines, in moussaka, ratatouille, curries, baba ganoush, parmigiana and stir-fries. Slice, salt and rinse older aubergines to draw out any bitterness (modern varieties rarely need this), and cook until completely soft and creamy.

Aubergines keep for about a week in a cool place or the fridge’s salad drawer, but not in the cold part. They do not freeze raw, but cooked aubergine dishes freeze well, and roasted flesh can be frozen for use in dips.
use_tips: Roast the flesh for baba ganoush.

care.job: Pot on young plants and keep them at 18C or above, in a bright greenhouse or sunny windowsill.
Pinch out the growing tip at about 30 cm to encourage bushy plants and stake as they grow.
Water regularly and feed every week with a tomato feed once flowers appear, and mist the leaves to deter red spider mite.
Limit each plant to about four to six fruits for good size, removing any extras and smaller flowers.
Pick remaining fruit before the first frost.

pests.label: Flower and fruit drop in cold spells

preserving.how: Keep whole in the warmest part of the fridge or a cool room, as they dislike cold.
Roast or grill slices, or make into a dip or ratatouille, cool and freeze in tubs. Raw aubergine freezes poorly.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator or very low oven. Rehydrate in hot water or stock.
Make into a spiced chutney or pickle with onions and vinegar.

crops.name: Basil
crops.sun_text: Full sun; warm and sheltered, or a bright windowsill

types.name: Sweet basil (Italian)
types.when: Sow April to July · Pick June to October
types.note: The classic for tomatoes, pasta and pesto.

types.name: Small-leaved (Greek) basil
types.when: Sow April to July · Pick June to October
types.note: Neat bushes with tiny leaves and a strong flavour. Good in pots.

types.name: Thai and spiced basils
types.when: Sow April to June · Pick July to October
types.note: Aniseed, cinnamon or lemon notes, for curries and stir-fries.

info: Basil is the great summer herb, sweet, peppery and fragrant, and it belongs next to the tomatoes. It needs warmth, so it is best grown on a sunny windowsill, in a greenhouse or in a sheltered, sunny spot outdoors after the last frost.

Beyond the classic Genovese, there are Thai, lemon, cinnamon, purple and tiny-leaved Greek basils, each with a distinct flavour. Pots are ideal, and sowing a little every few weeks gives plants through to autumn.
sow: Sow on the surface of moist seed compost from April to July, 5 mm deep, at 18–21°C on a bright windowsill. Seed germinates in 1–2 weeks. Prick out seedlings into 7 cm pots when they have two true leaves, or sow thinly into the final pot and thin out.

Plant outdoors in June, once nights are warm (above 10°C) and frost risk has gone, or pot on into 15–20 cm pots on a windowsill. Space plants 20–30 cm apart. Basil resents cold and wet; a cloche or greenhouse helps.
sow_tips: Harden off carefully; basil hates cold.
grow: Water in the morning, at the base of the plant, keeping the compost moist but not soggy, since wet leaves in cool nights encourage rot. Pinch out the growing tips when plants are 15 cm tall for bushy growth, and pinch off flower buds immediately to keep leaves coming.

Feed with a liquid fertiliser every two weeks. Slugs love basil, and aphids and downy mildew can affect plants, especially in damp conditions. Keep plants in good light and airflow, and remove affected leaves.
grow_tips: Pinch out the tips for bushy plants.
Water in the morning at the base.
harvest: Start picking leaves when plants are 15 cm tall, from about six weeks. Pinch off the tips of stems just above a pair of leaves, which prompts two new shoots, and harvest from the top down rather than stripping individual leaves from the base.

Pick regularly, and never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Harvest before flowering for the best flavour. Pick in the morning, as the flavour is best before the heat of the day. Take all remaining leaves before the first cold nights in autumn.
harvest_tips: Pinch above a pair of leaves.
Never take more than a third.
use: Add torn leaves to tomato salads, pizza, pasta, soups and sauces at the end of cooking, as heat destroys the flavour. Blend into pesto with pine nuts, garlic, parmesan and olive oil, or make basil oil and basil vinegar. Thai basil suits stir-fries and curries.

Fresh basil keeps best at room temperature with the stems in water, not in the fridge, where it blackens. For longer storage, freeze leaves in olive oil in ice-cube trays, or freeze pesto in portions. Drying loses most of the flavour.
use_tips: Add at the end of cooking.
Store stems in water at room temperature.
Tear, don’t chop, to avoid bruising.

care.job: Keep plants on a warm, sunny windowsill or in a greenhouse; basil dislikes cold nights and sulks below about 10C.
Pinch out the growing tips regularly to make bushy plants and remove flower buds as they appear, as flowering makes leaves bitter.
Water in the morning at the base of the plant, keeping the compost moist but never sitting in water.
Feed container plants every two weeks with a general liquid feed.
Bring pots indoors before nights drop below 10C, or harvest the last leaves and freeze them in oil.

preserving.how: Treat cut stems like flowers in a glass of water on the worktop. Cold damages the leaves, so keep it out of the fridge.
Blend leaves with olive oil and freeze the paste in ice cube trays, or freeze whole leaves layered in a tub.
Blend with pine nuts, garlic, parmesan and oil and top with oil. Freeze in portions for longest life.
Steep a handful of leaves in white wine vinegar. Use fresh leaves in oil only for immediate use, and keep it chilled.

crops.name: Bay
crops.sun_text: Full sun to partial shade; sheltered from cold winds

facts.Type: Evergreen shrub or tree, hardy in most areas
facts.Height: 2–5 m (or clipped to 1 m in a pot)

info: Bay is a handsome evergreen with glossy, aromatic leaves that are an essential in bouquet garni and slow-cooked dishes. It is easy to grow in a large pot or border, and can be clipped into standards, balls and cones to make decorative features.

It is hardy in most of Britain once established, but young plants and pot-grown specimens may need protection in cold winters, since hard frost can scorch leaves. A sheltered spot makes all the difference.
sow: Plant a pot-grown bay in spring or early autumn in a sunny or lightly shaded, sheltered position with free-draining soil. Add grit to heavy soil. Seed is slow and erratic, so buy a young plant or take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer.
In pots, use a loam-based compost with grit in a container at least 30 cm wide, and repot every 2–3 years. Water in well until established. A position out of cold east winds prevents leaf scorch.
sow_tips: Buy a plant rather than sow.
grow: Once established, bay is easy. Water pot-grown plants regularly in summer but keep the compost on the dry side in winter. Feed monthly in the growing season. Clip in summer with secateurs, cutting stems rather than trimming leaves, which turn brown at the cut edge.

In cold regions, protect potted plants with fleece or move under cover. Scale insects and sooty mould are the main pests; wipe off scale with soapy water. Leaf scorch from cold winds browns leaves; it normally recovers in spring. Bay suckers are common and can be dug out.
harvest: Pick leaves at any time of year, cutting or snapping individual leaves from the stem. Flavour develops as the leaves age, so older leaves, a year or two old, have the strongest taste. Avoid stripping any one branch.
For drying, pick in summer and dry flat in a warm, shady place for two weeks, then store in a jar. Dried bay keeps its flavour for about a year.
use: Add one or two leaves to stews, soups, stocks, casseroles, curries, rice, sauces and custards. Always remove the leaves before serving, since they are tough. Fresh leaves are mild and become more pungent when dried and aged.
Store dried leaves in an airtight jar in a dark cupboard. Fresh leaves keep on the plant all year, or freeze in bags. A bay leaf in a jar of rice or flour deters weevils.
use_tips: Store dried leaves in a jar.

care.job: Trim shoots lightly in spring to keep the shape, and feed potted plants with a slow-release fertiliser.
Water pots in dry weather, as bay hates drying out completely, but never leave it standing in water.
Clip topiary shapes in summer, cutting with secateurs rather than shears so the large leaves are not damaged.
Move pots to a sheltered spot against a wall or wrap in fleece in hard frosts, as bay can be damaged by cold winds.

preserving.how: Pick leaves and dry flat for 2–3 weeks in a warm, airy place, then store in a jar. The flavour mellows as they dry.
Freeze fresh leaves in a bag. They go brittle but keep their flavour well.
Bay is evergreen, so you can simply pick fresh leaves all year round.

crops.name: Beetroot

facts.Type: Hardy biennial root vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 8–10 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

varieties: Burpee’s Golden (sweet yellow roots, no staining)

types.name: Early globe beetroot
types.when: Sow March to May (under cloches early) · Harvest June to August
types.note: Quick, tender, round roots that are best pulled young at golf-ball to tennis-ball size.

types.name: Maincrop and storing beetroot
types.when: Sow May to July · Harvest September to October, store for winter
types.note: Larger roots that keep well in boxes of sand or a cool shed.

types.name: Coloured beetroot
types.when: Sow April to July · Harvest July to October
types.note: Golden and striped roots that do not bleed red, and have a milder, sweeter flavour.

info: Beetroot is one of the easiest and most forgiving root crops, giving both sweet roots and nutritious leaves that can be eaten like chard. It grows well in pots, beds and between other crops, and a few short rows sown every few weeks keep a steady supply going from early summer to late autumn.

Beetroot seed is actually a dried fruit that contains several seeds, so each ‘seed’ produces a small cluster of seedlings. Thinning is therefore part of the job, but the thinnings make a tasty salad leaf.
sow: Sow from March under cloches or fleece, then outdoors in April to July once the soil is above about 7°C. Colder soil can cause young plants to bolt. Sow seed 2 cm deep in rows 30 cm apart, one cluster every 5–10 cm. Seedlings appear in 10–14 days, and soaking the seed in water for a few hours before sowing speeds germination.

Sow a short row every three or four weeks for a steady supply, and finish with a late sowing in July for autumn roots. In containers, use a pot at least 20 cm deep and sow thinly across the surface, thinning to 5 cm for baby beets.
sow_tips: Choose a bolt-resistant variety such as Boltardy for early sowings.
Thin to one seedling per cluster when they reach 5 cm.
Sow thinly in a pot for a baby-beet crop on a balcony.
Do not sow into freshly manured soil.
grow: Thin seedlings in stages, finishing at 8–10 cm apart for full-size roots. Water regularly, because dry spells followed by rain cause splitting and tough, woody roots. A mulch of compost or grass clippings keeps the soil evenly moist and suppresses weeds, which beetroot dislikes competing with.

Beetroot is rarely troubled by serious problems. Leaf miners leave pale tunnels in the foliage, so pinch off affected leaves. Birds sometimes peck seedlings, and boron deficiency in very alkaline or sandy soil can cause dark, corky patches in the roots, which a light application of borax-containing fertiliser addresses.
grow_tips: Water consistently; uneven watering is the main cause of poor roots.
Pinch off leaves with miner damage and bin them.
Feed lightly if growth stalls, but avoid high nitrogen.
harvest: Baby beets can be pulled from about eight weeks, when they are the size of a golf ball. For maincrop roots, wait until they are 5–8 cm across, around 12 weeks. Larger roots tend to be woodier, so harvest before they exceed a tennis ball. Lift with a fork to avoid damaging the skin, as the roots bleed colour.

Twist off the leaves 2–3 cm above the root rather than cutting them, as cutting makes the beetroot bleed. Lift all roots from the ground by mid to late October, before hard frosts. Leaves can be picked sparingly throughout the season.
harvest_tips: Twist, do not cut, the leaves to stop colour loss.
Use a fork and keep it well away from the roots.
Pick a few leaves from each plant; taking too many weakens the root.
Harvest before hard frosts for the best storage.
use: Roast whole beets in foil for an hour, then peel the skins off, or boil them for 30–45 minutes. Grate raw into slaws, blend into hummus and chocolate cakes, or pickle with vinegar for a jar to enjoy through the winter. The young leaves can be wilted like spinach or added raw to salads.

Twist off the leaves, leave 2 cm of stalk and keep roots unwashed in a bag in the fridge for two to three weeks. For longer storage, pack undamaged roots in boxes of dry sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed, where they last three to five months. Cooked beetroot freezes well, or can be pickled and kept for a year.
use_tips: Wear gloves when peeling cooked beetroot to avoid stained hands.
Pickle small roots whole for a jar that keeps for months.
Wilt the leaves in butter like chard.
Freeze cooked, peeled cubes on a tray before bagging them.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 7 to 10 cm apart, as each seed cluster produces several, and use the thinnings in salads.
Water consistently, as uneven watering causes woody roots, and keep weeds down while the plants are small.
Add a boron-rich feed or seaweed extract if roots split or have black patches inside.
Lift the last roots before hard frost or cover with a thick layer of straw.

preserving.how: Twist off the leaves, leave a little stalk, and pack unwashed roots in boxes of slightly damp sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed.
Store unwashed, trimmed roots in a bag in the salad drawer.
Cook until tender, peel, slice and pack into jars of spiced vinegar. Classic and keeps well.
Cook, peel, slice or cube and freeze in bags. Raw beetroot freezes badly.
In mild areas, cover with a thick mulch of straw and lift as needed. Lift before hard frost to be safe.

crops.name: Blackberry
crops.sun_text: Full sun to shade; tolerates poor sites

facts.Spacing: 2–4 m apart (thornless types need more space)
facts.Planting depth: Same depth as in the nursery

types.name: Thornless blackberries
types.when: Harvest August to October
types.note: Easy to prune and pick. Excellent for small gardens.

types.name: Thorny blackberries
types.when: Harvest August to October
types.note: Often the best flavour and hardiest, and a wildlife barrier.

info: Cultivated blackberries are bigger, juicier and less seedy than wild ones, and the thornless varieties are easy to pick. They crop heavily in late summer and autumn, and grow in a wide range of conditions, including partial shade and poor soil.

They are vigorous climbers best trained along a wire fence, trellis or wall, and a single plant can cover several metres. They are ideal for hiding eyesores and for wildlife-friendly gardens, as the flowers and fruits are loved by pollinators and birds.
sow: Plant bare-root or potted canes between November and March in a sunny or partially shaded spot with fertile, well-drained soil. Dig in plenty of compost. Space plants 2–4 m apart depending on vigour, as they can spread widely.

Install posts and horizontal wires at 1 m, 1.5 m and 1.8 m. After planting, cut the cane to 20–30 cm above the ground. Water in well and mulch around the base. Compact varieties such as Waldo can be grown in large pots.
sow_tips: Cut canes to 25 cm after planting.
Choose thornless varieties for easy picking.
grow: Mulch each spring with compost and water in dry periods. Tie in new canes to the wires as they grow, keeping new growth separate from the old canes that will fruit this year: tie the new growth to one side and the fruiting canes to the other.

After fruiting, cut the old canes that bore fruit to the ground, and tie in the new canes to replace them. This is the main pruning job. Birds and wasps will take the fruit, and cane spot or botrytis can occur in wet years; good air flow helps.
grow_tips: Train new canes separately from fruiting ones.
Cut out fruited canes after harvest.
Keep ties loose to avoid girdling.
harvest: Pick blackberries when fully black and glossy, and they come off the plant with a gentle tug; unripe ones are shiny and stay stuck. Berries ripen gradually from August to October, so pick every few days. Ripe berries are soft and sweet.
Pick in the morning on a dry day, and handle gently, as berries bruise easily. Use shallow containers and do not stack deeply. Wear gloves and sleeves for thorny types.
harvest_tips: Pick when fully black and soft.
use: Eat fresh with cream or yoghurt, or cook in crumbles, pies, jams, jellies, sauces and cordials. Blackberries and apple is a classic autumn pairing. They also make wonderful ice cream, syrup, and brambly vinegars, and bring colour to puddings.

Fresh berries keep for only 2–3 days in the fridge, so process quickly. Freeze unwashed on a tray, then bag for up to a year, and use straight from the freezer in crumbles and jam. Bottled blackberry syrup and jelly store well on a shelf.
use_tips: Freeze on a tray and bag.

care.job: Tie in last year's canes to supports and cut out any dead or weak shoots. Feed and mulch around the base.
Train this year's new canes in a separate bunch away from fruiting canes, so you can find them easily at pruning time.
Water in dry spells while fruit swells, and net against birds.
After fruiting, cut the old fruited canes to the ground and tie in the best new canes, around 10 to 15 cm apart.
Plant new canes in the dormant season and cut back to a strong bud about 25 cm above the ground.

preserving.how: Spread unwashed berries in a single layer in a shallow container.
Open freeze on a tray, then bag. Berries stay separate and are ready for baking and smoothies.
Blackberry and apple jam is a classic. Jelly removes the seeds if you prefer.
Simmer with sugar for a cordial, or steep in gin or vodka with sugar for a few months.
preserving.keeps: Cordial: about 1 month in the fridge; liqueur: 1 year+

facts.Planting depth: 5 cm deeper than in the nursery

types.name: Early blackcurrants
types.when: Harvest early to mid July
types.note: Ripen before the main season, but are more at risk from spring frost.

types.name: Mid-season blackcurrants
types.when: Harvest mid to late July
types.note: Reliable and heavy, best for general use.

types.name: Late blackcurrants
types.when: Harvest late July to August
types.note: Frost-tolerant when flowering, with sweeter fruit.

info: Blackcurrants are exceptionally hardy and productive bushes, packed with vitamin C, giving heavy crops of glossy black berries from July. They thrive in the UK’s cool climate and tolerate some shade, and bushes crop reliably for 15 years or more.
They are simple to grow and prune, and the fruit is excellent for jam, cordials and desserts. Compact varieties such as Ben Sarek are suited to smaller plots and large pots.
sow: Plant bare-root bushes between November and March in a sunny or lightly shaded site with fertile, moisture-retentive soil, enriched with compost. Plant 5 cm deeper than they were in the nursery, as this encourages strong new shoots from the base.

Space bushes 1.5 m apart. After planting, cut all stems down to one bud above the ground; this feels drastic but promotes strong growth. Mulch generously and water in. No fruit will be borne in the first year, but crops begin in year two.
sow_tips: Plant deeper than in the nursery.
Cut stems to one bud after planting.
grow: Mulch every spring with compost and apply a nitrogen-rich feed such as chicken manure pellets. Water in dry spells while the fruit swells. Net the bushes against birds as the fruit ripens.

Prune in winter after fruiting: remove about a third of the oldest, darkest stems at ground level and cut out weak or low-lying growth, as blackcurrants fruit best on young wood. Big bud mite, which causes swollen buds, and reversion virus are the main problems. Pick off swollen buds in winter.
grow_tips: Remove a third of old stems each winter.
harvest: Pick berries when fully black and slightly soft, usually in July and August, with the whole truss at once. Dessert varieties can be picked as they ripen; for jam, the whole strig can be cut off with scissors. Pick on a dry day.
Berries ripen over a couple of weeks, and the whole bush can be harvested in one or two sessions. Berries can be left on the bush for a short time, but birds will find them, so net them early.
use: Blackcurrants are tart and strongly flavoured, so they suit cooking more than eating raw. Make jam (they set well), cordial, crumbles, pies, compotes, sorbets and sauces, or the classic summer pudding. Add sugar to taste. Remove the ‘tops and tails’ if you like, though it is not strictly necessary for jam.

Fresh berries keep for a week in the fridge. They freeze brilliantly: strip from the truss with a fork, freeze on a tray, then bag, and use straight from frozen. Blackcurrant cordial can be frozen or bottled.
use_tips: Strip from the truss with a fork.
Freeze whole and cook from frozen.

care.job: Mulch around the base and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser, as blackcurrants are hungry plants.
Protect flowers from frost with fleece, as blackcurrants flower early.
Net against birds as the fruit ripens, and water in dry spells to boost fruit size.
Prune straight after harvest: cut out about a third of the oldest, darkest stems down to the ground to stimulate new growth.
Plant bare-root bushes deeply in the dormant season and cut all stems back to one bud above the ground.

preserving.how: Strip from the strigs, freeze on a tray, then bag. They are tart and freeze exceptionally well.
Simmer with sugar and a little water, strain and bottle in sterilised bottles. Rich in vitamin C.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

preserving.how: High in pectin, so they set easily. Good for sauces, too.
Keep on the stalk in a covered container.

facts.Planting depth: Same depth as in the pot

types.name: Early blueberries
types.when: Harvest July
types.note: Ripen first and give a short, sweet flush.

types.name: Mid-season blueberries
types.when: Harvest late July to August
types.note: Reliable, heavy cropping, and the best all-rounders.

types.name: Late blueberries
types.when: Harvest August to September
types.note: Large, firm, late-keeping berries with excellent flavour.

info: Blueberries are attractive shrubs with white spring flowers, fine autumn colour and generous crops of nutrient-packed berries. They need acid soil, but grow very happily in pots of ericaceous compost, so any gardener can grow them.

Plant two different varieties for better pollination and bigger crops. Choose early, mid and late varieties for a long season. Compact varieties such as Sunshine Blue and Top Hat are ideal for patios.
sow: Plant in autumn or spring in a sunny site. Blueberries need acid soil with a pH of 4.5–5.5; if your soil is neutral or alkaline, grow them in pots of ericaceous (peat-free) compost, in containers of at least 40 cm. Plant two or more varieties for cross-pollination.

In pots, use a mix of ericaceous compost with a layer of crocks for drainage, and plant at the same depth as in the nursery pot. Mulch with pine bark or composted bracken. Water with rainwater, as tap water in hard-water areas gradually raises the pH.
grow: Keep the soil constantly moist, but not waterlogged, especially while the fruit swells; shallow roots dry out quickly in pots. Feed with an ericaceous fertiliser in spring. Pick off the flowers in the first year to build a stronger bush.

Prune lightly in the first years. From year four, in winter, remove a quarter of the oldest stems to the base, and any weak or crossing growth. Net the bushes as soon as fruit forms, since birds love blueberries. Yellow leaves with green veins signal iron deficiency from high pH.
harvest: Berries ripen over several weeks from July, in succession. Wait until they are fully blue all over, with no red tinge, then wait another few days for the best flavour, as they sweeten after turning blue. Ripe berries come off with a gentle roll of the thumb.
Pick every few days. Berries from the top of the bush ripen first. Net the fruit before it starts to colour. Autumn leaf colour in October is a bonus.
harvest_tips: Wait a few days after they turn blue.
Roll berries off with your thumb.
use: Eat fresh, add to porridge and yoghurt, bake in muffins, pancakes and pies, or cook into jam, compote and sauces. Blueberries pair with lemon, vanilla, almonds and cream. Their skins are rich in antioxidants and hold their shape when cooked.

Fresh blueberries keep for up to two weeks in the fridge, longer than most fruit. They freeze very well: spread unwashed on a tray, freeze, and bag for up to a year. Dried blueberries are a healthy snack.

care.job: Mulch with pine bark or ericaceous compost and feed with an ericaceous fertiliser, as blueberries need acidic soil.
Water with rainwater whenever possible, as tap water in hard-water areas raises the pH. Never let pots dry out.
Protect flowers from frost with fleece, and encourage bees, which pollinate the blossoms.
Net bushes against birds as the fruit ripens and water regularly to keep fruit plump.
Prune in winter, cutting out the oldest, darkest stems and any crowded growth, to stimulate fresh fruiting wood.

preserving.how: Keep dry and unwashed in a shallow, covered container. Wash just before use.
Open freeze on a tray and bag. They stay free-flowing and hold their shape for baking.
Dry in a dehydrator or low oven until chewy, then store in a jar.
Cook with sugar and lemon juice. Jam sets best with added pectin or a tart fruit.

info: Borage is a rugged, hairy annual that produces a haze of bright blue, star-shaped flowers from June until the first frost, and it is one of the best plants for bees. The flowers taste of cucumber and are edible, as are the young leaves.

It is superb alongside strawberries and tomatoes, where it attracts pollinators and may improve fruit set. It self-seeds so reliably that one sowing gives plants for years. It can grow large and sprawling, so give it space at the back of a bed.
sow: Sow seeds directly outdoors from April to June, 1 cm deep, in a sunny spot in any soil, including poor soil. Thin seedlings to 45 cm apart, since plants grow big. Borage has a long taproot and dislikes being moved, so sow where it will grow.
Seedlings appear in 1–2 weeks. Sow a second batch in mid-summer for a longer flowering season. Borage can be grown in large pots (30 cm or more), but plants grow best in the ground.
sow_tips: Sow in succession for longer flowers.
grow: Borage needs almost no care. Water in a prolonged drought, but avoid feeding. Support taller plants with twiggy sticks or canes if windy. The stems and leaves have bristly hairs, so wear gloves when handling.

Deadhead to extend flowering, or leave the seed to self-sow. Powdery mildew may occur in late summer. Plants can be cut hard back if they get untidy, and they will regrow. Pull out unwanted seedlings in spring.
harvest: Pick the flowers in the morning once fully open, pulling them gently from the green calyx. Pick young leaves when small and tender, before the hairs coarsen. Flowers are produced continuously from June to October.
Use flowers fresh, as they wilt within hours. Leave plenty of flowers for the bees, who love them. Young leaves are best before flowering.
use: Scatter the flowers on salads, desserts, cakes and cheese, or float them in drinks such as Pimm’s and gin and tonic; freeze them in ice cubes for pretty drinks. Young leaves taste of cucumber and can be chopped finely in salads and cream cheese, or cooked like spinach.

Flowers are best used immediately but keep for a day in the fridge. Candy them with egg white and sugar for decorating cakes, which preserves them for several weeks. Freeze in ice cubes for summer drinks.

care.job: Thin seedlings to about 45 cm apart, as borage grows large and bushy, and keep it away from delicate plants that it could swamp.
Pick flowers regularly for salads and drinks, which keeps the plants blooming and attracts bees all summer.
Let a few plants set seed so borage self-sows for the following year, and pull up the rest in autumn.

preserving.how: Freeze flowers in ice cube trays with water for drinks and summer cocktails.
Brush flowers with egg white, dust with caster sugar and dry on a rack for cake decorations.
Dry leaves lightly for tea, although the flavour is weaker than fresh.

crops.name: Borlotti bean
varieties: Lingua di Fuoco (climbing, fresh or dry)

info: Borlotti beans are beautiful beans with speckled crimson and cream pods and mottled seeds, grown to be eaten fresh or dried. They are rich, nutty and creamy, a staple of Italian cooking, and they are easy to grow in the same way as runner and French beans.
Climbing types need supports, while dwarf types are available for pots. They need a warm summer to ripen, but fresh shelling beans can be picked earlier if the season is cool.
sow: Sow indoors from late April to May in individual pots, 5 cm deep, or outdoors from mid-May to June, once the soil is warm, at the base of canes or a wigwam, 15 cm apart. Plant out after the last frost.
Choose a sunny, sheltered site with fertile, moisture-retentive soil, and give climbing types 2.4 m canes.
sow_tips: Sow indoors for an early start.
grow: Water regularly, especially in flowering and podding, and mulch to retain moisture. Pinch out the tops when plants reach the top of the support. Feed with tomato fertiliser fortnightly.
Slugs eat seedlings, and blackfly may colonise tips. In wet autumns, pods can rot; harvest early. Beans need a warm, dry end of summer to dry on the plant.
harvest: For fresh borlotti, pick pods when they turn streaked red and cream and the beans inside are plump, from August to September. Shell immediately. For dried beans, leave pods on the plant until papery, then pick, shell and dry fully.
Bring plants indoors to dry in a warm, airy spot if autumn is wet. Dry thoroughly before storing.

Beans are at their best as ‘fresh shelling’ beans when the pods have just coloured up, because they cook in half the time of dried beans and have a creamier texture. Leave a few pods to dry fully on the plant for next year’s seed, picking them once they rattle.
use: Fresh borlotti cook in 25–30 minutes, with onions, tomatoes, sage and olive oil for pasta e fagioli, in soups, stews and salads. The beans turn brown on cooking. Dried beans need soaking overnight and boiling hard for 10 minutes before simmering until tender.
Fresh beans keep for a few days in the pod in the fridge, or freeze shelled beans after blanching for 2 minutes. Dried beans keep for a year in jars.
use_tips: Boil dried beans hard for 10 minutes first.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost and provide canes or netting for climbing types, and protect young plants from slugs.
Water well during flowering and pod swelling, as dry soil makes flowers drop, and mulch to keep roots cool.
Pinch out the tips of climbing types once they reach the top of the supports.
Leave pods to mature on the plant until they turn mottled red and papery, picking before the first frosts and finishing the drying indoors.

preserving.how: Leave pods on the plant until brown and rattling, or hang whole plants in a dry shed. Shell and dry fully in a warm place before storing in jars.
Shell fresh beans, blanch for 2–3 minutes and freeze in bags.
Keep unshelled fresh pods in the salad drawer.
Soak and boil dried beans for at least 10 minutes at a full boil, then freeze in portions with their liquid.

crops.name: Broad bean

facts.Spacing: 20 cm apart in double rows 20 cm apart

varieties: Crimson Flowered (red flowers, rare and ornamental)

types.name: Autumn-sown (hardy)
types.when: Sow October to November · Harvest May to June
types.note: The earliest crop, from hardy Longpod types. Best in mild, sheltered areas.

types.name: Spring-sown
types.when: Sow February to April · Harvest June to July
types.note: Larger crops and more plants. Choose Longpod for the most beans per pod or Windsor for a sweeter flavour.

info: Broad beans are among the hardiest and easiest of vegetables, producing a heavy crop of plump pods in early summer, often before other beans are ready. They can be sown in autumn for the earliest harvest, or in spring, and they fix nitrogen in the soil.

Tall types need support, while dwarf varieties such as The Sutton are ideal for small gardens and exposed spots. The tops are edible, too: pinch them out when plants flower to deter blackfly and enjoy the tender tips in a stir-fry.
sow: Sow in October–November for an early harvest in sheltered areas, using a hardy variety such as Aquadulce Claudia, or in February–April for a later crop. Sow seeds 5 cm deep, 20 cm apart, in double rows 20 cm apart. Sow a few extra at the end of the row to fill gaps.

In cold or wet regions, start spring seed in pots under cover and plant out in March–April. Pick a sunny, sheltered site in well-drained, fertile soil. Autumn-sown plants may need protection with fleece or cloches in hard winters.
sow_tips: Sow in autumn for the earliest crop.
Start spring seeds in pots if soil is cold.
Sow extra seed to fill gaps.
Use a hardy variety for autumn sowing.
grow: Support taller varieties with posts and string running around the plants. Water in dry spells, especially at flowering and podding. Pinch out the top 8 cm of the growing tip once the first pods set, to deter blackfly and encourage pod formation.

Blackfly is the main pest; blast off with water, or spray with soapy water, and remove infested tips. Chocolate spot (brown marks on leaves) occurs in wet conditions; good spacing and potash help. Pea and bean weevil leaves scalloped edges, but rarely hurts.
grow_tips: Pinch out the tips once pods form.
harvest: Pick broad beans young while the pods are 7–10 cm long for tender, sweet beans, or leave them to swell for larger, starchier ones. Overgrown beans have tough grey skins and need double-podding. The pods are ready from May for autumn sowings and from June for spring sowings.

Pick regularly to keep plants producing, and pull pods downwards to avoid damaging stems. Tiny young pods are edible whole, cooked like mangetout. After cropping, cut plants off at ground level and leave the roots to rot and release nitrogen.
harvest_tips: Pick young for tender, sweet beans.
Pull pods down to snap off.
use: Shell the beans and cook in boiling water for 3–5 minutes, then eat with butter, add to salads, risottos, pasta and soups, or crush on toast with mint and feta. Larger beans can be double-podded by removing the grey outer skin after blanching, which makes them bright green and tender.

Fresh pods keep for a few days in the fridge. For storage, blanch shelled beans for 2–3 minutes, chill, then freeze in bags for up to a year. Late, mature beans can be left to dry on the plant and stored in jars for winter stews.
use_tips: Crush with mint and feta on toast.
Dry the last beans for winter.

care.job: Stake plants or support them with string between canes, as the tall types flop in wind.
Pinch out the growing tips once the first pods form to deter blackfly and encourage pod growth.
Check for blackfly on the young tips and wipe off or spray with soapy water.
Water in dry spells, especially while flowering and podding.
Cut plants to ground level after harvest, leaving the roots in the soil.
Protect autumn-sown plants with fleece in hard frost.

preserving.how: Pod, blanch for 2 minutes, cool quickly and freeze on a tray before bagging. The best way to keep them.
Keep in the pods in the salad drawer and shell as needed.
Leave a few pods to ripen fully on the plant for dried beans, and keep some for seed.
Make into a purée or dip and freeze in tubs.

images.alt: A handful of broad bean seeds in a gardener's palm, over a freshly prepared bed
A string line pulled tight across a raked bed, marking the row for broad beans, with the first seeds laid along it

facts.Time to harvest: Leaves from May; seed in Sep
facts.Good companions: Keep away from dill, tomatoes and beans

info: Bronze fennel is a tall, graceful perennial with feathery, smoky bronze foliage and flat yellow flower heads that attract hoverflies and lacewings. It tastes of aniseed and is used for its leaves, seeds and pollen, rather than the bulb of Florence fennel.
It looks wonderful in borders, but self-seeds freely and grows large, so deadhead before seeds ripen if you do not want a lot of seedlings. It dislikes being moved, thanks to a long taproot.
sow: Sow in situ from March to May, 1 cm deep, in a sunny spot with free-draining soil, and thin to 60 cm apart. Fennel hates root disturbance, so avoid transplanting. Alternatively, buy a young plant and plant in spring.
Allow plenty of room, since mature plants reach 2 m. Keep away from dill, with which it crosses, and from tomatoes and beans, which it inhibits. Water in until established.
grow: Little care is needed. Water in dry spells in the first year, then leave. Cut down old stems in autumn, and mulch with compost. Support tall stems in windy gardens.

Remove flower heads before seeds ripen to prevent self-seeding. Divide the clump in spring every 3–4 years if needed, although it resents disturbance. Aphids may colonise the stems but are quickly dealt with by hoverflies.
harvest: Pick the feathery fronds from late spring to autumn, cutting stems at the base, or snipping individual leaves. Young fronds are the sweetest. Harvest regularly to promote new growth.
Collect seeds in September when the flower heads turn brown, cutting the heads into a paper bag and shaking out the seeds. Dry for a week before storing.

The pollen from the flower heads is prized by chefs: shake the dry yellow flower heads over a sheet of paper in August and collect the golden dust, which has a concentrated sweet aniseed flavour. Seeds should be harvested before they scatter, so tie a paper bag over the heads.
use: Chop fronds into salads, fish dishes, soups, sauces, potato salad and egg dishes, or use whole sprigs to flavour grilled fish and pork. The flavour is a gentle aniseed. Use seeds in breads, sausages, curries and teas.
Fresh fronds keep for several days in the fridge with stems in water. Freeze chopped fronds in ice-cube trays. Seeds keep a year in a jar.

care.job: Cut back last year's dead stems and feed lightly in spring, then thin or move clumps if overcrowded.
Pick fronds regularly for flavour and cut off flower heads if you do not want self-sown seedlings everywhere.
Leave some flowers for hoverflies and ladybirds, which feed on aphids, and keep it away from dill to prevent cross-pollination.
Cut stems down to ground level once the foliage fades.

preserving.how: Cut seed heads when brown, dry in a paper bag and store seeds in a jar.
Chop the feathery fronds and freeze in ice cube trays with a little water or oil.
Wrap fronds in damp paper in a bag.

crops.name: Brussels sprouts
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open, sheltered site

facts.Type: Hardy biennial, grown as an annual

types.name: Early sprouts
types.when: Sow March · Harvest September to November
types.note: Quick to mature, with smaller sprouts that are best eaten fresh.

types.name: Mid-season sprouts
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest October to January
types.note: The best all-rounders, with reliable yields and good flavour.

types.name: Late sprouts
types.when: Sow April · Harvest December to March
types.note: Hardy types whose flavour improves after frost.

info: Fresh Brussels sprouts picked from the stalk are sweet and nutty, and have little in common with the soggy boiled version many remember. They grow into tall plants on a stout stem, with the sprouts forming up the stalk, and crop from autumn until the new year.

They need a long season, a firm, fertile bed and some protection from wind and pigeons, so they are best on a medium or large plot. Choose early, mid and late varieties for pickings from September to March.
sow: Sow in March and April indoors in modules or trays, 1–2 cm deep, then harden off and plant out in May to June, when plants are 10–15 cm tall. Alternatively, sow directly in a seedbed outdoors in April and transplant. Space plants 60–75 cm apart in each direction, which looks wide but sprouts need space.

The soil must be firm, so avoid digging deep in spring; if the bed is freshly dug, firm by treading before planting. Plant deeply up to the lowest leaves, firm in well, and water thoroughly. Net immediately against pigeons and cabbage whites.
sow_tips: Plant into firm soil and plant deeply.
Allow plenty of space, as plants get big.
Choose varieties that crop at different times.
grow: Water thoroughly in dry weather and feed in midsummer with a general fertiliser, then stop feeding in late summer to avoid soft, loose sprouts. Stake each stem or earth up around it by autumn, as the tall, top-heavy plants rock easily in gales and loosen the roots.

Remove yellowing lower leaves in autumn, which can carry fungal diseases, and check regularly for whitefly, aphids and cabbage caterpillars. Keep nets on until picking is finished. Clubroot is a risk on acid soil, so lime the bed and rotate crops.
grow_tips: Stake or earth up stems before autumn gales.
Pinch out the growing tip in autumn for even sprouts.
harvest: Pick sprouts from the bottom of the stem upwards when they are firm, about 2–4 cm across, usually from October onwards. Twist or snap them off, picking a few from each plant at a time. Frost improves the flavour, making them sweeter and milder.

Cut or break off the top of the plant in autumn to encourage the sprouts to mature at the same time. At the end of the season, the top ‘sprout tops’ can be cooked like cabbage greens. Pull up the stems when finished and chop them up for the compost heap.
harvest_tips: Pick from the bottom of the stem upwards.
Wait for a frost for the sweetest flavour.
Cook the sprout tops as greens.
use: Boil or steam whole sprouts for six to eight minutes, or roast them with olive oil and balsamic vinegar for caramelised flavour. Shred raw sprouts into slaws, fry with bacon or chestnuts, or stir-fry them with garlic. Cutting a small cross in the base of each helps larger ones cook evenly.

Sprouts keep on the stalk for weeks in the garden, which is the best way to store them. Picked sprouts keep in the fridge for up to a week, or you can leave whole stalks in a cool shed. Blanch for three minutes and freeze in bags for use at Christmas and beyond.
use_tips: Do not overcook, which makes them bitter and smelly.
Leave sprouts on the stalk until needed.

care.job: Plant very firmly, as loose plants make loose sprouts. Cover with mesh against pigeons and butterflies.
Water in dry weather and feed once with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser in early summer, then stop to avoid soft, loose buttons.
Stake tall plants and remove yellowing lower leaves, which can harbour disease, as the sprouts mature.
Pinch out the top of the stem in October to encourage the sprouts to mature together.
Pick sprouts from the bottom up and clear stalks afterwards, as they harbour pests and disease.

preserving.how: Sprouts keep best on the stalk. Harvest from the bottom up as needed, and flavour improves after frost.
Cut whole stalks, or loose sprouts, and keep in the salad drawer.
Trim, blanch for 3 minutes (small sprouts), 4 (medium) or 5 (large), cool and freeze in bags.
Halve and ferment in brine, or pickle in vinegar, for a tangy winter condiment.

facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors; plant out late May–June

info: Butternut squash has a sweet, nutty orange flesh, among the best of the winter squashes. It needs a longer, warmer season than courgettes, but compact varieties ripen reliably in sunny English summers, and it stores well into winter.

Plants are vigorous trailers that can be trained up a trellis or frame to save space. Choose an early variety such as Hunter or Harrier, bred for cooler climates, and give them rich soil and plenty of water.
sow: Sow indoors from mid-April to May, with seeds on their edge, 2 cm deep, in 9 cm pots of multipurpose compost at 18–21°C. Seedlings emerge in about a week. Keep them warm and bright, and avoid sowing too early.

Harden off and plant out in early June, once the frost has gone, in a sunny, sheltered place, in soil enriched with compost or manure. Allow 90 cm to 1 m between plants, or train up a strong trellis, supporting the fruits in nets or tights.
sow_tips: Plant in rich soil in a sunny spot.
grow: Water deeply and regularly, especially in dry spells, and feed weekly with tomato fertiliser from the time the first fruits form. Pinch out the main growing tip when the stem is 1.5 m long, and restrict the plant to 3–4 fruits for good-sized squashes.

Keep fruits off wet soil with a tile or board. Hand-pollinate if there are few bees about. Slugs, powdery mildew and aphids can be a problem; remove affected leaves and water at the base. In September, remove leaves that shade the fruit, to let the sun ripen them.
harvest: Harvest in late September to October, when the skins have turned from green to a deep tan colour and are hard enough that a fingernail will not dent them, and the stalks are dry and corky. Cut with secateurs, leaving a long stalk, and never carry by the stalk.

Bring in before the first frost. Cure the fruits in a sunny, dry place for 10–14 days to harden the skin. Unripe squashes can finish ripening on a sunny windowsill, but they are less sweet and keep less well.
harvest_tips: Leave a long stalk on each fruit.
Cure in the sun for 10–14 days.
use: Roast butternut squash in wedges with olive oil, garlic and herbs, blend into soups, mash, or add to risottos, curries, stews, lasagne and pies. The flesh is sweet and creamy; the skin is edible once roasted, saving peeling. Roast the seeds for a snack.

Cured whole squashes keep for 4–6 months in a cool (10–15°C), dry, well-ventilated place; do not stack them. Once cut, wrap and refrigerate for a week. Cooked squash and soup freeze well for up to six months.
use_tips: Roast with the skin on to save peeling.
Store whole squashes in a cool, dry place.

care.job: Harden off and plant out after the last frost on a rich mound of soil or compost with plenty of space.
Water generously at the base and feed every one to two weeks with a tomato feed once fruits start to set.
Pinch out the growing tips after four or five fruits have set so the energy goes into ripening those fruit.
Rest fruits on a piece of wood or straw to keep them off damp soil and turn them occasionally for even colour.
Harvest before frost when the skin is hard and cannot be dented by a fingernail, then cure in a warm, dry place for two weeks.

pests.label: Fruit not ripening in cool summers

preserving.how: Leave on the plant until the skin is hard, cut with a long stalk, then cure in a warm, sunny spot for 10 days. Store on shelves at 10–15°C.
Peel, cube, roast or steam, then freeze flat on a tray before bagging. Or freeze soup or purée.
Make big batches of soup, cool and freeze in portions.
Dice into a spiced chutney with apple and onion.

facts.Type: Hardy biennial leafy vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Mar–Jun in trays; plant out after about 6 weeks
facts.Spacing: 30–45 cm apart in rows 45 cm apart

types.name: Spring cabbage
types.when: Sow July to August · Harvest March to May
types.note: Loose, pointed heads (or spring greens), planted out in autumn to overwinter.

types.name: Summer and autumn cabbage
types.when: Sow March to May · Harvest July to November
types.note: Round, tender heads, best eaten fresh. Red cabbages sit here too.

types.name: Winter cabbage
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest October to February
types.note: Solid, frost-hardy heads that stand in the garden or store in a cool place. Savoys are the hardiest.

info: Cabbages are among the most dependable crops for UK gardens and, by choosing different types, you can pick them nearly all year round: spring cabbages, summer and autumn types, red cabbages, and frost-hardy Savoys for winter. A freshly cut head is sweeter and crisper than anything from a shop.

They are heavy feeders that like firm, fertile, limey soil, and they need protection from pigeons, butterflies and slugs. With netting and a little attention they are one of the most rewarding vegetables you can grow.
sow: Sow in modules or seed trays from March to June, 1–2 cm deep, in a cool, bright place. Prick out into larger pots if needed, and plant out when the seedlings have 4–5 true leaves, usually five to six weeks after sowing. For spring cabbages, sow in July and August and plant out in autumn.

Choose a sunny site with firm, fertile, well-drained soil, dug over the previous autumn and limed if acidic. Plant seedlings 30–45 cm apart, setting them deeply up to their first leaves and firming the soil well with your heel. Water in thoroughly, and cover with netting.
sow_tips: Firm the soil before and after planting; loose soil gives loose heads.
Plant deeply, up to the first true leaves.
Lime acidic soil to guard against clubroot.
Use a collar around each stem to deter cabbage root fly.
grow: Water regularly, particularly in dry spells, and feed with a high-nitrogen fertiliser a few weeks after planting. Keep weeds down, hoeing carefully, and mulch to hold moisture. Pull a little soil around the stems to help stability in windy weather.

Protect plants with netting or fine mesh from the start against pigeons and cabbage white butterflies, whose caterpillars can strip a plant. Check the underside of leaves regularly for eggs. Clubroot, a soil disease, is the biggest threat; liming, good drainage and crop rotation help keep it away.
grow_tips: Net as soon as you plant to stop pigeons and butterflies.
Squash yellow butterfly eggs on the undersides of leaves.
Feed with nitrogen for leafy growth.
Rotate brassicas on a four-year plan.
harvest: Cut cabbages when the heads are firm and have reached a good size, around 12–16 weeks after planting out. Squeeze a few; a solid head with a tight heart is ready. Cut at the base with a sharp knife on a dry day, leaving the stalk in the ground.

Cut a shallow cross in the top of the stump and you will often get a flush of small, tender loose-leaved ‘cabbage greens’ a few weeks later. Winter types stand in the ground through frost and are cut as needed. Do not let heads split, which happens after heavy rain.
harvest_tips: Cut a cross in the stump to get a second flush.
Harvest before heads crack after heavy rain.
Clear old stumps at the end of the season to deter pests.
use: Shred raw cabbage into coleslaw, steam wedges lightly, stir-fry, braise with apples and spices, or turn it into sauerkraut. Savoys are lovely stuffed and baked, and red cabbage is a traditional winter side dish braised with vinegar and sugar. Avoid overcooking, which gives a strong smell and a limp texture.

Whole heads keep for two to three weeks in the fridge and for several weeks in a cool, frost-free shed hung in nets. Firm winter varieties such as white and red cabbage keep longest. Shredded cabbage can be blanched for a minute and frozen, or fermented into sauerkraut that will last for months.
use_tips: Ferment shredded cabbage with salt for sauerkraut.
Cook briefly so it keeps its texture and sweetness.
Hang firm heads in nets in a cool shed.
Add caraway seeds for traditional flavour.

care.job: Plant firmly and cover with fine mesh or netting from day one to keep cabbage white butterflies, pigeons and root fly away.
Water well in dry spells, and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser to help hearts form.
Check the leaf undersides every week for butterfly eggs and caterpillars, and squash them.
Draw soil up around the stems of tall cabbages and stake in windy spots.
Remove yellowing leaves, which can harbour disease, and clear stalks after harvest. Do not plant brassicas in the same place next year.

preserving.how: Harvest firm heads in autumn, remove loose outer leaves and hang or store in a frost-free, airy shed, not touching each other.
Wrap a whole head loosely and keep in the salad drawer.
Shred and ferment with 2% salt by weight into sauerkraut, packed down under its own brine in a jar.
Shred, blanch for 90 seconds and freeze. Best used cooked afterwards.
Slice red cabbage and pack into jars with spiced vinegar.

crops.name: Calabrese
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open site

facts.Spacing: 30–45 cm apart in rows 45 cm apart

types.name: Early calabrese
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest June to July
types.note: Quick heads and side shoots in summer.

types.name: Autumn calabrese
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest September to November
types.note: Large, firm heads, with plenty of side shoots after the main head is cut.

info: Calabrese is the broccoli you buy in shops, forming a large central head followed by smaller side shoots. It is a quick brassica, ready in around three months, so you can sow several batches through spring and early summer for a long picking season in summer and autumn.

Calabrese dislikes cold checks, drought and transplant shock, which make the heads ‘button’ (form small, tight heads too early). Sow on time, plant firmly and keep the plants watered to get large, even heads.
sow: Sow indoors in March and April in modules, 1–2 cm deep, then plant out from late April in an open, sunny, firm bed. You can also sow directly outdoors from April to June in drills 1–2 cm deep, thinning to 30–45 cm apart. Make successional sowings every three or four weeks for a continuous supply.

Choose fertile, well-drained, firm soil with a pH above 6.5, adding lime if needed. Do not dig deeply in spring; settled ground gives bigger heads. Water seedlings well, and cover with fine mesh at once to deter pigeons, cabbage root fly and butterflies.
sow_tips: Sow a few modules every three to four weeks.
Do not let seedlings get pot-bound before planting.
Use fine mesh from the day of planting.
grow: Water regularly, especially when the heads are forming, as drought causes small, tight heads. Feed with a high-nitrogen fertiliser four weeks after planting, then keep the plants weed-free and well watered. Stake taller plants in exposed gardens.

Check for caterpillars, whitefly and aphids, and protect plants with fine mesh. Clubroot, cabbage root fly and pigeons are all potential trouble. Regular rotation and a firm, limed soil will reduce disease risk, and removing the old stumps in autumn helps break pest cycles.
grow_tips: Water well when the head begins to form.
Feed with nitrogen about four weeks after planting.
Cover with mesh the whole time.
Pull up old stumps in autumn.
harvest: Cut the central head when the flower buds are tight and dark green, at about 10–15 cm across, before any yellow flowers appear. Use a sharp knife and cut a few centimetres below the head at a slight angle. Heads left too long open into yellow flowers and become unusable.

After cutting the main head, side shoots develop from the leaf joints and can be cut over the following weeks, which extends the harvest a lot. Harvest regularly and in the morning for the best flavour and texture.
harvest_tips: Cut before any yellow petals show.
Leave the plant in place for side shoots.
Cut in the morning when buds are cool and crisp.
Check plants daily in warm weather.
use: Calabrese can be steamed, roasted, stir-fried, charred or eaten raw in salads with a good dip. Cut the head into florets and slice the stalk, which is tender and sweet, to cook alongside. Steam for three to four minutes, or roast at 200°C with olive oil, chilli and lemon.

Heads keep for up to five days in the fridge in a bag, though they are best fresh. To freeze, cut into florets, blanch for three minutes, chill in iced water, then drain well and freeze on trays before bagging. Do not wash before storing in the fridge, as damp encourages mould.
use_tips: Peel and slice the stalk; it is the sweetest part.
Roast with chilli, garlic and lemon.
Do not wash heads before storing.

care.job: Plant firmly 30 cm apart, protect from pigeons and butterflies with mesh and keep the soil evenly moist.
Feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser a few weeks after planting and water consistently, as stress causes premature flowering.
Cut the central head while the buds are still tight and green, then leave the plant to produce smaller side shoots for weeks.
Check leaf undersides for butterfly eggs and caterpillars, and remove them.

preserving.how: Keep unwashed in a loose bag in the salad drawer.
Cut into florets, blanch for 3 minutes, cool in iced water and freeze on a tray before bagging.
Blend into broccoli and stilton or cheddar soup and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Calendula

facts.Sow: Mar–Jun direct; Sep for early flowers

varieties: Pacific Beauty Mix (mixed yellows and oranges)

info: Calendula, the pot marigold, is a cheerful, easy-going annual with bright orange or yellow daisy flowers from early summer until the frosts. It is a great plant for beginners, children and wildlife-friendly gardens, attracting bees, hoverflies and butterflies.

The petals are edible and have been used for centuries to colour and flavour food and to make soothing skin balms. It self-seeds freely, producing new plants each year, and the flowers last well when cut.
sow: Sow seeds directly outdoors in March to June, 1 cm deep, in rows 30 cm apart, thinning to 20–30 cm. Seeds germinate in about 10 days in cool soil. For earlier flowers, sow in September and overwinter in a sheltered spot, or sow indoors in March.

Calendula thrives in average to poor soil and full sun, and tolerates partial shade. Rich soil produces leaves and fewer flowers. It does well in pots, as part of a vegetable bed, or in a cottage garden border.
sow_tips: Sow in September for earlier flowers.
Scatter seed where you want flowers.
grow: Deadhead regularly to keep the plants flowering for months; leaving the seed heads will lead to self-seeding. Water in dry spells but avoid feeding. Pinch out the tips of young plants for bushier growth.

Powdery mildew can appear in late summer, and aphids sometimes colonise the stems. Remove affected leaves and keep plants watered. Plants usually die after the first hard frost, but self-seeded plants will return in spring.
harvest: Pick the flowers when fully open on a dry, sunny morning, after the dew has dried. Cut the whole flower head, or pull off the petals and use them fresh or dry. Picking regularly encourages more flowers.
To dry, spread petals or whole heads on a tray in a warm, airy place and turn daily until crisp, then store in a jar in the dark. Harvest the flowers throughout the summer and autumn.
harvest_tips: Store dry petals in the dark.
use: Scatter fresh petals over salads, rice dishes and soups for colour and a mild peppery, tangy flavour: they are known as ‘poor man’s saffron’. Use them to colour butter, cheese, cakes, and bread. Infuse petals in oil to make a healing salve for dry or irritated skin.
Fresh flowers last a few days in the fridge. Dried petals keep for a year in an airtight jar in the dark, and make a calming tea. Calendula-infused oil makes a lovely handmade balm.
use_tips: Use as a saffron substitute for colour.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 20 to 30 cm apart and pinch out the tips to produce bushy plants with more flowers.
Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and pick petals for salads and rice dishes while they are fresh.
Check for aphids and encourage hoverflies by leaving some flowers, as calendula attracts the insects that eat pests.
Leave a few seed heads to self-sow, then pull up spent plants.

preserving.how: Pick open flowers and dry in a single layer in a warm, airy place. Use for tea, colouring rice and soaps.
Steep fully dried petals in olive or sunflower oil for 4–6 weeks, then strain, for skin balms and salves. Use dried petals, as fresh ones can make the oil go off.
Freeze petals in ice cube trays for drinks and salads.

safety: Infuse petals in oil to make a healing salve for dry or irritated skin.

crops.name: Carrot

facts.Type: Hardy biennial root vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 5–8 cm apart in rows 15–30 cm apart

varieties: Autumn King (heavy cropper that stores well)
Paris Market (round roots for shallow pots)

types.name: Earlies
types.when: Sow March to May · Harvest June to August
types.note: Short, sweet, quick roots for baby carrots. Sow under cloches in March for the first pickings.

types.name: Maincrop
types.when: Sow May to July · Harvest September to November
types.note: Longer, heavier roots that store well. Sow after the main carrot fly flight in May, and lift before hard frosts.

types.name: Coloured and fly-resistant
types.when: Sow April to July
types.note: Purple, yellow and white carrots for interest, and partly carrot-fly-resistant types for troubled sites.

info: Home-grown carrots are sweeter and more tender than most shop-bought ones, and they come in colours supermarkets rarely stock, from purple and yellow to white and deep orange. They are a cool-season crop that is sown where it will grow, and they suit raised beds and deep pots as well as open ground.

The main challenge in the UK is carrot fly, a small pest whose larvae tunnel into the roots. Everything else is straightforward: a light, stone-free soil, even moisture and sowings spread from spring to midsummer will give you fresh roots for most of the year.
sow: Carrots dislike being moved, so sow them where they will grow. Prepare a fine, stone-free bed in full sun, raking out lumps and stones that make roots fork. Avoid fresh manure, which also causes forking; soil that was improved the previous year is ideal. Water the drill first, sow thinly in rows 15–30 cm apart, cover with 1 cm of soil and firm lightly.
