Sow earlies under cloches or fleece from March, then maincrops from April to July. Seed can take two to three weeks to germinate, so mark the rows and keep the soil moist. In containers choose a pot at least 30 cm deep, using short or round varieties in shallower ones.
sow_tips: Sow thinly to cut down on thinning, which releases the scent that attracts carrot fly.
Mix the fine seed with dry sand to space it more evenly.
Sow a short row every three weeks to avoid a glut.
Cover the seedbed with fleece to keep it warm and damp until seedlings appear.
grow: Thin seedlings to 5–8 cm apart once they are about 5 cm tall. Water steadily, because roots split if the soil dries out and is then soaked. A thin mulch of grass clippings or compost keeps moisture even. Weed gently while the seedlings are small, as they are slow to start and easily smothered.

Protect against carrot fly with a 60 cm high barrier of fine mesh or fleece around the bed, as the female flies low to the ground. Sowing early or late to miss the main flights in May and again in August and September, and choosing resistant varieties, also helps. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which give hairy, forked roots and plenty of leaf.
grow_tips: A 60 cm barrier of fine mesh is the most effective carrot fly defence.
Thin on a calm evening, then water and take the thinnings away.
Rotate carrots to a new bed each year, away from parsnips.
Cover any shoulders poking out of the soil so they do not turn green.
harvest: Early varieties are ready 10–12 weeks after sowing and maincrops in 14–16 weeks. Pull one or two to check: baby carrots are delicious at finger width, while maincrops are best around 2–3 cm across the shoulder. Water the row the day before to soften the soil, then loosen it with a fork before pulling so roots do not snap.

Lifting disturbs the soil and releases scent, so pull in the evening or under a cover when carrot fly is about. Maincrops sown in late spring can stay in the ground and be lifted as needed until the soil freezes hard. In cold or very wet areas, lift them in November.
harvest_tips: Twist off the foliage straight away, as leaves draw moisture out of the root.
Pull every other carrot in a row first to give the rest room to swell.
Cover rows with straw in winter so you can still lift in frost.
Lift everything before slugs or hard frost damage the roots.
use: Carrots work raw and cooked: grate them into salads and slaws, roast with honey and thyme, boil and mash with swede, or simmer in soups and stews. Home-grown roots have thin, sweet skin, so scrubbing is usually enough. The feathery tops can be used in small amounts, for example blitzed into a salsa verde or pesto.

For short-term storage, twist off the tops and keep unwashed roots in a paper bag or box in the fridge, where they last three to four weeks. For longer storage, layer undamaged roots in boxes of slightly damp sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed, where they keep for three to five months. They also freeze well when sliced and blanched for three minutes.
use_tips: Store only undamaged roots, and eat any with slug holes or splits first.
Check stored roots every few weeks and remove any that are going soft.
Blanch for three minutes, cool quickly, then freeze in portions.
Roast at 200°C for about 30 minutes for the sweetest flavour.

care.job: Thin seedlings gradually to 5 to 8 cm apart in the evening, and remove the thinnings so the smell does not attract carrot fly.
Cover the crop with fine insect mesh from sowing to protect against carrot fly, which flies low to the ground.
Water evenly, especially after a dry spell, as irregular watering splits roots. Weed carefully.
Lift remaining carrots before hard frosts or protect with a thick layer of straw or fleece.

preserving.how: Twist off the tops, leave unwashed, and pack in boxes of slightly damp sand or compost in a frost-free shed. Keep boxes cool and dark.
Mulch thickly with straw and lift as needed, then cover with fleece to deter carrot fly in autumn.
Trim tops and keep in a bag in the salad drawer.
Slice or dice, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze in bags.
Pickle sticks with dill and garlic in vinegar, or ferment in brine.

images.alt: Freshly pulled carrots, still with soil on, among feathery carrot tops in a vegetable bed

crops.name: Cauliflower
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open site

types.name: Summer cauliflower
types.when: Sow February to April · Harvest June to September
types.note: Quick, compact heads, best given steady water.

types.name: Autumn cauliflower
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest September to December
types.note: The easiest group for most gardeners.

types.name: Winter cauliflower
types.when: Sow May · Harvest February to May
types.note: Slow, hardy heads that mature in the following spring. Best in mild areas.

info: Cauliflower has a reputation as a fussy crop, but with steady growth, regular water and firm soil it can be very rewarding, and fresh-cut heads are sweeter and more delicate than shop-bought ones. Summer and autumn types are the easiest in the UK.

Plants dislike any check to growth, such as drought, transplant shock or cold, so keep them growing steadily from sowing to cutting. Coloured varieties, including purple, orange and lime-green Romanesco, make the plot look attractive.
sow: Sow in March to May in modules or small pots indoors, 1–2 cm deep, at 15–20°C, and grow on in a cool, bright place. Harden off and plant out when seedlings are about 10 cm tall, from May to July. Space 45–60 cm apart in both directions in firm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun.

Avoid letting seedlings get pot-bound or dry, as stress causes ‘buttoning’, where tiny heads form too early. Water the plants in thoroughly, and put brassica collars around stems to deter cabbage root fly. Net against pigeons from planting.
sow_tips: Never let seedlings dry out or get root-bound.
Plant into firm soil and firm in well.
Fit a root-fly collar around each stem.
Choose summer or autumn varieties for an easier crop.
grow: Water steadily throughout, particularly in dry spells, and feed with a high-nitrogen fertiliser every few weeks. Mulch to hold moisture and keep weeds down. When the white head (the curd) begins to form, bend a few of the inner leaves over it, or tie them loosely, to keep it white and protected from sun and frost.

Cauliflowers suffer from the usual brassica problems: caterpillars, aphids, flea beetle, pigeons and clubroot. Net from the start and inspect regularly. Limed, firm soil and a four-year rotation give the best chance of healthy plants.
grow_tips: Tie leaves loosely over the head to keep it white.
Water regularly while the head develops.
Lime acid soils and rotate brassicas.
harvest: Cut when the head is firm, compact and 10–15 cm across, before it begins to separate and look ‘ricey’. Cut with a sharp knife just below the head, with a few leaves attached to protect it. Summer and autumn varieties ripen from July to November.

Harvest promptly, as heads deteriorate quickly in warm weather. If several ripen at once, cut them early as small heads, or lift the plants and hang them in a cool shed for a week or two. Coloured types turn green if they lose their colour when overcooked.
harvest_tips: Cut while the head is tight and smooth.
Leave a few wrapper leaves on the head.
use: Cauliflower is endlessly versatile: steam florets, roast them with spices, make cauliflower cheese or soup, shred into a rice substitute, or eat raw with a dip. Romanesco is delicious lightly steamed, and coloured varieties keep their hue best when cooked briefly.

Whole heads keep in the fridge for up to a week, or hang in a cool shed in a net for two weeks. Cut into florets, blanch for three minutes, cool quickly and freeze on trays before bagging. Do not store cut cauliflower near strong-smelling foods.
use_tips: Roast at 220°C with curry spices for crisp, golden edges.
Use the tender leaves in soup too.
Cook coloured varieties briefly to preserve their colour.

care.job: Plant firmly and cover with mesh from day one, as cauliflowers attract cabbage white butterflies, pigeons and root fly.
Water consistently, as checks in growth cause small, early heads (buttoning). Feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser.
When the curd begins to form, bend a few leaves over it to shield it from the sun and keep it white.
Cut heads promptly when firm and clear stalks afterwards. Do not plant brassicas in the same ground next year.

preserving.how: Keep whole heads in a loose bag in the salad drawer, or cut into florets in a container.
Cut into florets, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze on a tray before bagging.
Make piccalilli or pickled florets with turmeric and mustard seeds.
Ferment florets in a 2–3% salt brine for a tangy side dish.

facts.Type: Hardy biennial root vegetable, grown as an annual

info: Celeriac is a knobbly root with a smooth, nutty, celery-like flavour, and it is one of the most useful winter vegetables for soups, mash and the French salad céleri rémoulade. It is not difficult but has a long growing season and needs a good start indoors.

Celeriac loves a fertile, moisture-retentive soil and regular watering. In return it will stand in the ground through most of the winter, so it is a handy crop for a medium or large plot that wants late-season produce.
sow: Sow in March to early April in seed trays of moist, peat-free seed compost, pressing seeds onto the surface without covering, as they need light to germinate. Keep at about 15–20°C in a propagator or warm windowsill. Germination can take two to three weeks, so be patient.

Prick out seedlings into individual small pots when they have two true leaves, harden them off in May and plant out in late May to June, 30–40 cm apart each way. Plant with the base of the stems at soil level or slightly above, as burying the crown gives misshapen roots.
sow_tips: Do not cover the seed; it needs light to germinate.
Keep warm and moist until seedlings appear.
Harden off over two weeks before planting.
Plant with the crown at soil level, never buried.
grow: Water frequently and generously throughout summer: dry spells make celeriac woody and hollow. Mulch with compost or grass clippings to hold moisture, and feed every two to three weeks with a general liquid fertiliser. Remove any side shoots and the lowest leaves in late summer to expose the shoulders of the root.

Slugs are the main nuisance when plants are young, and celery leaf miner and celery fly can damage the foliage; pick off affected leaves. Celeriac is fairly hardy, but a thick mulch of straw protects the roots in cold winters.
grow_tips: Never let the soil dry out.
Remove the lowest leaves in late summer.
Feed every few weeks during summer.
Mulch heavily with straw in hard winters.
harvest: Roots are ready from October and size up through autumn, reaching 10–15 cm across. They are hardy and can stay in the ground, but lift before severe frosts or cover well with straw. Use a fork to loosen the soil, then lift and trim off the leaves and fibrous roots.
In mild areas, harvest as required until March. Roots left after that will start to produce a flower stem and become woody and hollow, so lift any remaining ones by early spring.
harvest_tips: Cover with straw for winter harvesting.
Lift before the soil freezes hard.
Trim off leaves and roots before storing.
Larger roots are not always better; check for hollows.
use: Peel off the knobbly skin, cut into pieces and put straight into water with a squeeze of lemon, as it browns quickly. Celeriac makes a creamy soup, an excellent mash with potatoes, a golden roast, or a crisp raw salad shredded in mustard mayonnaise. It also adds depth to stews and gratins.

Trimmed roots keep for two to three months in boxes of slightly damp sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed, or for several weeks in the vegetable drawer of the fridge. Cubed and blanched for three minutes, they freeze well, as does celeriac soup.
use_tips: Drop peeled pieces into acidulated water to stop browning.
Use a sturdy knife to cut off the skin.
Roast cubes with garlic and thyme.
Mash with potato for a lighter, nuttier purée.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost with the crown just above the soil, 30 to 40 cm apart, and water in well.
Water heavily and regularly, as celeriac is thirsty, and mulch to keep the roots moist and cool.
Feed every two weeks with a general liquid feed and remove the lower leaves in late summer to expose the swelling root.
Lift before hard frosts or cover with straw for protection, and store trimmed roots in a cool, dry place.

preserving.how: Trim the leaves and roots, brush off soil, and pack in boxes of damp sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed.
Wrap trimmed roots in a bag in the salad drawer.
Peel, cube and blanch for 3 minutes, or freeze as mash or soup.
Mulch over winter and lift as needed in mild areas. Lift before hard frosts to be safe.

crops.name: Celery
crops.sun_text: Full sun to light shade; moist soil essential

facts.Type: Hardy biennial, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Mar–Apr indoors; plant out late May–June

varieties: Victoria (stays pale without covering, good flavour)

types.name: Self-blanching celery
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest August to October
types.note: The easy type, grown in blocks so that plants shade each other.

types.name: Trench celery
types.when: Sow March · Harvest October to December
types.note: Hardier, with the finest flavour, but needs earthing up for blanching.

types.name: Leaf celery
types.when: Sow March to June · Harvest June to October
types.note: The easiest type, giving flavoursome leaves and thin stems.

info: Homegrown celery has a stronger, more aromatic flavour than shop celery, and is delicious cooked as well as raw. It needs a long season, rich soil and plenty of water, making it one of the more demanding crops, but it is worth the effort for a well-flavoured result.

Types that stay pale on their own, grown close together so they shade each other, are easier than traditional trench celery. Leaf celery and celeriac are easier alternatives with a similar flavour, while red varieties are hardier and tastier.
sow: Sow in March to April on the surface of seed compost, pressing in lightly but not covering, as light helps germination. Keep at 15–20°C; seed is slow and may take 2–3 weeks. Prick out into individual modules when large enough to handle.

Harden off in late May and plant out in early June, 25–30 cm apart in blocks, not rows, in rich, moisture-retentive soil in a sunny site. Types that stay pale on their own are best planted close together so they shade each other. Never let seedlings dry out or get cold, which makes them bolt.
sow_tips: Do not cover seeds with compost.
grow: Celery needs constant moisture: water deeply and regularly, and mulch thickly with compost. Feed fortnightly with a general liquid fertiliser. Dry spells cause stringy, hollow stalks and bolting.

These varieties can be wrapped in cardboard or paper in the last few weeks to keep out the light and keep the stalks pale and mild. Slugs and celery fly (leaf miner) are the main problems; pick off affected leaves and use fleece to protect plants. Celery leaf spot can be avoided with clean seed and good rotation.
grow_tips: Never let the soil dry out.
Cover with fleece against celery fly.
harvest: Cut self-blanching celery from August to October when the stalks are 25–30 cm tall and plump. Cut the whole head at ground level with a sharp knife, or pull individual stalks from the outside as needed. Harvest before the first hard frosts, which damage the plants.
Red and leaf types are hardier and can be picked into winter. Use the leaves as a herb, too. The roots are edible but not as large as celeriac.
harvest_tips: Cut the whole head at ground level.
Use the leaves as a herb.
use: Use celery raw in salads, with cheese and as a dipper, or cook it in soups, stews, stuffings, braises and as part of the base of many sauces. Homegrown celery has a stronger flavour, so you may need less. The leaves are a fragrant herb for soups and stocks.
Whole heads keep in the fridge for two weeks, wrapped in foil or in a bag. Chopped celery freezes for cooking, though it loses crunch. Dry the leaves for winter seasoning, or make celery salt.
use_tips: Use the leaves as a herb.
Wrap in foil in the fridge.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost into rich soil with plenty of moisture, and keep plants watered.
Water heavily, as celery is a bog plant at heart, and mulch to keep roots moist and cool.
Feed every two weeks with a general liquid fertiliser, and for self-blanching types, grow in a block so stems blanch each other.
Blanch trench celery by wrapping stems in cardboard or earthing up about three weeks before harvest.
Lift before hard frosts, as most celery is not hardy. Leaf celery types will often overwinter under a cloche.

pests.label: Bolting if checked by cold or drought

preserving.how: Wrap the whole head in foil, which keeps it crisp longer than a bag.
Chop and freeze for cooking only, as it turns soft. Ideal for soups, stews and stock.
Dry leaves in a low oven or dehydrator for a seasoning, and store in a jar.
Make celery soup or stock and freeze in portions.

info: Chamomile is a charming daisy-flowered herb best known for its calming tea. German chamomile is a taller annual, with more flowers and a stronger flavour, while Roman chamomile is a low-growing perennial often used for lawns and paths.
Both are easy and attractive, with feathery leaves and apple-scented flowers, and are excellent for pollinators. They self-seed freely, so one sowing may give plants for years.
sow: Sow seed on the surface of the soil in March to June, pressing in lightly and not covering, since it needs light to germinate. Sow where it is to flower, in rows 25 cm apart, in full sun and light, well-drained soil. Seedlings appear in 1–2 weeks.
Thin to 15–25 cm apart. Chamomile is tolerant of poor soil. Roman chamomile can also be bought as plants and set 15 cm apart for a lawn.
grow: Chamomile needs little attention. Water in dry weather, and weed carefully while seedlings are small. Don't feed, since rich soil makes plants leafy with fewer flowers. Support taller German chamomile with twiggy sticks if exposed.
Aphids and powdery mildew are the only likely problems. Remove old flowers regularly to promote more blooms. Roman chamomile should be trimmed after flowering and divided every few years.
harvest: Pick flower heads when fully open and the petals are flat or just starting to bend back, usually from June to September, on a dry morning. Pick regularly to encourage more flowers.
For drying, spread flowers on a tray in a warm, airy spot out of sun for a week, until crisp. Store in a jar in the dark.

A simple trick for picking lots of chamomile is to use a hand rake or a fork to comb through the plants and pull the flowers off in bulk, then pick out the stems. The more you pick, the more the plant flowers, so harvest at least once a week through summer.
use: Steep a handful of fresh flowers (or a teaspoon of dried) in boiling water for five minutes for a soothing tea. The flavour is mild, fruity and floral. Use flowers to flavour syrups, shortbread, custards and honey.
Dried flowers keep for a year in an airtight jar. Avoid chamomile if you are allergic to daisies or ragweed.

Chamomile tea tastes best made from fresh flowers; use a small handful per cup, cover and steep so the volatile oils do not escape. It makes a lovely cold infusion with lemon and honey, and can be added to bath sachets and homemade skincare.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 15 to 20 cm apart and keep the bed weed-free while plants are small.
Pick flowers regularly when fully open, as this keeps plants producing, and water only in dry spells.
Let a few plants set seed so annual German chamomile self-sows, and cut back perennial Roman chamomile after flowering.

preserving.how: Pick flowers at full bloom and dry on a tray in a warm, airy spot until crisp, then store in a jar for tea.
Freeze fresh flowers in ice cube trays for iced teas.
Steep dried flowers in honey or cooled syrup for soothing drinks.
preserving.keeps: Honey: 6 months; syrup: 1 month in the fridge

crops.name: Cherry
crops.sun_text: Full sun; sheltered, frost-free blossom position

facts.Height: 2.5–4 m on dwarfing rootstock (fans), 8 m+ unrestricted

types.name: Sweet cherries
types.when: Harvest June to August
types.note: Sweet and juicy for eating fresh. They need full sun and shelter, and a fan on a warm wall suits small gardens.

types.name: Acid (Morello) cherries
types.when: Harvest July to August
types.note: Sharp, deep red cherries for pies, jam and brandy. Tolerant of a north-facing wall and always self-fertile.

info: Cherries have been difficult for small gardens in the past, but modern dwarfing rootstocks such as Gisela 5 and self-fertile varieties like Stella and Sunburst have changed that. A fan-trained tree against a sunny wall is ideal, producing a heavy crop of glossy dark fruit and attractive spring blossom.
Sweet cherries are eaten fresh, while acid cherries such as Morello are for cooking, and tolerate a north-facing wall. Netting is essential, because birds will take every cherry given the chance.
sow: Plant bare-root trees between November and March in a sheltered, sunny spot with fertile, free-draining soil that holds some moisture. Cherry blossom opens early, so avoid frost pockets. Choose a self-fertile variety unless you have a neighbour with compatible trees.

Plant with the graft union 5 cm above ground, stake firmly and mulch with compost. For a fan, tie in branches to horizontal wires on a fence or wall. Water well in the first two summers. Cherries on Gisela 5 rootstock are suitable for large containers (50 cm) if watered and fed regularly.
sow_tips: Net as soon as fruit forms.
Plant fans on a warm wall.
grow: Prune cherries only in spring and summer, never in winter, to reduce the risk of silver leaf and bacterial canker. Fans need a summer prune in July to August: pinch back side shoots to 6 leaves, and tie in new growth. Remove dead or diseased wood at once.

Water regularly during dry spells and as fruit swells; irregular watering causes the fruit to split. Mulch each spring, and feed with a general fertiliser. Protect blossom from frost with fleece on cold nights in spring. Net the tree against birds, preferably over a frame.
grow_tips: Prune in spring and summer only.
harvest: Pick sweet cherries from June to August when fully coloured and slightly soft; they do not ripen further after picking. Taste one to test the sugar. Pick with the stalk attached, to prevent juice loss and mould. Acid cherries such as Morello are ready when deep red and come away from the stalk easily.
Pick on a dry day and eat promptly. Pick over the whole tree several times as fruit ripens unevenly, and remove cracked or rotting fruit to prevent spread of brown rot.
use: Eat sweet cherries fresh, or use in clafoutis, tarts, cakes and compotes. Acid cherries make superb jam, pies, sauces and cherry brandy, and have a fabulous sharpness. A cherry stoner makes preparation quick.
Fresh cherries keep for 3–5 days in the fridge. Freeze stoned cherries on a tray, then pack in bags for up to a year. Morello cherries can be bottled in syrup or preserved in alcohol.
use_tips: Freeze stoned cherries on a tray.

care.job: Feed with a general fertiliser and mulch around the base in spring, and net or fleece small trees if frost threatens blossom.
Net trees as the fruit colours to protect from birds, as they will strip a crop in days.
Prune in summer after harvest, never in winter, to avoid silver leaf and bacterial canker, taking out dead and crossing branches.
Water young trees regularly in dry weather, especially in pots, and avoid heavy watering after a dry spell as it splits fruit.
Look out for oozing gum or sunken patches on bark (bacterial canker), and cut out affected wood in summer rather than winter.

preserving.how: Keep unwashed, with stalks on, in a covered container.
Stone, or leave whole, and open freeze on a tray before bagging. Use for baking, sauces and smoothies.
Cook with sugar and lemon juice. Sour cherries make the best preserves.
Pack into jars with sugar and brandy, gin or vodka and leave for at least 6 weeks.
Stone and dry in a dehydrator until leathery. Sour cherries dry well.

crops.name: Chervil
crops.sun_text: Partial shade; protect from midday sun

info: Chervil is a delicate, lacy herb with a gentle aniseed-and-parsley flavour, one of the classic French fines herbes. It thrives in cool, damp, shady conditions where many herbs struggle, and is a good choice for a north-facing windowsill, a shady border or a pot beside the back door.

Chervil bolts quickly in hot, dry weather, so is best grown in spring and autumn, and in partial shade in summer. Sowing a little every few weeks keeps the supply constant, and in mild areas it will crop through winter.
sow: Sow thinly on the surface from March to September, pressing seed in lightly and barely covering it, as light helps germination. Sow where it is to grow, since chervil has a taproot and dislikes transplanting. Rows 20 cm apart, or scatter across a pot. Seedlings appear in 2–3 weeks.

In summer, sow in a shady position and keep the soil moist, since heat and dryness make the plants bolt. A sowing in late August or September under a cloche gives leaves through the winter. Sow a short row every three weeks for a steady supply.
grow: Keep the soil constantly moist and the plants shaded from hot sun. Thin seedlings to 15–20 cm apart. Chervil needs little feeding in reasonable soil. Remove flower buds as they form to extend leaf production, although allowing one or two plants to seed will give you self-sown seedlings.
Slugs are the main pest and love the tender leaves, so use traps or wool pellets around young plants. Aphids and mildew occasionally appear. Mulch the soil to keep the roots cool and moist.
harvest: Start picking leaves 6–8 weeks after sowing, when plants are about 10 cm tall, cutting the outer leaves first. Pick regularly to keep plants leafy and delay flowering. Leaves are best before the plant flowers.
Plants usually give 3–4 weeks of picking before bolting, which is why successional sowing matters. The leaves have the finest flavour when young and fresh, and lose it quickly after cutting.
use: Chervil is best fresh and added at the end of cooking, because heat destroys its delicate flavour. Chop into omelettes, soups, salads, potato dishes, fish sauces, butters and chicken dishes. It is a key part of fines herbes, with parsley, chives and tarragon.

Fresh chervil wilts fast, so use it within a day or two of picking, with stems in water in the fridge. Drying loses nearly all the flavour; freeze chopped in ice-cube trays or make chervil butter to keep it.
use_tips: Add at the end of cooking.
Freeze in butter or ice cubes.

care.job: Sow in a shady spot where it will not dry out, as chervil bolts quickly in hot, dry conditions.
Water in dry weather and pick leaves regularly from the outside, since chervil is best used fresh and young.
Give plants light shade in summer, and let one or two flower to self-sow for autumn and spring crops.
Protect autumn sowings with a cloche to keep leaves coming into winter.

preserving.how: Chop and freeze in ice cube trays with water or butter. It loses its flavour quickly when dried.
Wrap stems in damp kitchen paper in a bag.
Mix chopped leaves into softened butter, roll in baking paper and freeze in slices.

facts.Type: Hardy perennial, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: May–Jun for chicons; Mar–Aug for leaf

types.name: Witloof (forcing) chicory
types.when: Sow May to June · Lift roots October · Force December to March
types.note: Grown for the pale, tender chicons forced in the dark in winter.

types.name: Sugarloaf chicory
types.when: Sow June to July · Harvest September to November
types.note: Tall, upright heads of crisp leaves, similar to cos lettuce, but hardier and bitter-sweet.

types.name: Radicchio and leaf chicory
types.when: Sow June to August · Harvest October to December
types.note: Red and variegated, very hardy. The colour deepens with cold.

info: Chicory gives two crops: bitter-sweet leaves for salads in autumn, and pale 'chicons' (witloof) grown by forcing the roots in darkness in winter. Both are delicious, and the second is very rewarding, as it comes when little else is growing.
Sugarloaf chicory forms tall, upright heads; red-leaved types are radicchio. The blue flowers of chicory are pretty in a border, and the roots can be roasted for a coffee substitute.
sow: For chicons, sow Witloof types in May to June, 1 cm deep, in rows 30 cm apart, and thin to 20 cm. For leaf chicory, sow from March to August. Choose a sunny site with deep, fertile, stone-free soil. Do not use fresh manure.
Water in dry spells. The long taproots develop through summer, and should be lifted in October for forcing.
grow: Keep weed-free and water in dry weather. Cut off any flowering stems that appear. In October, cut the leaves to 2.5 cm above the crown and lift the roots, trimming them to about 20 cm long.

To force, pack roots upright in boxes or large pots of damp compost, with the crowns just exposed, and cover completely with a black bucket or place in a dark cellar at 10–15°C. Keep the compost damp.
harvest: Cut chicons when they are 10–15 cm long, about 4 weeks after forcing begins, taking them off the root with a sharp knife. Exposure to light turns them green and bitter, so harvest and keep in the dark.
A second smaller crop may sprout from the root after cutting. Leaf chicory can be cut from late summer, and the hardier types stand through winter.
use: Use chicons raw in salads, with walnuts, blue cheese, apple or orange, or braise or roast them in butter until soft and caramelised. The classic dish is chicons wrapped in ham in a cheese sauce. Leaf chicory goes well in salads and with warm dressings.
Wrap chicons in paper to keep them out of light, and store in the fridge for up to 5 days. Roots can be stored until needed for forcing in a cool, damp place.
use_tips: Pair raw chicons with walnuts and blue cheese.

care.job: Thin seedlings to about 25 cm apart, and water in dry weather to prevent bolting and bitterness.
Cut leaves of forcing types down to 2 cm above the soil, then lift roots for forcing in a dark place.
Pot forcing roots in damp compost and cover with a black pot or bucket in a dark, cool place so they produce pale chicons.
Remove any plants that bolt in spring, as the flowering stems turn the leaves bitter, and keep the soil moist.

preserving.how: Keep heads in a bag in the salad drawer, away from light, which turns the leaves bitter.
Lift roots in autumn, store cool, and pot a few at a time in the dark for fresh chicons all winter.
Braise or roast, cool and freeze in tubs.

crops.name: Chilli pepper
crops.sun_text: Full sun, 6+ hours; warm and sheltered

facts.Type: Tender perennial, grown as an annual in the UK
facts.Spacing: 45 cm apart, or one per 20–30 cm pot

varieties: Apache (compact, high-yielding, medium heat, ideal for pots)
Prairie Fire (very small and hot, ornamental)
Habanero (very hot, needs a long season)

types.name: Mild chillies
types.when: Sow January to March · Harvest July to October
types.note: Pleasant warmth without the burn, ideal for stuffing and for beginners.

types.name: Medium chillies
types.when: Sow January to March · Harvest August to October
types.note: The cook’s workhorses for curries, salsa and sauces.

types.name: Hot chillies
types.when: Sow January to February · Harvest September to October
types.note: Very hot, with a long season. They need a greenhouse or a very warm spot.

info: Chillies are surprisingly well suited to British gardens when started early and given warmth, and they are among the most ornamental of the edible crops. A single plant can produce dozens of fruits, in colours from green to red, yellow, orange, purple and chocolate brown.

They suit pots on a bright windowsill, in a greenhouse or on a sunny, sheltered patio. Heat levels range widely: mild types such as Hungarian Hot Wax are good for beginners, while Scotch bonnet and habanero need a long, hot season and are best under cover.
sow: Sow early, from January to March, because chillies need a long season to ripen. Sow seeds 5 mm deep in seed compost at 20–25°C in a heated propagator, as they germinate slowly, taking two to four weeks. Once seedlings are large enough to handle, pot on individually into 7–9 cm pots, holding them by the leaves.

Pot on into 12 cm pots when roots fill the pot, and again into final 20–30 cm containers in late spring. Plants can go outdoors in June in a sunny, sheltered spot once temperatures hold above 10°C at night. For hot varieties, a greenhouse or a conservatory is more reliable.
sow_tips: Sow in January to March; they need a long season.
Pot on gradually as roots fill the pot.
Harden off before moving outside in June.
grow: Keep plants in full sun and out of draughts. Water when the top of the compost feels dry, but avoid overwatering, which causes root rot; slightly drier conditions can also increase heat in the fruit. Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato feed once flowers appear.

Pinch out the growing tips of young plants when 20 cm tall, to encourage bushy growth. Support taller types with a cane. Aphids, red spider mite and whitefly are the main pests, especially under cover. Mist plants sparingly to deter spider mite, and wash off aphids.
grow_tips: Pinch out the tip of young plants for bushier growth.
Water when the top of the compost is dry.
Check under leaves for aphids and mite.
harvest: Pick chillies green or wait until they ripen to their final colour for a sweeter, fruitier, hotter taste. Cut fruits off with scissors or secateurs, leaving a short stalk. The first fruit usually ripens in August, and regular picking promotes more flowers and fruit.

Before the first frost in October, pick all the remaining fruits, including the green ones, which can be used in cooking or ripen on a sunny windowsill. In heated conservatories, plants can be overwintered and give a bigger crop in their second year.
harvest_tips: Cut with scissors, leaving a short stalk.
Pick regularly to encourage more fruit.
Pick all fruit before the first frost.
use: Use fresh chillies in curries, chilli con carne, salsas, stir-fries, marinades, hot sauces and sweet chilli jam. Remove the seeds and white pith to reduce the heat. Always wash your hands thoroughly after chopping, or wear gloves, and avoid touching your eyes.

Chillies keep for one to two weeks in the fridge, and freeze whole, with no blanching, ready to chop from frozen. For long-term storage, dry them on a string in a warm, airy place, or in a low oven, and store in a jar. Dried chillies can be ground into powder or flakes, or made into hot sauce.
use_tips: Freeze whole chillies straight from picking.
Dry on a string in a warm, airy spot.
Remove seeds and pith to reduce the heat.
Wear gloves when chopping hot types.

care.job: Pot seedlings on into small pots and keep them warm and bright, at least 15C, and move into larger pots as roots fill.
Pinch out the growing tip when plants reach about 20 cm to make them bushy, and harden off before moving outdoors.
Water when the top of the compost feels dry, as chillies like it slightly dry rather than soggy. Stress can make fruit hotter.
Feed every one to two weeks with a high-potash tomato feed once flowers appear.
Stake tall plants and tap or gently shake flowers on hot days to help pollination indoors.
Cut back and keep a favourite plant on a bright, frost-free windowsill over winter, watering sparingly.

pests.label: Blossom drop in cold or dry spells

preserving.how: Thread whole chillies on a string and hang in a warm, airy place, or dry in a dehydrator or low oven until brittle.
Freeze whole, or chopped, in bags. They soften when thawed but keep heat and flavour.
Blend with vinegar, garlic and salt, simmer and bottle into sterilised jars. Ferment first for a deeper flavour.
Grind dried chillies in a spice grinder into flakes or powder, and wear gloves.
Make chilli jelly with apples or peppers for cheese and cold meats.

info: Chinese cabbage forms tall, tight, crisp heads of pale, frilly leaves with a mild, sweet flavour. It is faster and juicier than ordinary cabbage, and is a staple for stir-fries, kimchi and salads in East Asia.
Sow in July and August, not earlier, since long days and cool nights in spring cause bolting. Plants are not frost-hardy, so harvest before hard frosts, in October and November.
sow: Sow from mid-July to August, 1 cm deep, directly where plants are to grow, in rows 40 cm apart, in rich, moist, firm soil. Thin seedlings to 30–40 cm apart. Chinese cabbage hates root disturbance, so avoid transplanting unless using modules.
Cover with fine mesh at sowing time to keep off flea beetles, which attack young seedlings. Water the row before sowing in dry weather.
sow_tips: Sow in place or in modules.
Cover with fine mesh at once.
grow: Keep the soil constantly moist, as dry spells cause loose, bitter heads and bolting. Mulch to hold moisture, and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser a month after sowing. Keep weeds under control.

Slugs, flea beetle and caterpillars are the main pests. Fine mesh is the best defence. Rotate with other brassicas to avoid club root. Plants tolerate light frosts but should be harvested before hard ones.
grow_tips: Use mesh on the whole crop.
harvest: Cut heads when they are firm and heavy, usually 8–12 weeks after sowing, from October. Cut at the base with a sharp knife. Loose heads can be harvested early as greens.
Harvest before hard frosts. Heads store for several weeks in a cool, frost-free place. Leave the stump in the ground; it may produce a few loose leaves.

If a hard frost is forecast and the heads are not quite solid, tie the outer leaves loosely around the heads with soft string to give extra protection. Pulled whole with the roots and hung in a cool shed, heads often keep for a month or more.
use: Use Chinese cabbage shredded raw in coleslaw and salads, stir-fried with garlic and ginger, in soups, dumplings and spring rolls, or fermented as kimchi. The leaves are sweet and tender, cooking in just a couple of minutes.
Whole heads keep for 2–3 weeks in the fridge, wrapped loosely. Ferment as kimchi or sauerkraut for long storage. It does not freeze well raw.

care.job: Water regularly and keep the soil moist, as dry spells make plants bolt, and cover with fine mesh against flea beetle.
Check for slugs and caterpillars, and pick off any you find, as the tender leaves are a favourite.
Cover plants with fleece in cool weather and cut the heads before hard frost.

preserving.how: Wrap whole heads in paper or a bag and store in the salad drawer.
Make kimchi with salt, chilli, garlic and ginger. It is the classic way to keep it.
Blanch for 90 seconds, drain well and freeze for cooked dishes only.

crops.name: Chives

facts.Sow: Mar–May, or divide clumps in spring or autumn
facts.Time to harvest: 8–10 weeks from sowing, then all year

varieties: Garlic chives (flat leaves with a mild garlic flavour)

info: Chives are the easiest of herbs: a hardy perennial that comes back every spring, thrives in pots and borders, and gives a mild onion flavour to many dishes. The pretty purple pompom flowers are edible and loved by bees.
Once you have a clump you will have chives for years, and dividing it gives free plants for friends. Chives are happy on a windowsill, so they suit even the smallest of gardens.
sow: Sow seed in trays or pots in March to April on a bright windowsill, or direct outdoors from April to May, 1 cm deep. Sow thinly in small clumps of 5–10 seeds, which can be planted out as a group. Germination takes two to three weeks. Plant out when seedlings are about 10 cm tall, 20–25 cm apart.

The simplest way is to buy a pot from a garden centre or divide an existing clump. Dig up a clump in spring or autumn, split it into small clusters of bulbs and replant. Chives grow in a pot at least 15–20 cm wide, and a pot kept outside near the kitchen door is handy.
sow_tips: Sow seed in small clumps, not single seeds.
Divide a clump to make free plants.
Keep pots near the kitchen for easy picking.
grow: Chives prefer moist, fertile soil and regular watering. Cut them to 5 cm above the ground a few times each summer to encourage fresh, tender growth, and cut back flowers after blooming unless you want seed. Mulch the plants in autumn and feed with a general liquid fertiliser during the growing season.

Clumps become congested after three to four years and flower less, so lift and divide them in spring or autumn. Aphids sometimes appear, and chive rust (orange pustules) and onion fly are rare problems. Cut back and discard affected leaves.
grow_tips: Cut back hard after flowering for fresh growth.
Divide clumps every three to four years.
Feed lightly every month in summer.
harvest: Begin picking when the leaves are about 15 cm tall, snipping them 2–5 cm above the soil with scissors. Cut only a third of the plant at one time. Regular cutting keeps the growth fresh and prevents the leaves from becoming tough and straggly.

The flowers can be picked as they open in late spring and early summer. Use them whole in salads or break the florets apart and scatter them over dishes. Chives die back in winter but sprout again in early spring, and a pot brought indoors will keep growing on a bright sill.
harvest_tips: Snip with scissors rather than tearing.
Never cut more than a third of the plant.
Pick flowers fully open for the best flavour.
Bring a pot indoors for winter pickings.
use: Chives are best raw or added at the end of cooking, as heat destroys their flavour. Scatter on scrambled eggs, baked potatoes, soups, cream cheese, salads and fish, or mix into butter and sour cream. The purple flowers add colour and a mild onion kick to salads.

Fresh chives keep in the fridge for a week, wrapped in damp kitchen paper in a bag. Drying loses most of the flavour, so freeze them instead: chop and pack into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or freeze in bags. Chive flower vinegar, made by steeping blossoms in white wine vinegar, turns a lovely pink.
use_tips: Add at the end of cooking to keep the flavour.
Freeze chopped chives in ice-cube trays.
Make pink chive-blossom vinegar in a jar.
Do not dry chives; they lose their taste.

care.job: Divide congested clumps in spring and replant in fresh soil, giving every clump a good water.
Cut stems down to 5 cm above the soil several times in the season, which encourages fresh, tender growth.
Cut off flower stalks if you want leaves, or leave some for bees, and use the flowers in salads.
Water in dry spells and feed pots with a general liquid feed every month or so.
Cut back dead foliage and lift a clump into a pot for winter leaves indoors on a bright windowsill.

preserving.how: Snip and freeze in bags or ice cube trays. Flavour is better frozen than dried.
Mix chopped chives into softened butter and freeze in rolls.
Steep flowers or leaves in white wine vinegar for 2 weeks and strain for a pink, oniony vinegar.
Pot up a clump in autumn and keep on a bright windowsill for fresh winter cuttings.

info: Cobnuts, the cultivated forms of hazel, are the English nut and especially popular in Kent. Fresh green cobnuts in late summer are sweet and milky, and fully ripe hazelnuts keep for months. Plants are hardy, reliable and long-lived.
Hazels are wind-pollinated, with catkins in February, so plant at least two different varieties for cross-pollination. They also make excellent hedging and provide wildlife habitat.
sow: Plant bare-root trees from November to March in fertile, well-drained soil in sun or partial shade. Plant two or more varieties 4–5 m apart. Stake and mulch; protect from rabbits and squirrels.
Avoid very rich soils, which produce leaf at the expense of nuts. After planting, cut the main stem to 60 cm.
grow: Train as a goblet-shaped bush with 8–10 main stems on a short trunk. Prune in late summer (August) by ‘brutting’, snapping side shoots part-way, and in February, cutting them back to 3 buds after pollination.
Water newly planted trees. Mulch each spring. Squirrels are the main enemy; netting or cages may be needed. Nut weevil and honey fungus are minor concerns.
grow_tips: Prune in late summer and February.
harvest: Pick fresh green cobnuts in late August to September when the husks turn pale. For storing, wait until nuts turn brown and fall, in late September to October. Collect from the ground daily before squirrels.
Dry fully before storing, in a warm, airy place for 2 weeks.

Squirrels and jays can strip a tree in a week, so keep an eye on the tree from August and pick fresh ‘green’ cobs a little early rather than lose them. Ripe nuts fall easily from their husks; nuts that sink when put in water are good, and floaters are empty.
harvest_tips: Pick fresh green cobs in August.
use: Eat fresh green cobnuts raw. Roast hazelnuts, chop in cakes, praline, chocolate spread, pesto and salads, or grind into flour. Their flavour is superb.
Dried nuts in shells keep for a year in a cool, dry place. Shelled nuts keep 3–6 months in the fridge or freezer.

Toast hazelnuts in a dry pan or a 180°C oven for 8–10 minutes until golden, then rub off the papery skins in a clean tea towel. They are wonderful in chocolate brownies, with roasted vegetables, ground in biscuits and cakes, and blended into a rich nut butter.

care.job: Prune in late winter, shortening side shoots to leave a few buds and removing suckers, to keep an open framework.
Water young trees in dry spells and keep the base clear of weeds.
Net or protect nuts from squirrels as they ripen, and pick them as they fall or when the husks turn brown.
Plant new trees bare-root in winter and mulch the base each spring.

preserving.how: Leave nuts in their husks to dry for a few weeks in a warm, airy place, then shell and keep in an airy container or net bag.
Fresh green nuts are milky and juicy and need eating within a week or two.
Shelled kernels freeze well in bags.
Roast shelled nuts on a tray for 10 minutes, cool and store in a jar.

crops.name: Coriander
crops.sun_text: Partial shade in summer; full sun in spring and autumn

facts.Time to harvest: 4–6 weeks for leaf; 12 weeks for seed
facts.Good companions: Not fennel; good with carrots and potatoes

info: Coriander is a fragrant herb that is notorious for bolting, but with the right timing and cool, moist conditions it is easy. The leaves and the seeds are both used in the kitchen, and the flowers attract hoverflies and bees.
To avoid bolting, sow often, choose a bolt-resistant ‘leaf’ variety, and grow it in partial shade in summer. For seed, let plants flower and set seed, and enjoy both.
sow: Sow thinly directly where it is to grow, 1 cm deep, from March to September, in rows 20 cm apart or scattered in a pot. Coriander dislikes root disturbance, so avoid transplanting. Seedlings appear in 1–3 weeks.

Sow a short row every 3 weeks for continuous leaves. Summer sowings do best in partial shade with moist soil, as heat and drought cause bolting. A late-summer sowing under cover provides winter leaves.
grow: Keep the soil moist, never letting it dry out, and shade from hot afternoon sun. Thin to 15–20 cm apart, or grow densely for cut-and-come-again leaves. Mulching helps keep the roots cool.

Plants will bolt at some point, which is natural. Let some plants flower for the pollinators, and collect the seeds when they turn brown. Aphids and slugs are the main pests, and leaf spot may occur in wet conditions.
grow_tips: Let some plants flower and seed.
harvest: Cut leaves when the plant is 15 cm tall, from 4–6 weeks. Cut outer stems first, or cut the whole plant 5 cm above ground for regrowth. Pick regularly to delay bolting. Lower, rounded leaves have the strongest flavour, while upper feathery leaves are milder.

To collect seeds, leave a few plants to flower and wait until the seed heads turn brown, then cut and dry them in a paper bag. The seed is called coriander and has a warm, citrusy flavour quite different from the leaf.
harvest_tips: Dry seed heads in a paper bag.
use: Use fresh coriander in curries, salsas, guacamole, salads, soups, chutneys and stir-fries, adding at the end for freshness. Stems and roots are packed with flavour and can be chopped into curry paste. Dried seeds, toasted and ground, form the base of many spice blends.

Fresh leaves keep a few days in the fridge with stems in water. Chop and freeze in ice-cube trays with water or oil for later use. Dried leaves have little flavour, but dried seeds keep for years in a jar.
use_tips: Add leaves at the end of cooking.

care.job: Water regularly and keep the soil evenly moist, as coriander bolts quickly if it dries out.
Give plants light shade in the afternoon in hot weather to slow bolting, and sow every few weeks for a steady supply.
Harvest leaves from the outside regularly, and let a few plants flower and set seed for coriander seeds.
Cut seed heads when they turn brown and dry them upside down in a paper bag to catch the seeds.

preserving.how: Chop leaves and freeze in ice cube trays with a little water or oil. Drying loses most of the flavour.
Stand stems in a glass of water with a bag loosely over the top, or wrap in damp kitchen paper.
Let some plants run to seed, dry the heads in a paper bag and store the seeds whole in a jar.
Blend leaves with garlic, chilli, ginger and oil and freeze in small portions.

facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors; plant out late May–June
facts.Height: 60–90 cm; trailing types spread more widely

types.name: Green courgettes
types.when: Sow April to May indoors · Harvest July to October
types.note: The usual dark green, glossy fruits, heavy and reliable.

types.name: Yellow courgettes
types.when: Sow April to May indoors · Harvest July to October
types.note: Golden fruit, easy to spot among the foliage, with a slightly sweeter flavour.

types.name: Round courgettes
types.when: Sow April to May indoors · Harvest July to September
types.note: Ball-shaped fruits that are perfect for stuffing.

info: Courgettes are among the most productive vegetables you can grow: two or three plants can feed a family all summer and still produce a glut. They are easy and reliable, thriving on rich soil, sun and water, and the large yellow flowers are edible.
Choose green, yellow or round types for variety. Plants are big, so need room, but a single plant in a large pot or growing bag works on a balcony. Compact bush varieties suit small gardens.
sow: Sow indoors from April to early May, placing seeds on their edge, 2 cm deep, in 9 cm pots of multipurpose compost at 18–20°C. They germinate in a week and grow fast. You can also sow directly outside in late May to June, under a cloche, where the soil has warmed.

Harden off plants for 10 days and plant out after the last frost, from late May, into fertile, moisture-retentive soil enriched with plenty of compost or manure. Space them 90 cm apart; a mound or shallow dish around each plant helps hold water.
sow_tips: Do not plant out until frosts have finished.
Dig in lots of compost first.
grow: Water deeply and regularly, particularly once fruits begin to form, aiming the water at the base and avoiding the leaves. Mulch around the plants with compost or straw. Feed fortnightly with a high-potash fertiliser once the first fruits appear.

Small fruits that rot at the end are generally poorly pollinated; in cool or wet weather, hand-pollinate by transferring pollen from the male flower to the female flower (with the baby fruit behind it) with a small brush. Powdery mildew often arrives in late summer; remove affected leaves and keep plants watered. Slugs target young plants.
grow_tips: Water at the base, not on the leaves.
harvest: Pick courgettes when they are 10–15 cm long, from July until the first frost. Cut with a sharp knife, leaving a short piece of stem. Check plants every day or two in midsummer: courgettes grow incredibly fast and can become marrows overnight.

Regular cutting keeps the plant producing, while a marrow left on the plant will stop further fruiting. The flowers are also edible and delicious stuffed and fried; choose male flowers (on a long thin stalk) and leave plenty of female flowers to fruit.
harvest_tips: Pick at 10–15 cm for best flavour.
Cut, don’t twist, off the plant.
use: Courgettes are versatile: grill, roast, fry, spiralise into noodles, grate into cakes and fritters, or stir into pasta sauces and ratatouille. Stuff the round types with rice and cheese. Small, young fruit can be eaten raw, thinly sliced in salads. Courgette flowers are a delicacy.

Fresh courgettes keep for a week in the fridge. To freeze, grate and squeeze out water before freezing in bags in portions, ideal for soups, bakes and cakes. Chutneys and relishes preserve larger gluts, and marrows can be stuffed and roasted.
use_tips: Salt and drain slices before frying.

care.job: Harden off plants and set them out after the last frost, in rich soil with plenty of room. Protect from slugs.
Water generously at the base, as courgettes are thirsty, and avoid wetting the leaves.
Feed every 1 to 2 weeks with a tomato feed once the first fruits form.
If few fruits set, hand-pollinate by dabbing a male flower into a female one (the female has a tiny courgette behind it).
Pick fruits small and often, as leaving them to grow into marrows slows the plant down.
Watch for white powdery mildew on the leaves. Remove badly affected leaves and keep plants watered.
Clear plants after the first frosts and compost the healthy foliage.

pests.label: Poor pollination in cold, wet summers

preserving.how: Grate, squeeze out the water and freeze in portions for baking and fritters, steam-blanching for 1–2 minutes first if you will keep it for months. Or slice, blanch for 3 minutes and freeze.
Keep small, firm courgettes unwashed in a bag in the salad drawer.
Cook into soup or a tomato and courgette sauce and freeze in tubs.
Make courgette relish or chutney, or pickle thin ribbons in vinegar.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator for chips or to add to soups.

images.alt: A young courgette growing beside an open yellow-orange flower

crops.name: Cucumber

facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors; plant out late May–June

varieties: Burpless Tasty Green (mild, easy to digest)

types.name: Greenhouse cucumbers
types.when: Sow March to May · Harvest June to September
types.note: Long, smooth fruit, needing heat and humidity.

types.name: Outdoor (ridge) cucumbers
types.when: Sow April to May indoors · Harvest July to September
types.note: Shorter, rougher-skinned and hardier, the best choice for UK gardens.

types.name: Mini and snack cucumbers
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest July to September
types.note: Small, thin-skinned fruit that crop heavily in pots.

info: Cucumbers are quick, productive plants with crisp, refreshing fruits that taste better when picked fresh. Greenhouse types have long, smooth fruits; outdoor or ridge cucumbers are shorter and slightly rough-skinned and hardier, ideal for UK gardens.

Grown up a trellis or wigwam, cucumbers use little ground and suit balconies and small gardens. They need warmth, shelter and plenty of water, and they reward you with a heavy crop through late summer.
sow: Sow indoors from April to early May, placing seeds on their edge 1–2 cm deep in individual 7 cm pots of seed compost at about 20°C. They germinate quickly, within a few days, and grow fast. Do not sow too early, because cold checks growth.

Harden off in late May and plant out in early June, once the frost risk has passed, in rich, moisture-retentive soil or a large pot. Add compost generously, plant 45–60 cm apart and train up a trellis, netting or canes. Under glass, plant a few weeks earlier.
sow_tips: Plant out in early June after the last frost.
Train up a trellis to save space.
grow: Keep the soil constantly moist, watering generously in hot weather, and mulch to help retain moisture. Feed every week to two weeks with tomato fertiliser once fruits start forming. Tie in stems as they climb, and pinch out the growing tip at about 1.5 m.

Outdoor ridge types need no pinching out of side shoots, but remove male flowers on greenhouse varieties to avoid bitter fruit. Powdery mildew, aphids, slugs and red spider mite are the main problems. Water at the base, keep the foliage dry and allow good air flow.
grow_tips: Pinch out the tip at 1.5 m.
Water at the base to avoid mildew.
harvest: Pick cucumbers when they reach a good size, from 15–20 cm for ridge types, usually from July to September. Cut with a sharp knife, leaving a short piece of stalk. Cut fruits regularly, because leaving ripe ones on the vine slows further production and the fruit turns bitter and seedy.
Pick in the morning when fruits are cool and crisp. The more you pick, the more the plant will produce. Pull plants up after the first frost, and use up the last small fruits for pickles.
harvest_tips: Harvest every few days at peak season.
use: Eat cucumber fresh in salads, sandwiches and tzatziki, or serve it chilled in cold soups such as gazpacho. Slice thinly for quick pickles, or make bread-and-butter pickles, dill cucumbers or relishes to preserve a glut. A few slices in a jug of water makes a refreshing summer drink.

Whole cucumbers keep for up to a week in the fridge, wrapped in cling film or in a bag, but they do not freeze well. For storage, pickle in brine or vinegar and keep in sterilised jars for a year, for a satisfying crunch long after the season ends.
use_tips: Wrap in cling film in the fridge.
Salt and drain slices for crisp pickles.
Leave the skin on ridge types for extra crunch.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost in a greenhouse or sheltered spot, and train the main stem up a support.
Water regularly and maintain humidity in a greenhouse by damping down the floor on hot days.
Pinch out side shoots after two leaves beyond a fruit, and remove male flowers on greenhouse types so fruits do not turn bitter.
Feed weekly with a tomato feed once fruits are growing.
Shade the greenhouse in hot weather, and watch for mildew and red spider mite, which both like hot, dry conditions.

preserving.how: Wrap in kitchen paper and keep in the salad drawer. Keep away from tomatoes and apples, which give off ethylene.
Slice for bread and butter pickles, or pickle small ones whole in dill and vinegar.
Ferment whole or sliced in a 3–5% salt brine with dill and garlic for sour pickles.
Cook with onions, sugar and vinegar for a sweet relish.
Blend cold soups and freeze in tubs. They are best eaten raw rather than frozen.

crops.name: Dill

facts.Time to harvest: 6–8 weeks for leaves; 14 weeks for seed
facts.Good companions: Cabbages, cucumbers, lettuce (not fennel or carrots)

varieties: Bouquet (tall, good for seed and leaf)

info: Dill is a delicate, feathery herb with a distinctive aniseed and citrus flavour, indispensable with fish, potatoes and cucumber pickles. It is quick and easy from seed, and the airy foliage and yellow flowers look attractive in borders and attract hoverflies.
It grows tall and can be knocked over by wind, so choose a sheltered spot. Keep it away from fennel, since the two cross-pollinate and the flavour suffers. Dwarf varieties suit pots.
sow: Sow directly outdoors from April to August, 5 mm deep, in rows 30 cm apart, in a sunny, sheltered spot with light, well-drained soil. Dill dislikes being transplanted as it has a taproot, so sow where it will grow, or use deep pots.
Sow a short row every 3 weeks for fresh leaves all summer, as plants bolt quickly in warm weather. Thin seedlings to 20–30 cm apart. Dill self-seeds readily if you let it flower.
grow: Water in dry spells, as drought triggers bolting, but avoid overwatering. Support tall plants with canes or twiggy sticks. Feeding is unnecessary in reasonable soil, as too much nitrogen reduces flavour.

Aphids and caterpillars may occur, but the flowers attract natural predators such as hoverflies and ladybirds. Cut back the flower heads to prolong the leaf harvest, or leave them to set seed. Dill is hardy, but dies at the end of the season.
grow_tips: Cut flower heads to extend leaf harvest.
harvest: Snip the feathery leaves (dill weed) when plants are 20 cm tall, from about six weeks. Take leaves from the outside, or cut the whole plant 5 cm above the base for regrowth. The flavour is strongest just before flowering.

For seed, wait for the flower heads to turn brown and form flat seeds, then cut the heads and dry them in a paper bag. Use the yellow flowers and green seed heads for pickling. Harvest in the morning.
harvest_tips: Pick before flowering for best taste.
Dry seed heads in a paper bag.
use: Add fresh dill to salmon, potatoes, egg dishes, cucumber salad, yoghurt sauces and soups at the end, as heat quickly reduces flavour. Use flower heads in pickled cucumbers (dill pickles) and in gravadlax. The seeds flavour breads and pickles.

Fresh dill keeps for a few days in the fridge with stems in water. Freeze chopped in ice-cube trays for the best flavour retention; dried dill loses most of its aroma. Dill vinegar and dill butter are good ways to preserve it.
use_tips: Add at the end of cooking.

care.job: Thin seedlings to about 20 cm apart and stake tall plants, as the hollow stems are brittle in wind.
Water in dry weather and pick fronds regularly to keep growth tender, keeping dill away from fennel to prevent cross-pollination.
Let a few plants flower for the seed heads (for pickling) and to attract hoverflies, which eat aphids.
Harvest the ripe seed heads and dry them, and leave some seed to self-sow for next year.

preserving.how: Chop fronds and freeze in bags or ice cube trays. Better than dried for flavour.
Cut seed heads when brown, dry in a paper bag and keep seeds in a jar for pickling.
Steep fronds in white wine vinegar, or mix into butter and freeze in rolls.
Add heads and fronds to jars of cucumbers, beetroot or cauliflower.

crops.name: Edamame

info: Edamame are young soya beans in their pods, a protein-rich snack that is simple to grow in a warm, sunny summer. Early-maturing varieties bred for cooler climates crop reliably in the south and midlands, and also under cover.
The plants are bushy and compact, so they suit large pots as well as beds. Like other beans, they fix nitrogen in the soil.
sow: Sow in individual pots or modules in May, 3 cm deep, at about 18°C. Plant out in early June after hardening off, 15–20 cm apart in a sunny, sheltered spot with fertile soil. Direct sowing is possible in late May in warm areas.
Early-maturing varieties are essential. Cover with a cloche or fleece in cold weather.

If you sow directly, wait until the soil has warmed to at least 15°C, usually late May. Cold, wet soil rots the large seeds, so cover seedlings with a cloche in the first few weeks. Sow a few extra seeds in case some fail.
grow: Water regularly, especially during flowering and pod fill, and mulch to retain moisture. No feed is needed, as beans fix their own nitrogen. Weed carefully.
Slugs are the main problem for young plants. Birds and mice can eat seed. Stake bushy plants if windy.

Edamame plants flower in midsummer, and pod set depends on warmth and steady moisture. A black plastic mulch can raise soil temperature and suppress weeds in cooler areas. Keep an eye out for aphids on the growing tips, and spray them off with water. In windy sites, a few short canes with string around the plants stop them flopping.
harvest: Pick pods when they are plump, bright green, about 5–6 cm long, and the beans inside are full, usually from late August to September, before the pods turn yellow. Cut whole plants or pick pods individually.
Eat quickly, since sugars turn to starch within hours. Harvest before frost.
use: Boil pods in salted water for 4–5 minutes, drain and serve warm or cold, squeezing the beans from the pods into your mouth, with sea salt. Shelled beans can be added to salads, stir-fries, hummus and rice dishes.
Freeze whole pods after blanching for 3 minutes, for up to a year. Fresh pods keep for 2–3 days in the fridge.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost and water in well, as edamame needs warmth to thrive.
Water regularly during flowering and podding, and mulch to keep the roots cool.
Pick pods when they are plump and still bright green, before they turn yellow.

preserving.how: Boil pods for 3–5 minutes, cool in iced water, drain and freeze in bags in the pod or shelled.
Keep fresh pods in a bag in the salad drawer.
Leave pods on the plant until brown and rattling, then shell and dry as soya beans.

safety: Don't eat the pods.

crops.name: Elder
crops.sun_text: Sun or shade; tolerates poor soil

facts.Type: Hardy deciduous shrub or small tree

info: Elder is a tough, native shrub with creamy scented flowers in early summer, and glossy purple-black berries in late summer, both good for the kitchen. It grows in sun or shade, in any soil, and is a magnet for wildlife.
Cultivated forms include Black Lace, with deep purple lacy leaves and pink flowers. Berries must be cooked, as raw they can cause upset stomachs.
sow: Plant bare-root or pot-grown plants from November to March in almost any soil in sun or shade. Dig a hole, plant at the same depth as in the pot, firm and water in. Space 3 m apart as a hedge, or singly as a specimen.
Elder grows rapidly; cut back to 30 cm after planting to encourage a bushy habit. Hardwood cuttings taken in winter root readily.
grow: Prune in late winter, removing a third of the oldest stems to ground level, and shortening others, to keep plants vigorous and fruitful. Elder can be cut hard back and will regrow.
Water in the first year. Few problems: aphids on young shoots and elder leaf spot are the main ones. Elder spreads by seed, so remove unwanted seedlings.
harvest: Pick flower heads in May to June on a dry, sunny day when fully open and fragrant, shaking off insects. Pick berries in August to September when deep black and hang heavily; cut whole heads and strip with a fork.
Never eat berries raw; always cook. Remove all stalks, which are toxic. Leave some berries for birds.

Pick elderflowers on a dry, sunny morning when the flowers are a creamy colour and smell sweet, not musty, and shake them to remove insects, but do not wash them, as this removes the pollen that carries the flavour. Use within a few hours of picking for the best cordial.
harvest_tips: Pick flowers on a dry day.
use: Make elderflower cordial, champagne, fritters, or infuse in gooseberry jam. Cook berries for syrup, jelly, wine, chutney and pies; elderberry syrup is a traditional winter remedy. Combine with blackberries and apple.
Cordial keeps 6 months in sterilised bottles, or freeze it. Berries freeze whole. Dry berries for tea.

Elderflower cordial is made by steeping about 20 flower heads with sliced lemons, sugar and citric acid in boiling water for 24 hours, then straining and bottling. Elderberry syrup, simmered with sugar and a few cloves, is a classic winter cordial that can also be frozen.

care.job: Prune in late winter, cutting out the oldest wood and shortening branches to keep the bush manageable and productive.
Keep the plant in check by cutting back suckers, and feed with a general fertiliser if growth is weak.
Pick berries when fully ripe and dark, removing stalks, and always cook them before eating. Raw elderberries are mildly poisonous.
Plant new bushes bare-root in winter and mulch the base each spring.

preserving.how: Strip berries from the stalks with a fork, freeze on a tray and bag. Cook before eating, as raw berries upset the stomach.
Simmer cooked berries with sugar and spices, strain and bottle in sterilised bottles.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

preserving.how: Dry berries in a dehydrator or low oven until hard, then simmer later for syrups and teas.
Steep flowers with sugar, lemon and citric acid for 24 hours, strain and bottle or freeze.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

preserving.how: Combine with apple for a firm set.

safety: Never eat berries raw; always cook.
Remove all stalks, which are toxic.
Raw elderberries are mildly poisonous.

facts.Type: Hardy perennial, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: 20–25 cm apart in rows 40 cm apart

info: Elephant garlic is actually a relative of the leek, producing enormous bulbs with a handful of huge cloves and a much milder, sweeter flavour than true garlic. It is easy to grow, hardy and productive.
The tall flower stalks carry large, spherical purple heads, which are beautiful in a border and attract bees. It tolerates most soils, and bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball.
sow: Plant individual cloves in October to November (or February to March) 5–8 cm deep, pointed end up, 20–25 cm apart in rows 40 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with fertile, free-draining soil. On heavy clay, plant in raised beds or start in pots.
Use bulbs from a reputable supplier, as supermarket bulbs may carry disease. Autumn planting gives bigger bulbs. Mulch lightly over winter in cold areas.
grow: Keep the bed weed-free, since garlic competes poorly. Water in dry spring weather, and stop watering in June as bulbs ripen. Feed with a general fertiliser in spring.

Cut off flower stems if you want larger bulbs, or allow them to bloom for ornament. Rust and white rot are the main diseases; rotate beds and don't replant garlic in the same soil for at least four years.
grow_tips: Remove flower stems for larger bulbs.
harvest: Harvest in July and August when the lower leaves turn yellow and flop over. Ease bulbs out with a fork rather than pulling, to avoid damage. Handle gently, as the skins are thin.
Dry bulbs in a warm, airy place for 2–3 weeks, until the skins are papery. Trim roots and stems or plait. The bulbs reach their full size and ripeness in sun.

Because elephant garlic can grow quickly in wet weather, lift bulbs on a dry day and leave them to dry on a rack with the leaves on for a week before trimming. Large bulbs also produce small ‘rounds’ (bulbils) that can be replanted to give a fresh crop in two years.
use: Elephant garlic has a mild, sweet flavour that is excellent roasted whole, sliced raw into salads, or sautéed in butter. Use more than you would regular garlic. The huge cloves are easy to peel.
Cured bulbs keep for about 6 months in a cool, dry, airy place. Roast cloves and freeze them, or make garlic confit in oil in the fridge.
use_tips: Store in a cool, dry place.

care.job: Keep beds weed-free and water in dry spring weather, as elephant garlic needs steady moisture while the bulbs swell.
Cut off the flower stems when they appear so the energy goes into the bulb.
Stop watering once the leaves yellow, and lift the bulbs when the tops die back.
Check autumn-planted cloves are firm in the soil and mulch beds in cold areas.

preserving.how: Dry in a warm, airy place for 2–3 weeks, then hang in nets or plait and store somewhere cool and dry, not in the fridge.
Peel and chop, or roast whole bulbs, then freeze in tubs.
Roast whole bulbs and squeeze out the cloves. Keep in the fridge for a week.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator or low oven, then grind into garlic powder.

images.alt: Two large elephant garlic cloves held in a gardener's hand beside a string line on a prepared bed

types.name: Curly endive (frisée)
types.when: Sow June to August · Harvest September to November
types.note: Finely cut, frilly leaves with a pale heart. Sharp and crisp, best blanched.

types.name: Broad-leaved endive (escarole)
types.when: Sow June to August · Harvest October to December
types.note: Broader, smoother leaves with a milder taste. Hardier and better in winter.

info: Endive is a bitter-sweet salad plant related to chicory, forming frilly curly heads (frisée) or broad-leaved heads (escarole). It is at its best in autumn and early winter, when lettuce is over, and its slight bitterness is a welcome change.
Sown in summer, endive resists bolting better than lettuce. Covering the hearts for a few days to keep the light out makes them paler and less bitter and gives tender, pale leaves.
sow: Sow from June to August, 1 cm deep, in modules or directly in rows 30 cm apart, and thin or plant out to 25–30 cm. Sowing before June risks bolting. Seeds germinate best in cool conditions, so sow in the evening in summer.
Choose a sunny spot with fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Late sowings under cloches carry the crop through winter.
sow_tips: Sow in the evening in hot weather.
grow: Water regularly and evenly, since drought makes leaves bitter and tough. Feed lightly if the plants look pale. Mulch to keep the soil moist.

To blanch, about 10 days before harvest, tie the outer leaves loosely together or cover the head with a plate or bucket, excluding light. Slugs and aphids are the main pests. Do not blanch in wet weather, which leads to rot.
harvest: Cut whole heads when they are firm and 20–25 cm across, from September to December, once the hearts have turned pale. Cut at ground level with a knife. The plants are hardy to about -5°C, but heads rot in prolonged wet or hard frost.
Loose outer leaves can be picked as needed. Take heads in before severe frost, or protect with fleece.

If you do not wish to blanch, you can simply cut the leaves young for a milder taste. Curly types may hold water in their frills, so drain and shake well before storing. Tying the outer leaves with a rubber band or soft string is a quick method of blanching.
harvest_tips: Cut blanched heads at ground level.
use: Use endive raw in salads, mixed with sweet ingredients such as oranges, apples, walnuts or bacon to balance the bitterness, with a mustardy dressing. Larger leaves can be braised, sautéed or added to soups.
Heads keep 1–2 weeks in the fridge, wrapped in damp paper. Soak cut leaves in cold water to mellow the bitterness and crisp them up.
use_tips: Balance with sweet and salty flavours.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 25 to 30 cm apart, and water regularly to avoid bitterness and bolting.
Blanch the hearts by tying the outer leaves loosely together or covering with a plate for about 10 days before cutting, to reduce bitterness.
Protect late plants with a cloche from frost and cut before hard freezing weather.

pests.label: Rot when blanched in wet weather

preserving.how: Keep whole heads in a bag in the salad drawer.
Tie up outer leaves a week before cutting, or cover with a plate, to blanch the heart and make it sweeter.
Braise or wilt in soups, cool and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Fig
crops.sun_text: Full sun; a warm, sheltered, south-facing wall is ideal

facts.Sow: Plant Mar–Apr, or container trees in spring
facts.Planting depth: Same depth as in the pot

varieties: Brown Turkey (hardy and reliable, the usual UK choice)
Little Miss Figgy (compact, perfect for pots)
White Marseilles (pale, sweet, good in warm sites)
Rouge de Bordeaux (compact, good in pots)

types.name: Hardy figs for outdoors
types.when: Harvest August to October
types.note: Well suited to a warm wall in the UK.

types.name: Figs for pots and greenhouses
types.when: Harvest July to October
types.note: Compact or less hardy types that reward some shelter.

info: Figs are surprisingly happy in the UK, especially in the south, with a warm wall and a restricted root run. Their bold lobed leaves are very ornamental, and the sweet, honeyed fruits are a delicacy you rarely taste at their best in a shop.

Restricting the roots, in a large pot or a pit lined with paving slabs, encourages fruit rather than leaves. Only the figs that form in late summer and overwinter as embryo fruit need protecting; the following year they ripen. Figs are self-fertile, so one tree is enough.
sow: Plant in spring in a hot, sunny, sheltered spot, ideally against a south- or west-facing wall. For good fruiting, restrict the roots by planting in a 40–50 cm pot, or in a pit 60 cm square lined with concrete slabs or thick plastic, with rubble in the bottom for drainage.

Use a loam-based compost such as John Innes No. 3 mixed with grit. Plant at the same depth as in the nursery pot and water well. Keep potted figs in the sunniest spot, and move to a sheltered location or wrap with fleece in cold winters.
sow_tips: Restrict the roots for more fruit.
grow: Water potted figs regularly through the summer, and feed with a high-potash fertiliser every two weeks from the time fruit forms. Pot-grown figs dry out quickly in a heatwave. Repot into a slightly larger pot every few years, or refresh the top 5 cm of compost annually.

In late autumn, remove all fruit larger than a pea (they will not survive winter), and keep the pea-sized fruit that will ripen next year. Protect with fleece or straw in cold areas. Prune in spring to keep the shape, removing damaged shoots, and in early summer pinch out new shoot tips to five leaves.
grow_tips: Remove large unripe figs in late autumn.
Pinch out shoot tips in summer.
harvest: Figs are ripe in August to October when the fruit droops on its stalk, the skin is soft, slightly wrinkled and coloured, and a drop of nectar may appear at the base. Gently twist or cut the stalk to pick. An unripe fig will not continue to ripen after picking.
Pick figs when you are ready to eat them, as they bruise easily and keep poorly. Wear gloves, since the sap can irritate skin. Cover trees with netting to keep birds and wasps from ripe fruit.
use: Eat figs fresh, on their own or with cheese such as goat’s cheese, blue cheese or mozzarella, with ham, honey or yoghurt. Roast or grill halved figs with honey, make jam, chutney, or bake them in tarts and cakes. Dried figs, made in a low oven, keep well.

Ripe figs keep only 2–3 days in the fridge, so eat or process them quickly. They freeze whole or halved on a tray, then bagged, for up to a year, for use in baking or sauces. Fig jam keeps for a year.

care.job: Prune lightly in spring, cutting out dead or damaged branches, and feed with a high-potash fertiliser such as tomato feed.
Water pot-grown figs regularly in summer, as they dry out quickly, and keep roots restricted to encourage fruit instead of leaves.
Pinch out the tips of new shoots after five leaves to encourage fruiting wood and keep the plant manageable.
Remove any fruits larger than a pea at the end of autumn that will not ripen before winter, to leave tiny embryo figs to overwinter for next year.
Wrap outdoor figs in horticultural fleece or straw in hard frosts, and keep potted plants in an unheated, frost-free spot.

preserving.how: Keep ripe figs in a single layer in the fridge and eat quickly, as they are very fragile.
Freeze whole on a tray, then bag. Thawed figs are soft, so are best cooked.
Cook with sugar and lemon, or in spiced chutney with onions and vinegar.
Halve and dry in a dehydrator or very low oven until leathery.
Pack in sugar syrup with brandy for long keeping.

safety: Wear gloves, since the sap can irritate skin.

facts.Good companions: Not beans, tomatoes or dill (it cross-pollinates and stunts)

types.name: Quick-maturing bulb fennel
types.when: Sow June to July · Harvest August to October
types.note: Bolt-resistant varieties for summer sowing.

types.name: Traditional bulb fennel
types.when: Sow June to July · Harvest September to November
types.note: Larger bulbs, but more prone to bolting.
