info: Florence fennel is grown for its swollen, crisp, aniseed-flavoured bulb, which is delicious raw or cooked. It also produces feathery fronds as a bonus herb. It is a little temperamental, bolting if checked by cold or drought, but with good timing it is rewarding.

Sow after midsummer in the UK to avoid bolting in long days, and choose bolt-resistant varieties. Bulbs form in late summer and autumn, and they are good in pots as well as beds. Keep it away from dill, with which it crosses.
sow: Sow from mid-May to July, as seed sown earlier in cool weather tends to bolt. Sow directly outdoors 1 cm deep in rows 45 cm apart, or in modules to avoid root disturbance, planting out at 3–4 weeks. Final spacing is 25–30 cm apart.

Choose a sunny spot with light, fertile, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil. Fennel dislikes root disturbance, so sow in modules or biodegradable pots. A later sowing in July gives a late autumn crop. Fleece protects early plantings against cold snaps.
sow_tips: Sow after mid-May to avoid bolting.
Sow in modules to avoid root disturbance.
grow: Water regularly and consistently, since drought or irregular watering leads to bolting. Weed carefully. When the bulbs begin to swell, in late summer, draw soil up around them to keep the light out, producing tender, white bulbs.

Slugs and aphids are the main pests. Fennel is generally trouble-free, but flower stems should be removed as soon as they appear. Mulching helps keep the roots cool and moist. The foliage is an excellent insect-attracting plant, especially for hoverflies.
grow_tips: Earth up bulbs as they swell.
harvest: Harvest bulbs when they are about the size of a tennis ball, around 12–16 weeks from sowing, usually from August to October. Cut at ground level with a sharp knife, leaving the stump, which will often resprout fronds that can be used as a herb.
Harvest before bulbs get oversized and tough. Pick fronds all summer as a herb. Pull out any bolting plants, though the bulbs are still edible if small. Lift the remaining bulbs before hard frosts.
harvest_tips: Cut at ground level and leave the stump.
Pick fronds as a herb all summer.
Don’t let bulbs get too large.
use: Slice the bulb thinly and eat raw in salads with orange, olive oil and parmesan, or roast, braise or grill it, which makes it sweet and mellow. Fennel pairs well with fish, pork, and tomato dishes. The fronds make a pretty garnish and flavour sauces, soups and fish dishes.

Bulbs keep for one to two weeks in the fridge, in a bag. They can be blanched and frozen for cooking. Fennel seeds, harvested from bronze fennel, are good for tea or baking, but Florence fennel seed is less aromatic.
use_tips: Use the fronds as a garnish.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 20 to 30 cm apart, as crowded plants bolt, and avoid disturbing the roots.
Water regularly and consistently, as dry spells cause bolting, and keep fennel away from dill to avoid cross-pollination.
Earth up the swelling bulbs when they reach the size of an egg to blanch them and keep them tender.
Lift bulbs before hard frost and cut off the feathery tops for use as herbs.

preserving.how: Trim the fronds and keep bulbs wrapped in a bag in the salad drawer.
Slice, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze for cooked dishes.
Slice thinly and pickle in vinegar with fennel seeds and chilli.
Dry seed heads in a paper bag, and freeze the chopped fronds.

crops.name: French bean
varieties: Purple Teepee (purple pods, easy to spot)

types.name: Dwarf French beans
types.when: Sow May to July · Harvest July to October
types.note: Compact, no supports, and quick to crop. Good in pots.

types.name: Climbing French beans
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest July to October
types.note: Longer cropping season and bigger yields. Needs canes or netting.

types.name: Yellow and purple French beans
types.when: Sow May to July · Harvest July to October
types.note: Easy-to-spot pods; purple varieties turn green when cooked.

info: French beans are quick, slender, tender beans without strings, and they crop heavily from midsummer through to the first frosts. They are easier than runner beans and flower more reliably in hot weather, and dwarf types suit pots and small plots.

Pods come in green, yellow (wax), purple and speckled colours. Climbing varieties crop for longer and use vertical space, while dwarf varieties need no support. Many can also be left to mature and dried as haricot beans.
sow: Sow indoors from mid-April to May in individual pots, 5 cm deep, at 15–18°C, and plant out in late May to June once the frosts have gone. Alternatively, sow directly outdoors from mid-May to early July, 5 cm deep, 10–15 cm apart for dwarf types, in rows 45 cm apart.

Soil should be warm, well-drained and fertile. Give climbing types wigwams or rows of canes 1.8–2.4 m tall. Sow every three weeks for a continuous supply. Cold, wet soil rots seed, so wait for warmth if the weather is poor.
grow: Water regularly, especially during flowering and pod formation, and mulch to retain moisture. Feed with a tomato fertiliser every two weeks once flowers appear. Dwarf types may benefit from twiggy sticks for support, and from earthing up the stems.

Slugs love young plants, and blackfly can colonise the growing tips. Remove infested tips and use traps. Watering and mulching prevent flowers dropping. Avoid working among wet plants to avoid spreading bean rust and other diseases.
harvest: Begin harvesting dwarf varieties after 8–10 weeks, and climbers a little later. Pick pods when they are about 10–15 cm long, slim and snap cleanly, before the seeds inside swell. Pick every two or three days, as regular picking keeps plants producing for weeks.

Use two hands, one to hold the plant and the other to pick, or use scissors. Pods picked young are sweet and tender; overgrown pods become stringy. Harvest in the morning, and eat or process soon after picking.
harvest_tips: Use scissors to avoid damaging stems.
use: Top and tail the pods and steam or boil for 3–5 minutes until just tender but still crisp. Serve with butter, in salads, or with tomatoes, garlic and olive oil. They are good in stir-fries, stews and pasta, and they pickle well (dilly beans). Yellow and purple types are particularly attractive in salads, though purple pods turn green on cooking.

Fresh pods keep for up to a week in the fridge in a bag. To freeze, top and tail, blanch for 3 minutes, cool quickly, and freeze whole or sliced for up to a year. Leave a few pods to mature on the plant and dry the beans for winter use.

care.job: Plant out or sow after the last frost, and protect young plants from slugs.
Water regularly, especially during flowering, and mulch to keep roots cool.
Support climbing types on canes and dwarf types with short twigs or string.
Pick every two or three days while young and tender, as this keeps the plant cropping.
Clear plants after the first frost, leaving the roots in the soil.

preserving.how: Top and tail, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze on a tray before bagging.
Keep unwashed in a loose bag in the salad drawer.
Pack whole beans into jars with dill, garlic and hot spiced vinegar for dilly beans.
Ferment in 3% brine for a tangy, crunchy snack.
Leave pods on the plant until brown and rattling, then shell and dry the beans.

images.alt: A heap of freshly picked green French beans

crops.name: French tarragon
varieties: French tarragon (Artemisia dracunculus ‘Sativa’, the best flavour)
Mexican tarragon (Tagetes lucida, a tender substitute)

info: French tarragon has a delicate, aniseed-like flavour that is one of the great classics of French cooking, especially with chicken, fish and eggs. It never sets seed, so it must be bought as a plant or propagated by division or cuttings.

It likes a warm, sunny, sheltered position in well-drained soil, and dies down in winter. In cold or wet gardens, grow in a pot and bring under cover in winter. Avoid Russian tarragon, which is easier to grow but tastes bland and bitter.
sow: Buy a plant of French tarragon from a nursery (seed sold as tarragon is usually the inferior Russian type). Plant from April to June in full sun, in light, free-draining soil with added grit. Space 45–60 cm apart. In heavy soil, plant in a raised bed or pot.
In pots, use a loam-based compost with grit, at least 30 cm wide. Water in well until established. Tarragon can be propagated by dividing the roots in spring or taking cuttings in early summer.
sow_tips: Buy French tarragon as a plant.
Plant in a sheltered, sunny site.
grow: Water moderately in summer, but avoid wet soil, which rots the roots, particularly in winter. Pinch out the flowering stems to keep the plant producing leaves. Cut stems back to ground level in autumn once they die back, and mulch the crown with dry bracken or straw in cold areas.

Divide plants every 3 years in spring to keep them vigorous, as old plants lose flavour. In pots, move to a sheltered spot and keep dry over winter. Tarragon is relatively pest-free, though rust and powdery mildew can occur.
grow_tips: Keep the soil on the dry side.
harvest: Pick young shoots and leaves from May to September, snipping off the top 10–15 cm of stems regularly to encourage bushy growth. The flavour is best before the plant flowers in midsummer. Take more extensively in June and July, when the plant is growing fast.

For drying, which loses much of the flavour, cut stems in summer before flowering. It is better to preserve tarragon in vinegar or oil, or by freezing. Light picking in the first year allows the plant to establish.
harvest_tips: Pick lightly in the first year.
use: Tarragon is a key part of béarnaise sauce, and it complements chicken, fish, eggs, mushrooms, asparagus and creamy sauces. Add fresh leaves at the end of cooking, since long heating dulls the flavour. It is one of the fines herbes, with chervil, chives and parsley.

Fresh tarragon keeps for a week in the fridge wrapped in damp paper. Make tarragon vinegar by steeping sprigs in white wine vinegar for a few weeks. Freeze leaves whole or chopped in oil, which holds the flavour far better than drying.
use_tips: Add at the end of cooking.
Use in béarnaise and chicken dishes.

care.job: Cut back old stems and divide plants every three years in spring, as clumps lose flavour as they age.
Pinch out the growing tips to keep plants bushy and water pots lightly, as tarragon hates wet roots.
Cut stems back by half in late summer, drying or freezing the trimmings for winter use.
Protect French tarragon pots from winter wet by moving them under cover or into a sheltered position.

preserving.how: Freeze whole sprigs or chopped leaves in bags or ice cube trays. This keeps the flavour far better than drying.
Steep fresh sprigs in white wine vinegar for 2 weeks and strain. A classic for sauces.
Mix chopped leaves into butter for chicken and fish, and freeze in rolls.
Dry quickly in a warm place, though it loses much of its aroma.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open site

facts.Type: Hardy perennial bulb, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: 15 cm apart in rows 25–30 cm apart

types.name: Hardneck
types.when: Plant October to December · Harvest June to July
types.note: Stronger flavour and a flower stalk (scape) you can eat. Hardier, but stores only 4–6 months.

types.name: Softneck
types.when: Plant November to March · Harvest July to August
types.note: Milder flavour, plaits well, and stores for 8–12 months. Best for storing and for milder areas.

info: Garlic is one of the easiest crops to grow, and home-grown bulbs have a sweeter, fresher taste than supermarket ones. A single clove planted in autumn becomes a full bulb by early summer, and garlic is useful in the kitchen all year round.

There are two main types: hardneck varieties, which have a flowering stem and often better flavour but store for fewer months, and softneck varieties, which store for longer and can be plaited. Garlic needs a cold spell to form bulbs, so autumn planting is usually best in the UK.
sow: Plant cloves from October to November in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; heavy, wet soil makes them rot, so improve it with grit or plant on a ridge. Break up the bulbs just before planting and plant the largest outer cloves. Set each clove with the pointed end up, 2.5–5 cm deep, 15 cm apart in rows 25–30 cm apart.

In a cold or wet area, start cloves in modules in a cold frame or greenhouse in November and plant out in spring. February and March plantings are possible, but the bulbs will be smaller. Always buy certified garlic for planting, because supermarket bulbs may carry disease and are not suited to British growing conditions.
sow_tips: Plant certified, UK-grown garlic, not supermarket bulbs.
Plant with the pointed end up.
Use raised beds or ridges in heavy soil.
Net or fleece new plantings if birds pull out cloves.
grow: Garlic needs little attention. Keep the bed weed-free, as garlic is a poor competitor, and water in dry spells during spring until the bulbs start to swell in early summer, then stop. A feed of general fertiliser in spring helps strong growth, but avoid high nitrogen later in the season.

Hardnecks send up a flower stem in early summer; cut off the curly scape when it appears, which redirects energy to the bulb, and enjoy the scapes in cooking. The main problems are garlic rust, which appears as orange pustules on the leaves, and white rot. Wide spacing, good air flow and crop rotation help prevent both.
grow_tips: Remove hardneck scapes for bigger bulbs.
Stop watering once the leaves begin to yellow.
Rotate with a three- or four-year gap to prevent white rot.
harvest: Lift bulbs between June and August when the lower leaves have turned yellow and brown but the top few leaves are still green. Check a test bulb: it should be plump with firm, well-formed cloves. Loosen the soil with a fork and lift carefully without bruising.

Dry the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded place for two to three weeks, with the leaves still attached, hanging them in bundles or laying them on racks. Garlic dried in direct strong sun can scorch. They are ready to store when the outer skins are papery and the stems are dry.
harvest_tips: Harvest before the leaves die completely, as the skins split.
Dry in the shade, not direct sun.
Handle gently; bruised bulbs do not store.
Save the best bulb for planting next autumn.
use: Use garlic crushed, sliced or roasted whole until sweet and spreadable. Fresh, wet garlic eaten shortly after lifting is milder and juicier. Young green garlic can be used like spring onion in spring, and hardneck scapes are good in stir-fries, pesto and omelettes.

Store cured bulbs in a cool, dry, airy place at 5–15°C: softnecks keep for six to eight months, often longer if plaited into ropes, and hardnecks for three to five. Do not store in the fridge, which can trigger sprouting. Peeled cloves can be frozen or preserved in oil in the fridge for up to a week.
use_tips: Plait softneck garlic into ropes for attractive storage.
Roast whole bulbs at 180°C for about 40 minutes.
Use hardneck scapes in pesto and stir-fries.
Keep out of the fridge to prevent sprouting.

care.job: Keep the bed weed-free, as garlic hates competition, and water in dry spring weather.
Feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser in spring if growth looks pale.
Cut off the curled flower stems (scapes) from hardnecks and eat them, which sends energy to the bulb.
Stop watering once the leaves yellow, to allow the bulbs to dry.
Check autumn-planted cloves are firm in the soil, as frost can heave them up, and firm them back in.

preserving.how: Dry bulbs in a warm, airy place for 2–3 weeks, then hang in nets or plait and keep somewhere cool, dry and airy. Softneck types store longest.
Freeze whole peeled cloves, or chopped garlic in ice cube trays with a little water, in small portions.
Roast whole bulbs until soft and squeeze the cloves into a tub in the fridge.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator or low oven, then grind into garlic powder.
Pickle cloves in vinegar or ferment in brine. Do not store raw garlic in oil at room temperature, as there is a risk of botulism.

safety: Do not store raw garlic in oil at room temperature, as there is a risk of botulism.

images.alt: A handful of garlic cloves, split from the bulb and ready to plant
A single garlic clove held between two fingers, papery skin still on

facts.Sow: Mar–May direct; or plant any time

info: Garlic chives, or Chinese chives, have flat, grass-like leaves with a mild garlic flavour, and produce pretty white starry flowers in late summer. They are tougher and easier than garlic, grow in sun or part shade, and come back each year.
They are widely used in East Asian cooking and are excellent in pots. Cut flowers before the seed ripens, since they self-seed freely.
sow: Sow in March to May, 1 cm deep, in rows 20–25 cm apart, in any reasonably fertile soil, and thin to 20 cm. Seed germinates in 2–3 weeks. Clumps can be divided in spring or autumn.
Plants are happy in pots at least 20 cm wide. Water until established, then tolerate dry spells.
grow: Little care is needed. Water in dry spells and feed lightly in spring. Remove flower stems before seed sets if you want to avoid self-seeding. In autumn, cut the leaves back to 5 cm.
Divide clumps every 3–4 years to keep them vigorous. Onion fly, rust and slugs may occur but are rarely serious.
harvest: Cut leaves with scissors 5 cm above the ground, from about 8 weeks after sowing, taking about a third of the plant at a time. Plants regrow quickly. The white flower buds and flowers are edible and attractive.
Harvest regularly from spring to autumn. Plants die back in winter.

If you grow a patch, it is a good idea to cut the whole clump back to 5 cm in midsummer to refresh it; fresh young leaves will appear within two weeks. Cut flower stems for the vase as they last well and add a mild garlic scent.
harvest_tips: Take a third at a time.
use: Chop leaves into stir-fries, omelettes, dumplings, noodles, soups, salads, potatoes and dips. The flavour is delicate; add at the end of cooking. The flowers make a pretty garnish and an edible decoration.
Fresh leaves keep a week in the fridge. Freeze chopped in bags. Garlic chives lose flavour when dried.

Garlic chives are the classic filling for Chinese dumplings, mixed with minced pork and ginger. They are also delicious in scrambled eggs, stirred into hot noodles just before serving, or as a topping for congee and potato dishes.

care.job: Divide congested clumps in spring and replant, giving them plenty of water to re-establish.
Cut leaves to 5 cm above the soil regularly, as this encourages fresh, tender growth.
Deadhead flowers before they set seed, as garlic chives self-sow freely, or enjoy the star-shaped flowers in salads.
Cut back dead foliage and mulch the clumps lightly.

preserving.how: Snip and freeze in bags or ice cube trays. Drying loses most of the flavour.
Mix chopped leaves into softened butter and freeze in rolls.
Steep flowers or leaves in white wine vinegar for 2 weeks and strain.

info: Gherkins are small, prickly cucumbers bred for pickling, producing masses of crisp little fruits on vigorous plants that scramble over supports. They are easy, reliable and heavy croppers, even in cool summers.
Harvesting the fruit small and often keeps the plants productive. They make a fine crop for a trellis or a large pot.
sow: Sow indoors from April to May, seeds on edge, 1–2 cm deep, in pots at 20°C. Plant out in early June after hardening off, 45 cm apart, against a trellis or net in a sunny, sheltered spot.
Rich soil with compost gives the best crops.

Gherkins hate cold and wet. If the weather turns chilly after planting out, cover them with a cloche or fleece overnight, and keep slug pellets or wool pellets around young plants, because slugs can strip a seedling in a night. In a greenhouse, plants can go in earlier, in mid-May, and will crop a few weeks sooner.
grow: Water regularly and mulch. Feed weekly once fruiting. Tie in stems as they climb. Pinch out growing tips at 1.5 m.
Powdery mildew and slugs are the main problems. Pick regularly.

Gherkins are shallow-rooted and thirsty, so water deeply at the base every day or two in hot weather and never let the soil dry out and then flood, which makes fruits misshapen and bitter. A mulch of compost or straw keeps the roots cool. Picking the fruit while it is small is the most important job, since a single oversized gherkin left on the plant tells it to stop flowering.

Powdery mildew usually appears in late summer, particularly in dry weather and crowded plants. Growing vertically improves air circulation, and watering the soil rather than the leaves helps. Remove badly affected leaves and keep picking.
harvest: Pick gherkins at 5–8 cm long, every 2–3 days, from July to September. Cut with scissors. Regular picking keeps plants producing; oversized fruit stops further cropping.
Pick in the morning and pickle on the day for the crispest results.

Check plants every other day in July and August, lifting the leaves to find small fruits hidden below, as gherkins hide well among the foliage. A good plant will give you a handful of fruit several times a week, which is just the right amount to make a jar of pickles at a time. You can keep a bowl of salted cucumbers in the fridge until you have enough to fill a jar.
use: Pickle gherkins in vinegar with dill, garlic, mustard seeds and peppercorns, or ferment in brine. Use fresh in salads and sandwiches. Salt first to draw out moisture for crisp pickles.
Pickles keep for a year in sterilised jars. Fresh gherkins keep for 1 week in the fridge.

For quick refrigerator pickles, pack the gherkins into a jar with dill, garlic and mustard seeds, cover with a warm brine of vinegar, water, salt and a little sugar, and leave for a week. For longer storage, process in sterilised jars. Sliced gherkins are good in tartare sauce, potato salad and sandwiches.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost in a sunny, sheltered spot and give climbing types a support to scramble up.
Water regularly, as dry soil causes bitter, misshapen fruit, and feed every two weeks with a tomato feed.
Pick small gherkins regularly, as leaving fruit to grow stops the plant producing more.
Watch for powdery mildew on the leaves and remove affected foliage, keeping plants well watered and spaced.

preserving.how: Pack small gherkins whole into jars with dill, garlic, mustard seed and hot vinegar brine.
Ferment in a 3–5% salt brine with dill and garlic for sour half-sours and full sours.
Keep fresh gherkins in a bag in the salad drawer and pickle within a few days.
Chop and cook into sweet relish with onions, sugar and vinegar.

crops.name: Globe artichoke

facts.Sow: Seed Mar–Apr indoors, or plant offsets Mar–Apr

varieties: Imperial Star (flowers in the first year from seed)

info: Globe artichokes are handsome architectural perennials with silvery, deeply cut leaves and large edible flower buds. They are as ornamental as any border plant and crop for around four to five years before needing replacing.

They prefer sun, shelter and free-draining soil, and need winter protection in cold areas. The buds are harvested before they open, and any left to flower produce spectacular purple thistle-like blooms loved by bees.
sow: Sow seed in March to April, 1 cm deep, in individual pots at 15–18°C. Seedlings vary in quality, so select the best. Plant out in May to June, 90 cm to 1 m apart, in a sunny, sheltered spot with deep, fertile, well-drained soil. Alternatively plant rooted offsets (suckers) from a friend or nursery in spring.

Dig in plenty of compost before planting and water in well. Plants grown from seed will crop later than those from offsets. Offsets from named varieties give a more reliable crop and are the usual method for propagation.
sow_tips: Offsets give a more reliable crop than seed.
Pick a sunny, sheltered, free-draining site.
grow: Water in dry weather and mulch each spring with compost or manure, and feed with a general fertiliser. In late autumn, cut back leaves and mulch the crown thickly with straw or bracken for winter protection, particularly in cold areas.

Blackfly can colonise the buds and stems, and slugs eat young shoots. Divide plants every three to four years in spring, taking healthy offsets with roots and replanting them. Renewing the planting regularly keeps up the quality of buds.
harvest: Cut the large central bud first, while it is tight and plump, before the scales begin to open, usually from June to July. Use a sharp knife and leave a short stalk. Side buds follow over the next few weeks, and are smaller but just as tasty.
Pick regularly to encourage more buds. Leave a few to open into purple flowers if you wish, as bees love them. After harvest, cut down the flower stalks.
harvest_tips: Let one flower for the bees.
use: Boil or steam whole globes for 30–40 minutes until a leaf pulls away easily, then eat the soft base of each leaf dipped in melted butter or vinaigrette, and finish with the tender heart. Baby artichokes can be trimmed, halved and roasted, grilled or braised, or eaten raw in salads.
Fresh buds keep for a few days in the fridge in a bag. The hearts can be cooked, then frozen or preserved in oil. Dip the cut hearts in lemon water to avoid browning.
use_tips: Dip leaves in butter or vinaigrette.

care.job: Mulch with well-rotted compost in spring, remove any frost-damaged growth and feed generously, as artichokes are hungry plants.
Water in dry weather and remove side shoots (suckers) to leave two or three of the strongest on each plant.
Cut the central bud when plump and tight before the scales open, and cut the smaller side buds after.
Cut stems to the ground after cropping and protect crowns with a thick mulch or straw for winter.

preserving.how: Keep whole, unwashed heads in a bag in the salad drawer.
Trim to the hearts, simmer in lemon water for 5 minutes, cool and freeze in bags.
Simmer hearts in vinegar and water, pack into a jar with herbs and cover with oil. Keep it in the fridge and use within a week, as vegetables in oil can carry a botulism risk.
Pickle in a vinegar brine in sterilised jars for longer keeping.

safety: Keep it in the fridge and use within a week, as vegetables in oil can carry a botulism risk.

facts.Planting depth: Same depth as in the nursery

types.name: Cooking gooseberries
types.when: Pick late May to June, while hard and green
types.note: Tart and green, best cooked with sugar in pies, fools and sauces.

types.name: Dessert gooseberries
types.when: Pick July, when soft and coloured
types.note: Left to ripen fully, they become sweet and juicy enough to eat raw.

info: Gooseberries are one of the first soft fruits of the year, from late May, and are tough, hardy and adaptable plants, tolerating shade and cold. Green cooking varieties are tart and wonderful in puddings, while red and yellow dessert types are sweet enough to eat raw.

Bushes are thorny, which makes picking a challenge, but also deters wildlife and works as a barrier. They can be trained as standards or cordons, or grown in large pots, and they rarely suffer from frost.
sow: Plant bare-root bushes between November and March in a sunny or lightly shaded position in fertile, well-drained soil. Gooseberries dislike very wet or very dry soil. Space bushes 1.5 m apart, and plant at the same depth as in the nursery, leaving a clear ‘leg’ of 15 cm.

After planting, cut back stems by half, to an outward-facing bud. Mulch with well-rotted compost and keep weeds down. Choose mildew-resistant varieties, since American gooseberry mildew is the main disease.
sow_tips: Cut stems by half at planting.
grow: Mulch each spring and water in dry spells, particularly when the fruit is forming. Prune in winter to an open, goblet shape, cutting back new growth by half and side shoots to two buds. Thin the fruits in May: picking every other berry as a ‘thinning’ gives larger berries and the thinnings are good to cook.

Gooseberry sawfly caterpillars can strip a bush in a few days in spring, so check regularly from April and remove by hand. American gooseberry mildew leaves white powder on fruits and shoots; prune out affected tips and keep the bush open to air flow.
grow_tips: Thin berries in May and use the thinnings.
harvest: Pick cooking gooseberries when they are hard and green, from late May, when still tart, and later pick the rest to ripen for sweetening. Dessert types are ready in July when soft and coloured. Wear thick gloves and long sleeves, and use scissors for awkward berries.
Pick in two goes: thin the bush in May for cooking, and leave the rest to ripen for eating raw. Berries keep on the bush for a while, but birds and wasps may take them.
harvest_tips: Pick half green and leave half to ripen.
Net if birds are a problem.
use: Cook green gooseberries with sugar into crumbles, pies, fools, sauces (classic with mackerel), chutneys and jam. A sprig of elderflower in the pan adds a beautiful muscat flavour. Ripe dessert types are lovely raw, in fruit salads and with cream.

Fresh gooseberries keep for a week in the fridge. They freeze well: top and tail, freeze on a tray and bag for up to a year, and cook from frozen. Gooseberry jam and chutney are good for storing a glut.
use_tips: Freeze on a tray and bag.
Serve the sauce with oily fish.

care.job: Prune in late winter, removing crossing branches and shortening the side shoots, to an open goblet shape that lets air in.
Mulch with compost and feed with a potash-rich fertiliser, and keep weeds away from the base.
Check for gooseberry sawfly caterpillars, which can strip a bush in days. Pick them off by hand as soon as you spot holes.
Thin the crop in early summer, eating the first fruit green and leaving the rest to ripen sweet.
Net against birds, water in dry weather and look out for American gooseberry mildew, a white powder on the fruit and shoots.

preserving.how: Top and tail, then freeze on a tray and bag. They keep their tartness for pies and fools.
Keep firm, under-ripe berries in a covered container.
High in pectin, so they set well. Chutney is excellent with cheese and pork.
Stew with sugar into a sauce for mackerel, or into a cordial with elderflower.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

types.name: Outdoor dessert grapes
types.when: Harvest September to October
types.note: Hardy, disease-resistant varieties that ripen on a sunny wall or pergola without any heat.

types.name: Outdoor wine grapes
types.when: Harvest late September to October
types.note: Early-ripening varieties for juice or home winemaking, hardy enough for most of southern Britain.

types.name: Greenhouse grapes
types.when: Harvest August to October
types.note: The finest dessert flavour, but they need a heated or sunny greenhouse and careful pruning.

info: Grapes grow well in Britain on a sunny wall, over a pergola, or in a greenhouse. Modern disease-resistant varieties bred for cool climates, such as Solaris, Regent and Phoenix, produce excellent dessert or wine grapes outdoors.
Vines are decorative, covering walls with lovely foliage and autumn colour, and plants are long-lived. Greenhouse varieties such as Black Hamburg give sweeter dessert grapes.
sow: Plant a pot-grown vine between November and March in a sunny, sheltered, south-facing position with fertile, well-drained soil. Dig in compost and, on acid soils, add some lime. Space plants 1.2–2 m apart.
Provide a sturdy support: horizontal wires 30 cm apart on a wall or fence, or a pergola. Cut the plant to 2–3 buds after planting. Mulch with compost.
grow: Train a main stem (rod) up the support, and in winter prune side shoots (spurs) back to 2 buds. In summer, tie in new shoots and pinch out the tips beyond 2 leaves past the last flower cluster. Thin fruit bunches to improve grape size.

Water in dry spells in the first years, then plants mostly look after themselves. Mildew and botrytis can be a problem in wet summers; keep air flowing by removing leaves around the fruit. Prune in winter before the sap rises, in December to January.
harvest: Taste grapes before picking; they should be sweet and fully coloured, with brown pips. Outdoor grapes ripen in September to October. Cut whole bunches with scissors, and pick on a dry day.
Net the fruit against birds and wasps. Leave late grapes on the vine as long as possible, until frost threatens.

Wasps are a particular nuisance in September, so bag the ripening bunches in muslin or fine netting from late August. If birds are a problem, cover the entire vine with netting. Unripe bunches that fail to sweeten can still be used for verjuice.
use: Eat dessert grapes fresh, serve with cheese, or make juice, jelly and jam. Wine grapes can be pressed and fermented; a modest vine yields several bottles. Grape leaves can be pickled for dolmades.
Grapes keep for 1–2 weeks in the fridge. Freeze whole grapes as a snack. Juice can be pasteurised and bottled.

Dessert grapes are excellent baked with roast chicken or pork, in focaccia, or in a sticky chutney. To make juice, crush the grapes in a bowl, simmer gently for 10 minutes and strain through muslin. Grape leaves are traditional for stuffing with rice and herbs.

care.job: Prune vines hard in the dormant season, cutting side shoots back to one or two buds, but never later than February or they will bleed sap.
Tie in new shoots as they grow and pinch out the tips beyond the last flower cluster.
Thin bunches by snipping out the middle berries with scissors, giving the rest room to swell.
Water well in dry weather, feed with a high-potash feed and ventilate greenhouse vines to avoid mildew.
Remove some leaves to expose ripening bunches to the sun, and net outdoor crops against birds and wasps.

preserving.how: Keep bunches unwashed in a bag in the fridge. Remove any split or mouldy fruit.
Freeze whole on a tray for eating as a cold snack, or in smoothies.
Press and bottle juice, or make into jelly. Strain through muslin.
Dry seedless varieties in a dehydrator or low oven into raisins.
Ferment the surplus into wine, if you wish.

crops.name: Hardy kiwi
crops.sun_text: Full sun to light shade; sheltered

info: Hardy kiwi, or kiwi berry, is a vigorous climber producing grape-sized, smooth-skinned fruits that are sweet and can be eaten whole, with no peeling. Unlike the supermarket kiwi, it tolerates UK winters, down to about -25°C.
Most varieties need a male and a female plant, though self-fertile ones such as Issai exist. They need a strong support and annual pruning. Fruit is packed with vitamin C.
sow: Plant in a sunny, sheltered spot with fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Provide a strong support, such as a pergola or wires on a wall. Plant a male for every 5–6 females, unless using self-fertile Issai.
Space 3 m apart. Protect young shoots from late frosts with fleece. Mulch around the roots with compost and water well.
sow_tips: Plant a male for the females.
grow: Train a main stem and side branches onto wires. In winter, prune side shoots to 3–5 buds beyond the last fruit; in summer, cut back extra growth. Overgrown plants become tangled, so prune regularly.
Water in dry spells and feed in spring. Cats love scratching young plants, so protect them with a wire cage. Few pests trouble hardy kiwi.
harvest: Fruit is ready in October when it softens slightly and the seeds turn dark. Pick when slightly firm and ripen indoors for a few days. Pick all before hard frosts.
Fruits come in clusters and ripen at different times, so pick over several weeks.

Hardy kiwis are very productive once mature, and a single established vine can crop several kilos. Fruits ripen unevenly along a branch, so check often. They get sweeter if left a day or two on a windowsill after picking and taste best when they just yield to gentle pressure.
use: Eat the whole fruit fresh, skin and all, or add to fruit salads, smoothies, tarts and jams. Their sweet, tangy flavour is like a small kiwi. Slice to garnish desserts.
Ripe fruit keeps 1–2 weeks in the fridge. Unripe fruit stores for 2–3 months in a cool place. Freeze whole.

care.job: Prune in late winter to remove dead and crossing growth, and tie in shoots to wires or trellis.
Summer prune by cutting side shoots back to five or six leaves beyond the last fruit, and cut away unwanted growth.
Water well in dry weather and mulch around the roots, keeping it away from the stem.
Pick fruit when it is slightly soft and sweet, and net against birds if necessary.

preserving.how: Ripen on the vine or on a windowsill, then eat or refrigerate.
Pick slightly under-ripe in autumn and keep in a cool, frost-free place to ripen slowly.
Freeze whole berries on a tray and eat as a cold treat or in smoothies.
Cook with sugar and lemon juice, and pot into sterilised jars.

facts.Planting depth: Root cuttings 5 cm deep, at an angle

info: Horseradish is a tough, fiery root that will thrive for years with almost no care. Its pungent flavour is the classic accompaniment to roast beef, smoked fish and beetroot, and homegrown roots are far stronger than the jarred sauce.
It is so vigorous that it can become a weed: any bit of root left in the ground will regrow, so confine it to a large pot, a bed of its own, or a bottomless bucket sunk into soil.
sow: Plant root cuttings (called thongs) in February to April, 20–30 cm long and pencil-thick, at a slight angle with the top 5 cm below the surface. Space 45 cm apart in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil in sun or part shade.

To keep it under control, plant in a bottomless bucket, a tall pot, or a bed edged with deep paving. Cut the top of the thong flat and the bottom at a slant, so you always know which end is up. Water until established.
sow_tips: Contain it so it can't spread.
Mark the flat top and slanted bottom.
grow: Horseradish needs little attention. Water in dry spells, and mulch with compost to keep the roots moist and tender. Remove any flower stalks so that the plant puts its energy into the roots.

Leaves are sometimes holed by flea beetle or caterpillars, which does no harm. White blister fungus can mark the leaves. To improve root size, you can thin the crown to the strongest shoots in early summer.
grow_tips: Never let roots escape into the garden.
harvest: Dig roots from October to March, when the foliage has died back and the roots are at their strongest, once the first frosts have sweetened them. Lift with a fork, taking care to get out as much as possible; leave a few thin pieces to regrow, or replant thongs in spring.
Roots from the first year are small; the largest and hottest come from plants in their second year. Rake the soil fully to remove all fragments if you want to clear the bed.
harvest_tips: Clear all root fragments if you move it.
use: Wash, peel and grate the roots finely, ideally outside or near an open window, since the fumes are powerful. Mix with a little vinegar, cream or crème fraîche to make horseradish sauce, which is superb with roast beef, smoked mackerel, ham and beetroot.

Whole roots keep for several weeks in the fridge, or in damp sand in a cool shed. Grated horseradish in vinegar keeps for a few months in a jar in the fridge, though the heat fades. Freeze grated root in small portions.
use_tips: Grate outside; the fumes are strong.
Add vinegar quickly to fix the heat.

care.job: Weed around the plants and mulch with compost, and contain the roots in a bed or large pot, as horseradish spreads.
Water in dry spells to keep the roots tender, and remove any flower stems that form.
Lift roots after the foliage dies back and replant a few pencil-thick pieces to keep a supply going.

preserving.how: Lift roots in autumn and pack in damp sand in a cool, frost-free shed.
Wrap whole roots in a bag in the fridge.
Grate root, mix with a little vinegar and salt and jar. The flavour fades over a few months.
Freeze grated or whole peeled roots and grate straight from frozen.

crops.name: Hyssop
varieties: Rock hyssop (Hyssopus officinalis subsp. aristatus, compact)

info: Hyssop is a bushy, aromatic evergreen with spikes of blue, pink or white flowers from midsummer, adored by bees and butterflies. The leaves have a minty, slightly bitter flavour and are a traditional herb in old cookery.
It is hardy, drought-tolerant and long-lived, making a neat low hedge or edging for a herb or vegetable bed. Cabbage white butterflies are said to be deterred by its scent.
sow: Sow seed on the surface of seed compost in spring at 15–18°C, and plant seedlings 30–45 cm apart in June. It is quicker to buy plants or take softwood cuttings in early summer. Plant in full sun in free-draining soil, ideally poor and alkaline.
Add grit to heavy soils. Water until established, then plants need little care. Use as an edging 30 cm apart.
sow_tips: Buy a plant or take cuttings.
grow: Trim in spring to keep the plant bushy, cutting back to about 10 cm above the ground, and again lightly after flowering. Don’t cut into old wood. Water only in prolonged drought and don’t feed.
Replace plants every 5–6 years when they get woody. Hyssop is generally free of pests and diseases, though wet winter soils cause root rot.
harvest: Pick young leaves and shoot tips from spring through to autumn, cutting stems with scissors. The flavour is strongest just before flowering. Flowers are edible and attractive in salads.
For drying, cut stems before flowering and hang in a warm, airy spot.

Hyssop flowers are among the best for attracting bees, so only take half the flower spikes and leave the rest for the pollinators. Leaves can be harvested year-round in mild winters, though the flavour is milder than in summer.
use: Use sparingly, as the flavour is strong and slightly bitter: chop into salads, soups, stews, game, stuffings and fruit dishes. Add to herbal tea, or to liqueurs. The flowers are a pretty garnish.
Dried leaves keep a year in a jar. Hyssop honey from the bees that visit it is excellent. Avoid in pregnancy and with epilepsy.

care.job: Trim plants lightly in spring and remove any winter-damaged growth.
Deadhead to prolong flowering, or let the blue flowers feed bees and butterflies, and water pots sparingly.
Cut plants back by about a third after flowering to keep them tidy and prevent them becoming woody.

preserving.how: Hang small bunches in a warm, airy place, then crumble into jars for teas and cooking.
Freeze chopped leaves in ice cube trays.
Steep in honey or syrup for a minty, soothing flavour.
preserving.keeps: Honey: 6 months; syrup: 1 month in the fridge

crops.name: Jerusalem artichoke

facts.Type: Hardy perennial sunflower grown for its tubers
facts.Spacing: 30–40 cm apart in rows 90 cm apart

varieties: Fuseau (long, smooth tubers that are easy to clean)

info: Despite the name, Jerusalem artichokes are neither from Jerusalem nor artichokes: they are the knobbly tubers of a tall native North American sunflower. They are very hardy, almost impossible to kill, and give a heavy crop of sweet, nutty tubers from autumn to early spring with almost no attention.

The plants grow 2–3 m tall and make an excellent windbreak or summer screen. The main caution is that they spread: every tuber left in the ground regrows, so plant them in a spot where this is welcome, such as a corner of the plot or a large raised bed.
sow: Plant tubers from February to April in any reasonably fertile soil, in sun or part shade. You can buy tubers from garden centres or use ones from a greengrocer, as they are not prone to the same diseases as potatoes. Plant them 10–15 cm deep and 30–40 cm apart, in rows about 90 cm apart.

Because they spread vigorously, consider planting in a contained area such as a large bottomless pot or a bed edged with a barrier sunk 30 cm deep. Choose a site where tall plants will not shade neighbouring crops, such as the north side of the plot, or use the plants as a windbreak.
sow_tips: Plant at the north end of the plot so they do not shade other crops.
Even small tuber pieces will grow.
Edge with a buried barrier if you need to limit spread.
grow: Jerusalem artichokes need almost no care. Water in the first few weeks and during very dry spells, and earth up the stems lightly when they reach 30 cm to improve stability. Tall plants can blow over in strong winds, so cut them back to about 1.5 m in midsummer or support them with stakes and string.

Cut off any flower buds if you want to maximise the tuber crop, though the bright yellow blooms are attractive and loved by pollinators. Slugs eat tubers, and sclerotinia and powdery mildew can affect the stems in damp summers, but severe problems are rare.
grow_tips: Cut stems to 1.5 m in midsummer to prevent wind rock.
Remove flower buds for a bigger crop.
Grow them on their own, as they are very competitive.
harvest: When the foliage has turned brown and died back in October or November, cut the stems down to about 15 cm and lift the tubers with a fork as you need them. They store best in the ground and have thin skins that dry quickly once lifted. Dig carefully, as the knobbly tubers snap easily.

Harvest through to March, then lift all the tubers so the bed does not become overrun, saving some of the smoothest ones to replant. Any small pieces left in the soil will re-sprout, so check carefully if you want to move or clear the bed.
harvest_tips: Leave tubers in the ground until needed.
Cut stems to 15 cm and use them as markers.
Pick out every piece if you want to stop regrowth.
Save your best tubers for replanting.
use: The tubers have a creamy, nutty flavour a bit like artichoke hearts. Scrub, peel if you wish, and use in soups, roasts, gratins or purées, or slice raw into salads. They are rich in inulin, which can cause wind for some people, so start with small portions and cook them thoroughly. Adding a little lemon juice keeps the cut flesh from browning.

Tubers shrivel quickly once lifted, so dig only what you need. Unwashed tubers keep for one to two weeks in a bag in the fridge, or you can store scrubbed tubers in slightly damp sand. Cooked purée and soup freeze very well.
use_tips: Start with small portions, as inulin can cause wind.
Roast with olive oil, garlic and thyme at 200°C.
Add lemon juice when cutting to prevent browning.
Make a velvety soup with stock and cream.

care.job: Plant tubers about 10 cm deep and 30 cm apart, in a spot where tall plants will not shade other crops.
Stake or cut back plants to 1.5 m in June to reduce wind rock, and water in dry spells.
Cut stems to about 30 cm after leaves turn brown, leaving the stumps to mark the plants.
Lift tubers as needed over winter and be sure to remove every piece, as even small tubers will regrow next year.

preserving.how: Tubers store best in the soil, so lift as you need them from autumn until the plants regrow in spring.
Keep unwashed tubers in a bag in the salad drawer. They go limp quickly once out of the soil.
Make into soup or a purée and freeze in tubs.
Slice and pickle in spiced vinegar. Crisp and good with cheese.

crops.name: Kale

facts.Type: Hardy biennial leaf vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Apr–Jul in trays or a seedbed

varieties: Cavolo Nero (also called Nero di Toscana)

types.name: Curly kale
types.when: Sow April to June · Harvest October to March
types.note: The hardiest group, with frilly leaves that sweeten after frost.

types.name: Cavolo nero (Tuscan kale)
types.when: Sow April to June · Harvest October to March
types.note: Dark, savoury, puckered leaves with a deeper flavour. Superb braised.

types.name: Red and Russian kale
types.when: Sow April to July · Harvest August to March
types.note: Tender, flat or frilly leaves in red and purple. Good as baby leaf too.

info: Kale is among the hardiest and most productive winter crops, giving fresh leaves from autumn to spring when little else is available. It tolerates cold, partial shade and poor soil, and the flavour is even sweeter after frost.

It is a cut-and-come-again plant, so you can pick leaves for months from the same plant. There are curly, flat and ruffled types, with colours from deep blue-green to purple, making it attractive enough to grow in ornamental borders and pots.
sow: Sow in April to July in modules, trays or a seedbed, 1–2 cm deep, and thin or prick out as they grow. Transplant when plants are about 10–15 cm tall, usually four to six weeks after sowing, spacing them 45–60 cm apart. In small gardens, sow thickly and pick the young seedlings as baby leaf.

Choose a position in full sun or light shade with fertile, well-drained, firm soil. Plant deeply and firm in, and water in well. Kale also grows well in large containers of at least 30 cm. Cover with netting from planting to protect from pigeons and butterflies.
sow_tips: Plant firmly into soil that has not been dug recently.
Sow thickly for baby kale leaves.
Use pots at least 30 cm wide on a balcony.
grow: Water well in dry weather and mulch to hold in moisture. Kale does not need much feeding, but a nitrogen-rich fertiliser a month after planting encourages leaf growth. Stake tall varieties in exposed sites, and earth up the stems in autumn to stop the wind rocking them.

Cabbage white caterpillars, whitefly and aphids can be a problem, along with pigeons, so net the plants and check regularly under the leaves. Clubroot may be a problem in acid soil; liming and rotation help. Remove yellowing leaves, which can harbour disease.
grow_tips: Check under leaves for butterfly eggs and squash them.
Stake tall varieties in windy areas.
Remove old yellow leaves to keep plants healthy.
Lime acid soil and rotate crops.
harvest: Pick the lower leaves when they are 15–20 cm long, taking a few from each plant and leaving the crown at the top to keep producing. Pick young, tender leaves often and avoid stripping a plant, which weakens it. Remove any flower buds in spring to extend the harvest.

Harvest continues from autumn to March, with the flavour improving after frost. In spring, the plants send up flower shoots that can be picked like sprouting broccoli, and the yellow flowers are edible. Pull out the plants once the shoots go over.
harvest_tips: Take a few leaves from each plant rather than stripping one.
Pick after frost for the sweetest flavour.
Harvest the spring flower shoots too.
Remove flower buds to prolong leaf picking.
use: Strip the leaves from the tough stems and add to soups, stews and curries, sauté with garlic and chilli, bake into crispy kale crisps, or massage with oil and lemon for a raw salad. Cavolo nero is the classic choice for Italian ribollita, and young leaves can go into smoothies.

Kale keeps in a bag in the fridge for four to five days. It freezes very well: wash, strip from the stalks, blanch for three minutes, drain thoroughly and freeze in portions. Bunches can be stood in water in the fridge to stay fresh for longer.
use_tips: Massage raw kale with oil and lemon to soften it.
Bake at 150°C with oil for crisps.
Remove the tough central stalks before cooking.

care.job: Net against pigeons and cabbage white butterflies, and check the undersides of leaves for yellow eggs and caterpillars.
Water young plants in dry spells and firm the soil around the base so the stems stay stable.
Remove yellowing lower leaves, and stake tall plants against winter winds.
Keep netting in place against pigeons, which can strip a plant over winter.
Pick the young flowering shoots in spring, then pull up plants once they bolt.

preserving.how: Kale is very hardy and tastes better after frost, so pick as needed all winter.
Strip from the stalks, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze in bags.
Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Make kale crisps in a low oven or dehydrator, or crumble dried leaves into soups.
Ferment shredded leaves with salt, similar to sauerkraut.

facts.Type: Hardy biennial, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 15–20 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

info: Kohlrabi looks like an alien: a swollen, bulb-shaped stem that grows above the ground, with the flavour of a sweet, mild turnip crossed with broccoli stalk. It is one of the quickest and least troublesome brassicas, and gives fresh crisp crops from early summer through autumn.
It is ideal for small plots, as it grows fast, takes up little room and is often untroubled by pigeons and caterpillars. The stems are best eaten young, at tennis-ball size, before they become woody.
sow: Sow thinly outdoors from March to August in shallow drills 1–2 cm deep, in rows 30 cm apart, in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in sun or light shade. Sow a short row every two or three weeks for a continuous supply. March sowings under fleece or cloche are possible for an early crop.

Thin seedlings to 15–20 cm apart once they have a few true leaves. Kohlrabi can also be started in modules and transplanted at 3–4 weeks, taking care not to bury the stem. Late sowings in August give crops in October and November.
sow_tips: Sow short rows every two or three weeks.
Thin early to give each plant room.
Do not bury the swelling stem when transplanting.
grow: Keep the plants growing steadily: water regularly, as slow or stressed growth leads to woody, fibrous stems, and mulch to keep the soil cool and moist. Hoe between plants carefully because the roots are shallow. They rarely need feeding in fertile soil.

Flea beetle on young seedlings can be prevented by fine mesh or by keeping the soil moist. Cabbage root fly, caterpillars and clubroot may also appear, as with other brassicas. Rotate with other brassicas, and lime acid soils.
grow_tips: Use fine mesh against flea beetle.
Mulch to keep soil cool and moist.
harvest: Harvest kohlrabi when the stems are about the size of a golf ball to a tennis ball, around 5–7 cm across, usually 8–10 weeks after sowing. Larger ones can turn woody and fibrous, apart from giant varieties such as Superschmelz. Pull or cut at the base with a knife.

Pick regularly as plants ripen, because the swollen stems can quickly become tough in warm weather. Cut off the leaves, which are edible and can be cooked like cabbage. Late-sown crops can stand in the ground into November.
harvest_tips: Pick at golf-ball to tennis-ball size.
Eat the young leaves as greens.
Lift late crops before hard frosts.
use: Peel off the tough skin and eat kohlrabi raw, grated into slaws or sliced thinly with lemon and salt for a crunchy snack. It can also be steamed, roasted, stir-fried, mashed or added to soups and curries, where it tastes like a sweet turnip. Young leaves can be sautéed like spring greens.

Trimmed stems keep for two to three weeks in the fridge in a bag. Peeled, cubed kohlrabi can be blanched for two minutes and frozen. Do not wash until needed, and keep it away from strong-smelling foods.
use_tips: Peel thickly, as the skin is tough.
Slice thinly raw with lemon, salt and olive oil.
Cook the young leaves like cabbage.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 15 to 20 cm apart and water evenly, as irregular watering makes bulbs woody and split.
Cover with mesh against flea beetle and cabbage root fly, and keep weeds down around the shallow roots.
Harvest bulbs at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best flavour and tenderness.

preserving.how: Remove the leaves and keep the bulbs in a bag in the salad drawer.
Store trimmed bulbs in damp sand in a cool, frost-free shed.
Peel, cube and blanch for 2 minutes, cool and freeze.
Slice or grate for pickle or sauerkraut.

info: Komatsuna, or Japanese mustard spinach, is a fast, vigorous leaf crop with glossy green leaves and a mild, spinach-like flavour with a gentle mustard edge. It tolerates both heat and cold, and bolts much less than spinach.
It is one of the easiest leaf crops to grow, giving repeated cuts over months. Use it as a baby leaf, or let plants grow to full size for cooking.
sow: Sow from March to September, 1 cm deep, in rows 20–30 cm apart, or scatter thickly. Thin to 15–20 cm for full-sized plants, or leave closer for baby leaf. Seeds germinate in a few days.
In a polytunnel or under a cloche, komatsuna can be sown in autumn for winter leaves. Fine mesh at sowing helps keep flea beetle off. Sow successionally every 2–3 weeks.
sow_tips: Sow from spring to early autumn.
grow: Keep the soil moist and weed-free. It will bolt in drought, so water in dry spells. Feed lightly if growth is slow.
Flea beetle, slugs and aphids can be problems, and caterpillars may attack in summer. Cover with fine mesh. Rotate with other brassicas.

Komatsuna is a quick, forgiving crop. A fortnightly sowing keeps the table supplied. For tender leaves, grow it quickly with plenty of water and avoid letting it get too stressed. The plants recover well from cutting, giving three or four harvests before they flower.
harvest: Cut baby leaves at 10–15 cm, from three to four weeks, or whole plants at 6–8 weeks. Cut 2.5 cm above the base for regrowth, up to three times. Pick outer leaves for a longer harvest.
Harvest before the flower stalks appear. The flower buds are edible like broccoli raab.
harvest_tips: Cut above the base for regrowth.
use: Cook komatsuna as you would spinach: stir-fry, steam, or add to soups, noodles, curries and omelettes. Young leaves are good raw in salads. It requires no special preparation, and stems cook as fast as leaves.
Keeps for 3–4 days in the fridge. Blanch for 1 minute and freeze in portions for winter cooking.

Komatsuna doesn't turn bitter or stringy, and the thick, juicy stems are as good as the leaves. Try it in a miso soup, with garlic and soy sauce in a stir-fry, or lightly steamed with sesame oil. The flowers in spring are lovely in salads.

care.job: Water regularly and cover with fine mesh against flea beetles, which can pepper the leaves with holes.
Harvest leaves young and often, as this keeps the plant productive and prevents bolting.
Protect plants with a cloche for winter leaves and sow a fresh batch every few weeks.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Blanch for 1–2 minutes, squeeze out the water and freeze in portions.
Ferment leaves in brine, as is done with similar greens in Asian cooking.
Cook into soup or stir-fry bases and freeze in tubs.

facts.Spacing: Thin to 10 cm, or sow thickly for baby leaf

info: Lamb’s lettuce, also called corn salad or mâche, is a very hardy, low-growing salad plant that provides mild, nutty rosettes of leaves right through the winter, when there is little fresh salad around. It is one of the best crops for a cold frame, pot or sheltered border.

The compact, spoon-shaped leaves are tender and delicious, and plants will stand frost, snow and shade. Sow it in late summer and autumn, and you will have pickings from October until spring, when it flowers and goes to seed.
sow: Sow from August to October, scattering seed thinly or in rows 10–15 cm apart, 1 cm deep, into fine, firm, moisture-retentive soil. Seed can be slow to germinate in warm soil above 20°C, so sow in a shaded spot in late summer and keep it watered. Seedlings usually appear in 10–14 days.

In cold regions, sow in pots or trays and keep in a cold frame, unheated greenhouse or under a cloche for an easy winter crop. You can sow again in March and April for a spring crop, although it bolts faster in warmth. Thin seedlings to 10 cm for larger rosettes.
sow_tips: Sow in late summer in the shade, as heat stops germination.
Scatter-sow into a pot for winter leaves.
Cover with a cloche in the coldest areas.
grow: Lamb’s lettuce needs very little care. Keep the soil moist while seeds germinate and keep weeds out, as the plants are small and easily overcome. Water occasionally in dry spells. No feeding is needed in reasonably fertile soil.

Slugs can damage seedlings, so check regularly on damp nights. In very wet winters, grey mould (botrytis) can affect plants, so remove any yellowing leaves and keep the foliage dry in a covered position. Established plants survive snow and hard frost.
grow_tips: Weed carefully, as plants are small.
harvest: Pick whole rosettes when they are 5–8 cm across, from October onward, by cutting just above the root with scissors. You can also pick individual outer leaves, leaving the plant to continue. Harvest regularly, as plants flower from March.

Plants grow slowly in winter, so harvest a few at a time from each row rather than clearing one patch. Spring sowings are ready in about eight weeks. The small pale blue flowers are edible, and plants will self-seed if you let one or two flower.
harvest_tips: Cut whole rosettes just above the root.
Take a few from each row.
Pick often in spring before bolting.
Let a few flower to self-seed.
use: Lamb’s lettuce is best raw, with its soft texture and mild, nutty flavour, in salads with beetroot, walnuts, goat’s cheese or oranges. Serve with a simple vinaigrette, and add at the last moment, as the leaves are delicate. It can also be lightly wilted into soups or used as a bed for fish.

The leaves keep for two to three days in the fridge in a bag lined with kitchen paper. For longer storage, the plants themselves are the best store, as they stay fresh in the ground all winter. It does not freeze well.
use_tips: Pair with beetroot, walnuts and goat’s cheese.
Dress lightly at the last moment.
Rinse gently, as the leaves bruise.
Leave plants in the ground until needed.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 5 to 10 cm apart and keep weeds away, as lamb's lettuce is small and slow growing.
Cover with a cloche or fleece in very hard frost, though it is hardy, and pick rosettes whole or leaf by leaf.
Let a few plants flower in spring to self-sow for autumn, or pull up spent plants.

preserving.how: Keep unwashed rosettes in a bag with a piece of kitchen paper. Very delicate, so best eaten quickly.
It stands outdoors over winter, so pick fresh leaves from the plant rather than storing them.
Wilt into soups and freeze, as it does not freeze well raw.

crops.name: Land cress
crops.sun_text: Partial shade; tolerates sun and shade

facts.Type: Hardy biennial peppery salad leaf, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 10–15 cm apart in rows 20 cm apart

varieties: Winter cress (another common name for the same plant)

info: Land cress, also called American cress or Belle Isle cress, tastes just like watercress but grows in ordinary garden soil, with no need for running water. The dark, glossy leaves are peppery and rich in vitamins, and the plant is tough enough to stand hard winters.

It is a useful crop for autumn and winter, when it provides fresh leaves in cold weather, and for spring, when it is very early to grow. It tolerates partial shade and thrives in cool, moist conditions, so is ideal for a damp, sheltered corner of the garden.
sow: Sow from March to April for early summer crops, and from August to September for the best autumn and winter pickings. Sow thinly 1 cm deep in rows 20 cm apart, in moist, fertile soil in partial shade. Seedlings appear in about a week and should be thinned to 10–15 cm apart.

Cress dislikes heat and drought, so sow in cool conditions and keep the soil moist. Late summer sowings under cloches or in a cold frame provide leaves all winter. Land cress also grows well in pots and containers on a shady patio.
sow_tips: Choose a partly shaded spot in summer.
Sow in August for a winter crop.
Grow in a container of moist compost.
grow: Keep land cress watered, because dry spells make the leaves bitter and cause bolting. Mulch to keep the soil cool and moist, and keep weeds down. No feeding is needed in fertile soil. Plants form a leafy rosette in the first year and flower in the second.

Flea beetle can damage the leaves in spring, so cover with fine mesh. Slugs are a nuisance in damp weather, and caterpillars sometimes appear. As a brassica, land cress should be rotated with other members of the cabbage family.
grow_tips: Water regularly to stop bitter, woody leaves.
Cover with fine mesh in spring.
Check for slugs on damp nights.
harvest: Pick the outer leaves when they are 5–8 cm long, usually from eight weeks after sowing, leaving the centre to grow more. Plants can be cut hard back to 2.5 cm above the base and will regrow. Picking regularly keeps the leaves tender and delays flowering.

In spring, the plants send up flower stalks with yellow flowers, which are edible and attractive to bees. Cut these off to prolong leaf production, or leave one or two to set seed for next year. Dig up the plants after flowering and resow.
harvest_tips: Pick young leaves for the mildest flavour.
Remove flower stalks to extend cropping.
Eat the yellow flowers in salads.
use: Use land cress raw in salads, sandwiches and as a garnish, where the peppery bite livens up bland flavours. It is delicious in egg sandwiches, with smoked fish and in potato salad. It can also be made into soup, in the style of watercress soup, or lightly wilted into hot dishes.

Fresh leaves keep for up to three days in the fridge in a bag, wrapped in damp kitchen paper. It does not freeze or dry well, but soup made from it freezes nicely. Plants in the garden are the best form of storage, as they stay fresh until you need them.
use_tips: Make a peppery soup with potato and stock.
Pair with smoked salmon or egg.
Use as a garnish for flavour and colour.

care.job: Water well in dry weather, as dry soil makes leaves tough and hot, and thin seedlings to 15 cm apart.
Pick leaves regularly from the outside through autumn and winter, and cover plants in severe frost.
Pull up plants as they flower in spring, or let a few self-sow.

preserving.how: It is hardy and keeps cropping through winter, so pick fresh from the plant.
Wrap leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Blend peppery leaves into soup or pesto and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Lavender
varieties: Imperial Gem (deep purple, good for drying)

info: Lavender is a classic scented shrub that is also edible, with flowers and leaves used in baking, preserves, teas and drinks. It thrives in hot, sunny, dry spots and is a magnet for bees and butterflies, making it useful in any garden.
English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is the hardiest and best for cooking, with a sweeter flavour than French lavender, which is more camphor-like. Plants are best replaced every 8–10 years.
sow: Plant in spring or early autumn in full sun in poor, free-draining soil; it hates wet roots. Add plenty of grit or plant on a raised bed or slope on clay. Space plants 40–60 cm apart, or 30 cm for a hedge.
Pots work well with gritty, loam-based compost. Do not enrich the soil, since too rich a diet gives leafy plants with few flowers. Water until established, then rarely.
grow: Trim immediately after flowering in August, cutting back the flowering stems and about 2.5 cm of green growth, but never into old wood, which rarely regrows. A light trim in spring helps too. This keeps plants compact and prolongs their life.
Water only in prolonged drought once established. Wet winters are the main cause of death, so ensure good drainage. Lavender is generally trouble-free, though rosemary beetle may occasionally appear.
harvest: Cut flower stems when about half the buds on the spike have opened, usually June to August, on a dry morning after the dew has gone. Cut long stems for drying, tying small bundles and hanging them upside-down in a dark, airy place for 2–3 weeks.
For cooking, pick fresh flowers just as they open. Leaves can also be used in cooking, though sparingly, as they are strong.
harvest_tips: Cut when half the buds are open.
use: Use culinary lavender sparingly: a few buds in shortbread, scones, cakes, ice cream, jam, honey, sugar, lemonade and herbes de Provence. Pair with lemon, honey, berries and chocolate. Too much tastes soapy. Lavender-infused sugar is a lovely gift.
Dried flowers keep their flavour and scent for a year in an airtight jar. Use dried buds in sachets, or sprinkle into baking. Only use lavender grown without pesticides.

care.job: Remove any frost-damaged growth in spring but avoid hard pruning into old wood, as it may not reshoot.
Cut flower stems when about half the buds have opened for drying, and water pots only when the compost is dry.
Trim plants straight after flowering, taking off the flower stalks and about 2.5 cm of green growth, to keep them compact.
Replace plants every 8 to 10 years once they become woody, taking softwood cuttings to propagate new ones.

preserving.how: Cut flower stems just before the buds open fully, bundle and hang in a warm, dark, airy place. Strip buds into jars.
Layer dried buds with caster sugar in a jar for 2 weeks for baking.
Steep in syrup, honey or cream for desserts and drinks.
preserving.keeps: Honey: 6 months; syrup: 1 month in the fridge

preserving.how: Fill small cloth bags with dried buds for drawers and wardrobes.

facts.Type: Hardy biennial, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Mar–Apr in trays or a seedbed; plant out Jun–Jul
facts.Spacing: 15 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

types.name: Early leeks
types.when: Sow February to March · Harvest August to November
types.note: Slimmer, milder leeks for earliest picking.

types.name: Mid-season leeks
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest October to January
types.note: Reliable and thick, the usual choice.

types.name: Late leeks
types.when: Sow April · Harvest January to April
types.note: Very hardy and slow-growing, standing through the toughest winters.

info: Leeks are one of the best winter vegetables: hardy, productive and happy in a wide range of soils, and they are ready to harvest when little else is. They grow slowly, so a March sowing gives you a crop from autumn right through to spring.

They are very forgiving, and take little attention other than watering and weeding, making them a great choice for beginners. Planting them in deep holes (dibbling) is the traditional way to get long, blanched white stems.
sow: Sow in March and April, either in trays or modules indoors, or thinly in a seedbed outdoors, 1 cm deep. Seedlings look like thin blades of grass and are slow to start. Keep them watered and weeded until they are about as thick as a pencil, which takes 8–12 weeks.

In June or July, transplant them into their final position. Use a dibber to make holes 15 cm deep and 15 cm apart, in rows 30 cm apart. Trim the roots and leaf tips, drop one leek into each hole and water in, letting the water wash soil around the roots. Do not fill the holes with soil.
sow_tips: Do not fill the dibbed holes; water settles the soil.
Trim leaf tips by a third before planting.
Interplant with quick catch crops like radishes.
grow: Water in dry spells and keep weeds down while plants are young. Feed with a general fertiliser every few weeks through the summer. As the leeks swell, gradually draw soil up around the stems, a process called earthing up, to blanch the stems and keep them white and tender.

The main problems are leek rust (orange spots on the leaves), leek moth, allium leaf miner and white rot. Rust-resistant varieties and wide spacing help; cover with fine mesh to keep out moths and leaf miners. Rotate leeks with other onion-family crops.
grow_tips: Earth up gradually in late summer for longer white stems.
Net with fine mesh against leek moth and leaf miner.
Feed in summer and stop in autumn.
harvest: Lift leeks from September through to April, when they are at least 2 cm across. Early varieties are ready first, while hardy types stand all winter. Loosen the soil with a fork alongside the row and lift the whole plant, taking care not to snap the stem.

Leeks stand well in the ground, so lift only what you need. In freezing weather, harvest before the soil is frozen solid. In spring, lift any remaining leeks before they run to seed, when they develop a hard central core.
harvest_tips: Lift a few at a time throughout autumn and winter.
Use a fork rather than pulling by hand.
Take out all leeks before they bolt in spring.
Leave small ones to grow on.
use: Slice leeks into soups, pies and stews, braise them in butter, bake them in a cheese sauce, or use as the base of potato and leek soup. Smaller baby leeks are tender enough to eat whole with vinaigrette. The dark green tops are tougher but work well in stock.

Trim the roots and tops, wash off any soil between the layers, and keep in the fridge in a bag for up to two weeks. Leave hardy leeks in the ground until needed. For the freezer, slice, blanch for two minutes, drain well and freeze in portions.
use_tips: Slice and wash thoroughly to remove grit trapped between layers.
Use the dark green tops for stock.
Blanch for two minutes before freezing.
Cook slowly in butter to bring out the sweetness.

care.job: Plant out young leeks into 15 cm holes made with a dibber, dropping a plant in each and watering in, without filling the hole.
Water in dry weather and hoe off weeds, then draw soil around the stems to blanch them white.
Check for leek moth and rust, which shows as orange spots. Remove badly affected leaves, and cover with fleece or mesh.
Lift as needed and heel in any spare leeks if the ground is very frozen.

preserving.how: Leeks are very hardy and keep well in the soil, so lift as needed all winter.
Trim and keep unwashed in a bag in the salad drawer.
Slice, wash well, blanch for 2 minutes, cool and freeze in bags. Ideal for soups.
Cook leek and potato soup in large batches and freeze in portions.
Lift and replant tightly together in a spare corner if you need the bed back.

info: Lemon balm is a soft, bright green perennial with crinkled, lemon-scented leaves. It is easy, cheerful and vigorous, thriving in sun or shade, and it is a favourite of bees (its name comes from the Greek for honey bee). It makes a refreshing tea and a pretty edge to a border.

It can self-seed freely, so cut off the flowers before the seeds ripen unless you want a lot of plants. The golden-leaved form ‘Aurea’ lights up shade but can scorch in full sun. Like mint, it can be restrained in a pot.
sow: Sow seed on the surface of seed compost from March to May at 15–20°C, pressing in lightly, as it needs light to germinate. Germination takes up to 3 weeks. Transplant to pots, then plant outside when large enough. Space plants 45–60 cm apart.

Alternatively, buy a plant or divide an existing clump in spring or autumn. It tolerates most soils, in partial shade or sun, but best leaf flavour comes from moist, fertile soil. A large container controls its spread.
sow_tips: Divide in spring for new plants.
Use a pot to contain it.
grow: Water in dry spells, particularly in pots. Cut the plant back hard to 5 cm in midsummer after flowering for a fresh flush of leaves, and again in late autumn. Remove flowers before they set seed to prevent self-seeding.

Divide clumps every 3 years in spring. Powdery mildew can affect plants in dry weather; cut back affected stems to the base. Cutting back also brings fresh new shoots with the best flavour. Plants die down in winter and regrow in spring.
harvest: Pick young leaves and shoot tips from spring through to autumn, using scissors. The leaves are most aromatic before flowering and in the morning. Cutting the whole plant back to 5 cm in midsummer yields a large harvest for drying, while new leaves grow back.
Harvest regularly, and leave some flowers for pollinators. The leaves darken and lose their scent when dried slowly, so dry quickly in a warm, shady, airy place. Fresh leaves are best.
harvest_tips: Cut hard back for a large harvest.
use: Steep fresh leaves in hot water for a calming, lemony tea, or add to iced drinks, cordials and fruit salads. Chop into fish dishes, salads, stuffings, desserts, and custards, or use as a substitute for lemon zest. Add it at the end of cooking, as the flavour is delicate.
Fresh leaves keep a few days in the fridge in water. Freeze leaves in ice cubes for summer drinks, or dry for tea, though flavour is weaker. Lemon balm vinegar and cordial capture the aroma.
use_tips: Make a fresh tea with hot water.
Add to ice cubes for drinks.
Chop into fish dishes at the end.

care.job: Divide clumps in spring and cut back dead stems, and contain the plant in a pot or bed edge, as it spreads and self-seeds freely.
Cut stems back by half every few weeks for fresh, flavourful leaves, and remove flowers before they set seed.
Give plants a hard cut back mid-summer if they look tired, then water and feed to encourage fresh growth.
Cut dead stems to the ground and mulch the crown lightly.

preserving.how: Dry quickly in a warm place for tea. Colour and flavour fade, so use within the year.
Freeze leaves in ice cube trays with water for drinks.
Simmer leaves with sugar and water, then strain and bottle.
preserving.keeps: 1 month in the fridge; longer frozen

preserving.how: Stand stems in a glass of water, loosely covered.

info: Lemon verbena has the most intense, true lemon fragrance of any herb, and its slim leaves make superb tea, desserts and drinks. It is a deciduous shrub that dies back in cold winters and needs protection from frost in most of the UK.
Grow it in a large pot that can be moved into a greenhouse or porch for winter, or against a warm, sheltered wall in milder areas. Cuttings root easily, so you can always keep a spare.
sow: Plant in May or June in a sunny, sheltered spot with fertile, free-draining soil, or in a large pot (30 cm) of loam-based compost with added grit. Seed is rarely available and unreliable, so buy a plant or take softwood cuttings in early summer.
Place against a south-facing wall for protection. Water in well, and mulch the roots for winter.
grow: Water regularly in summer, keeping the compost moist, and feed fortnightly with a general fertiliser. Pinch out the tips in spring for bushy growth. In October, bring pots into a frost-free place; plants shed their leaves, which is normal, and should be kept almost dry.
Prune in spring, when new growth shows, cutting back to healthy buds. Mulch outdoor plants thickly with straw or bracken for winter. Whitefly and red spider mite may attack under glass.
harvest: Pick leaves from June onwards, harvesting stem tips or individual leaves. Flavour is best just before flowering in midsummer. Regular picking promotes bushy growth.
For drying, pick whole stems in late summer, dry in a warm, shady place, and strip leaves. Dried leaves hold their scent well.

Before the first frost in October, take a final large harvest of leafy stems and dry them for winter tea. Even after plants drop their leaves in autumn, you can sometimes gather the last few that fall in a tray and dry them.
use: Make a fragrant tea with a few fresh or dried leaves in boiling water. Use in custards, ice creams, sorbets, cakes, fruit salads, syrups and gin. Wrap fish or chicken in leaves before grilling.
Dried leaves keep their scent for a year in an airtight jar. Fresh leaves freeze well.

care.job: Move pots outdoors only once frost has passed, and harden off gradually, as lemon verbena is tender.
Water in dry weather and feed pots every two weeks, and pinch out the tips to keep plants bushy.
Bring pots indoors before the first frost to a cool, bright, frost-free place. Leaves will drop, which is normal.
Water sparingly through winter and prune back by about a third in early spring as new growth appears.

preserving.how: Dry on a tray in a warm, airy place. It keeps its lemon scent well when dried, so is great for tea.
Freeze whole leaves in a bag for later use.
Steep leaves in syrup, sugar or milk for desserts.
preserving.keeps: Syrup: 1 month in the fridge; milk or cream: use within 2–3 days

preserving.how: Take cuttings or overwinter in a frost-free place so you can pick fresh again next year.

crops.name: Lemongrass

facts.Type: Tender perennial grass, grown as an annual

varieties: West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus, the culinary type)
