info: Lemongrass is a tall, tropical grass with intensely citrus-scented stems, essential to Thai and Vietnamese cooking. It will grow in the UK in a large pot in summer, and be moved to a bright, frost-free windowsill for winter.
The easiest method is to root fresh stalks from a supermarket in a glass of water. In a hot summer it can reach 1 m and give you a harvest of fat stems.
sow: Buy fresh lemongrass stalks with the base intact and stand them in a glass of water on a warm windowsill. After 2–3 weeks, roots appear; pot up into 15 cm pots of multipurpose compost. Seed is available but slow.
Pot on to 30 cm containers by May and move outdoors in June to a sunny, sheltered spot. Keep warm and well watered.
grow: Water generously in summer, since lemongrass is thirsty, and feed fortnightly with a general liquid fertiliser. Keep in the sunniest, warmest spot. Divide clumps in spring.
Bring into a bright, frost-free room in September, and keep nearly dry over winter. Cut leaves back by half before bringing indoors. Spider mite may attack indoors; mist regularly.
harvest: Harvest stems when they are at least 1 cm thick at the base, from late summer. Cut or twist off stalks near the base, taking the outer ones. The tender lower 10 cm is the culinary part.
Leaves can be dried for tea. Harvest before the first frost.

To harvest, grasp a stem low down and twist and pull it away from the clump; this encourages new stems to develop. Peel off the dry outer layers to reveal the tender pale core, which is the part to bruise, slice and cook with.
use: Bruise the stalks, then slice thinly or add whole to curries, soups, stir-fries, marinades and tea, removing the tough pieces before serving. Pair with chilli, ginger, coconut and lime. Leaves make an aromatic tea.
Stalks freeze well chopped or whole. Fresh stalks keep 2–3 weeks in the fridge.

care.job: Plant out or move pots outside only after the last frost, and place in the sunniest, warmest spot.
Water generously and feed every two weeks, as lemongrass is a thirsty, hungry plant, and harvest stalks from the outside.
Bring pots indoors before frost and cut leaves back to about 15 cm, keeping plants on a bright windowsill.
Water sparingly over winter, as lemongrass hates cold and wet together.

preserving.how: Trim, chop or freeze whole stalks in bags. Works as well as fresh in curries and soups.
Wrap stalks in damp paper in the fridge.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator for teas.
Blend with garlic, ginger and chilli and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Lettuce
crops.sun_text: Full sun in spring; partial shade in summer

facts.Type: Hardy to half-hardy annual salad leaf
facts.Sow: Mar–Aug outdoors; Feb and Sep–Oct under cover

varieties: Salad Bowl (loose-leaf, cut and come again)
Winter Density (hardy cos for autumn sowing)

types.name: Cut-and-come-again (loose-leaf)
types.when: Sow March to August · Harvest from 4–8 weeks
types.note: Pick leaves repeatedly from one plant. The easiest and most forgiving type.

types.name: Hearting (cos, butterhead, crisphead)
types.when: Sow March to August · Harvest 8–12 weeks
types.note: Cut whole heads. Little Gem is the best compact cos; butterheads are soft and sweet.

types.name: Hardy winter lettuce
types.when: Sow September to October under cover · Harvest March to April
types.note: Slow but tough types for overwintering in a cold frame or greenhouse.

info: Lettuce is the classic salad crop and one of the easiest to grow, giving fresh, tender leaves for months from a few packets of seed. There are many types: crisp cos and iceberg, soft butterheads, frilly and colourful loose-leaf varieties, and hardy winter types.

Homegrown lettuce is crisper and sweeter than bagged leaves, and cut-and-come-again types give repeat pickings from a single sowing. Lettuce grows well in pots and window boxes as well as in beds, and tolerates light shade in the heat of summer.
sow: Sow thinly outdoors from March, 5 mm deep, in rows 15–30 cm apart, and thin to the final spacing as seedlings grow. Make a new sowing every two weeks until August to avoid gluts. In hot weather, lettuce seed can fail to germinate above about 25°C, so sow in the cool of the evening and water the drill beforehand.

For early crops, sow in trays or modules indoors from February and plant out under cloches in March. In autumn, sow hardy winter varieties in September and October under cloches or in a cold frame. For baby leaves, sow thickly and cut when 5–10 cm tall.
sow_tips: Sow a short row every two weeks.
Sow in the evening in summer to avoid heat blocking germination.
Choose heat-tolerant, bolt-resistant varieties for midsummer.
Use modules for early and winter sowings.
grow: Lettuce needs even moisture: water regularly, especially in dry spells, because stressed plants turn bitter and bolt (run to seed). In midsummer, give plants some afternoon shade, for example beside taller crops. Mulch to hold moisture and keep roots cool.

Slugs and snails are the main enemies, so use traps, wool pellets or night-time patrols and keep the bed free of hiding places. Aphids, lettuce root aphid and grey mould can also appear. Remove damaged outer leaves, space plants generously for air flow and rotate the crop.
grow_tips: Water consistently to keep leaves sweet and crisp.
Give afternoon shade in hot weather.
Set slug traps around young plants.
Thin to the right spacing early.
harvest: Pick loose-leaf lettuces by taking the outer leaves from around the plant, leaving the centre to grow on and produce more. Hearting types such as cos and butterhead are ready when the heart feels firm; cut them at the base with a sharp knife, leaving the stump, which will often resprout.

Harvest in the morning when the leaves are full of water and the plants are crisp. Cut the whole row of overgrown plants before they start to bolt, because once a flower stem forms the leaves become bitter. Baby leaves are ready within three to four weeks.
harvest_tips: Harvest in the morning for the crispest leaves.
Take outer leaves first from loose-leaf types.
Leave the stump; it often regrows.
use: Use lettuce in salads, sandwiches and wraps, or lightly cook outer leaves in soups and with peas, as the French do. Little Gem is excellent halved and grilled. Mix a variety of leaf types together for colour and flavour, and dress just before serving so the leaves stay crisp.

Wash, spin dry and keep in the fridge in a bag lined with kitchen paper, where they stay fresh for three to five days. Cut-and-come-again lettuce stays best in the garden, picked as required. Lettuce does not freeze or dry successfully, so sow little and often.
use_tips: Dress at the last minute to keep leaves crisp.
Store in a bag lined with kitchen paper.
Try grilled halved Little Gem hearts.

care.job: Thin seedlings early to 15 to 30 cm apart, depending on the type, so hearts can form.
Water regularly in the morning, as dry spells make lettuce bitter and bolt to seed.
Protect from slugs and snails with a barrier, nematodes or evening checks.
Give plants shade or a damp mulch in hot weather to prevent bolting.
Cover winter lettuce with a cloche or fleece and remove dead outer leaves to prevent grey mould.

preserving.how: Wash, dry thoroughly and wrap leaves in kitchen paper in a container or bag, or keep whole heads unwashed in the salad drawer.
Harvest outer leaves only and the plants regrow, which avoids having a glut at once.
Cook surplus lettuce into pea and lettuce soup and freeze in portions. It cannot be frozen raw.
Braise gem or cos hearts in butter and stock for a cooked side dish.

info: Loganberries and tayberries are hybrid berries, crosses between raspberries and blackberries, with large, aromatic, richly flavoured fruits that are too soft to travel and so are rarely seen in the shops. They are excellent for the home garden, and easier to grow than most berries.
Plants are vigorous and are trained like blackberries on a wall or wires. Thornless forms are available. They tolerate partial shade and heavy soils, and crop reliably even in poor summers.
sow: Plant bare-root canes between November and March in fertile, well-drained soil in sun or partial shade, 2–3 m apart. Dig in plenty of compost, and set up a wire support system with wires at 1 m, 1.5 m and 1.8 m.
Cut canes to 25 cm after planting. Mulch generously and water in. These are vigorous, so leave plenty of room for growth, or train against a fence.
grow: Water in dry spells and mulch each spring. Feed with a general fertiliser. Tie in new canes as they grow, separating this year’s growth from last year’s fruiting canes, as with blackberries.
After fruiting, cut all old canes to the ground and tie in the new ones. Birds and wasps are the main pests, and cane spot may appear in wet seasons. Thin new canes to 6–8 per plant.
grow_tips: Cut out fruited canes after harvest.
harvest: Pick fruits when they are fully coloured, deep red-purple, and they come away from the plant easily, from July to August. They are soft, so pick carefully, and use shallow containers. Fruit is best when slightly overripe, when the flavour is richest.
Pick every 2–3 days. Fruit does not travel well, so eat or process quickly.

Loganberries ripen to a deep red-purple and will taste sharper than tayberries, which are sweeter when fully ripe and a dark crimson. Because the cores come away with the fruit, they are easier to use than blackberries, and they do not need hulling.
use: Eat fresh with cream, or cook in pies, tarts, jams, sauces and ice creams. The flavour is more intense and tart than raspberries; it holds well in baking. Tayberry jam is exceptional.
Fresh fruit lasts 1–2 days in the fridge. Freeze whole on trays and bag for a year. Make jam with surplus.

care.job: Tie in last year's canes to supports and cut out any dead or weak wood, then feed and mulch around the base.
Keep this year's new canes separate from the fruiting canes by tying them in a different part of the support.
Water in dry weather and net against birds as the fruit reddens.
After fruiting, cut the old fruited canes to the ground and tie in the new ones in their place.

preserving.how: Open freeze on a tray, then bag. Perfect for jams and baking later.
Keep unwashed in a single layer in a shallow container.
Tart and richly flavoured, with enough pectin to set well.
Simmer into a cordial, or steep in gin with sugar.
preserving.keeps: Cordial: about 1 month in the fridge; liqueur: 1 year+

crops.name: Lovage
crops.sun_text: Full sun to partial shade; moist soil

facts.Sow: Seed Mar–Apr or Aug; plant Mar–Oct
facts.Good companions: Most vegetables; give it its own space

varieties: Common lovage (the only widely available form)

info: Lovage is a tall, majestic perennial with glossy, celery-like leaves and a strong, savoury flavour, like a concentrated celery with hints of curry. It is a traditional kitchen garden herb that reaches 2 m, and a single plant is plenty for the average household.

It is hardy, long-lived and very easy, thriving in sun or part shade and rich, moist soil. Its umbels of yellow-green flowers attract hoverflies and ladybirds. It dies back in winter and returns each spring, getting bigger every year.
sow: Sow fresh seed in late summer (August), or in March to April, on the surface of seed compost or in pots at 15°C; germination is slow and patchy, 2–4 weeks. Plant seedlings out at 60–90 cm apart once they are large enough. Fresh seed germinates best.

Alternatively, buy a plant or divide an established clump in spring or autumn, lifting and splitting the crown with a spade into sections with buds. Choose a rich, moist, well-drained soil in a sunny or lightly shaded position, and allow plenty of room.
sow_tips: Allow space: it grows 2 m tall.
grow: Water in dry spells and mulch each spring with compost. Feed once in spring with a general fertiliser. Cut back the flowering stems in summer to encourage more leaves, unless you want seeds. In late autumn, cut the dead stems down to the ground.

Divide the crowns every 3–4 years. Lovage is rarely troubled, though leaf miner and slugs may nibble leaves, and aphids may colonise the flower heads. It can be grown in a large pot (at least 40 cm), but it will need regular watering.
grow_tips: Cut flower stems for more leaves.
harvest: Pick young leaves from spring, from the second year, and the stems and leaves through summer. Cut individual stems at the base or pick leaves; young leaves are the tenderest and most flavoursome. Cut back the whole plant to the ground in midsummer for a fresh flush of growth.
Collect the seeds in late summer when they turn brown, and dry them in a paper bag. The hollow stems can be blanched and used like celery, or candied like angelica. Harvest in the morning.
harvest_tips: Cut back in midsummer for fresh growth.
Collect seed heads in late summer.
use: Use lovage sparingly, as a little goes a long way. Chop leaves into soups, stews, stocks, potato salad, tomato juice, Bloody Marys and egg dishes as a substitute for celery. The hollow stems can be used as a straw in a Bloody Mary. The seeds can season bread, cheese and pickles.

Fresh leaves keep for a few days in the fridge, and freeze very well chopped in ice-cube trays. Dry leaves quickly in a warm place, and store in an airtight jar; they keep much of their flavour. The seeds keep for a year.
use_tips: Freeze chopped leaves in ice cubes.
Try a stem as a Bloody Mary straw.

care.job: Mulch with compost and feed in spring, as lovage is a large, hungry perennial, and divide clumps every few years.
Cut stems back regularly to encourage fresh young leaves, and cut flower stems as they appear unless you want seed.
Water in dry weather, as plants can wilt in drought, and stake very tall plants.
Cut stems to the ground when they die back and mulch the crown.

preserving.how: Chop leaves and freeze in bags or ice cube trays. Very strong, so use sparingly.
Dry leaves and stems in a warm, airy place and crumble into jars for soups and stocks.
Blend leaves with coarse salt, spread on a tray to dry and store in a jar.
Dry seed heads and keep the seeds in a jar to use like celery seed.

info: Marrows are overgrown courgettes, though they are best grown as a separate crop, left to reach 30–45 cm long. They have a mild flavour that is wonderful stuffed and baked, and they keep for weeks. A British classic for harvest festivals.
Plants are as easy and as vigorous as courgettes. Choose bush or trailing types, depending on space.
sow: Sow indoors in April to early May, seeds on edge, 2 cm deep, in 9 cm pots at 18–20°C. Plant out in early June after hardening off, 90 cm to 1 m apart, in rich, moisture-retentive soil.
Prepare a pit with compost or manure beneath each plant. Trailing types can be trained up a trellis.
grow: Water regularly, deeply and at the base. Feed fortnightly with tomato fertiliser once fruit sets. Mulch to retain moisture.
Hand-pollinate if few bees are about. Slugs and powdery mildew are the main problems. For large marrows, limit to 3–4 fruits per plant.

Marrows need rich, moisture-retentive soil, so dig in plenty of compost or manure before planting. Water thoroughly once a week in dry weather, rather than frequently and lightly, and keep the leaves dry. Slugs are a particular nuisance in young plants, so use traps or nematodes. As the fruit swell, put a tile or straw under each to keep them off damp soil, which causes rot.
harvest: Cut marrows at 30–40 cm, when the skin is still tender and a thumbnail pierces it, from August to September. For storing, leave on the plant until the skin hardens in early autumn. Cut with a stalk.
Bring in before frost. Cure in the sun for 10 days.
use: Stuff marrow halves with mince, rice or vegetables and bake, or slice into soups, stews, ratatouille, chutney and marrow and ginger jam. The flavour is mild, so it needs strong seasonings.
Hardened marrows keep for 2–3 months in a cool, dry place. Peel, deseed and freeze cooked chunks.

Marrows have a high water content and a mild flavour, so the secret is strong accompaniments: chilli, garlic, ginger, tomato sauce, cheese or spiced mince. Peel and deseed older marrows, because the skin is tough. Slice and roast with olive oil until golden to concentrate flavour.
use_tips: Store in a cool, dry place.

care.job: Harden off and plant out after the last frost on a rich, sunny mound, leaving plenty of room for trailing stems.
Water generously at the base and feed every one to two weeks with a tomato feed once fruits form.
Hand-pollinate if fruit does not set, by dabbing a male flower into a female one.
Cut marrows when 30 to 40 cm long for eating fresh, or leave on the plant to harden for storing.

preserving.how: Let fruit mature on the plant until the skin is hard, then cure in the sun for a week and store somewhere cool, dry and frost-free.
Peel, cube and blanch for 3 minutes, or freeze cooked marrow in sauces or soup.
Marrow chutney is a classic. Marrow and ginger jam is old-fashioned and good.
Make stuffed marrow or marrow and tomato bake and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Melon
crops.sun_text: Full sun; needs heat, best under glass

info: Melons can ripen in British summers with the right variety and a warm spot, ideally in a greenhouse or polytunnel, though early varieties such as Sweetheart and Emir can do well against a south-facing wall in good summers. A homegrown melon is a real triumph.
They need warmth, plenty of water, and a long season. Cantaloupe and charentais types are the best choices for UK conditions.
sow: Sow in April, seeds on edge, 1–2 cm deep, in individual pots at 20–25°C in a heated propagator. Germination takes 5–10 days. Pot on as they grow, and plant out in late May to June into a greenhouse border or large pot with rich compost.
Outdoors, plant against a south-facing wall in June, under cloches, on a mound with black plastic to warm the soil.

Melon seeds rot easily in cold, wet compost, so use a free-draining mix and water sparingly until the seedlings emerge. Germination is quick at 25°C. Once seedlings have two true leaves, pot them on into individual 9 cm pots, taking care not to disturb the roots.
grow: Train the main stem up a string or trellis and pinch out at 1.5 m. Allow side shoots to develop, pinching them out after 2 leaves beyond a fruit. Restrict to 3–4 fruits per plant.

Water regularly but lightly, reducing as fruit ripens. Hand-pollinate flowers by transferring pollen from male to female flowers. Feed weekly with tomato fertiliser once fruits set. Support fruits in nets.

Pollination is crucial. Female flowers have a tiny melon behind the petals; pick a male flower, remove the petals and dab the pollen into the centre of the female flower. When fruits are the size of a golf ball, choose the best three or four and remove the rest. Ensure good ventilation in greenhouses to deter mildew.
harvest: Melons are ripe when the stalk end smells sweet and the fruit gives slightly at the stalk end, and the fruit comes away easily from the stem, from August to September. Charentais types develop a distinctive aroma.
Cut with a short stalk. Eat immediately for best flavour.
Mark the date when fruit sets, since many varieties ripen about 6–8 weeks later. A ripening melon changes colour, becomes fragrant and the stalk begins to crack where it joins the fruit.
use: Eat chilled slices on their own, with Parma ham, in fruit salads, sorbets and smoothies. Scoop the seeds out first. A sweet, ripe, homegrown melon needs no embellishment.
Whole ripe melons keep for 2–3 days; cut melon keeps 3 days in the fridge. Freeze cubes for smoothies.

care.job: Plant in a greenhouse, polytunnel or sheltered, sunny spot after the last frost, and train the main stem up a support.
Pinch out the tip after about five leaves, then train the side shoots and pinch them back after two leaves beyond a female flower.
Hand-pollinate female flowers with male flowers in the morning, and limit each plant to three or four fruits.
Water regularly and feed weekly with tomato feed once fruits start to swell, and support heavy fruits in nets.
Reduce watering slightly as fruits ripen to concentrate the sugars, and check for the fruit stalk cracking.

preserving.how: Keep whole ripe melons in the fridge, wrapped to stop the smell spreading.
Cut into cubes and freeze on a tray for smoothies and sorbets. They are soft once thawed.
Make melon and ginger jam, or pickle small pieces in spiced vinegar.
Blend into sorbet, freeze and keep in a tub.

crops.name: Microgreens
crops.sun_text: A bright windowsill or any well-lit indoor spot

facts.Type: Seedlings of salad, herb and vegetable plants harvested young
facts.Sowing depth: On the surface, or lightly covered

info: Microgreens are the young seedlings of salad and vegetable plants, cut after their first true leaves emerge, and they are packed with flavour and colour. They can be grown on any windowsill in as little as a week or two, in any month, with no garden at all, making them the best year-round crop in this guide.

Good choices include radish, mustard, pea shoots, sunflower, broccoli, rocket, coriander, basil, beetroot and fenugreek. They need almost no equipment: a shallow tray or old food container, a little compost or kitchen paper, seed and water.
sow: Use a shallow tray, about 3–5 cm deep, with drainage holes if possible. Fill with 2–3 cm of moist peat-free multipurpose compost, or use a layer of damp kitchen paper or a coir mat. Firm and level the surface, then scatter seed thickly and evenly so the seeds are almost touching but not overlapping.

Press the seed gently into the surface and mist it well. Some seeds, such as peas and sunflowers, benefit from soaking overnight before sowing. Cover with a lid, plate or another tray for two to three days to keep the seeds dark and moist, then uncover and move to good light. Use seed sold for sprouting or microgreens.
sow_tips: Sow thickly: microgreens are crops in a tray.
Cover for two to three days, then move into the light.
Use a bright windowsill, ideally south-facing.
Soak large seeds like peas and sunflowers overnight.
grow: Water the trays from below or with a gentle mist, keeping the compost moist but never waterlogged. Overwatering and poor air flow lead to mould. Keep the tray in a bright, well-ventilated spot at room temperature, and turn it every day so the seedlings grow straight.

If you see white fuzz on the surface, it is usually fine root hairs rather than mould; mould is grey or cottony and smells musty. Good ventilation, thinner sowing and careful watering prevent it. Wash trays between batches in hot water and use fresh compost each time.
grow_tips: Water from below to keep leaves dry.
Turn trays daily for even growth.
Use fresh compost for each sowing.
harvest: Cut microgreens with scissors just above the compost when the first pair of seed leaves has fully opened and, for some types, the first true leaves have started to appear. Radish and mustard take about a week, sunflower and pea shoots two to three weeks, and basil and coriander three weeks or more.

Harvest in the morning when the leaves are crisp, and snip the whole tray or take just what you need. Most do not regrow well after cutting, apart from pea shoots, which may give a second smaller crop. Compost the used compost and roots, then start another tray.
harvest_tips: Cut just above the compost with clean scissors.
Harvest when the first leaves are open.
Sow a new tray every week for a steady supply.
Pea shoots may give a second cut.
use: Use microgreens as a fresh topping for salads, sandwiches, soups, eggs, pizza and curries, where they add intense flavour and bright colour. Peppery radish and mustard greens liven up bland dishes, sweet pea shoots are lovely in stir-fries and sunflower greens add a satisfying crunch.

Microgreens are best eaten the day they are cut. Keep unwashed, dry greens in a container lined with kitchen paper in the fridge for up to five days. Rinse gently just before use. They do not freeze, so harvest only what you need.
use_tips: Add at the last moment to keep their crunch.
Store dry in a lined container.
Mix different types for flavour and colour.

care.job: Water from below or with a fine mist once or twice a day, keeping the compost moist but not soggy.
Keep trays in bright light but out of direct midday sun, and make sure there is airflow to avoid mould.
Harvest with scissors once the first true leaves appear, usually in one to three weeks, and resow a tray every week.

preserving.how: Cut just before use if you can, or keep dry in a container lined with kitchen paper.
Re-sow every week or two rather than storing, as microgreens are best fresh.
Blend into pesto, soups and smoothies to use up a surplus.

crops.name: Mint
crops.sun_text: Partial shade to full sun; moist soil

types.name: Spearmint and garden mint
types.when: Pick April to October
types.note: The classic mint for sauces, new potatoes and peas.

types.name: Peppermint
types.when: Pick April to October
types.note: Strong menthol flavour, the best for tea and desserts.

types.name: Fruit and fancy mints
types.when: Pick April to October
types.note: Milder, with apple, pineapple, ginger or orange notes. Good in salads and drinks.

info: Mint is one of the easiest herbs, thriving in damp, partly shaded places where many others struggle. It spreads rapidly by underground runners, so always confine it in a pot or sunk container, or it will take over the bed.

There are dozens of flavours: spearmint for sauces and teas, peppermint for tea, apple mint with woolly leaves, and chocolate, ginger and pineapple mints. Mint is invaluable for bees and other pollinators when it flowers.
sow: Mint is best grown from a small plant or a root cutting, as seed is unreliable and doesn’t come true to flavour. Plant from March to October in a large pot (at least 30 cm), or a bucket sunk into the ground with drainage holes, with rich, moisture-retentive compost.

Take cuttings easily: lay a piece of runner with roots in soil, or place stem cuttings in a jar of water until roots form. Plant at the same depth as in the original pot, water in well, and place in partial shade.
sow_tips: Grow from plants or cuttings, not seed.
Use a pot of at least 30 cm.
grow: Water regularly, since mint likes moist soil and quickly wilts in drought. Cut the plants back by half in mid-summer to renew foliage and prevent mint rust. Pinch off flowers to prolong leaf production, although bees love them.

Every 2–3 years, tip the plant out, divide it, discard the woody centre and replant healthy portions in fresh compost, as mint becomes woody and weak. Mint rust (orange spots) is the main disease; destroy affected plants and start with healthy stock.
grow_tips: Cut back by half in midsummer.
harvest: Pick leaves and stem tips from spring, when the growth is a few inches tall, to autumn. Pinch out the tips above a pair of leaves for bushy growth. Regular harvesting keeps the plant productive, and flavour is best before flowering.

Cut the plant to a few inches above the ground a couple of times in the season for a big harvest to dry or freeze; it regrows quickly. Mint dies back in winter, though in a mild spell, new shoots may appear. Bring a pot indoors for winter leaves.
harvest_tips: Cut hard back for a big harvest.
Bring a pot inside for winter.
use: Chop fresh mint into new potatoes, peas, lamb, salads, yoghurt raita and cold drinks, or make mint sauce, mojitos and fresh mint tea by steeping leaves in boiling water. It pairs with chocolate, lemon and watermelon. Peppermint is the best for tea.

Fresh mint keeps for a week with stems in water in the fridge. Freeze leaves in ice cubes for drinks, or dry bunches hung upside down in a warm, airy place and store in a jar. Mint jelly and mint sauce preserve the flavour in jars.
use_tips: Freeze leaves in ice cubes for drinks.
Add to peas and new potatoes.
Infuse in boiling water for tea.

care.job: Divide and replant congested clumps, and keep mint in a pot or sunk container to stop it taking over the bed.
Cut stems back by half every few weeks to keep growth fresh and bushy, and pinch out flowers.
Water pots regularly, as mint wilts quickly in dry compost.
Look out for orange rust spots on the leaves. Remove and bin affected stems; pot-grown mint can be cut to the ground and will regrow.
Cut back dead stems and mulch the crown, and bring a pot indoors to a bright windowsill for winter leaves.

preserving.how: Freeze whole or chopped leaves in ice cube trays with water or oil.
Hang bunches in a warm, airy place and crumble into jars for teas and cooking.
Chop with sugar and vinegar and jar for lamb.
Simmer with sugar and lemon, strain and bottle for drinks.
preserving.keeps: 1 month in the fridge; longer frozen

preserving.how: Make with apple juice and set in jars.

crops.name: Mizuna
crops.sun_text: Partial shade to full sun; tolerates shade

facts.Sow: Mar–Sep outdoors; autumn sowings under cover

varieties: Mibuna (a close relative with spoon-shaped leaves)
Misome (very mild, from the same group)

info: Mizuna is a Japanese salad leaf with feathery, deeply cut leaves and a mild, peppery flavour. It is one of the most useful winter salads because it is very hardy, grows well in cool weather and shade, and regrows after cutting.

It is also very easy: one sowing can be cut several times, and the plants tolerate cold and partial shade better than lettuce. It fills pots, window boxes and winter beds with little effort, and the thin leaves are beautiful in mixed salads.
sow: Sow thinly outdoors from March to September in shallow drills 1 cm deep, in rows 15–20 cm apart, or broadcast across a bed or pot. For baby leaves, sow close together and cut when 5–10 cm tall. For larger plants, thin to 10–20 cm apart.

For winter salad, sow in August and September, in the ground, in pots in a cold frame, unheated greenhouse or under a cloche. In midsummer, choose a shady position, as heat and dry conditions make the leaves hot and cause bolting. Sow short rows every few weeks.
sow_tips: Sow in September for winter leaves under cover.
Choose a shady spot in midsummer.
Broadcast sow in pots for baby leaf.
Cover with fine mesh against flea beetle.
grow: Mizuna needs very little care. Keep the soil moist, as drought makes the leaves hot and woody, and water in the morning. Cut back flowering shoots to prolong picking. It will grow in poor soil, though a little compost gives better leaf.

Flea beetle makes small holes in the leaves, mainly in spring and summer, and is kept away with fine mesh. Slugs may feed on autumn sowings. Plants in the ground survive hard winters, but those under cloches give fresher leaves in freezing weather.
grow_tips: Cut hard to regrow fresh leaves.
Cover winter crops with a cloche or fleece.
harvest: Begin cutting baby leaves about three weeks after sowing, using scissors to snip them 2.5 cm above the soil. The plants regrow, and you can cut several times over a few weeks. Larger leaves can be harvested individually from the outside of each plant for stir-fries.

Plants will eventually flower, usually in spring, producing yellow blooms that are edible and attractive to pollinators. Let one or two plants go to seed to collect seeds for future sowings. Pull up the old plants after flowering and resow.
harvest_tips: Cut with scissors and leave the base to regrow.
Pick young leaves for the mildest flavour.
Save seed from a bolted plant.
use: Mizuna adds a gentle mustardy bite to salads, and the leaves also work well wilted into soups, stir-fries and noodle dishes at the last minute. It is lovely paired with Asian dressings of soy, sesame and ginger, or with a simple lemon and olive oil dressing.

Fresh leaves keep for up to five days in a bag in the fridge, though they are at their best straight after picking. Mizuna does not freeze or dry well, so sow it little and often. Winter-hardy plants in the ground act as living storage.
use_tips: Mix with other salad leaves for variety.
Wilt into hot soup at the end of cooking.
Dress with soy, sesame oil and lemon.
Pick just before you need it.

care.job: Water regularly and cover with fine mesh against flea beetles, which can riddle the leaves with holes.
Harvest the outer leaves regularly, as this keeps plants productive, and cut the whole plant 5 cm above the soil to regrow.
Protect plants with a cloche or fleece in winter, as mizuna is hardy but benefits from shelter.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
It is hardy and regrows after cutting, so pick fresh from the plant through winter.
Blanch for 1 minute, squeeze out the water and freeze for cooked dishes.
Pickle stems and leaves in a light vinegar brine.

facts.Spacing: 15–20 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

info: Mooli, or daikon, is a giant white winter radish with a crisp, juicy, mildly peppery flesh. It is easy and quick, produces roots up to 40 cm long, and sown in late summer, provides autumn and winter crops when most radishes have finished.

Mooli is milder than the small red radishes and is used raw and cooked in Asian cuisine. Sown in spring it tends to bolt, so late summer is the best time. The seed pods and young leaves are also edible.
sow: Sow from July to August, 1 cm deep, directly into light, fertile, moisture-retentive, stone-free soil in sun or partial shade. Space rows 30 cm apart and thin seedlings to 15–20 cm apart. Sowing in spring risks bolting, so wait until after midsummer.
Mooli can also be grown in deep containers (30 cm or more). Water the drill before sowing, and cover with fine mesh to protect from flea beetle. Sow a short row every two weeks to spread the crop.
sow_tips: Use fine mesh against flea beetle.
grow: Keep the soil moist, since irregular watering causes cracked, woody roots and bolting. Weed carefully, and earth up the shoulders of roots exposed above the soil to prevent greening.

Flea beetle is the main pest, leaving tiny holes in leaves, especially on young plants. Slugs may also bite roots. Fine mesh is the best protection. As a brassica, it should be rotated with the cabbage family.
harvest: Pull roots 8–10 weeks after sowing, when they are 20–30 cm long and about 5 cm wide, from October onwards. Loosen the soil with a fork first if the soil is firm. Roots left in the ground too long turn woody and hot.
In mild areas, roots can stay in the ground over winter under straw, but lift before hard frosts. Pull the tender leaves for use as greens.
harvest_tips: Loosen soil with a fork first.
use: Eat mooli raw, grated in salads and slaws, sliced into sticks for dips, or pickled in Japanese and Korean styles. Cook in soups, stews, stir-fries and braises, where it turns sweet and tender. Grated mooli is a classic with sushi and tempura.
Roots keep for 1–2 weeks in the fridge. Pickle in vinegar and sugar or ferment as kimchi for long storage. Dry slices in a low oven to make crisp chips.

care.job: Water regularly and evenly, as dry spells make roots woody and fiery, and thin seedlings to 15 cm apart.
Cover with fine mesh against flea beetles and cabbage root fly, which attack all brassica roots.
Lift roots before hard frosts and store them in damp sand, trimming the tops.

preserving.how: Remove the leaves and keep in a bag in the salad drawer.
Store roots in damp sand in a cool, frost-free place.
Slice or grate and pickle in sweet and sour vinegar for banh mi and noodle dishes.
Make kimchi-style fermented radish, such as kkakdugi.
Cut into strips and dry in a dehydrator. Traditional in Japanese cooking.

info: Mustard greens are fast, peppery and very hardy, available in green, red and purple, and with frilly, smooth or crinkled leaves. They are ideal for baby leaf salads and stir-fries, and give a fiery punch to mixed leaves.
They can be sown almost all year round, and make a good winter crop. Red Giant and Green in Snow are particularly decorative. Mustard also works as a green manure.
sow: Sow thinly, 1 cm deep, from March to September in rows 20 cm apart, or scatter in pots. Thin to 10–25 cm for full plants, or leave dense for baby leaf. Seeds germinate in 3–5 days.
Cover with fine mesh against flea beetle. Sow in shade in hot weather to avoid bolting. Autumn sowings under cover give winter leaves.
A mixed sowing of red, green and frilly mustards gives a very attractive plot as well as variety in flavour. For continuous cut-and-come-again crops, sow a 1 m row every fortnight.
grow: Water regularly; stress makes leaves hot and bitter and causes bolting. Weed carefully. No feed is needed.
Flea beetle, slugs and caterpillars are the main pests. Rotate with other brassicas. Plants tolerate frost, and leaf flavour mellows in cold.

Hot, dry weather makes mustard greens extremely pungent and quick to bolt, so grow them in partial shade through summer and water well. In autumn and winter, the plants sweeten and soften in the cold. A cloche or fleece extends the harvest through the coldest months, protecting the leaves from wind and rain damage.
harvest: Pick baby leaves from three weeks, cutting 2.5 cm above the ground for regrowth. Full leaves are ready from six to eight weeks. Pick outer leaves first.
Younger leaves are milder. Flowers and flower buds are edible. Cut before flowering for the best flavour.
The cooler it is, the milder the leaves. Autumn-sown mustards are often the best flavoured. If plants bolt, the yellow flowers and buds can be eaten and are very attractive in salads.
use: Use baby leaves in salads and sandwiches for peppery heat. Cook larger leaves in stir-fries, soups, curries and braises, or wilt like spinach. They are traditional in Southern US and Asian cooking.
Keeps 3–4 days in the fridge. Blanch and freeze for cooking.

For a milder flavour, blanch large leaves for one minute before stir-frying, or braise slowly with bacon, onion and a splash of vinegar, the Southern US way. The peppery taste is also good in sandwiches in place of rocket.

care.job: Water regularly to stop plants bolting and cover with fine mesh against flea beetles.
Pick leaves while young, as older leaves become hot and tough, and sow a little every few weeks.
Protect with a cloche or fleece in cold weather, as some winter types are very hardy and will carry on cropping.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Blanch for 2 minutes, drain and freeze in portions for cooked dishes.
Ferment in brine or salt for tangy pickled greens.
Hardy types will crop outdoors through autumn and winter, so pick fresh.

crops.name: Nasturtium
crops.sun_text: Full sun; tolerates partial shade and poor soil

facts.Good companions: Cabbages, courgettes, beans, apple trees (traps blackfly)

varieties: Empress of India (dark red flowers, blue-green leaves, compact)

info: Nasturtiums are among the most generous plants: easy from seed, flowering for months, and edible from the leaves and flowers to the seeds. The peppery, watercress-like flavour adds colour and spice to salads, and the flowers come in orange, red, yellow and cream.

They thrive in poor soil, in full sun and in pots, hanging baskets and borders, and they trap blackfly away from beans and brassicas. Trailing types scramble over walls and banks, while dwarf types suit pots.
sow: Sow seeds directly outdoors in April to June, 2 cm deep, 25–30 cm apart, where they are to flower, after the last frost. Seeds are large and easy to handle, so are ideal for children. Soak overnight to speed germination, which takes 7–14 days.

For earlier flowers, sow in pots indoors in March and April, in individual biodegradable pots. Plants thrive in poor, dry soil; rich soil gives lots of leaves and few flowers. Harden off and plant out in late May.
sow_tips: Sow in poor soil for more flowers.
grow: Little care is needed. Water in dry spells, particularly in pots, but do not feed, as it encourages leaves at the expense of flowers. Deadhead to prolong flowering, and trim back any straggly growth in midsummer.

Blackfly love nasturtiums, which can be useful as a sacrificial plant to keep them off crops. Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on the leaves; check and remove caterpillars. Dig out the plant after the first frost, or let it self-seed.
grow_tips: Use as a trap crop for blackfly.
harvest: Pick flowers, leaves and young seed pods from about eight weeks onward, in the morning. Pick flowers when fully open, and leaves when young and tender; older leaves can be tough. Regular picking encourages more flowers.
The green seed pods can be picked while still young and used as ‘poor man’s capers’. Pick flowers just before using, as they wilt quickly. Check for insects before eating.
use: Add the peppery leaves and colourful flowers to salads, sandwiches, pesto and herb butters. The flowers can be stuffed with soft cheese or used as a garnish for cakes and savoury dishes. The unripe seed pods can be pickled in vinegar to make a caper substitute.

Use flowers and leaves fresh, as they do not keep, though they last a day or two in the fridge in a sealed box with damp paper. Pickled seed pods keep for months in a jar. Nasturtium pesto can be frozen.
use_tips: Pickle green seed pods as capers.
Use as a colourful salad garnish.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost and avoid rich soil, as too much fertiliser makes lots of leaves but few flowers.
Deadhead and pick flowers and leaves regularly for salads, which keeps plants blooming right up to the first frosts.
Check for blackfly and cabbage white caterpillars, and hose off or hand-pick as needed. They often draw pests away from vegetables.
Leave a few seed pods to self-sow, or collect the large seeds and dry them for next year.

preserving.how: Pickle green seed pods in brine and vinegar as poor man’s capers.
Steep flowers in white wine vinegar for 2 weeks for a peppery pink vinegar.
Blend peppery leaves into pesto with nuts, cheese and oil and freeze.
Freeze flowers in ice cubes for decoration. They do not dry well.

crops.name: Onion
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open site

facts.Type: Hardy biennial bulb, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Mar–Apr from sets; Jan–Feb from seed indoors
facts.Spacing: 10 cm apart in rows 25–30 cm apart
facts.Planting depth: Tip of the set just showing

types.name: Spring-planted sets
types.when: Plant March to April · Harvest July to September
types.note: The simplest method. Small bulbs give reliable bulbs for storing through winter.

types.name: Autumn-planted (overwintering) sets
types.when: Plant September to November · Harvest June to July
types.note: Hardy types that fill the gap before spring-planted onions are ready. They do not store as long.

types.name: Grown from seed
types.when: Sow January to March indoors · Harvest August to September
types.note: Cheaper and gives larger onions, including show types, but needs a longer season.

info: Onions are the backbone of the kitchen, and a well-grown crop can feed a household for most of the year. Home-grown onions will not always be bigger than shop-bought ones, but the red varieties in particular are far sweeter and more colourful.

Most gardeners grow from sets, which are small immature bulbs that are quick, easy and reliable. Growing from seed gives a wider choice of varieties and is cheaper, but needs more time and a sunny, fertile bed with lots of weeding in the early weeks.
sow: Plant sets from mid-March to April in fertile, free-draining soil in full sun, ideally dug over the previous autumn. Push each set in with the tip just showing above the surface, 10 cm apart in rows 25–30 cm apart. Firm the soil and cover with a net if birds pull them out. Autumn-planting varieties go in during October for an early crop the following summer.

To grow from seed, sow in trays indoors in January and February at 10–15°C, prick out and plant out in April. You can also sow direct outdoors in March to April in rows 25–30 cm apart, thinning gradually. Seed-grown onions are far less prone to bolting than sets, as they have not been through a cold–warm cycle.
sow_tips: Plant the tip just above the soil so birds cannot pull the set out.
Buy heat-treated sets to reduce the risk of bolting.
Fine, firm soil gives the best crop.
Do not plant onions in the same bed more than once every three years.
grow: Keep the bed weed-free, as onions are poor at competing and have shallow roots, so hoe carefully or hand-weed. Water during dry spells in the first half of the season, but stop watering altogether from mid-July so the bulbs can ripen. Avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which leads to soft growth, bulb rot and poor storage.

Onion white rot, a soil fungus that persists for years, is the worst disease; if you have it, grow onions in containers or move to a different part of the plot. Onion fly, downy mildew and neck rot are the other problems. Avoid thick overcrowding, rotate crops and remove any diseased plants quickly.
grow_tips: Stop watering from mid-July so bulbs can ripen.
Do not mulch directly against the bulbs, which should sit near the surface.
Rotate onions every year with a three- or four-year gap.
Grow in containers if white rot is a risk.
harvest: Onions are ready from late July to September when the tops turn yellow and begin to flop over. Lift them carefully with a fork on a dry day, leaving the bulbs on the soil surface or on a wire rack in the sun to dry for a week or two. Bend over any stubborn tops by hand to encourage ripening.

If the weather is wet, move them under cover to a greenhouse, shed or porch. Onions are ready to store when their skins are papery and the necks are fully dry. Use any thick-necked or damaged bulbs first, as these will not keep.
harvest_tips: Let the foliage die back naturally before lifting.
Dry them in a warm, airy spot for two weeks.
Do not bruise onions during lifting.
use: Onions go into almost everything: fry them slowly until golden for a sweet base, caramelise them for soup, pickle small ones whole, or eat red varieties raw in salads. A freshly harvested onion is juicy and mild, and a few weeks of curing intensifies the flavour.

Cured onions keep for four to six months in nets, trays or plaited ropes in a cool, dry, airy place (4–10°C), out of frost. Check them often and remove any with soft necks. Peeled and chopped onions can be frozen raw in freezer bags for use in cooked dishes, though they will not suit salads afterwards.
use_tips: Store in nets or trays with good airflow, never in a plastic bag.
Check stored onions monthly for rot.
Freeze chopped onion in portions for cooking.
Soak sliced red onion in cold water for a milder bite.

care.job: Keep the bed weed-free by hoeing carefully, as onions have shallow roots and hate competition.
Water in dry spells but stop once bulbs begin to swell and the tops start to yellow.
Look out for white rot and downy mildew. Remove affected plants and do not grow onions there again for several years.
When the tops flop over, loosen the roots with a fork to help the bulbs ripen and then lift on a dry day.
Plant overwintering sets and firm them down if birds or frost lift them.

preserving.how: Dry in the sun or a warm, airy place until the necks are tight and the skins papery, then hang in nets or plaits and store somewhere cool, dry and frost-free.
Chop or slice and freeze raw in bags. Great for cooking, though they are soft when thawed.
Pickle small onions and shallots whole in spiced vinegar.
Make caramelised onion chutney or marmalade with sugar and balsamic vinegar.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator, or crisp in a low oven, then grind into powder.

info: Orache, or mountain spinach, is a tall, easy plant with arrow-shaped leaves in red, purple, green or gold. It tastes like a mild spinach, and the colourful forms are as ornamental as any border plant. It tolerates heat and drought far better than spinach.
It self-seeds enthusiastically, so one sowing will provide plants for years. The red variety is the most popular, adding colour to salads.
sow: Sow from March to June, 1 cm deep, in rows 30–40 cm apart, and thin to 30 cm. Seeds germinate in 1–2 weeks. Sow a short row every 3 weeks for baby leaves, or let plants grow tall for ornamental interest.
Orache grows in any soil and is tolerant of poor or alkaline soil. A sunny position gives the best colour.

Orache seeds are of two sizes; the larger black seeds are best discarded, and the small brown ones are more reliable. It needs no special care, but germinates best in cool soil, so a late March or April sowing is ideal. In hot weather, plants run quickly to seed.
grow: Water in dry spells, and pinch out the growing tip to stop plants getting too tall and to encourage branching. Remove flowers to extend leaf production. Support tall plants.
Leaf miner, aphids and slugs may attack; pick off affected leaves. Plants are generally trouble-free. Let a few go to seed for self-sown plants next year.

Orache can reach 1.5 m in rich soil, so grow it at the back of a border or along a fence. The red forms make a striking backdrop for flowers. Because it self-seeds freely, remove the flower spikes if you do not want volunteers in every corner of the garden next year.
harvest: Pick young leaves from six weeks, cutting leaf tips or whole stems regularly. Young leaves are best; older leaves get coarse. Pick in the morning.
Regular harvesting keeps the plants producing. Cut plants back hard to renew growth. Seeds are edible as well.
The leaves are best in spring and early summer; later leaves can be tough. Cut stems back hard in midsummer to promote a fresh flush of young leaves.
use: Use young orache leaves raw in salads for colour, or cook as spinach, in soups, quiches, curries, pasta and omelettes. Red varieties lose some colour when cooked. The flavour is mild and slightly salty.
Keeps 3–4 days in the fridge. Blanch and freeze for winter.
use_tips: Use red leaves raw for colour.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 30 cm apart, and water in dry weather to prevent bolting.
Pick leaves regularly and pinch out the growing tips to keep plants bushy and productive.
Remove flower spikes if you want more leaves, or let a few set seed, as orache self-sows readily.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Blanch for 1–2 minutes, squeeze out and freeze like spinach.
It self-seeds, so keep picking young leaves rather than store them.

facts.Time to harvest: Light picking in year 1; fully from year 2

info: Oregano, also called wild marjoram, is a hardy, aromatic perennial and a staple of Italian, Greek and Mexican cooking. It makes dense, spreading clumps, produces masses of pink flowers loved by bees and butterflies, and needs little care.

Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) has the strongest flavour, while golden and variegated forms are ornamental. In poor, dry, sunny places it develops the most intense flavour. Sweet marjoram is tender and best grown as an annual.
sow: Plant potted oregano from March to October in a sunny spot with poor to moderately fertile, well-drained soil. Space 30–45 cm apart. In heavy soil, mix in grit or plant in a raised bed or container. Seed can be sown on the surface of seed compost in April–May at 15–18°C, but plants vary.

Divide existing clumps in spring, replanting rooted pieces, or take cuttings in early summer. Water in until established; after that, it needs little care. Oregano makes an excellent edging plant along a path.
grow: Oregano is easy and low-maintenance. Water only in extended drought, and don’t feed. Cut back stems to 5 cm in late autumn or early spring to refresh growth, and trim after flowering to keep plants compact.

Divide clumps every 3–4 years as the centre becomes woody. Oregano can spread by creeping roots in rich soil. Aphids and mint rust occasionally appear. Wet winter soil may rot the roots, so provide good drainage.
harvest: Pick sprigs from spring, choosing the fresh tips, with the flavour peaking just before the plant flowers in midsummer. In the first year, pick lightly. Cut stems with scissors, leaving enough foliage for regrowth.
To dry, cut stems just before flowering in the morning after dew has gone, and hang bunches in a warm, airy place. Leaves dry on the stem easily. The flowers are edible and attract many pollinators.
harvest_tips: Peak flavour is just before flowering.
Leave some flowers for the bees.
use: Oregano is essential on pizza, in tomato sauces, with grilled meat, in Greek salad, and in marinades, bean dishes and roasted vegetables. Its flavour becomes more intense when dried, and it stands up well to cooking, so can be added early.

Fresh oregano keeps for a week in the fridge, wrapped in damp paper. Dried oregano keeps its flavour for a year or more in a sealed jar, and is stronger than fresh. Freezing in oil ice cubes also works.

care.job: Cut back last year's dead stems and feed lightly, as oregano prefers poor soil and full sun.
Pinch out the tips to keep plants bushy and cut stems before the plant flowers for the best flavour.
Water pots only when dry, and let a section flower to attract bees and hoverflies.
Cut back flowered stems by about half after flowering and tidy the plant before winter.
Divide established clumps every 3 to 4 years to renew them.

preserving.how: Hang bunches in a warm, airy place until crisp. Oregano is one of the herbs that dries best, with a stronger flavour than fresh.
Freeze sprigs in bags, or chopped in ice cube trays with oil.
Steep dried sprigs in oil in the fridge for dressings and pizza. Use within a week and always keep it chilled.
Mix dried leaves with thyme and marjoram for a homemade Italian seasoning.

facts.Sow: Apr–Aug, straight into the soil or in trays

types.name: White-stemmed pak choi
types.when: Sow April to August · Harvest 6–8 weeks later
types.note: The common type, with crisp white stems and dark leaves.

types.name: Green-stemmed and baby pak choi
types.when: Sow April to September
types.note: Tender and quick, ideal for baby leaves.

info: Pak choi is a fast, mild-flavoured Asian cabbage with crisp white stems and smooth green leaves, ready to eat from only four weeks. It is one of the best crops for a small space, thriving in pots, window boxes and between other vegetables.

It prefers cool conditions and can bolt in hot weather or after a cold snap in spring, so sow from late spring to late summer. Autumn sowings can be protected for winter pickings, filling a gap when there is little salad around.
sow: Sow outdoors from April to August in shallow drills 1 cm deep, in rows 20–30 cm apart, in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Avoid sowing too early, as cold nights can trigger bolting. Sow thinly and thin to 10–20 cm for full-size heads, or leave closely spaced for baby leaves.

Make successional sowings every two to three weeks for a continuous supply. Pak choi grows well in containers at least 15 cm deep, or in modules for transplanting after three weeks. Sow hardy varieties in late summer and early autumn, covered with a cloche or fleece, for winter crops.
sow_tips: Wait until late April to avoid bolting.
Sow every two or three weeks.
Use fine mesh immediately to block flea beetle.
Grow in containers for balcony cropping.
grow: Water regularly, because dry soil leads to bolting and tough leaves. Mulch to retain moisture and keep the roots cool. Feed with a liquid fertiliser every two weeks if growth slows. Pak choi has shallow roots, so weed carefully by hand.

Flea beetle, slugs and caterpillars are the main pests; cover with fine insect mesh from sowing. Keep plants well spaced for air flow and rotate with other brassicas to avoid clubroot. Overwintering plants benefit from a cloche or fleece in hard frosts.
grow_tips: Cover with fine mesh from sowing.
Pick off slugs on damp evenings.
harvest: Harvest baby leaves from about three to four weeks, cutting them with scissors about 2.5 cm above the base so the plant regrows. Full-size heads are ready in six to eight weeks, cut at the base with a knife. Harvest when the stems are plump and the leaves are smooth and glossy.

Do not let plants stand too long, as they bolt quickly and the stems become tough. A bolted plant can still be used: eat the flower shoots, which are tender and sweet like tender-stem broccoli. In winter, pick leaves from plants under cover as needed.
harvest_tips: Cut baby leaves for repeated pickings.
Harvest whole heads before they bolt.
Cut in the morning for crispness.
use: Pak choi cooks in minutes: halve it lengthwise and steam, stir-fry or grill, or add it to soups, noodle dishes and broths at the last minute. The leaves are tender and the stems stay crisp, so cook them for a little longer. Baby leaves are delicious raw in salads.

Unwashed heads keep for up to a week in the fridge in a bag. Pak choi does not freeze well, so it is best eaten fresh. Sow small amounts regularly rather than a big batch, and harvest only what you plan to eat.
use_tips: Stir-fry with garlic, ginger and soy sauce.
Halve and char on a hot grill pan.
Add to noodle soup at the end.
Eat raw as baby leaf in salads.

care.job: Cover with fine mesh straight after sowing or planting against flea beetles and cabbage root fly.
Water regularly, as dry spells cause bolting, and keep slugs under control.
Harvest the whole head when about 15 to 20 cm tall, or pick outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again crop.

pests.label: Bolting in heat or cold stress

preserving.how: Keep whole heads unwashed in a bag in the salad drawer.
Chop, blanch for 1 minute, cool and freeze for cooked dishes.
Pickle in rice vinegar, or ferment in kimchi.
Take outer leaves or cut baby plants and let them regrow.

crops.name: Parsley
varieties: Giant of Italy (flat-leaved, vigorous, strongly flavoured)
Hamburg (root parsley, grown for its root)

types.name: Flat-leaved (Italian) parsley
types.when: Sow March to August · Pick year-round
types.note: The strongest flavour, best for cooking.

types.name: Curled parsley
types.when: Sow March to August · Pick year-round
types.note: Frilly leaves, ideal for garnish and hardier in winter.

types.name: Hamburg (root) parsley
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest October to December
types.note: Grown for its parsnip-like root as well as its leaves.

info: Parsley is the most useful culinary herb, fresh and green with a clean, grassy flavour, and it grows through the year in a mild climate. It does well in partial shade, which makes it useful for awkward spots, and in pots by the back door.
Flat-leaved (French) parsley has more flavour for cooking, while curly parsley is a classic garnish. Parsley is slow to germinate, but sown in succession, it gives an almost year-round supply.
sow: Sow from March to August, 1 cm deep, directly in the soil in rows 20–30 cm apart, or in pots. Parsley seed is notoriously slow, taking 3–6 weeks to germinate. Pouring boiling water along the drill before sowing, or soaking seeds overnight, can help.

Sow in a moisture-retentive, fertile soil in partial shade in summer. Thin seedlings to 15–20 cm apart. Sow again in July–August for winter pickings in a sheltered spot or cold frame. Parsley dislikes being moved, so sow where it will grow or use deep pots.
sow_tips: Be patient: germination can take 6 weeks.
Sow again in summer for winter leaves.
grow: Keep the soil moist, since dry spells cause bolting, and give the plant a little afternoon shade in summer. Feed occasionally with a liquid feed. Remove flower stems as soon as they appear in the second year to extend picking.

Parsley is a biennial: in the second spring it flowers and the leaves lose quality, so resow each year. Carrot root fly can attack parsley, so cover with mesh. Slugs and aphids are the other pests. Protect winter plants with a cloche.
grow_tips: Cover with mesh against carrot fly.
harvest: Begin picking when plants have several leaf stems, about 10–12 weeks after sowing. Cut the outer stems at the base, leaving the inner ones to grow, and never take more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting prompts new growth.

In mild areas, parsley crops through the winter. In spring of the second year, plants will flower; leave one or two to seed for self-sown plants, and discard the rest. Pull up old plants after flowering.
harvest_tips: Cut outer stems at the base.
Take no more than a third at once.
use: Chop fresh parsley over almost any savoury dish, from soups and stews to salads, fish, potatoes and eggs. Flat-leaved parsley is the base of tabbouleh, gremolata, salsa verde, chimichurri and persillade. Add the stalks to stocks, and finish dishes with the leaves.

Fresh parsley keeps for a week in the fridge with stems in a glass of water, loosely covered. To preserve, chop and freeze it in ice-cube trays with water or oil, or freeze whole sprigs in bags. Dried parsley is a poor substitute.
use_tips: Stand stems in water in the fridge.
Add at the end for freshness.

care.job: Feed with a general fertiliser and keep the bed weed-free as growth restarts in spring.
Water regularly in dry weather, as parsley runs to seed quickly if it dries out, and harvest regularly from the outside.
Cut off flower stems from second-year plants to prolong the leaf harvest, or let a few seed for free new plants.
Cover plants with a cloche or fleece for winter pickings, or lift a few into pots on the windowsill.

preserving.how: Chop and freeze in bags or ice cube trays. It freezes better than almost any herb.
Stand stems in a glass of water with a bag over the top, or wrap in damp paper.
Mix chopped leaves into softened butter and freeze in rolls.
Blend with nuts, garlic, lemon and oil and freeze in portions.
Dry quickly in a low oven or dehydrator, though flavour is milder than fresh.

crops.name: Parsnip

facts.Type: Hardy biennial root vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 15 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

types.name: Short and wedge-shaped parsnips
types.when: Sow March to May · Harvest October to March
types.note: Suited to shallow or stony soil.

types.name: Long parsnips
types.when: Sow March to May · Harvest October to March
types.note: The biggest roots and the best flavour, needing deep, stone-free soil.

info: Parsnips are a classic winter root: sweet, nutty and completely hardy, so they stay in the ground until you need them. They are slow, taking most of the growing season, but need little attention once they are up.

They need a long, deep, stone-free soil to grow straight, which makes them a better choice for medium and large plots or deep raised beds than for small containers. Always sow fresh seed, as parsnip seed loses viability within a year.
sow: Sow from March to April once the soil has started to warm, ideally in a bed dug over deeply the previous autumn. Parsnips germinate slowly and unevenly, taking three to four weeks, and cold, wet soil rots the seed. Sow three seeds every 15 cm in drills 1–2 cm deep, then thin to the strongest seedling.

Mark the row with a quick-growing radish, as the parsnips are slow to appear and you will not want to hoe them out by accident. Do not add fresh manure, and remove stones to at least spade depth. Pre-germinating seed on damp kitchen paper for a week can speed things up, but handle the fragile roots gently.
sow_tips: Use seed from this year’s packet only.
Sow in mid-March to April; earlier sowings often rot in cold wet soil.
Interplant with radishes to mark the row and loosen the soil surface.
Keep the soil surface moist, as a crust stops seedlings emerging.
grow: Keep the bed weeded while the plants are small, then the leaves quickly shade out weeds. Water in dry spells, as uneven moisture causes splitting and forked roots. Parsnips need little feeding; too much nitrogen gives a lot of leaf and poor roots.

The main problems are carrot fly, canker (rusty-brown patches on the shoulders) and leaf miner. Resistant varieties and sowing in well-drained soil limit canker, and a barrier of fine mesh deals with carrot fly. Always wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the foliage in sun, as the sap can cause skin blistering.
grow_tips: Choose canker-resistant varieties if the disease has been a problem before.
Wear gloves when weeding and harvesting: parsnip sap can burn skin in sunlight.
Mulch lightly in summer to hold moisture.
Rotate with carrots, celery and parsley, which share the same pests.
harvest: Roots are ready from October, but the flavour improves after the first hard frosts, which convert starch to sugar. Water first if the soil is dry, then loosen with a fork well to the side of the row and lift the roots carefully, as long roots snap easily.

You can leave parsnips in the ground until early spring and lift them as needed. Lift any left by March, as new growth turns them woody and bitter. In very cold areas, cover the row with straw so you can dig in a freeze.
harvest_tips: Always loosen the soil before pulling; do not tug by the leaves.
Harvest after the first frosts for the sweetest roots.
Lift all roots by early spring before they start to regrow.
Mark the rows if you use cover, so you can find them in snow.
use: Roast parsnips with honey or maple syrup for a Sunday-lunch favourite, or make creamy parsnip and apple soup, mash them with butter, bake them into cakes or cut them into crisps. Younger, smaller roots can be eaten whole, while larger ones have a woody core that is worth cutting out.

Unwashed roots keep for two to three weeks in a bag in the fridge, or for several months layered in damp sand in a cool, frost-free place. Leaving them in the ground is the simplest storage of all. For the freezer, peel, slice, blanch for two minutes and freeze in portions, or freeze after roasting.
use_tips: Cut out the woody core from large roots before cooking.
Parboil for five minutes before roasting for crispy edges.
Do not store alongside apples, whose ethylene turns roots bitter.
Roast and freeze in trays for easy meal-prep.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 10 to 15 cm apart once they are big enough to handle, and water in the thinning gaps.
Weed carefully, as parsnips are slow starters, and keep the soil moist to avoid cracking.
Look out for parsnip canker (orange-brown patches) and carrot fly. Rotate the crop to a new bed each year.
Leave roots in the ground and lift as needed, as frost improves the flavour. Cover rows with straw in very cold spells so you can dig them.

preserving.how: Parsnips are very hardy and taste sweeter after frost, so lift as needed until early spring.
Lift, trim and keep in boxes of damp sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed.
Peel, cut into batons, blanch for 2 minutes, cool and freeze. Or freeze roasted parsnips.
Make curried parsnip soup and freeze in portions.

safety: Always wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the foliage in sun, as the sap can cause skin blistering.
Wear gloves when weeding and harvesting: parsnip sap can burn skin in sunlight.

info: Patty pan squashes are saucer-shaped summer squashes with scalloped edges, in white, yellow or green. They are as easy and productive as courgettes, with a firm texture and a delicate, nutty flavour.
Plants are compact bushes, ideal for medium gardens. Pick them small for the best flavour.
sow: Sow indoors from mid-April to May, seeds on edge, 2 cm deep, in 9 cm pots at 18–20°C. Plant out after frost in early June, 75–90 cm apart, in rich soil in full sun.
Direct sowing under cloches is possible in late May. Add compost to the planting site.
grow: Water well, at the base, and feed fortnightly with tomato fertiliser once fruiting. Mulch around the plants.
Slugs, mildew and poor pollination are the main issues. Hand-pollinate in poor weather. Remove yellowing leaves.

Patty pans are less sprawling than trailing squashes, and a single plant fits into a space about 90 cm across, so they suit raised beds and large pots (at least 40 cm). Mulch with straw to keep fruit clean and the soil moist, and remove old leaves that block light and air flow in late summer. Feeding with a high-potash fertiliser every two weeks keeps them flowering and fruiting.
harvest: Pick when 5–8 cm across, tender and firm, from July to October. Cut with a sharp knife and a short stalk. Check plants daily, since fruit grows quickly.
Regular picking prolongs cropping. Larger fruits have tougher skin, but can be stuffed.

Pick small and often. A patty pan at 4–5 cm across, with a glossy skin and tender flesh, has a far better texture and flavour than one the size of a saucer, which becomes tough and seedy. Use a sharp knife and avoid knocking the plant, because stems are brittle. The flowers are edible, too; pick male flowers in the morning for stuffing and frying.
use: Steam, grill, sauté or roast small whole patty pans, or slice and use like courgettes. Larger ones can be hollowed and stuffed. The flavour is buttery and mild.
Keeps for a week in the fridge. Slice and freeze after blanching.

Small patty pans can be steamed whole and dressed with butter and herbs, or threaded on skewers and grilled. Larger specimens can be hollowed out, stuffed with rice, herbs and cheese and baked. They also make good fritters, soups and pickles. Their firm flesh keeps its shape better than courgette.

care.job: Harden off and plant out after the last frost in a sunny spot with plenty of space.
Water at the base regularly and feed every one to two weeks with a tomato feed once fruits form.
Pick patty pans at about 5 to 8 cm across, while the skin is tender, and check plants every couple of days.

preserving.how: Keep small, firm squashes in a bag in the salad drawer.
Slice, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze in bags.
Pickle small squashes whole in spiced vinegar.
Chop into relish or chutney with onions and spices.

crops.name: Pea

facts.Sow: Mar–Jun outdoors; Oct–Nov for overwintering types
facts.Height: 45 cm to 1.8 m, depending on variety
facts.Spacing: 5 cm apart in a double row, 15 cm between rows

varieties: Hurst Green Shaft (heavy cropping, good flavour)

types.name: Earlies (round-seeded)
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest June (11–12 weeks)
types.note: Hardy, quick and compact, with sweet small peas. The best choice for the first sowings and for overwintering.

types.name: Maincrop (wrinkled)
types.when: Sow April to June · Harvest July to September (12–14 weeks)
types.note: Taller plants and heavier crops of sweeter peas, but less hardy. They need support.

types.name: Mangetout and sugar snap
types.when: Sow April to June · Harvest July to September
types.note: Eaten whole, picked young. Sugar snaps have plump, crisp pods; mangetout have flat, tender ones.

info: Peas are sweet and tender when picked fresh, and the sugars start turning to starch the moment they are harvested, which is why homegrown peas taste so different from shop-bought ones. They are easy to grow, and the crops include shelling peas, mangetout and sugar snap types.

Varieties range from dwarf types ideal for pots to tall climbers that need supports. Pea shoots, the young tips, are also delicious in salads and stir-fries, and can be grown on a windowsill in winter.
sow: Sow from March to June, in succession every 2–3 weeks, directly into well-prepared soil. Make a flat-bottomed trench about 15 cm wide and 4–5 cm deep, scatter seeds 5 cm apart, and cover with soil. Sow in a double row for support and a better crop. Water the trench first if dry.

Cold, wet soil can rot seed, so start earlier sowings in lengths of guttering in a greenhouse or cold frame, and slide them into a trench later. Hardy overwintering varieties can be sown in October to November under cloches. Mice love pea seeds, so protect with netting or mesh.
sow_tips: Sow every 2–3 weeks for a long harvest.
Sow in a wide, flat trench.
grow: Provide support as soon as seedlings appear: use pea netting, twiggy sticks (pea sticks) or canes with string. Tall varieties need a 1.8 m support; dwarf types need less. Water well during flowering and pod-swelling, and mulch to hold moisture.

Pea moth, whose caterpillars feed within the pods, can be avoided by sowing early or late, so peas flower outside June–July, or by covering with fine mesh. Birds sometimes eat young shoots; cover with netting. Powdery mildew appears in dry late summers.
grow_tips: Cover with mesh against pea moth.
harvest: Pick shelling peas when the pods are well filled but still bright green and the peas are still sweet, around 11–14 weeks from sowing. Mangetout are picked when flat and 6–7 cm long, and sugar snaps when the peas have just formed. Pick regularly, as this keeps the plants flowering.

Hold the plant with one hand and pull the pod off with the other so you don’t pull up the plant. After the final harvest, cut plants at the base and leave the roots in the soil, where nitrogen-rich nodules will feed the next crop.
harvest_tips: Pick every day or two at peak.
Pick before pods turn dull and tough.
Pick in the morning for best flavour.
use: Eat peas raw straight from the pod, steam or boil for two to three minutes, or add to risottos, pasta, soups and salads. Mangetout and sugar snaps are good raw or in stir-fries. Pea shoots are delicious in salads and as a garnish.

Peas turn starchy within hours, so cook them on the day. Freeze surplus peas quickly: shell, blanch for two minutes, cool in iced water, drain and freeze on a tray before bagging. They keep for a year. For dried peas, leave the pods on the plant until brown and rattling, then shell and dry.
use_tips: Blanch for one minute before freezing.
Cook just two or three minutes.

care.job: Cover seedlings with netting to protect from mice and pigeons, and add twiggy sticks or netting for the tendrils to climb.
Water at the base once flowers appear, as watering during flowering and podding gives a heavier crop.
Mulch the roots to keep them cool and moist, and keep weeds under control.
Pinch out the growing tips of tall types once they reach the top of the support.
Cut plants down after cropping but leave the roots in the soil to release nitrogen.

preserving.how: Shell, blanch for 2 minutes, cool in iced water and freeze on a tray. Freezing straight after picking keeps them sweet.
Keep pods unshelled in a bag in the salad drawer and shell just before use.
Leave pods on the plant until brown and rattling, then shell and dry for soups, or save seed.
Make pea and mint soup and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Peach
crops.sun_text: Full sun; a warm, sheltered wall or greenhouse

info: Peaches are self-fertile and cropping well in the UK against a warm wall or in a greenhouse. Compact varieties such as Garden Lady and Bonanza grow in large pots on patios and give a surprising harvest.
The major problem is peach leaf curl, a fungal disease spread by rain in winter and spring. Keep trees dry in winter by covering with a clear plastic sheet or growing under glass.
sow: Plant in November to March in a sheltered, sunny spot against a south or west wall, in fertile, free-draining soil. Fan-train on wires. Dwarf types can be grown in a 45 cm pot in loam-based compost.
Peaches are self-fertile. Dig in compost, plant graft 5 cm above ground, mulch, and water in. Protect from rain in winter and spring.
sow_tips: Use a large pot for dwarfs.
grow: From January to May, cover the tree with a clear plastic sheet (open at the sides) to keep rain off the leaves and prevent peach leaf curl. Hand-pollinate the flowers in March with a soft brush. Thin fruitlets to 10–15 cm apart in May to June.
Water regularly in summer, particularly pots. Feed with high-potash fertiliser. Prune in spring and summer, never winter, to avoid silver leaf. Protect blossom from frost.
harvest: Peaches are ready when the flesh near the stalk gives slightly under gentle pressure and they have a sweet scent, in August to September. They should come away from the tree with a gentle twist. Cup the fruit in your palm.
Pick over several weeks. Eat immediately for the best flavour.

Peaches ripen quickly once they colour, so check trees every day. Unripe fruits that are picked too early will soften but never gain full sweetness. When harvesting from a fan, take care not to knock branches, as fruit bruises easily.
use: Eat fresh, grill, poach, bake in pies and cobblers, or make jam, chutney and ice cream. Peaches pair with raspberries, vanilla and almonds. Skin by dipping in boiling water for 30 seconds.
Ripe fruit keeps for 2–3 days; keep unripe fruit at room temperature. Freeze slices with lemon juice, or bottle in syrup.

care.job: Cover trees against peach leaf curl from late winter until late spring with a clear plastic sheet or rain cover, keeping the sides open for pollinators. Never let rain wet the leaves.
Hand-pollinate flowers on indoor or covered trees with a soft brush on warm, dry days, as few insects are around.
Thin fruitlets to about 10 cm apart once they reach the size of a hazelnut for large, juicy peaches.
Water consistently and feed with a high-potash feed once the fruit swells. Mulch to hold moisture.
Prune after harvest in summer, cutting out the shoots that have fruited and tying in new replacements.

preserving.how: Keep ripe fruit in a single layer in the fridge.
Peel, stone and slice, toss in lemon juice and freeze on a tray.
Make peach jam with a little lemon, or spiced chutney.
Preserve halves in light sugar syrup in sterilised jars, processed in a water bath.
Slice and dry in a dehydrator until leathery.

crops.name: Pear
varieties: Doyenné du Comice (the finest flavour, needs warmth)

types.name: Early pears
types.when: Pick late August to September · Eat within days
types.note: Juicy but short-lived. They go soft from the inside very quickly, so pick slightly under-ripe and eat within a week.

types.name: Mid-season pears
types.when: Pick late September to early October · Keep 2–4 weeks
types.note: The reliable all-rounders, best ripened indoors for a week after picking.

types.name: Late pears
types.when: Pick October · Store until December or later
types.note: Slow to ripen but the richest in flavour. Store hard in a cool place and bring into the warm to ripen.

info: Pears are rewarding trees with spectacular spring blossom, and they thrive in the UK, especially in the south and east. Trees on a quince rootstock are compact enough for small gardens when trained as cordons, espaliers or fans against a wall.
Most pears need a pollination partner, and pears flower early, so shelter from frost is important. Dessert pears need to be picked slightly unripe and ripened indoors for the best flavour.
sow: Plant bare-root trees from November to March in a warm, sheltered position with fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil. Pears hate waterlogging and extreme dryness. Check the pollination group of your variety, and plant partners flowering at the same time, or use compatible varieties from neighbours.

Stake firmly, plant with the graft union 5 cm above ground, and mulch with compost. Quince A rootstock gives a semi-dwarf tree; Quince C is more dwarfing. Cordons and espaliers need a post-and-wire frame.
sow_tips: Use dwarfing rootstock for small gardens.
grow: Prune in winter (November to February) to an open framework, and in summer for trained forms. Cordons and espaliers are summer-pruned in August by cutting side shoots to 3 leaves beyond the basal cluster. Thin fruitlets in June to one or two per cluster.

Water young trees and mulch every spring. Pear scab, pear midge and fireblight are the main problems. Remove diseased branches and burn them. Clear fallen leaves in autumn. Protect blossom from frost with fleece.
harvest: Pick pears while they are still hard. Early varieties are ready in August to September, while late types are picked in October. To test, lift the fruit gently: if it comes off easily with the stalk, it is ready. Do not wait until they are soft on the tree, since they rot from the inside.
