Ripen pears indoors at room temperature: Conference takes about a week, Comice up to two weeks after cool storage. Check daily, and eat when they give slightly at the neck.
harvest_tips: Do not leave on the tree to soften.
use: Eat fresh, poach in wine or syrup, bake in tarts and crumbles, or pair with blue cheese, walnuts and rocket in salads. Pears make wonderful chutney, jam, and perry. Poached pears with chocolate sauce are a classic.
Store hard, unblemished pears in a cool (0–4°C), dark, frost-free place for 1–3 months, wrapped in paper and not touching. Bring to room temperature to ripen. Poached or stewed pears freeze well.

care.job: Prune established trees in the dormant season, taking out dead, crossing and congested branches and shortening overlong shoots.
Mulch around the base with compost and feed with a general fertiliser, keeping the mulch away from the trunk.
Protect blossom with fleece on frosty nights where you can, as pears flower early and frost easily ruins the crop.
Thin heavy crops in June to one or two fruits per cluster for larger pears and a steadier crop each year.
Summer prune trained trees such as cordons and espaliers, and water young trees in dry spells.
Clear fallen fruit and leaves to reduce disease, and check stakes and ties before winter winds.

preserving.how: Pick before fully ripe and keep unbruised fruit in single layers, not touching, in a cool, dark, frost-free place. Bring into the warmth to ripen.
Keep ripe pears in the salad drawer.
Peel, core and poach lightly, then freeze in syrup. Raw pears go brown and mushy.
Make pear chutney or pear and ginger jam, or bottle in syrup.
Press into juice and freeze, or ferment into perry.

crops.name: Perpetual spinach
crops.sun_text: Full sun to shade; tolerates poorer light

facts.Type: Hardy biennial leaf vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 20–30 cm apart in rows 30–45 cm apart
facts.Time to harvest: 8–12 weeks, then for up to 18 months

info: Perpetual spinach, also called spinach beet or leaf beet, is a reliable, hard-working relative of chard that gives you spinach-style leaves almost all year. Unlike true spinach, it resists bolting in summer and tolerates cold, shade and poor soil.

It is a good choice for beginners and for those who find spinach difficult: one sowing in spring can crop for up to eighteen months. The leaves are slightly coarser than true spinach but cook just as well and have a mild, earthy flavour.
sow: Sow in March to July in shallow drills 2–3 cm deep, 30–45 cm apart, in ordinary garden soil in sun or partial shade. The seeds are corky clusters, so thin seedlings to the strongest when 5 cm tall, finishing at 20–30 cm apart. A second sowing in August gives winter leaves.

You can also sow into modules in March and April and plant out, which is useful if slugs are a problem. Perpetual spinach does well in large containers of at least 20 cm depth, and can be picked as baby leaf from only four to five weeks.
sow_tips: Thin to the strongest seedling per cluster.
Sow in August for winter leaves.
Choose partial shade in hot spots.
A 20 cm pot is enough for baby leaf.
grow: This is a low-effort crop. Water in dry weather to keep the leaves tender, and mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Feed with a general fertiliser a couple of times in summer. Cut off flower stems in the second year to keep the plants cropping.

Slugs, leaf miner and birds are the main problems. Pinch off damaged leaves and use nets or fleece when seedlings are young. In cold regions, cover winter plants with a cloche. Replace plants after 12–18 months, when they tend to run to seed.
grow_tips: Mulch to cut watering and weeding.
Remove flower stems to extend picking.
Protect winter plants with a cloche.
harvest: Pick leaves when they are 10–15 cm long, a few from each plant at a time, working from the outside in. Regular cutting encourages new growth. Young leaves are the tenderest and can be eaten raw in salads, whereas older ones should be cooked.

Plants will often crop right through winter in sheltered gardens and send up flower stems in the second spring. Remove these to extend the harvest, and clear the old plants in summer once they become tough and bitter, replacing them with a new sowing.
harvest_tips: Pick regularly from the outside in.
use: Cook perpetual spinach like true spinach: wilt it in a pan with garlic, stir it into curries, soups, pasta and bakes, or use it in pies and omelettes. The leaves are sturdier than spinach, so allow a couple of extra minutes. The midribs are edible when young, or can be chopped finely.

Fresh leaves keep for three to four days in a bag in the fridge, but it is easier to leave them growing and pick as needed. To freeze, wash, blanch for two minutes, squeeze out the water and freeze in portions.
use_tips: Wilt with garlic and a squeeze of lemon.
Cook slightly longer than true spinach.

care.job: Water in dry spells and pick leaves regularly from the outside to keep growth coming.
Cut off any flower stalks that appear to prolong cropping, and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser if growth slows.
Cover plants with a cloche or fleece in winter and pick sparingly through cold weather.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Blanch for 2 minutes, cool, squeeze out the water and freeze in portions.
It crops almost all year and survives frost, so pick fresh from the plant.
Make into soups, sauces, or spinach and ricotta fillings and freeze.

facts.Type: Tender perennial, grown as an annual

info: Physalis, the Cape gooseberry, forms papery lantern-like husks, each containing a sweet-tart golden berry. Easy to grow like tomatoes in a warm, sunny site, the plants are compact, productive and ornamental.
They are self-fertile, so one plant is enough. Each lantern ripens inside its husk, protected from birds.
sow: Sow in March to April, 5 mm deep, in pots at 18–20°C. Prick out into pots. Plant out in June, 60 cm apart, in a sunny, sheltered spot or large pots (30 cm) of compost.
Grow under glass for best results. Stake plants when they get tall.

Seedlings grow quickly and can be lanky if kept too warm and shaded, so give them the brightest windowsill you have, and turn the pots regularly. Pot on into 9 cm pots, then 3-litre pots, before moving them to the final position. Harden off for two weeks to avoid shock.
grow: Water regularly and feed fortnightly with tomato fertiliser once flowering. Pinch out the growing tip when 1 m tall. Not much side-shoot pinching is needed.
Aphids and whitefly are the main pests. Plants tolerate poor soil; rich soil gives too much foliage.

Physalis are thirsty, so water regularly, and mulch the soil to conserve moisture. Over-feeding with nitrogen produces tall, leafy plants with few fruits; use a tomato fertiliser once the first flowers appear. If plants become too tall, cut the tops to keep them manageable. Insects pollinate the flowers, but in a greenhouse, a gentle shake of the stems helps.
harvest: Pick when the husks turn papery and golden, and berries are orange, from September to October. Ripe fruits fall to the ground, where they can be collected. Pick before frost.
Fruit ripens inside the husk; unripe fruit can be ripened indoors in the husk.

Pick the fruits when the husks are straw-coloured and papery. The berries inside are orange and sweet. If frost threatens, cut the whole plant and hang it upside-down in a frost-free, airy place such as a shed or garage; the fruits will continue to ripen in their husks for several weeks.
use: Peel back the husk and eat the berries raw, dip in chocolate, add to fruit salads, or make jam. They are sweet and tangy with a tropical flavour. Cook in sauces for desserts.
Fruit keeps for weeks in its husk in a cool place. Freeze berries on a tray, or dry for snacks.

care.job: Harden off and plant out after the last frost in a sunny, sheltered spot or greenhouse, and support plants with canes.
Water regularly and feed every two weeks with a tomato feed once flowers appear, and pinch out the tips to keep plants compact.
Pick fruits when the papery husks turn pale gold and dry, or when they fall naturally.

preserving.how: Keep fruit in its papery husk in a cool, dry, airy place, as the husk protects it.
Slice or leave whole and dry in a dehydrator like raisins.
Freeze husked fruit on a tray, then bag.
Make a tangy jam with lemon juice.

crops.name: Plum

facts.Sow: Plant Nov–Mar, or container trees in spring

varieties: Marjorie’s Seedling (late, self-fertile, good in the north)

types.name: Early plums
types.when: Harvest August
types.note: Quick-ripening dessert types.

types.name: Mid and late plums
types.when: Harvest late August to September
types.note: Heavy croppers for eating, cooking and freezing.

types.name: Gages and damsons
types.when: Harvest September to October
types.note: Gages are sweet and rich; damsons are sharp and ideal for jam and gin.

info: Plums, damsons and gages are among the most rewarding tree fruits, with a juicy, sweet flesh and a rich flavour you rarely find in shops. Many varieties are self-fertile, so a single tree gives good crops without a pollination partner.

Plums flower early, so a sheltered spot is important; blossom damaged by late frost is the main cause of poor crops. Fan-trained trees on a sunny wall are space-saving and well protected, and compact rootstocks such as Pixy suit smaller gardens.
sow: Plant bare-root trees in November to March, or container-grown trees in spring, in a sunny, sheltered, frost-free spot with fertile, well-drained soil. Avoid frost pockets at the bottom of slopes, since blossom is very susceptible to late frosts.

Stake firmly and plant with the graft union 5 cm above ground level. Water well and mulch around the trunk. Plums are pruned in spring or summer, never winter, to avoid silver leaf disease. Fan-trained trees need a frame of horizontal wires on a warm wall or fence.
sow_tips: Fan-train against a sunny wall for shelter.
grow: Water well in the first years and in dry spells, and mulch each spring. Prune in spring or summer only, when the sap is rising, to lessen the risk of silver leaf and bacterial canker. Remove dead, diseased and crossing branches, and keep the centre open.

In good years, trees overload, so thin fruitlets in June to 5–8 cm apart, preventing broken branches and improving the size. Support heavy-laden branches. Plum moth causes maggots in fruit, aphids attack young leaves, and wasps attack ripe fruit. Brown rot is common in wet weather.
grow_tips: Prune only from spring to late summer.
harvest: Plums are ready from August to September, depending on variety. They should be fully coloured and slightly soft, and come away from the tree with a gentle twist. Pick over several visits, since a tree’s fruit ripens over two or three weeks. Cooking plums can be picked a little earlier.

Leave dessert plums to ripen on the tree for the best sugar. Handle the delicate skin carefully, as bruises spoil the fruit. Pick regularly to reduce wasp and brown-rot damage, and remove rotten fruit.
harvest_tips: Leave dessert plums to ripen fully.
use: Eat ripe plums fresh, or bake in tarts, crumbles, cakes and clafoutis, roast with spices, or turn into jam, chutney, sauces (such as Chinese plum sauce) and plum gin. Damsons are tart and ideal for jam, cheese and gin. Plums pair well with almonds, cinnamon and duck.

Ripe plums keep 3–5 days in the fridge. To freeze, halve and stone, freeze on a tray and bag for up to a year. Plum jam and chutney preserve gluts nicely, and plums can be bottled in syrup or dried into prunes in a low oven.

care.job: Protect early blossom with fleece when frost is forecast, and feed and mulch around the base in spring.
Thin heavily laden branches in June so fruit grows bigger, and prop or tie up branches before they bend or snap under the weight.
Water young trees in dry weather and tackle aphids on shoot tips by encouraging natural predators.
Prune only in summer, never in winter, to avoid silver leaf disease. Remove dead, crossing and diseased wood on dry days.
Harvest promptly to limit wasp damage, and remove any rotting fruit hanging on the tree, as it spreads brown rot.

preserving.how: Keep ripe fruit in a single layer in the fridge.
Halve and stone, then freeze on a tray and bag.
Plum jam sets easily with sharper varieties. Chutney uses up windfalls.
Preserve halves in light sugar syrup in sterilised jars and process in a water bath.
Dry halved plums into prunes in a dehydrator or low oven.

crops.name: Popcorn

facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors; plant out late May–June
facts.Time to harvest: 16–24 weeks from sowing, plus 2–4 weeks drying

varieties: Strawberry (small red cobs, ornamental and a reliable popper)
Tom Thumb (compact and early, suits cooler areas)
Dakota Black (dark kernels that pop white)
Glass Gem (multicoloured cobs; check the supplier says it pops)
Any early variety sold as popcorn (availability varies by supplier)

info: Popcorn is a type of maize with hard, starchy kernels that burst when they are heated. It is grown much like sweetcorn, and the reward is a jar of your own kernels that pop into fresh, tender popcorn. The plants are tall and handsome, and the small cobs in red, blue and yellow are a talking point on the plot, which makes it a lovely crop to grow with children.

It needs more summer than sweetcorn, because the cobs must ripen fully and then dry. In the UK that means a warm, sunny, sheltered spot, an early or compact variety and a good start indoors. In a poor summer the crop may be small, so treat it as a fun extra, not a main crop. Do not grow it near sweetcorn, because cross-pollination makes the sweetcorn starchy and tough and spoils the popcorn kernels.
sow: Sow indoors from mid-April to mid-May, 2.5 cm deep, one seed per 7–9 cm pot or loo-roll tube at 18–21°C, because the roots dislike disturbance. Seedlings appear in about a week. An early start gives the cobs the long season they need to ripen and dry.

Harden off for about 10 days and plant out in late May to June, once the frost has passed, in a sunny, sheltered spot with rich soil that holds moisture. Plant in a block of at least 4 by 4 plants, 30–40 cm apart, because corn is pollinated by the wind. Keep popcorn at least 10 m from any sweetcorn, or sow one of them two to three weeks later so they do not flower together.
sow_tips: Sow early to give the cobs time to dry.
Plant in a block, not a row.
Use deep pots or loo-roll tubes.
grow: Water well in dry spells, particularly when the tassels and silks appear and the cobs are filling. Mulch to hold in moisture, and feed with a high-potash fertiliser once the cobs start to swell. Earth up around the base of the stems and stake in exposed spots, as the plants are tall and shallow-rooted.

Weed gently. Mice, squirrels, badgers and birds will raid the cobs, so net or fence the patch as they ripen. Unlike sweetcorn, popcorn is not picked at the milky stage but left on the plant to ripen and dry, so it needs protecting for longer.
grow_tips: Water when the tassels and silks appear.
Earth up and stake in windy spots.
Protect the cobs for longer than sweetcorn.
harvest: Do not pick popcorn green. Leave the cobs on the plant until the husks turn brown and papery and the stalks begin to die back, usually in September or October. If frost or wet weather threatens, cut the cobs with a short stalk and bring them indoors to finish drying.

Peel back the husks and hang the cobs in a warm, dry, airy place, such as a porch, shed or airing cupboard, for 2 to 4 weeks, until the kernels are hard and you cannot dent one with a fingernail. Twist the kernels off with your thumbs, then test-pop a small handful. Kernels that are too moist chew rather than pop, and kernels that are too dry leave many unpopped, so adjust the drying time if you need to.
harvest_tips: Leave the cobs on the plant until the husks are brown.
Dry for 2–4 weeks in a warm, airy place.
Test-pop a few kernels before storing.
Rub the kernels off with your thumbs.
use: Pop the kernels in a heavy pan with a lid and a little oil until the popping slows, then season with salt, or with smoked paprika, cinnamon sugar, grated Parmesan or chopped rosemary. The popcorn recipe on this site shows how, step by step.

Dried kernels keep well in an airtight jar in a cool, dark place for a year or more, which makes popcorn one of the easiest crops to store. Popped corn goes stale within a day or two, so pop only what you will eat. Popcorn is a choking hazard for babies and toddlers, so wait until children are older.
use_tips: Store dried kernels in an airtight jar.
Pop only what you will eat.
Season with herbs from the garden.
Keep popcorn away from babies and toddlers.

care.job: Harden off and plant in a block, 30 to 40 cm apart, and keep it well away from sweetcorn to avoid cross-pollination.
Water regularly, particularly when the tassels and silks appear and while the cobs fill out.
Earth up around the base of the stems and weed carefully, as roots are shallow. Stake in exposed sites.
Feed with a high-potash fertiliser once the cobs start to swell, and net them against mice, squirrels and birds.
Leave the cobs on the plant until the husks are brown and papery, then pick and hang them to dry for 2 to 4 weeks.

pests.label: Poor pollination if grown in a single row

preserving.how: Leave the cobs on the plant until the husks are brown and papery, then hang them in a warm, airy place for 2–4 weeks until the kernels are hard. Rub the kernels off and keep them in airtight jars in a cool, dark place.
Pop a small handful of the dried kernels. If many stay unpopped, dry the cobs for another week or two and test again.
Let popped popcorn cool completely, then keep it in an airtight container. It goes stale quickly, so pop only what you will eat.

crops.name: Potato
crops.sun_text: Full sun (6+ hours); tolerates light shade with a smaller crop

facts.Type: Half-hardy tuberous perennial, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: 30–40 cm apart in rows 60–75 cm apart

varieties: Maris Peer (second early, creamy and versatile)
Pink Fir Apple (late salad, superb flavour)

types.name: First earlies
types.when: Plant mid-March to April · Harvest June to July (10–12 weeks)
types.note: Quick-maturing, small to medium new potatoes with thin skins and a waxy, sweet flavour. They are lifted before blight arrives and do not store, so eat them fresh. Ideal for pots and bags.

types.name: Second earlies
types.when: Plant late March to April · Harvest July to August (13–15 weeks)
types.note: A slightly larger, heavier crop than first earlies, just as good boiled or in salads. Many are at their best in July and can be stored for a few weeks.

types.name: Maincrop
types.when: Plant mid-April to May · Harvest September to October (18–20 weeks)
types.note: The biggest yields and the best keepers. Lift in autumn once the foliage dies back, cure the skins and store them in the dark for winter. Best for roasting, chips, baking and mash, and they need the most space.

info: Potatoes are among the most productive and satisfying crops you can grow, and freshly dug new potatoes taste far better than anything from a shop. They are grown from ‘seed’ potatoes, which are small tubers saved or sold for planting, and come in three groups: first earlies, second earlies and maincrops.

You can grow them in open ground, raised beds, large pots, sacks or bags, making them suitable for gardens of almost any size. Always buy certified seed potatoes, as supermarket potatoes can carry disease and are not treated for planting.
sow: From late January, stand seed potatoes in egg boxes with the end with most ‘eyes’ upwards, in a cool, bright, frost-free place. This is called chitting, and gives short, sturdy shoots that give earlier crops. Plant first earlies in mid-March to early April, second earlies in early to mid April and maincrops from mid-April to May.

Dig a trench or individual holes 10–15 cm deep, plant with the shoots upwards, space 30–40 cm apart and cover with soil. In large pots or potato bags, put 15 cm of compost in the base, plant three tubers per 30–40 cm pot, then add compost as they grow. Protect emerging shoots from frost with fleece or soil.
sow_tips: Chit seed potatoes in a bright, cool place for six weeks before planting.
Rub off all but 3–4 of the strongest shoots for bigger potatoes.
Cover shoots with fleece if a late frost is forecast.
Never plant shop-bought potatoes: use certified seed.
grow: When shoots reach 20–25 cm, ‘earth up’ by drawing soil from between the rows up around the stems, leaving just the tops showing. This stops tubers turning green and poisonous and boosts yield. Repeat every two weeks until the foliage meets across the row. Water well in dry weather, especially once the plants flower.

Potato blight, a fast-spreading disease in warm, humid weather, is the biggest threat, usually from July. Check leaves regularly for brown patches; if you see them, cut off all foliage straight away and bin it, leaving tubers in the soil for two weeks before lifting. Choosing blight-resistant varieties and growing earlies, which are lifted before blight arrives, are the best defences.
grow_tips: Earth up regularly to stop tubers turning green.
Water deeply once plants are in flower.
Lift earlies before blight season to dodge the disease.
Rotate with a three- or four-year gap, as potatoes share diseases with tomatoes.
harvest: First earlies are ready from June, when plants flower, around 10–12 weeks after planting. Lift carefully with a fork well away from the stems, and dig a test plant first. Second earlies follow from July. Lift maincrops from September, when the foliage has yellowed and died back.

For maincrops, cut off the haulm (the top growth) about two weeks before lifting so skins can set, which helps storage. Dig on a dry day and leave the tubers on the surface for a few hours to dry, then brush off the soil. Remove any damaged or slug-eaten tubers and eat them first.
harvest_tips: Dig a test plant of earlies before lifting the whole row.
Use a fork, pushing it in well away from the stems.
Cut off maincrop foliage two weeks before lifting.
Do not wash potatoes you plan to store.
use: New potatoes are best boiled with mint and tossed in butter, while salad varieties suit potato salads. Maincrops are the roasting, mashing, chipping and baking potatoes, and the waxy or floury texture of each variety decides what it does best. Never eat green or sprouting tubers, as they contain solanine, which is toxic; cut off any green patches completely.

Earlies are best eaten within days. Cure maincrops by drying them for a few hours, then store in paper or hessian sacks in a cool, dark, frost-free place at 4–10°C, where they keep for five months or more. Never store potatoes in plastic bags or in the fridge, which makes them sweet and damp. Store them away from onions.
use_tips: Keep potatoes in the dark to stop them turning green.
Check stored potatoes monthly and remove any rotting ones.
Never eat green or sprouting tubers.
Boil waxy varieties and bake or roast floury ones.

care.job: Chit seed potatoes on a cool, bright windowsill with the eyes upwards until short, sturdy shoots form.
Earth up by drawing soil over the shoots when they reach 20 cm, leaving the tips showing, to stop tubers turning green. Repeat every two weeks.
Cover shoots with fleece if a late frost is forecast, as frost blackens the foliage.
Water well in dry spells, especially once the plants flower, as this is when tubers swell.
Check for blight in warm, humid weather. If leaves blacken, cut off all the foliage and wait 2 to 3 weeks before lifting.
Cut down the haulms of maincrops two weeks before lifting so the skins set for storing.

preserving.how: Let skins harden, brush off soil, discard damaged tubers and store in paper sacks or hessian in a cool, dark, frost-free place at around 5–10°C. Exclude light to avoid green tubers.
Cold turns starch to sugar, giving sweet taste and dark chips and roasties, so avoid the fridge for raw potatoes.
Freeze as chips, roasties or mash, or par-boiled wedges, on a tray first.
Maincrop potatoes can stay in the soil for a few weeks after the foliage dies, but lift before slugs and blight spores do harm.
Make leek and potato soup and freeze in portions.

safety: This stops tubers turning green and poisonous and boosts yield.
Never eat green or sprouting tubers, as they contain solanine, which is toxic; cut off any green patches completely.
Never eat green or sprouting tubers.

images.alt: Freshly harvested potatoes spilling from a hessian sack onto soil

crops.name: Pumpkin

facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors; plant out late May–June

varieties: Baby Bear (small, sweet, good for pies)
Rouge Vif d’Etampes (French heirloom, good for soup)

types.name: Carving pumpkins
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest September to October
types.note: Big, smooth fruit with thin flesh. Perfect for lanterns.

types.name: Eating pumpkins
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest September to October
types.note: Smaller, sweeter, denser flesh that is better for soup and roasting.

info: Pumpkins are great fun to grow and rewarding, producing a spectacular crop of large orange fruits in autumn for Halloween carving and for the kitchen. They are vigorous, hungry and thirsty plants that need space, sun and rich soil, but they need little else.
Choose between giants grown for show, carving types and smaller varieties good for eating. Trailing stems can be trained up a fence or over a compost heap to save ground.
sow: Sow indoors in late April to May, putting seeds on their edge 2 cm deep in 9 cm pots of compost at 18–20°C. Germination takes about a week. Grow on in good light, and harden off over 10 days in late May.

Plant out in June once the frost has passed, into a sunny site and into soil enriched with plenty of compost or well-rotted manure, preferably in a shallow dip to hold water. Allow 1–1.5 m between plants, with their trailing stems given room to spread.
sow_tips: Plant into a mound or dip with lots of compost.
Give each plant at least a square metre.
grow: Water deeply and regularly, especially while fruits swell, and feed weekly with tomato fertiliser from the time the first fruits set. Mulch to retain moisture. For larger fruits, limit each plant to two or three pumpkins and remove the rest, and pinch out the tips of stems beyond the last fruit.

Hand-pollinate female flowers (the ones with a tiny pumpkin behind them) with a male flower, if bees are scarce. Slide a tile or piece of wood under the fruits to keep them off wet soil. Powdery mildew, slugs and aphids are the main pests.
grow_tips: Limit to 2–3 fruits per plant for larger pumpkins.
harvest: Harvest pumpkins in late September to October when the skin is hard enough that a thumbnail will not dent it, the stalk is dry and woody, and the leaves have started to die back. Cut with a sharp knife, leaving a 10 cm piece of stalk as a handle. Never carry by the stalk.
Bring them in before the first hard frost, which spoils the fruit. To harden the skins for storage, leave them in a sunny, dry place such as a greenhouse or windowsill for 10 days.
harvest_tips: Harvest when the skin is hard and the stalk is dry.
Pick before the first hard frost.
Cure in the sun for 10 days.
use: Pumpkin flesh is good roasted, in soups, curries, pies, risottos, breads and muffins. Smaller, sweeter types are best for eating; large carving pumpkins are watery and bland, but can still be used for soup. Roast the seeds with salt or spices for a snack.

Cured pumpkins with the stalk attached will store for three to six months in a cool (10–15°C), dry, frost-free place such as a garage or spare room. Cut pumpkins keep for a week in the fridge. Roast or purée surplus flesh and freeze in portions.
use_tips: Store cured pumpkins in a cool, dry place.

care.job: Harden off and plant out after the last frost, on a mound of rich soil or compost, leaving 90 cm or more between plants.
Water generously at the base, and feed every one to two weeks with a tomato feed once fruits set.
Pinch out the tips of vines after four or five fruits set so energy goes into ripening fewer, bigger pumpkins.
Place a piece of wood or straw under developing fruit to keep it off damp soil and discourage rot.
Cut pumpkins with a piece of stalk once the skin is hard and sounds hollow when tapped, then cure in a sunny, dry spot before storing.

preserving.how: Harvest with a long stalk before frost, cure in the sun for 10 days, then store on shelves somewhere dry and cool at about 10–15°C.
Roast or steam, scoop the flesh and freeze as purée in tubs, or cube and freeze on a tray.
Make soup and freeze in portions.
Cook with apple, onion and spices.
Rinse, dry and roast pumpkin seeds with salt for a snack.

info: Quince is a beautiful small tree with large pink-white blossom in spring, and golden fragrant fruit in autumn. It is undemanding, self-fertile, and cropping reliably in sheltered spots in the south of England.
The fruit is hard and astringent raw, but cooks to a gorgeous rosy red with a perfumed, honeyed flavour. A single tree can yield dozens of fruits, making it great for preserves.
sow: Plant bare-root trees from November to March in a sunny, sheltered position with moist but well-drained soil. Quince tolerates heavy soils better than most fruit trees, but dislikes drought. Stake and mulch.
Self-fertile, so one tree is enough. It flowers late, avoiding most frosts. Container-grown plants can be planted year-round with watering.
grow: Little pruning is needed. Remove dead, crossing and diseased branches in winter and keep the centre open. Water young trees in dry weather. Mulch every spring.
Quince leaf blight and fireblight may occur in wet summers; remove affected shoots. Thin heavy crops of fruit in June to improve size.
harvest: Harvest in October when the fruit turns from green to golden yellow and smells fragrant, before frosts. Pick gently with the stalk, since they bruise. Hold fruit for a few weeks to develop aroma.
Rub off the grey down before using.

Quinces ripen gradually; if frost threatens before they colour, harvest regardless and let them ripen indoors, where their perfume will fill the room. Do not store them next to other fruit, as they can taint the flavour of apples and pears.
use: Quince is too hard to eat raw. Poach it in sugar syrup for an hour until rose pink, bake in tarts, make quince jelly, membrillo (quince paste, perfect with cheese), or add a slice to apple pie for fragrance.
Store whole fruit in a cool, dark place for 2–3 months. Membrillo keeps for a year. Cooked quince freezes well.

care.job: Prune lightly in late winter, taking out dead, crossing and congested branches, and feed and mulch around the base.
Protect blossom with fleece when frosts are forecast, as quinces flower relatively early.
Water young trees in dry spells and thin heavy crops of fruit for larger quinces.
Pick fruit when it turns golden yellow and is fragrant, before the first hard frosts, and store carefully as it bruises easily.

preserving.how: Pick when yellow and fragrant, wrap in paper and store in single layers in a cool, dark place, away from other fruit as the scent spreads.
Cook quince pulp with sugar into a thick paste, set in tins and slice for cheese boards.
Rich in pectin, quince makes a deep pink jelly or jam.
Peel, core and poach, then freeze in syrup. Raw quince is hard and not worth freezing.
Make Spanish-style membrillo and wrap in baking paper.

facts.Type: Hardy perennial chicory, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Jun–Jul for autumn and winter heads
facts.Spacing: Thin to 25–30 cm apart in rows 30–40 cm apart

info: Radicchio is a red-leaved Italian chicory with a bold, pleasantly bitter flavour and a striking colour. It is hardier than lettuce, so provides fresh salads in autumn and winter, and it is less demanding to grow than many people assume.

There are round-headed types such as Palla Rossa, and elongated ones such as Treviso. The red colour develops as the weather cools, and the bitterness mellows after cold or when the plants are blanched. They are a good crop for medium or large plots.
sow: Sow in June and July for a crop in autumn and early winter. Sowing too early causes the plants to bolt rather than head up. Sow thinly in a seedbed or in modules, 1 cm deep, and thin or transplant to 25–30 cm apart when the seedlings are 10 cm tall.

Choose a sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil. In very dry conditions, water the drill before sowing. Pests rarely trouble the young plants but slugs may nibble, so protect with traps. Plants establish well, and the roots develop deeply, making them reasonably drought-tolerant.
sow_tips: Sow in June–July; earlier sowings bolt.
Keep the soil moist during germination.
grow: Water regularly through the summer, keeping the soil moist but not waterlogged. Hoe between plants to control weeds. Cut off the foliage 2.5 cm above the ground in late summer or autumn to encourage a tight head of leaves to form; this also makes the plant produce a neat, red, round head of leaves.

Slugs and snails are the main problem, along with aphids. Fleece or a cloche in late autumn protects the heads from frost damage and wet. Radicchio is hardy but heads can suffer in very hard winters; harvest before prolonged freezing.
grow_tips: Cut the foliage back in late summer to promote tight heads.
Protect heads with fleece in frost.
harvest: Cut heads when they feel firm and are about the size of a grapefruit, from October to December. Cut just above ground level with a sharp knife, leaving the root in the soil; many plants will re-grow loose heads in spring. Harvest before hard frosts to protect the heads.

To tame the bitterness, you can lift whole plants in November, trim the leaves to 3 cm and pack the roots in boxes of damp compost in a dark, cool place. The pale, tender new leaves (chicons) grow in three to four weeks and are sweet and delicate.
harvest_tips: Force roots in the dark for pale, sweet chicons.
Leave the root; it may regrow.
use: Slice radicchio into salads for colour and crunch, balancing the bitterness with sweet fruit, nuts, honey or a creamy dressing. It is also delicious grilled or roasted, which softens the flavour and turns it sweet and smoky. Add it to risotto, pasta and pizza, or braise it gently in butter and wine.

Whole heads keep in the fridge for two weeks, wrapped in damp kitchen paper in a bag. Remove the outer leaves before eating. Cooked radicchio can be frozen, but fresh leaves lose their crisp texture on freezing.
use_tips: Soak shredded leaves in cold water to soften the bitterness.
Grill wedges with olive oil and balsamic vinegar.
Balance with honey, pears or walnuts.
Add to risotto at the end.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 25 to 30 cm apart and water regularly to prevent bitterness and bolting.
In late summer, cut back plants that have not hearted up to 2.5 cm above the soil to encourage a tight new heart to form.
Protect hearts from frost with a cloche or fleece and cut when firm and tightly closed.

preserving.how: Keep whole heads in a bag in the salad drawer.
Late heads keep well in a cool, frost-free shed.
Grill, roast or braise and freeze in tubs.
Pickle strips in vinegar for a bitter-sweet relish.

crops.name: Radish

facts.Spacing: Thin to 2–3 cm apart in rows 15 cm apart

varieties: Rat-tail (grown for its edible seed pods)

types.name: Summer radishes
types.when: Sow March to September · Harvest in 3–5 weeks
types.note: Small, crisp, quick roots. Sow a short row every fortnight and pick young before they turn woolly.

types.name: Winter radishes
types.when: Sow July to August · Harvest October to December
types.note: Large, dense roots with a sharper taste that store well. Mooli is the best known.

info: Radishes are the fastest crop you can grow, going from seed to salad in as little as three weeks. They are ideal for beginners and children, for sowing between slower crops and for filling gaps, and they grow in a pot on a windowsill as happily as in a bed.

They prefer cool, moist weather and turn hot, woody and bitter if they dry out or are left too long. Small, frequent sowings give the best flavour, while winter radishes such as mooli and Chinese radish are sown in summer for autumn and winter roots.
sow: Sow thinly in shallow drills 1 cm deep from March to September, in rows 15 cm apart, and cover lightly. Seedlings appear within a few days. For a continuous supply, sow a short row every two weeks rather than all at once. In summer, choose a spot with partial shade to stop plants bolting in heat.

Sow winter radishes such as mooli, black Spanish and China Rose in July and August, and thin to 15 cm apart as they grow larger. Radishes are great sown between slower crops like parsnips, where they mark the row and are harvested long before they compete.
sow_tips: Sow little and often, ideally every two weeks.
Sow in part shade in summer to avoid bolting.
Use a pot at least 15 cm deep for a windowsill crop.
Sow winter radishes in midsummer for autumn harvests.
grow: Radishes need very little care apart from steady moisture. Water regularly, particularly in dry weather, because drought gives hot, woody roots that split. Thin seedlings to 2–3 cm apart once they are about 2 cm tall, giving each root room to swell.

Flea beetle is the main pest, peppering the leaves with tiny holes. Cover rows with fine mesh or fleece from sowing and keep plants watered, as healthy plants grow away from damage. Keep weeds down early, and rotate radishes with the rest of the brassica group to avoid clubroot.
grow_tips: Cover with fine mesh at sowing to keep flea beetle off.
Water during dry spells for sweet, crisp roots.
Thin early so the roots can swell.
Grow in a different bed each year, as radish is a brassica.
harvest: Most varieties are ready three to five weeks after sowing, when the roots are about 2–3 cm across. Pull a few to check. Left too long, they turn woody, pithy and fiery, so harvest promptly and eat while crisp. Pull gently and in the morning, when the roots are at their juiciest.

Winter radishes need 8–12 weeks and can be left in the ground until needed, though lift them before hard frosts in cold areas. If a plant bolts, let it flower and form seed pods: the green pods are crunchy, peppery and delicious in salads and stir-fries.
harvest_tips: Harvest quickly: older radishes turn woody fast.
Pick in the morning for the crispest texture.
Twist off the leaves right away.
Let one plant go to seed to eat the pods.
use: Slice radishes into salads, eat them with butter and salt, add them to sandwiches and tacos, or roast them for a surprisingly sweet side dish. Pickle them in vinegar and sugar for a bright garnish in about an hour. The young leaves are edible too and can be stir-fried or made into a peppery soup.

Remove the leaves, wash the roots and store them in the fridge wrapped in damp kitchen paper for one to two weeks. Revive floppy ones in iced water for 15 minutes. Radishes do not freeze or dry well, so sow little and often and enjoy them fresh, or quick-pickle surplus roots.
use_tips: Revive limp radishes in iced water for 15 minutes.
Roast at 200°C for 15–20 minutes to mellow the heat.
Quick-pickle with vinegar, sugar and salt.
Add the leaves to soups for a peppery kick.

care.job: Water regularly and evenly so roots swell quickly, as slow growth makes them woody and hot.
Cover with fine mesh to keep flea beetles from peppering the leaves with small holes.
Thin seedlings to 2.5 cm apart and sow a small row every two weeks for a steady supply.

preserving.how: Remove the leaves, and keep roots in a bag or a container of water in the fridge.
Quick pickle sliced radishes in vinegar, sugar and salt.
Ferment whole or sliced in brine.
Blend young leaves into soup or pesto and freeze.

facts.Spacing: 45–60 cm apart in rows 1.8 m apart
facts.Planting depth: Same depth as in the nursery

types.name: Summer-fruiting
types.when: Harvest June to July
types.note: Fruit on last year’s canes. Cut the fruited canes to the ground after harvest and tie in the new ones.

types.name: Autumn-fruiting
types.when: Harvest August to October
types.note: Fruit on this year’s canes. Simply cut everything to the ground in February.

info: Raspberries are among the easiest soft fruits, cropping heavily for ten years or more once established. They are expensive and fragile in shops, so a few canes are well worth growing for freshly picked, perfumed fruit.

Summer-fruiting types crop in June and July, autumn-fruiting types in August to October on the current year’s canes, and are simpler to prune. They tolerate light shade and suit large pots, but they are best in the ground with a simple support.
sow: Plant bare-root canes between November and March, when the soil is not frozen or waterlogged. Choose a sunny or lightly shaded site with moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and dig in plenty of compost. Raspberries dislike waterlogging, so use raised beds on heavy soils.

Space canes 45–60 cm apart in rows 1.8 m apart, planting at the same depth as they grew in the nursery. After planting, cut canes to 25 cm above the ground. Install posts and wires (at 60, 90, 120 and 150 cm) to support them, and mulch with compost.
sow_tips: Cut canes to 25 cm after planting.
grow: Mulch each spring with compost or well-rotted manure and water in dry spells, particularly when the fruit forms. Tie in new canes to the wires as they grow. Weed carefully by hand as the roots are shallow, and remove any suckers that appear outside the row.

Prune summer-fruiting types after harvest by cutting all canes that have fruited to the ground, and tie in 6–8 of the best new canes per metre. Autumn-fruiting types are simply cut to the ground in February. Raspberry beetle can infest fruit, and cane diseases can occur in wet soil.
grow_tips: Cut out fruited canes after harvest (summer types).
Cut autumn types to the ground in February.
harvest: Pick raspberries when they are fully coloured and come away easily from the plug (the core remains on the plant). Ripe berries are plump and soft. Pick every two or three days, preferably in the morning when dry, and handle gently.

Berries do not ripen further after picking, so wait until they are fully ripe. Use shallow containers to avoid crushing. Net the plants to protect from birds. Autumn varieties give fruit until the first frosts.
harvest_tips: Pick when they come away easily.
use: Eat fresh with cream or yoghurt, in desserts such as cranachan, pavlova and Eton mess, or turn into jam, coulis, ripple sauces, vinegars and liqueurs. They freeze very well. Raspberries pair with chocolate, almonds, peach and lemon.

Fresh berries keep for 2–3 days in the fridge, so use them quickly. Freeze on a tray without washing, then bag for up to a year; frozen raspberries hold their shape better than most berries. Raspberry jam is one of the best preserves.

care.job: Cut back autumn-fruiting raspberries to ground level and tie in new canes to supports.
Mulch with compost and feed with a general fertiliser, and keep the roots moist.
Net against birds as the fruit colours, and water in dry spells.
After fruiting, cut out the old fruited canes of summer varieties and tie in the strongest new canes, about 10 cm apart.
Plant new canes now, while dormant, and keep them well watered the following year.

preserving.how: Open freeze on a tray, then bag. They keep their flavour very well.
Keep unwashed in a single layer in a shallow container.
Sets easily with a little lemon juice, and freezer jam keeps the freshest flavour.
Steep in vinegar for a fruit vinegar, or in gin or vodka with sugar.
Sieve cooked or raw fruit with sugar and freeze in small tubs.

crops.name: Redcurrant
crops.sun_text: Sun or shade; one of the best fruits for a north wall

facts.Planting depth: Same depth as in the nursery

info: Redcurrants are among the most trouble-free fruits and tolerate partial shade, making them useful for a spot where little else will crop. The translucent red berries hang in jewel-like trusses and are delicious in preserves, sauces and desserts.

Bushes can be trained as cordons against a fence or wall, saving space, and suit small gardens. White currants are a similar, sweeter relative. Plants live for 20 years and rarely suffer from frost damage.
sow: Plant bare-root bushes between November and March in moisture-retentive, fertile soil, in sun or partial shade. Space bushes 1.2–1.5 m apart, or cordons 30–40 cm apart against a fence or wall. Plant at the same depth as in the nursery, with the stem clear of the soil.

Use a ‘leg’ of 10–15 cm of clear stem, as this makes picking and pruning easier. Cut back the stems by half after planting to encourage a good framework. Mulch with compost and water in well. Redcurrants also grow in 30 cm pots.
sow_tips: Cut stems by half after planting.
Train as cordons to save space.
grow: Water in dry spells and mulch each spring with compost. Redcurrants fruit on spurs on older wood, unlike blackcurrants. In winter, prune the main branches by half of the new growth, and cut side shoots back to two buds, to create an open, goblet-shaped bush. Cordons are summer-pruned in July.

Net the bushes before the fruit starts to colour, because birds adore them. Currant blister aphid, which makes red blisters on the leaves, and sawfly caterpillars, which strip the leaves in spring, are the main pests; hand-pick the caterpillars.
grow_tips: Prune to open, spurred branches in winter.
Look for sawfly caterpillars in spring.
harvest: Pick whole trusses in July and August when the berries are fully red and glossy, using scissors or by pulling the truss off the stem. Fruits will hang on the bush for weeks if netted, which extends the season. Pick when dry.

Handle trusses gently, as the berries are fragile, and hold the stalk, not the berries. Berries in the shade stay on the bush longer and keep the flavour. White varieties are sweeter and better eaten fresh.
harvest_tips: Net to keep fruit on the bush for longer.
use: Redcurrants are tart, so they are best used in cooking: make jelly (the classic accompaniment for lamb and game), sauces such as Cumberland sauce, jam, coulis, tarts and summer pudding. A few fresh sprigs make a lovely decoration on desserts and cocktails.
Fresh trusses keep for up to a week in the fridge. To freeze, leave the berries on their stalks on a tray, freeze, then strip off with a fork and pack. Redcurrant jelly keeps for a year.
use_tips: Make jelly with lamb or game.
Freeze trusses and strip with a fork.

care.job: Prune in late winter, cutting back the previous year's growth on side shoots to two buds and removing crossing branches.
Mulch around the base with compost and feed with a potash-rich fertiliser.
Protect flowers from frost where possible, as currants blossom early.
Net bushes against birds before the fruit reddens, and water in dry spells.
Check leaves for blistered red patches (aphids) and pick off any sawfly caterpillars on the leaf undersides.

pests.label: Coral spot fungus on dead wood

preserving.how: Freeze on the strig, then pull off with a fork when frozen. Bag and freeze.
Redcurrant jelly is the classic, with a high pectin set. Serve with meat and cheese.
Keep on the strigs in a covered container.
Simmer into a cordial or Cumberland-style sauce.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

crops.name: Rhubarb

facts.Planting depth: Crown buds just at soil level
facts.Time to harvest: Light picking in year 2; full cropping from year 3

varieties: Glaskins Perpetual (grows from seed, long cropping)

types.name: Early rhubarb
types.when: Pick March to April (force from January)
types.note: Pink, tender stalks that respond well to forcing under a bucket.

types.name: Maincrop rhubarb
types.when: Pick April to June
types.note: The heaviest cropper, with thick red-green stalks.

types.name: Late rhubarb
types.when: Pick May to July
types.note: Extends the season into summer with tender, sweet stalks.

info: Rhubarb is one of the easiest and longest-lived perennial crops, giving stems for puddings from March to July for ten years or more with minimal care. It is among the first fruit-like crops of the year, and forced rhubarb gives pink stalks in midwinter.

The plant is large, with big leaves, so allow plenty of space and use it as a feature at the back of a border. It tolerates part shade. The leaves are toxic and should never be eaten, but they are safe to compost.
sow: Plant dormant crowns from November to March in a sunny or lightly shaded spot, in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with a bucketful of well-rotted manure or compost. Dig a hole big enough for the crown, and plant so the buds are just at or just below the surface. Space plants 75–90 cm apart.

Water in well and mulch with compost, leaving the buds uncovered. Avoid harvesting in the first year so that the plant establishes. Buying crowns from a reputable nursery or dividing an established plant is more reliable than seed. Rhubarb also grows in a large pot (40 cm or more).
sow_tips: Plant crowns with the buds at soil level.
Do not pick in the first year.
grow: Each spring, mulch around the crown with well-rotted manure or compost, and feed with a general fertiliser. Water in dry spells, and remove any flower stems as soon as they appear, by pulling or cutting at the base, so that energy goes into the stalks.

Divide the crowns every five to seven years in winter, when they become congested and produce thin stems: lift, cut into sections with at least one bud each and replant. Crown rot occurs in waterlogged soil, so ensure good drainage.
harvest: Pick stems from the second year, lightly, and from the third year onward from March to July. Hold a stalk near the base and pull and twist it to detach it, rather than cutting, which can leave stumps that rot. Never take more than half the stalks at once, and stop picking by mid-July to let the plant recover.
Cut off the leaves and discard or compost them; they contain oxalic acid and are poisonous. For early pink stems, cover a crown with a bucket or forcer in January and pick in about 6–8 weeks.
harvest_tips: Leave at least half the stalks.
use: Stew chopped stalks with sugar and a little orange juice for 10 minutes until soft, and use in crumbles, fools, pies, tarts, jams, chutneys and compotes. Rhubarb is tart, so it pairs well with ginger, orange, strawberry, custard and cream. Forced rhubarb is sweeter and less stringy.

Fresh stalks keep for a week in the fridge. To freeze, chop into chunks, spread on a tray, freeze and pack in bags for up to a year; no blanching is needed. Rhubarb jam, chutney and cordial preserve a glut.

care.job: Mulch generously with well-rotted manure or compost, keeping it clear of the crown, and feed with a general fertiliser.
Force a few crowns in March by covering with a bucket or forcing pot to get early pink stems.
Remove flower stalks as they appear, and water in dry spells.
Stop harvesting by July and let the plant build energy for next year. Never eat the leaves, which are poisonous.
Divide crowns every five years or so in winter, replanting healthy pieces with at least one bud.

preserving.how: Chop raw stalks and freeze on a tray, or freeze stewed rhubarb in tubs.
Trim leaves, which are poisonous, and keep stalks wrapped in a bag.
Rhubarb and ginger jam is a favourite, with chutney for savoury use.
Simmer with sugar and orange into a syrup and bottle.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

preserving.how: Preserve in sugar syrup in sterilised jars.

safety: The leaves are toxic and should never be eaten, but they are safe to compost.
Cut off the leaves and discard or compost them; they contain oxalic acid and are poisonous.
Never eat the leaves.
Trim leaves, which are poisonous, and keep stalks wrapped in a bag.
Never eat the leaves, which are poisonous.

facts.Type: Hardy annual salad leaf (wild rocket is perennial)
facts.Spacing: Thin to 10–15 cm apart, or sow thickly for baby leaf

info: Rocket is a quick, peppery salad leaf that is ready in about four weeks and is easy to grow in pots, window boxes and any gap in the vegetable bed. Fresh homegrown leaves have a nuttier, stronger flavour than bagged supermarket rocket.

There are two main types: salad rocket, an annual with broader leaves and mild flavour, and wild rocket (also called sylvetta), a perennial with narrow, deeply cut, hotter leaves. Both are productive and will self-seed freely if allowed to flower.
sow: Sow thinly outdoors from March to September, 1 cm deep, in rows 15 cm apart, or scatter seeds across a pot or tub. Seedlings come up in a few days. Sow a short row every two to three weeks for a constant supply, as plants soon bolt in warm weather.

For summer crops, sow in light shade and keep the soil moist, as hot and dry conditions lead to hot, peppery leaves and early flowering. Autumn sowings in September, under a cloche or in a cold frame, give leaves right into winter.
sow_tips: Sow a short row every two to three weeks.
Cover with fine mesh from sowing against flea beetle.
Scatter-sow into a pot for the windowsill.
grow: Rocket needs little care, but regular watering is important, as drought makes the leaves bitter and fiery and causes bolting. Keep it weeded and thin plants to 10–15 cm for larger leaves, or leave them close for baby leaf.

Flea beetle is the main pest, leaving numerous small holes in the leaves. Fine mesh from sowing, plus consistent watering, protects the crop. Slugs can eat young seedlings. Rotate rocket with other brassicas, as it is in the same family.
grow_tips: Water regularly to avoid fiery, bitter leaves.
Use fine mesh to keep out flea beetle.
Sow in partial shade during summer.
harvest: Start picking when the leaves are 5–10 cm long, from four weeks after sowing, using scissors to cut leaves about 2.5 cm above the base. Leave the centre to regrow, and you can cut again two or three times. Young leaves are the mildest, and older ones become hotter.

Pick regularly to delay flowering. Once rocket bolts, the cream flowers are edible and peppery in salads, and wild rocket will go on flowering for weeks. Allow one or two plants to set seed, and they will self-sow around the garden.
harvest_tips: Cut with scissors and allow to regrow.
Pick young leaves for a milder taste.
Let a plant seed for next year.
use: Toss rocket into salads, scatter on pizza and pasta just before serving, blend into pesto, or wilt into omelettes and soups. Its pepperiness pairs well with sweet fruit such as pear, with parmesan, with lemon and with olive oil. Add it at the last minute, because heat quickly wilts the leaves.

Rocket is best eaten fresh, as it wilts quickly. Keep leaves in a bag lined with kitchen paper in the fridge for up to four days. It does not dry or freeze well, though you can blend it into pesto and freeze that in small pots.
use_tips: Add to hot dishes at the last moment.
Blend into pesto and freeze in small pots.

care.job: Water regularly and give plants light shade in summer, as rocket bolts quickly in hot, dry conditions and turns hot and bitter.
Cover with fine mesh against flea beetles, which make small holes in the leaves.
Pick leaves regularly from the outside, and sow a little every two to three weeks for a constant supply.
Protect winter rocket with a cloche or fleece and pick sparingly through the colder months.

preserving.how: Wash, dry thoroughly and keep in a container lined with kitchen paper.
Take a few leaves from each plant and re-sow every few weeks, rather than storing.
Blend peppery leaves into pesto with nuts, cheese and oil and freeze.
Cook into a soup with potato and freeze in portions.

facts.Type: Hardy biennial brassica, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors or in a seedbed

info: Romanesco is a striking brassica with lime-green, spiralling fractal heads and a nutty, delicate flavour, milder than cauliflower. It is as much a conversation piece as a vegetable, and crops from late summer to autumn.
It is somewhat easier than cauliflower but still needs steady moisture, firm soil, and a protective net. Good for medium to large plots.
sow: Sow in April to May, 1 cm deep, in modules or a seedbed, then transplant seedlings when they have 4–5 leaves, about 5–6 weeks later. Plant them firmly, 60 cm apart, in rich, firm soil that has been limed to pH 6.5–7.
Bury the stems up to the first leaves and firm in well, as loose soil causes small, ‘blown’ heads. Cover with mesh at planting to protect from cabbage root fly, pigeons and butterflies.
grow: Water regularly, especially in dry summers, as a check in growth means small heads. Feed in mid-summer with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser. Weed with care.
Protect from cabbage white caterpillars, aphids, pigeons and slugs. Bend a few outer leaves over the developing head to protect it from sun and frost. Club root is a risk in acid soils.
grow_tips: Tie leaves loosely over the developing heads.
harvest: Cut heads when the florets are tight and well-formed, usually 10–15 cm across, between September and November. Cut with a sharp knife, leaving some leaves attached to protect the head.
Harvest promptly once ready, since heads open up and become coarse. Plants do not produce side shoots after the main head is cut.
harvest_tips: Cut when tight and bright green.
use: Steam or roast Romanesco in florets, or cook briefly in boiling water for 3–4 minutes, to keep its colour and structure. It is delicious with lemon, garlic, chilli and olive oil, in pasta, or as a roasted side. It can also be eaten raw in salads.
Whole heads keep for 1–2 weeks in the fridge. Blanch florets for 3 minutes, cool and freeze for up to a year.

Romanesco is tender and nutty when roasted at a high heat (220°C) with olive oil, garlic and chilli flakes until the edges are charred. It is also lovely raw, finely sliced, with lemon juice and olive oil, or steamed whole and served with a garlic and anchovy butter.
use_tips: Don't overcook; it loses its shape.
Serve a whole head as a centrepiece.

care.job: Plant firmly 60 cm apart and cover with mesh from day one against pigeons and cabbage white butterflies.
Water consistently and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser, as romanesco is a hungry plant that sulks if checked.
Bend a few leaves over the developing head to shield it from frost and sun, and cut when firm and bright.

preserving.how: Keep whole heads unwashed in a loose bag in the salad drawer.
Cut into florets, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze on a tray before bagging.
Pickle florets in spiced vinegar.
Roast florets until just tender and freeze in a single layer.

crops.name: Rosemary

facts.Time to harvest: All year, from the first spring

varieties: Miss Jessopp’s Upright (tall, hardy, good for hedges)

types.name: Upright rosemary
types.when: Pick all year
types.note: Tall, bushy shrubs, ideal for hedges and borders.

types.name: Prostrate rosemary
types.when: Pick all year
types.note: Trailing stems that tumble over walls and pots. A little less hardy.

info: Rosemary is a bold, aromatic evergreen shrub with needle-like leaves and blue spring flowers beloved by bees. It thrives in sun and poor, dry soil, and it grows for years with little attention, making a handsome hedge or specimen in a pot.

Upright forms grow to 1.5 m, while prostrate types trail over walls. It is hardy in most of the UK, though young plants need protection in cold winters and wet soil can kill it. In cold gardens, grow it in a pot that can be moved to shelter.
sow: Buy a plant or take cuttings, as seed is slow and unreliable. Plant from March to October in full sun in free-draining soil; add plenty of grit to clay or heavy soil, or plant in raised beds or pots. Space plants 60–90 cm apart.

To take cuttings, snip 10 cm non-flowering shoots in summer, strip the lower leaves, and insert into pots of gritty compost. They root in about 4–8 weeks. Water in new plants until established, then they are very drought-tolerant.
sow_tips: Use a gritty compost in pots.
grow: Water sparingly: rosemary prefers dry conditions, and wet roots in winter are the main cause of death. Don’t feed. Prune lightly after flowering in late spring to maintain shape, cutting back soft new growth but never into old, leafless wood, which rarely regrows.

In cold areas, protect potted plants with fleece or bring them under cover in severe weather. Rosemary beetle, a shiny metallic green-and-purple insect, feeds on leaves; pick it off by hand. Replace very old woody plants every 8–10 years.
harvest: Harvest sprigs year-round by cutting the top 10 cm of stems, taking from different parts of the plant to keep the shape. Don’t cut into old wood. The flavour is strongest in early summer, and flowers are edible and pretty in salads.
For drying, cut longer stems before flowering and hang in a warm, airy spot. Light picking in the first year helps plants establish. Regular harvesting keeps plants compact and bushy.
harvest_tips: Cut the top 10 cm of stems.
use: Use rosemary with roast lamb, chicken, potatoes, focaccia, tomato sauces, and roasted root vegetables. The needles are tough, so chop finely, or use whole sprigs and remove before serving. Woody stems make aromatic skewers for kebabs. Infuse it in olive oil, vinegar or sugar.
Fresh rosemary keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge wrapped in damp paper, and freezes well on the stem. Dry stems keep their flavour for a year in a jar. Rosemary salt and oil are lovely gifts.
use_tips: Chop finely or use whole sprigs.

care.job: Prune lightly after the main flush of growth begins, taking off the tips of shoots to keep the plant compact.
Water pots in dry spells but avoid overwatering, as rosemary hates wet roots.
Trim after flowering, cutting back about a third of the growth but never into old, bare wood.
Take softwood cuttings in early summer to make new plants.
Protect plants in pots from hard frost by moving them against a sheltered wall or wrapping in fleece.

preserving.how: Hang small bunches in a warm, airy place, then strip the needles into jars. It dries well and keeps its flavour.
Freeze whole sprigs in bags, or chopped in ice cube trays with oil.
Rosemary is evergreen, so pick fresh sprigs all year round.
Blend leaves with salt or sugar and dry out before storing.
Steep sprigs in white wine vinegar for 2 weeks and strain.

crops.name: Runner bean
crops.sun_text: Full sun to light shade; sheltered

facts.Type: Tender perennial climber, grown as an annual

varieties: White Lady (white flowers, set well in heat)

types.name: Tall (climbing) runner beans
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest July to October
types.note: The classic type, needing 2.4 m canes. The heaviest crops.

types.name: Dwarf runner beans
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest July to September
types.note: No supports needed, so they suit pots and windy plots.

types.name: White-flowered runner beans
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest July to October
types.note: White flowers set better in hot weather and the pods are stringless.

info: Runner beans are the classic British summer bean: vigorous climbers with bright red, white or pink flowers, which produce heavy crops of long, flat, tender pods from July to October. They are decorative enough for the front garden and grow up wigwams, fences and arches.

They need a sturdy support, rich soil and plenty of water, and they are not frost-hardy. Dwarf varieties are available for pots. Flowers sometimes drop without setting in hot, dry weather, so water plants and mist the flowers.
sow: Sow indoors from mid-April to mid-May, 5 cm deep, in individual pots of multipurpose compost. Or sow direct outdoors from mid-May to June, after the frost risk has passed, 5 cm deep and 15–20 cm apart at the base of each support. Plant two seeds per cane and remove the weaker.

Prepare the soil well in advance: dig a trench in winter and fill with kitchen waste and compost to hold moisture. Build a wigwam or double row of 2.4 m canes before planting, tied firmly at the top. Harden off indoor-sown plants before planting out.
sow_tips: Never plant out before frost has finished.
Dig in compost to hold moisture.
Use 2.4 m canes with firm ties.
Sow a few extra seeds in pots as replacements.
grow: Guide young shoots to their cane, winding them anticlockwise. Pinch out the tip when the plant reaches the top of the support. Water thoroughly every few days in dry weather, especially in flowering, and mulch to retain moisture. A weekly tomato feed helps pods develop.
Mist flowers in dry weather to help them set. Blackfly may colonise the tips, and slugs eat seedlings. Pick regularly to keep plants producing. Wind can topple wigwams, so anchor them well.
grow_tips: Pinch out at the top of the support.
Water and mist in dry spells.
harvest: Begin picking pods when they are about 15–20 cm long and slim, before the beans inside swell, usually from mid-July. Pick at least every few days, as leaving pods to mature stops the plant flowering. Hold the stem and pull the pod down to avoid damaging the vine.

At the end of the season, leave a few pods to mature and dry on the plant for seed. Cut the plants off at the base and leave roots in the ground to release nitrogen. Roots of runner beans can be lifted and stored over winter in frost-free places.
harvest_tips: Pick every 2–3 days at the peak.
Pick while pods are slim and tender.
Leave some pods to dry for seed.
Cut plants off at the base.
use: Top and tail the pods, string if necessary, slice diagonally and steam or boil for 4–5 minutes, until just tender. Serve with butter, add to curries, stir-fries, stews and salads, or pickle for chutney. Use young pods for the best flavour; large, old pods are tough.

Pods keep for up to a week in the fridge in a bag. Freeze by slicing, blanching for 3 minutes, cooling and freezing in bags for up to a year. Salting beans in layers of coarse salt, as in the old way, also preserves them. Dried mature beans can be used in stews.
use_tips: Add to chutney to use gluts.

care.job: Build a sturdy wigwam or double row of 2.4 m canes, tied at the top, before planting out after the last frost.
Help young plants find the canes, twining them anticlockwise, and protect from slugs and snails.
Water well during dry spells, especially while flowering, and mulch to keep the roots cool. Dry soil makes flowers drop.
Pinch out the tops once plants reach the top of the canes to encourage side growth and keep it picking.
Pick every few days, as pods left to mature stop the plant producing more.
Cut plants down at ground level but leave the roots in the soil, as they release nitrogen that helps next year's crop.

pests.label: Red spider mite in hot summers

preserving.how: Top, tail and slice, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze on a tray before bagging. The best way to keep a glut.
Keep unwashed in a bag in the salad drawer.
Make runner bean chutney with onions and vinegar, a classic way to use a glut.
Layer sliced beans with salt in jars, the traditional way. Rinse well before cooking.
Leave pods on the plant until brown and rattling, then shell and dry the beans for winter, and save seed.

images.alt: Runner bean pods hanging from the plant

crops.name: Sage

facts.Time to harvest: Light picking in year 1; fully from year 2

varieties: Tricolor (pink, cream and green; less hardy)

types.name: Common sage
types.when: Pick all year
types.note: The strongest flavour and the hardiest.

types.name: Purple and variegated sage
types.when: Pick all year
types.note: Decorative leaves in purple, gold or cream. Slightly less hardy.

info: Sage is a hardy, silvery-leaved evergreen shrub with a strong, earthy flavour and attractive purple-blue flowers in early summer that bees adore. It is easy to grow, and it keeps its leaves through most winters.

Besides common sage, there are purple, golden and tricolour forms that are as ornamental as they are useful. Plants grow well in pots and borders, in sun and free-draining soil, and they are long-lived with minimal care.
sow: Plant potted sage from March to October in full sun and free-draining soil, with plenty of grit added on heavy ground. Space plants 45–60 cm apart. Sage can be sown in April and May on the surface of seed compost at 15–18°C, but plants take longer and vary.
Cuttings are easy: take 10 cm softwood cuttings in late spring, root in gritty compost and pot on. Layering low stems also works. In pots, use a loam-based compost with extra grit.
sow_tips: Plant in sun and good drainage.
grow: Water sparingly once established, and avoid feeding, since rich soil reduces flavour. Cut back the plant by one third after flowering in summer, avoiding cutting into bare old wood, to prevent a leggy, woody plant. A light trim in spring helps, too.

Replace the plant every 4–5 years when it becomes woody and unproductive. Wet winters and heavy soils are the main threats, so ensure good drainage. Sage is generally untroubled by pests; powdery mildew can occur in dry, congested plants.
harvest: Pick leaves at any time of year, choosing young, fresh leaves from the tips for the best flavour. Pick lightly in the first year. The flavour is strongest in early summer, before flowering. Cut sprigs with scissors.
For drying, cut stems before flowering and hang in bunches in a warm, airy place. The flowers are edible and make a pretty salad garnish. Harvest in the morning after the dew has dried.
harvest_tips: Pick lightly in the first year.
use: Sage is a classic with pork, sausages, chicken, liver, onion stuffing, pumpkin, squash, and in brown butter sauce for gnocchi and pasta. Fry whole leaves in butter or oil until crisp for a garnish. The flavour is strong, so use it sparingly.

Fresh sage keeps for a week in the fridge wrapped in damp paper. It dries well and keeps the flavour for a year in a jar, and also freezes well on the stem. Sage tea is a traditional remedy for sore throats.
use_tips: Fry leaves in butter until crisp.

care.job: Trim off winter-damaged shoots and feed lightly in spring, as sage prefers poor, well-drained soil.
Pinch back growing tips to encourage bushy growth, and cut off flower stalks if you want more leaves.
Give plants a light trim after flowering, but avoid hard pruning into old wood late in the season.
Replace plants every 4 to 5 years as they become woody, or layer stems to create new plants.
Keep the soil free-draining and clear fallen leaves from around the base to prevent damp rot.

preserving.how: Hang small bunches in a warm, airy place until crisp, then rub the leaves into jars.
Freeze whole leaves in a bag, or chopped in ice cube trays with oil.
Sage is evergreen in most gardens, so pick fresh leaves through the year.
Mix chopped leaves into butter and freeze in rolls.

facts.Spacing: 10–15 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

info: Salsify, known as the 'oyster plant', is a long, slender, creamy-white root with a delicate flavour reminiscent of oysters or artichoke. It is an old-fashioned winter vegetable that is rarely seen in shops but is easy to grow in deep, stone-free soil.
Related scorzonera has black skin and is grown the same way. If left in the ground for a second year, salsify produces purple dandelion-like flowers, and its young shoots, called chards, are edible.
sow: Sow in April and May, 2 cm deep, in rows 30 cm apart, in deep, light, stone-free soil. Prepare the bed well, as stones cause forked roots. Seed is viable for only a year, so always use fresh seed; sow a few extra seeds as germination is patchy.
Thin seedlings to 10–15 cm apart. Keep weeds under control in the early stages, as seedlings are slow. Raised beds or large deep containers work well on heavy soil.
sow_tips: Use a raised bed for heavy soil.
grow: Water in dry spells to prevent roots from becoming woody and bitter, and keep weeds out by hoeing carefully. No feeding is needed in reasonable soil, and manure should be avoided, as it causes forking.
Salsify is little troubled by pests, though slugs and aphids may appear. White rust causes pale blisters on leaves; remove affected leaves. Plants are hardy and can stay in the ground all winter.
harvest: Lift roots from October onwards, as needed through winter, when the foliage has died back. Dig with a fork well away from the row to avoid snapping the long, brittle roots, which bleed a milky sap. Roots left in the ground are best, as they keep their quality.
In spring, young flower shoots can be harvested before they open and cooked like asparagus. Lift remaining roots before they start to grow in spring, as they become woody.
harvest_tips: Leave roots in the ground over winter.
use: Scrub the roots and peel them under running water or drop them immediately into water with lemon juice or vinegar, as the flesh discolours quickly. Boil for 15–20 minutes and serve with butter, or roast, fry, or add to gratins, soups and stews.
Roots keep for several weeks in the fridge, or in damp sand in a cool shed. Unpeeled roots can be left in the ground until needed. Cooked salsify can be frozen, though the texture softens.
use_tips: Serve with butter or cream sauce.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 10 to 15 cm apart and keep the bed weed-free, as salsify is slow to start.
Water in dry spells to prevent woody roots, and cover with fine mesh if carrot fly is a problem.
Leave roots in the ground over winter and lift as needed, taking care not to damage them, as they bleed milky sap.

preserving.how: Lift as needed through winter, as roots keep best in the soil.
Lift and store in damp sand in a cool, frost-free shed.
Peel, cut into lengths, blanch for 3 minutes in acidulated water and freeze.
Make into soup and freeze in portions.

facts.Type: Summer savory: annual; winter savory: hardy perennial

info: Savory is a peppery, thyme-like herb, famous as the ‘bean herb’ because its flavour complements broad, French and runner beans so well, and is thought to aid digestion. Summer savory is a delicate annual, and winter savory is a hardy, evergreen, stronger-flavoured perennial.
Both are easy, attractive plants with small pink-white flowers loved by bees. They suit pots, edges and the herb garden.
sow: Sow summer savory from April to May on the surface of fine, well-drained soil in a sunny spot, in rows 25 cm apart. Seed is tiny and needs light, so do not cover it. Thin to 15 cm. Seedlings appear in 2–3 weeks.
Winter savory can be bought as plants or sown similarly, then planted 30 cm apart. Both prefer poor, free-draining soil and full sun.
grow: Water sparingly and avoid feeding. Pinch out the tips of young plants to encourage bushiness. Trim winter savory in spring to keep it neat and productive, avoiding cutting into old wood.
Few pests trouble savory. Slugs sometimes eat seedlings. Replace winter savory every 4–5 years when woody. Summer savory finishes after flowering in late summer.
harvest: Pick sprigs from summer savory from about 8 weeks, cutting the top 10 cm before flowering. Winter savory can be picked all year, though it is best in summer.
Hang cut stems in bunches to dry for winter use. Harvest on a dry morning.

Summer savory is best picked just as the first flower buds appear, when the oils are strongest. Harvest the whole plant at once, leaving a few centimetres, for a big batch to dry, as the plant does not regrow well after flowering.
use: Add a sprig to the cooking water for broad beans, French beans or lentils, and use in stuffings, sausages, stews, soups and with roast meat. The flavour is peppery, between thyme and mint. Winter savory is stronger, so use less.
Dried savory keeps a year in a jar. Fresh sprigs keep a week in the fridge. A sprig of savory is a great addition to herb vinegars.

care.job: Cut back winter savory in spring to encourage fresh growth, and thin summer savory seedlings to 10 to 15 cm apart.
Pinch out the tips to keep plants bushy and cut stems regularly, particularly before they flower.
Cut summer savory stems to dry just as flowers begin to open, when the flavour is strongest.

preserving.how: Hang bunches in a warm, airy place and store leaves in jars. Summer savory dries well.
Freeze sprigs in a bag, or chopped in ice cube trays.
Dried leaves are the traditional herb for bean dishes, so keep a jar near your bean stores.

facts.Type: Hardy perennial root vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: 15 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

info: Scorzonera, or black salsify, produces long black-skinned roots with creamy white flesh and a delicate, nutty, slightly sweet flavour. It is easier than salsify, bolts less, and the roots are less prone to bleed when cut.
It is a handsome plant that produces yellow flowers in summer, and left for a second year, the roots become larger. A rare luxury vegetable, it is simple to grow in deep, light soil.
sow: Sow in April to May, 2 cm deep, in rows 30 cm apart, in deep, light, stone-free soil that has not been recently manured. Fresh seed gives the best germination; sow a few extra and thin to 15 cm apart.
Roots are long, so deep beds or large containers are best. Water the row if dry and keep weeds down. Seedlings take a couple of weeks to emerge and grow slowly at first.
grow: Water in dry spells, and mulch to maintain moisture and suppress weeds. Remove flower buds if you want the roots to keep growing. Hoe carefully, since the roots are brittle.
White rust may occur on leaves, but it rarely damages the crop. Slugs and aphids are minor problems. Scorzonera is very hardy and can be left in the ground all winter.
grow_tips: Do not damage the crown when hoeing.
Leave in the ground over winter.
harvest: Lift roots from October, using a fork to dig well down and out from the row, since the roots can reach 30 cm and snap easily. They can be harvested through the winter as required, and improve in flavour after frost.
Leave roots in the ground for a second year for larger roots, removing flower stalks. Lift all remaining roots by early spring. The young flower shoots are edible and tasty.
use: Scrub roots and peel under water or drop into lemon water to avoid browning, or boil in their skins and peel afterwards, which is easier. Cook for 15–20 minutes, then serve with butter, in a white sauce, roasted or in gratins and soups.
Roots keep for a couple of weeks in the fridge or in damp sand, but freshly dug is best. Cooked roots can be frozen, though the texture softens.
use_tips: Use lemon water to stop browning.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 10 to 15 cm apart and weed carefully, as roots grow slowly and are easily outcompeted.
Water in dry spells to prevent woody roots and avoid heavy feeding, which makes roots fork.
Leave roots in the ground over winter and lift carefully as needed, taking care not to snap them.

preserving.how: Lift as needed through winter, as roots keep best in the soil.
Lift carefully and store in damp sand in a cool, frost-free shed.
Peel, cut into lengths, blanch for 3 minutes and freeze.
Make into soup and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Sea kale
crops.sun_text: Full sun to light shade; free-draining soil

facts.Time to harvest: Light picking in year 2; full from year 3

info: Sea kale is a British native of the shingle coast, grown as a gourmet perennial vegetable for its tender, pale shoots, grown in the dark, in early spring, a Victorian delicacy. The blue-green waved leaves and white honey-scented flowers are also attractive.
Plants live for 10 years or more. They thrive in free-draining, even stony or sandy soil, and need very little care once established. A good choice for the vegetable border or ornamental bed.
