sow: Plant root cuttings (thongs) in March to April, 60 cm apart, with the crown at soil level, in fertile, free-draining soil in sun. Sea kale can be raised from seed sown in spring, but root cuttings give a quicker crop. Prepare the bed with compost and some grit.
Water well in the first season. Do not harvest in the first year. Sea kale makes a good ornamental plant for sandy and coastal gardens.
grow: Mulch each spring with compost or seaweed and water in dry spells. Cut off flower stalks in summer if you want more energy to go into the roots, or allow them to flower for the bees. In autumn, cut off the dying leaves.

To blanch shoots, cover the crowns in early spring with a large pot, bucket or forcing jar, excluding all light. Slugs and cabbage white caterpillars can attack leaves. Rotate away from other brassicas.
grow_tips: Blanch with a pot in early spring.
harvest: Force the crowns from year 3: cover with a bucket in February, and cut the pale shoots when they are 15–20 cm long, in April, with a sharp knife just below the soil surface. Cut over 3–4 weeks, then remove the cover to let the plant recover.
Unblanched young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked like kale. Flower buds, harvested in May, are like purple sprouting broccoli.
use: Steam the pale shoots for 10 minutes and serve with butter, hollandaise sauce, or a squeeze of lemon, like asparagus. The flavour is delicate and nutty, with a faint cabbage tang. The flower buds are good steamed or stir-fried.
Shoots keep for a few days in the fridge, wrapped in damp paper. They are best fresh. Cooked shoots can be frozen.

care.job: Mulch with compost in spring and give plants space, as sea kale is a long-lived perennial that forms a large clump.
Cover crowns with a bucket or forcing pot in early spring for blanched shoots, and cut when 20 cm tall.
Remove the cover once cropping ends, let the plant grow freely to build up strength, and water in dry weather.
Cut dead foliage down in autumn and protect crowns with a mulch for winter.

preserving.how: Keep blanched shoots wrapped in damp paper in the salad drawer.
Blanch for 2 minutes, cool and freeze shoots in bags.
Cover crowns in turn with pots through early spring to spread the harvest.

crops.name: Shallot
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open site

facts.Type: Hardy perennial bulb, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: 15–20 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

types.name: Banana and long shallots
types.when: Plant February to April · Harvest July to August
types.note: Long, tapered bulbs that are easier to peel and slice.

types.name: Round shallots
types.when: Plant February to April · Harvest July to August
types.note: The classic type, strongly flavoured and a great keeper.

types.name: Shallots from seed
types.when: Sow February to March · Harvest August to September
types.note: Cheaper, and avoid virus. Produce a single, medium bulb.

info: Shallots are a gourmet cousin of the onion, with a finer, sweeter flavour that chefs prize. Unlike onions, one planted set multiplies into a cluster of six to a dozen bulbs, which makes them a very productive crop for a small amount of space.

They are easier than onions in many ways: more reliable in wet years, less likely to bolt and happy in poorer soils. They are grown from sets (small bulbs), which you can buy in late winter or save from your own crop.
sow: Plant sets from late February to April when the soil is workable, in a sunny, open site with free-draining soil. Push each set in so that the tip is just visible, 15–20 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart. Birds may pull newly planted sets out, so firm them in and net or fleece them for the first few weeks.

Shallots can also be planted in autumn in mild areas for an earlier crop, using suitable varieties. Avoid overly rich or freshly manured soil, which encourages leaf growth and poor ripening. Raised beds and light soils suit shallots well.
sow_tips: Plant sets with the tip showing above ground.
Net after planting to stop birds pulling sets up.
Choose firm, healthy sets about 2–3 cm across.
Avoid very rich, freshly manured soil.
grow: Keep the bed weeded and water only in dry spells while the plants establish. Stop watering from early July to let the bulbs ripen. As the clusters swell, gently pull a little soil away from the bulbs to let the sun reach them and speed ripening. They need little or no feeding.

Problems are similar to onions: white rot, downy mildew, onion fly and neck rot. Rotate crops on a four-year plan, avoid overcrowding and remove any diseased plants as soon as you see them. Birds and slugs can damage newly planted sets.
grow_tips: Pull soil back from the bulbs in midsummer.
Rotate with other alliums on a four-year plan.
harvest: Shallots are ready to lift from July, when the foliage turns yellow and begins to die back. Ease clumps out of the ground with a fork on a dry day, and separate the bulbs by hand. Lay them out in a warm, airy place or on a wire rack for two to three weeks to dry fully.
Rub off loose soil and old skin, but do not wash them. Pick out any with thick necks or damage and use these first. Save a few of the best, smallest bulbs to replant next spring.
harvest_tips: Dry in a warm, airy spot for two to three weeks.
Do not wash shallots you intend to store.
use: Shallots are mild and sweet, ideal for vinaigrettes, sauces, roasting whole and caramelising. Their fine layers melt into dishes without overpowering them, and they are the classic base for béarnaise, beurre blanc and French-style stews. Small ones are perfect for pickling.

Cured shallots keep for six to eight months in nets or trays in a cool, dry, frost-free place, often longer than onions. Peeled and chopped shallots can be frozen in small bags. Check regularly for rot, and use any soft bulbs promptly.
use_tips: Roast whole in their skins until soft and sweet.
Pickle small shallots in vinegar for a jar to enjoy all winter.
Store in nets or trays with good airflow.
Chop and freeze for quick cooking.

care.job: Plant sets so the tips just show above ground, and cover with netting or a cloche if birds pull them out.
Keep the bed weed-free and water in dry spells. Avoid overwatering, as shallots rot in wet soil.
As the leaves yellow, ease the soil back from the bulbs to let the sun ripen them, and stop watering.
Lift on a dry day when the foliage has died and dry the bulbs for a few weeks in a sunny, airy place before storing.

preserving.how: Dry in a warm, airy place until the skins are papery, then store in nets or trays somewhere cool, dry and frost-free.
Pickle small shallots whole in spiced vinegar. Pickled shallots are excellent with cheese.
Chop and freeze raw in bags for cooking.
Make shallot marmalade or chutney with balsamic vinegar.

crops.name: Sorrel
crops.sun_text: Full sun to partial shade; tolerates shade

facts.Time to harvest: 8–10 weeks from sowing, then for years

varieties: Buckler-leaf sorrel (Rumex scutatus, mild and compact)
Blood-veined sorrel (Rumex sanguineus, red-veined and ornamental)

info: Sorrel is a hardy perennial with arrow-shaped leaves and a sharp, lemony flavour. It is among the first greens to appear in spring, and it crops for many years, which makes it one of the most reliable perennial crops for the kitchen garden.

Broad-leaved sorrel has a strong flavour. French or buckler-leaf sorrel (Rumex scutatus) is smaller, gentler and slower-growing. Both are easy in sun or part shade and thrive in pots. The tang comes from oxalic acid, so enjoy it in moderation.
sow: Sow in March to June, 1 cm deep, either indoors in modules or directly outside in rows 30 cm apart. Seedlings emerge in two to three weeks and can be thinned to 30 cm apart. Moist, fertile soil in sun or light shade gives the biggest leaves. Do not allow plants to dry out.

The easiest route is to buy a small plant or to divide an existing clump in spring, replanting the pieces 30 cm apart. Sorrel grows well in pots at least 20 cm wide. One or two plants are enough for most households, as the leaves are strong.
sow_tips: One or two plants are enough for a household.
Divide clumps in spring every three years.
Choose a non-flowering variety to save effort.
grow: Keep plants watered in dry weather and cut off flower stems as soon as they appear, to keep the leaves coming and prevent self-seeding. A mulch of compost each spring, and a general liquid feed once or twice in summer, keep the leaves tender and productive.

Sorrel is rarely troubled by disease, though slugs, sawfly larvae and downy mildew can mark the leaves. Cut hard back after a bad attack, and fresh leaves will grow. Divide old, congested clumps every three to four years to renew them.
grow_tips: Cut back hard if leaves look tired.
Feed lightly once or twice in summer.
Divide every three to four years.
harvest: Pick young leaves from about eight weeks after sowing, taking a few from each plant, from the outside of the clump. Young leaves are tender and lemony; older leaves become tough and very sharp. In the first year, pick lightly to let the plants establish.

Regular picking and removing flower stems keep fresh growth coming from March to November. In mild winters, sorrel keeps growing slowly. Do not eat huge quantities, because oxalic acid can be a problem for people with kidney stones or gout.
harvest_tips: Pick young leaves; they are less sharp.
Take leaves from the outside of the clump.
Cut back flowers to keep it productive.
use: Sorrel gives a bright lemony zing to sauces, soups and salads. Add a few young leaves to salads, or cook larger ones until they melt into a sharp purée, ideal with fish, eggs, chicken or potatoes. Classic uses include sorrel soup, French omelettes and sauce for salmon.

The leaves lose their bright green colour when cooked, turning an olive shade, which is normal. Fresh sorrel keeps for two to three days in the fridge. To keep surplus leaves, cook them to a purée and freeze in ice-cube trays, ready to add to sauces and soups.
use_tips: Cook briefly: sorrel melts in a minute or two.
Pair with fish, eggs and cream.
Use small leaves raw in salads.

care.job: Divide clumps every three or four years in spring and feed with a general fertiliser.
Cut off flower stems as soon as they appear to keep the leaves tender, and pick regularly from the outside.
Water in dry weather, as sorrel leaves turn tough and bitter if the plants dry out.
Cut back old foliage in autumn and mulch the crowns lightly.

preserving.how: Blanch briefly for 10 seconds or purée with a little butter and freeze in ice cube trays. The leaves go dark but the flavour holds.
Wrap in damp paper in a bag.
Make sorrel soup, and freeze in portions.
Cook into a creamy sauce for fish, then freeze in small tubs.

safety: The tang comes from oxalic acid, so enjoy it in moderation.
Do not eat huge quantities, because oxalic acid can be a problem for people with kidney stones or gout.

crops.name: Spinach
crops.sun_text: Partial shade; full sun in cool weather

facts.Sow: Mar–Apr and Aug–Sep, straight into the soil
facts.Spacing: Thin to 10–15 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart

varieties: Giant Winter (very hardy, for autumn sowing)

types.name: Spring and summer spinach
types.when: Sow March to May · Harvest May to July
types.note: Bolt-resistant types for spring sowing.

types.name: Winter spinach
types.when: Sow August to September · Harvest October to April
types.note: Hardy, slower types that overwinter.

info: Spinach is a cool-season leaf crop that gives tender, sweet leaves in spring and autumn, often a month before the summer salad crops arrive. It is quick to grow, tolerates part shade and is happy in containers.

The main challenge is bolting, which spinach does readily in heat, drought or long days. Sow at the right time, keep the soil moist, and choose slow-bolting varieties, and you will get a heavy crop. In summer, grow perpetual spinach or chard instead.
sow: Sow outdoors in rows 30 cm apart from March to April for spring crops, and from August to September for autumn and winter crops. Sow seeds 2–3 cm deep, thinly, and thin to 10–15 cm for full-size plants, or leave them close and cut as baby leaf. Soaking seed overnight can help germination.

Spinach prefers cool, moist, fertile, slightly alkaline soil, so add lime if yours is very acid, and dig in compost to hold moisture. In summer, sow in partial shade or choose bolt-resistant varieties. Autumn crops can be protected with cloches in cold areas.
sow_tips: Sow in spring and autumn, not midsummer.
Sow little and often, every two to three weeks.
grow: Water regularly, as dry soil triggers bolting, and mulch to keep the roots cool and moist. Feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser if the leaves turn pale. Keep weeds down, hoeing carefully, as spinach roots are shallow.

Downy mildew, leaf miner, slugs and aphids are the main problems. Remove affected leaves and avoid overcrowding to improve air flow. A pinch of fleece in spring protects against cold snaps and flea beetle, and also helps against leaf miner.
grow_tips: Pinch off leaves affected by leaf miner.
Cover autumn crops with a cloche.
harvest: Begin picking baby leaves from about four weeks, taking a few from each plant and leaving the centre to produce more. Full leaves are ready at about 8–10 cm long, from six to eight weeks. Pick from the outside of the plant, working inwards. Pick in the morning for the best flavour.

If plants start to bolt, harvest the whole lot right away, because the leaves turn bitter. Winter sowings can be picked sparingly through winter and give a big flush in early spring. Pull out the plants after harvesting and replace with a different crop.
harvest_tips: Pick little and often from the outside.
Harvest the whole plant if it starts to bolt.
Leave a few leaves on each plant to keep it growing.
use: Eat baby leaves raw in salads and sandwiches, or wilt larger leaves in a pan with garlic and a squeeze of lemon in a couple of minutes. Spinach goes well in curries, pies, quiches, soups, pasta and omelettes. Cook it briefly to keep its colour and flavour; a large bowlful shrinks to a few spoonfuls.

Fresh leaves keep for three to five days in the fridge in a bag, so eat them soon after picking. To freeze, wash, blanch for two minutes, cool quickly, squeeze out the water and freeze in portions. Spinach also makes a good soup that freezes well.
use_tips: Squeeze out excess water after cooking.
Blanch for one minute before freezing.
Add to curries and soups at the last minute.
Remove thick stalks from large leaves.

care.job: Keep plants well watered, as dry spells make spinach bolt, and pick leaves regularly from the outside.
Give plants a little shade in hot weather and sow in cooler, shadier spots to avoid bolting.
Protect from slugs and look out for mildew in damp conditions.
Cover winter spinach with a cloche or fleece and pick lightly, as growth is slow.

preserving.how: Blanch for 2 minutes, cool, squeeze out all the water and freeze in portions. This is by far the best way to keep a glut.
Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Make into sauces, soups or spinach and ricotta fillings and freeze.
Blend raw leaves with water and freeze in ice cube trays for smoothies.

crops.name: Spring onion

facts.Type: Hardy perennial grown as a salad annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 2.5 cm in rows 15 cm apart

varieties: Ishikura (bunching type that does not form bulbs)

info: Spring onions are fast, compact and easy, and they add a fresh oniony bite to salads, stir-fries and sandwiches. Because they hardly take any space, they suit pots, window boxes and gaps between other crops as well as vegetable beds.

Sow them in short rows every few weeks from spring to late summer for a continuous supply, and sow hardy varieties in late summer to stand through the winter for very early spring pickings. They are also known as salad onions or scallions.
sow: Sow thinly in shallow drills 1 cm deep, in rows 15 cm apart, from March to August. Seedlings appear in one to two weeks. For a regular supply, sow a short row every three weeks. Spring onions do well in containers and window boxes; use a pot at least 15 cm deep and sow thinly across the surface.

For an early crop the following spring, sow hardy winter varieties in late August to September and protect them with a cloche or fleece in hard weather. Thin gradually to 2.5 cm apart, using the thinnings in salads.
sow_tips: Sow a short row every three weeks.
Sow winter-hardy varieties in late summer.
Use a pot at least 15 cm deep.
Keep seedlings weeded; they are slow to start.
grow: Spring onions are low-maintenance. Water them during dry spells, as the shallow roots dry out fast, and keep the bed weeded because they are poor competitors. They do not need feeding in reasonably fertile soil.

Onion fly, thrips and downy mildew are occasional problems, but sowing in different beds each year and covering with fine mesh minimises the first two. Thin out overcrowded seedlings, as dense stands are more prone to disease.
grow_tips: Cover with fine mesh to prevent onion fly.
Grow in a new bed each year.
Do not let them dry out in pots.
harvest: Pull spring onions when they are 15–20 cm tall and about as thick as a pencil, usually 8–12 weeks after sowing. They are best when young and tender; leave them too long and they become tough and strong. Loosen the soil with a fork before pulling to avoid breaking the stems.
Harvest some from each row at a time so you have a succession. Overwintered crops are ready from March to May. Any that you leave will keep growing and produce flower heads in their second year.
harvest_tips: Pick when pencil-thick for the mildest flavour.
Loosen the soil first to avoid snapped stems.
Harvest from each row in turn.
Overwintered plants are ready in spring.
use: Use spring onions raw in salads, sandwiches, salsas and slaws, or cook them briefly in stir-fries, omelettes and noodle dishes. Both the white base and the green leaves are edible. Char them on a barbecue or grill pan for a sweet, smoky side dish.

Trim the roots, wrap in damp kitchen paper and keep in the fridge for up to a week. You can also stand the roots in a glass of water on the windowsill and they will keep growing. Chopped spring onions freeze well in small bags and are handy for cooking.
use_tips: Grill whole spring onions for a smoky side.
Regrow the roots in a glass of water.
Chop and freeze for cooked dishes.
Use the green tops for garnish.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 2.5 cm apart and keep weeds down, as spring onions are poor competitors.
Water regularly, as dry spells make them tough and strong-flavoured.
Cover with fine mesh against onion fly and carrot fly where they have been a problem, and sow a small batch every two to three weeks.
Protect winter crops with a cloche or fleece and thin gently.

preserving.how: Wrap in damp kitchen paper or stand in a glass of water in the fridge.
Chop and freeze in bags for cooked dishes.
Place roots in a glass of water on a windowsill and they regrow, or leave a few in the ground to keep cropping.
Pickle whole or sliced in a light vinegar brine.

crops.name: Sprouting broccoli
crops.sun_text: Full sun, in an open site

facts.Type: Hardy biennial, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Apr–May in trays; plant out Jun–Jul
facts.Spacing: 60 cm apart in rows 75 cm apart

varieties: Purple Sprouting Late (extends picking to May)

types.name: Early purple
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest February to March
types.note: The first to crop, usually from late winter. Quick but less hardy.

types.name: Late purple
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest March to May
types.note: Heavier and hardier, carrying on into spring.

types.name: White sprouting
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest March to April
types.note: Cream-white spears, milder and sweeter.

info: Purple sprouting broccoli is one of the highlights of the vegetable year, producing tender, sweet spears in late winter and early spring, during the ‘hungry gap’ when little else is ready. It is a large, hardy plant that takes up space for almost a year.

That investment pays off with weeks of pickings from each plant. It suits medium and large plots, and needs staking and netting, but needs little more than watering. White-sprouting types are also available.
sow: Sow in April and May in seed trays or modules, or in a seedbed outdoors, 1–2 cm deep, and keep watered. Seedlings are ready to plant in a month to six weeks, at 10–15 cm tall. Plant them in June to July, 60 cm apart in rows 75 cm apart, setting them deeply into firm soil.

Choose an open, sunny site with firm, fertile, well-drained soil, ideally where legumes grew the previous year, and lime if the soil is acidic. Tread the soil firm before planting and water in well. Net the plants straight away, as pigeons are the main threat.
sow_tips: Plant into firm soil and tread it down.
Choose early, mid and late varieties for a long season.
Do not plant in soil recently manured, which gives soft growth.
grow: Water in dry spells during summer, and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser in midsummer. Remove weeds, and earth up the stems in autumn and stake the plants in exposed places, as tall plants rock in winter gales and the roots loosen.

Pigeons, cabbage white caterpillars and aphids are the main nuisances, and a fine-mesh brassica cage deals with all three. Remove yellow leaves, which attract slugs and disease. Clubroot is the risk in acid soil; lime and rotate.
grow_tips: Stake or earth up plants for winter.
A fine-mesh cage keeps out pigeons and butterflies.
Remove yellowing leaves to stop slugs and rot.
Lime the soil and rotate brassicas.
harvest: Pick spears from February to May, when the flower buds are well formed but before the yellow flowers open. Snap or cut each shoot 10–15 cm from the tip, taking the central spear first. Side shoots then grow, and picking regularly keeps the plant producing for weeks.

Pick every few days in the peak, as unpicked shoots flower quickly and the plant stops cropping. Cook and eat the spears soon after picking; the sugar content falls fast. The leaves just below the buds are edible and delicious too.
harvest_tips: Pick regularly: flowering stops further growth.
Cut spears at an angle so water does not collect.
Use the young leaves as greens.
use: Steam or boil the spears for three to four minutes until tender but still bright, or roast them with olive oil and garlic. Serve with hollandaise, add them to stir-fries and pasta, or char them on the barbecue. The purple colour fades to green when cooked.

Fresh spears keep for only three or four days in the fridge in a bag, so eat them promptly. For freezing, blanch the spears for three minutes, chill quickly in cold water, dry them and freeze on trays before bagging. Do not leave harvested spears in a warm kitchen.
use_tips: Steam for three to four minutes to keep the colour.
Blanch for two minutes before freezing.
Roast at 200°C with garlic and chilli flakes.

care.job: Plant out firmly, cover with mesh against pigeons and butterflies, and keep the soil moist while plants establish.
Stake tall plants and earth up the stems, as they stand over winter and are easily rocked by wind.
Keep netting or mesh in place over winter against pigeons, and clear yellowing leaves from the base.
Pick spears regularly once they appear, as picking encourages more side shoots and prolongs cropping.
Pull up plants after cropping and clear the bed. Rotate brassicas to a fresh site.

preserving.how: Keep unwashed in a loose bag in the salad drawer.
Trim, blanch for 3 minutes, cool and freeze on a tray before bagging.
Harvest frequently and the plant produces more shoots, so pick little and often.

crops.name: Strawberry

facts.Spacing: 30–45 cm apart in rows 75 cm apart
facts.Planting depth: Crown level with the soil surface

varieties: Mara des Bois (perpetual, aromatic, wild flavour)

types.name: Summer-fruiting
types.when: Harvest June to July (early, mid, late varieties)
types.note: One heavy crop. Choose early, mid and late varieties to extend the season to about six weeks.

types.name: Perpetual (everbearing)
types.when: Harvest July to October
types.note: Lighter crops over a long period. Good for pots and small spaces.

types.name: Alpine
types.when: Harvest June to October
types.note: Tiny, intensely flavoured fruits that tolerate partial shade and grow from seed.

info: Strawberries are the most popular soft fruit and are easy to grow in beds, pots, hanging baskets and growbags, so suit gardens of every size. Nothing beats the flavour of a fully ripe homegrown berry, warm from the sun.

There are three main types: summer-fruiting varieties give a big crop in June and July, perpetual (everbearing) types fruit lightly from summer to autumn, and alpine strawberries produce tiny, intensely flavoured fruit and tolerate part shade.
sow: Plant bare-root runners in late summer (August to September) for the best crop the following summer, or in March–April for a lighter first crop. Potted plants can go in almost any time. Choose a sunny, sheltered spot with fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and dig in compost before planting.

Plant with the crown (where the leaves emerge) exactly level with the soil: too deep and it rots, too shallow and it dries out. Space 30–45 cm apart, in rows 75 cm apart. In pots, use a 25 cm pot for three plants, or a hanging basket or strawberry tower. Water in well.
sow_tips: Plant the crown level with the surface.
Plant in August for the best first crop.
grow: Water regularly, especially when the fruits form, but aim at the base, not the fruit. Mulch with straw around the plants just as the fruits begin to swell, to keep berries clean and suppress weeds. Net the plants to keep birds off, and use slug traps or wool pellets.

After the summer harvest, cut off the old foliage 5 cm above the crowns, clear it away, feed with a general fertiliser and remove excess runners. Peg runners into pots of compost to create new plants. Replace plants every three to four years, as the yield falls and viruses build up.
grow_tips: Mulch with straw as berries form.
Peg runners to make new plants.
harvest: Pick strawberries when fully red all over, with no white or green near the stalk, usually from late May or June for summer types. Pick every two days in the warm, preferably in the morning when the fruit is cool. Leave the green calyx and a short stalk on the fruit by pinching the stalk off with your fingernails.
Remove any rotting or mouldy fruit promptly to avoid spreading grey mould. Perpetual types give small flushes through the summer. Avoid picking when wet, which makes fruit rot quicker.
harvest_tips: Pick with the stalk, not the berry.
Pick in the cool of morning.
use: Eat fresh with cream, add to salads and desserts such as Eton mess, pavlova and tarts, or make jam, coulis, sorbet and smoothies. Strawberries pair well with mint, balsamic vinegar and black pepper. Over-ripe fruit is best for jam and sauces.

Fresh strawberries keep for only 1–3 days in the fridge, so use them quickly, and bring them to room temperature before eating. Freeze whole berries on a tray, then bag, for up to a year; they will be soft when thawed, so are best for sauces, smoothies and baking.
use_tips: Don’t wash until just before eating.
Freeze on a tray, then bag.

care.job: Remove dead leaves, weed around the plants and mulch with compost. Feed with a balanced fertiliser as growth starts.
Cover plants with a net or fleece if frost threatens open flowers.
Tuck straw or a mat under the trusses once the fruit sets to keep it clean and off the soil, and net against birds.
Water regularly at the base while fruiting, and feed every 10 to 14 days with a high-potash feed.
After fruiting, cut off old leaves on summer varieties and peg down a few runners into pots to make new plants. Remove the rest.
Plant new plants and clear weeds. Replace any plants more than three years old.

preserving.how: Freeze whole on a tray, then bag. They go soft when thawed, so use for sauces, smoothies and baking.
Strawberries are low in pectin, so use jam sugar or add lemon juice and set carefully.
Keep unwashed and unhulled in a single layer, and discard any mouldy fruit at once.
Slice and dry in a dehydrator until leathery for snacks and muesli.
Blend with sugar and lemon and freeze in small tubs, or sieve and bottle as syrup.

images.alt: Ripening strawberries, from green-white to ripe red, hanging from the plant

facts.Type: Hardy biennial root vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 23 cm apart in rows 38 cm apart

types.name: Yellow-fleshed swede
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest October to February
types.note: The classic swede, sweet and heavy.

types.name: Purple-top swede
types.when: Sow May to June · Harvest October to February
types.note: Hardy and mildew resistant, with a rich flavour.

info: Swede is a hardy, undemanding winter root that is ideal for the cold part of the year when little else is cropping. The flesh is sweet and golden, a lot more flavoursome when freshly grown, and it stands in the ground from October to March.

It belongs to the brassica family, so it shares cabbage’s problems, such as clubroot and flea beetle, and it likes a firm, moist soil that is not too acidic. A sowing in early summer is all you need, making swede one of the lowest-effort crops for a medium or large plot.
sow: Sow in late May to June, directly where plants will grow, in a sunny site with firm, fertile, moisture-retentive soil that has been limed if it is acidic. Sow thinly in shallow drills 1–2 cm deep and 38 cm apart. Later sowings are less prone to mildew and flea beetle but will not reach full size, so do not leave sowing past mid-June.

Seedlings emerge in a week to ten days. Thin them in two stages, first to 10 cm and later to 23 cm apart, so the final plants have room to swell. A prepared bed raked to a fine tilth gives the most even germination.
sow_tips: Sow in late May to mid-June, not later.
Lime acidic soils to guard against clubroot.
Firm the seedbed by treading before sowing.
Cover with fine mesh to protect from flea beetle.
grow: Keep the bed weeded and water in dry weather, because irregular moisture causes splitting, woody roots and brown heart (a boron deficiency). A mulch after thinning conserves moisture. Swedes need little feeding on reasonably fertile soil, and too much nitrogen gives leafy plants with small roots.

Clubroot is the serious disease, causing swollen, distorted roots, and it lives in the soil for many years, so lime the soil and rotate brassicas. Flea beetle on seedlings, caterpillars on the leaves and powdery mildew on older ones are the other likely troubles. Mildew-resistant varieties and watering well help most.
grow_tips: Lime acidic soil to a pH of 6.5–7 before sowing.
Water steadily to avoid split and woody roots.
Rotate brassicas on a four-year plan.
Net against pigeons and cabbage white caterpillars.
harvest: Roots are ready from October, when they are about the size of a tennis ball, although they can grow larger without becoming woody. Frosts improve the flavour, so there is no hurry. Lift with a fork, twist off the leaves and trim the roots, taking care not to damage the skin.

Swedes will stand in the ground until March in most areas and are lifted as needed. In hard winters, cover rows with straw or fleece to keep the soil workable. Lift any remaining roots before spring regrowth turns them hard and fibrous.
harvest_tips: Harvest after the first frost for sweeter roots.
Use straw or fleece in severe frost.
Do not leave them in the ground after March.
use: Boil and mash swede with butter and black pepper, or with carrots for a classic ‘neeps’ dish. It roasts beautifully, goes into stews, soups and pasties, and can be grated raw into slaws when young. Cubed swede is a good low-carbohydrate alternative to potatoes in curries.

Lifted roots store for several weeks in a cool, airy place, or for months layered in dry sand in a frost-free shed, though they are best left in the ground until needed. Peel thickly, as the skin is tough and waxy. Cubed and blanched for three minutes, swede freezes well.
use_tips: Peel thickly to remove the tough outer layer.
Roast cubes in oil with rosemary at 200°C.
Blanch for three minutes before freezing.
Mash with butter and plenty of black pepper.

care.job: Thin seedlings to about 25 cm apart, and water evenly, as irregular watering splits roots.
Cover with fine mesh against flea beetles and cabbage root fly, and watch for club root in brassicas.
Feed lightly with a general fertiliser if growth is slow, but avoid fresh manure.
Lift roots before hard frosts or protect with a thick layer of straw, and store in boxes of sand.

preserving.how: Lift as needed through winter, as swedes are very hardy.
Trim, brush off soil and store in damp sand or a box in a cool, frost-free shed.
Peel, cube, blanch for 3 minutes and freeze, or freeze as mash.
Make swede soup and freeze in portions.

crops.name: Sweet cicely
crops.sun_text: Partial to full shade; moist soil

facts.Sow: Sow fresh seed Sep–Oct, or plant Mar–Oct

info: Sweet cicely is a graceful, ferny perennial with lacy foliage, frothy white flowers in spring, and a sweet aniseed flavour. It thrives in shade, where many herbs will not grow, and is among the earliest herbs to appear in spring.
The leaves have a natural sweetness that can reduce the sugar needed when cooking sharp fruit such as rhubarb and gooseberries. It self-seeds readily, so deadhead if you do not want it everywhere.
sow: Sow fresh seed in September to October, 1 cm deep, as it needs a cold spell to germinate, and may take until spring. Stored seed is slow and unreliable, so it is easier to buy a young plant or divide an established clump in autumn.
Plant in partial or full shade in moist, fertile soil, 60–90 cm apart. Water until established.
grow: Little care is required. Water in dry spells and mulch with compost in spring. Cut back after flowering to produce a second flush of fresh leaves. Deadhead before seeds ripen to prevent self-seeding.
Powdery mildew may appear in dry weather. Divide every few years in autumn. The plant dies down in winter and reappears in March.
harvest: Pick young leaves from March, before flowering, when they are mildest and sweetest. Green seeds, picked in early summer, can be eaten raw as a nibble or added to salads and desserts; they taste of aniseed.
Roots can be dug in autumn and boiled as a vegetable, though plants are usually left. Cut back after flowering to renew the leaves.

Sweet cicely is one of the first herbs to emerge in spring, so you can harvest it when little else is ready. The big hollow stems can also be sliced and added to stewed fruit, and the large black seeds can be cracked and added to ice cream.
use: Add chopped leaves to stewed rhubarb, gooseberries, apples and plums to reduce the sugar needed, or use in salads, soups and omelettes. The aniseed flavour is mild. The green seeds are a delicious sweet nibble.
Leaves lose flavour when dried. Use fresh. The plant stays green into winter in mild areas.
use_tips: Cook with rhubarb to cut sugar.

care.job: Mulch with compost in spring and give plants room, as sweet cicely forms a large clump in light shade.
Pick leaves for sweetening rhubarb and tart fruit, and cut stems back after flowering if you do not want self-sown seedlings.
Collect the green seeds, which taste of aniseed, or let them self-sow for new plants.
Cut stems to the ground when they die back.

preserving.how: Freeze chopped leaves in bags, or ice cube trays for use with tart fruit.
Dry green or ripe seeds and keep in jars to flavour desserts.
Cook leaves with rhubarb or gooseberries to cut down on sugar.

facts.Type: Tender perennial, grown as an annual

info: Sweet marjoram is a more delicate, sweeter and less peppery cousin of oregano, with small velvety grey-green leaves and knotted flower buds that give it its other name, knotted marjoram. It is a tender plant in the UK, grown as an annual.
It needs warmth and sun, and does well in pots on a patio or windowsill. It is a classic for sausages, poultry, stuffings and tomato dishes.
sow: Sow in March to May on the surface of seed compost, pressing in lightly, at 18–20°C. Seed is tiny, so mix with sand to sow thinly. Germination takes 1–3 weeks. Prick out into modules and pot on.
Plant outside in late May or June in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot, 20 cm apart, in free-draining soil. In pots, use a gritty compost. Harden off carefully.
grow: Water sparingly, since it prefers drier conditions, and avoid feeding. Pinch out the tips to encourage bushiness. Remove flower buds to extend leaf production, unless you want the knots for drying.
In a mild area, plants may survive winter in a sheltered site with mulch, or bring pots indoors. Aphids and spider mite may occur under glass. Cut back in autumn.
harvest: Pick sprigs from about 10 weeks after sowing, snipping the top 5 cm. Flavour is strongest just before flowering in midsummer. Cut regularly to promote bushy growth.
For drying, cut stems before flowering and hang in bunches in a warm, airy place.

Marjoram flavour peaks as the knotted flower buds form in July, so cut stems at this stage if you intend to dry them. Strip the leaves and buds from the stems when dry, and store whole to preserve the flavour, crumbling just before use.
use: Use fresh or dried in stuffings, sausages, roast chicken, pork, soups, tomato sauces, beans and egg dishes. The flavour is sweet and floral. Add at the end of cooking for the best flavour, or early for slow cooked dishes.
Dried marjoram keeps a year in an airtight jar. Fresh sprigs keep a week in the fridge.
use_tips: Use fresh at the end of cooking.

care.job: Plant out after the last frost, as sweet marjoram is less hardy than oregano, and pinch out the tips for bushy plants.
Water pots only when dry, and cut stems before flowering for the best flavour.
Harvest stems for drying before the first frost and bring potted plants indoors to a bright windowsill.

preserving.how: Hang bunches in a warm, airy place and rub leaves into jars. Dries well.
Freeze leaves in bags, or chopped in ice cube trays with oil.
Mix chopped leaves into butter and freeze in rolls.

crops.name: Sweet pepper
crops.sun_text: Full sun; warm and sheltered, ideally under cover

facts.Type: Tender perennial, grown as an annual

varieties: Mini Bell (compact, early, ideal for pots)
Marconi Rosso (long, sweet Italian frying pepper)
Sweet Banana (yellow ripening to red, early)

types.name: Bell peppers
types.when: Sow February to March · Harvest August to October
types.note: Thick-walled blocky fruit that turn red, yellow or orange when ripe.

types.name: Pointed and sweet frying peppers
types.when: Sow February to March · Harvest August to October
types.note: Long, tapered and thin-skinned. Sweeter than bells and more productive.

info: Sweet peppers give crisp, juicy fruit in red, yellow, orange and green and are a satisfying crop in a greenhouse, polytunnel or sunny spot. They need a long, warm season, so start early and give them the sunniest place you can.

Compact varieties are good in pots on a sunny patio or balcony, but in cooler summers, peppers outdoors can be slow to ripen. Green fruit is simply unripe red; waiting for colour brings out the sweetness.
sow: Sow in February or March, 5 mm deep in seed compost, at 20–25°C in a heated propagator, as they need warmth to germinate and take two to three weeks. Prick out seedlings into individual pots, and pot on as they grow.

Plant into final 25–30 cm pots or growing bags in the greenhouse in May, or outdoors in early June if the nights are warm and the site sheltered. Harden off for two weeks. Use a tall pot with good drainage and a rich compost, and put a cane in as support.
sow_tips: Plant out only when nights are warm.
grow: Water regularly but do not overwater, and feed weekly with tomato feed once the first fruits appear. Pinch out the central growing tip when the plant is 30 cm tall for a bushier plant. Remove the first flower to let the plant establish, then allow fruits to develop.

Support laden branches with canes and ties. Mist flowers lightly to help fruit set in dry weather. Aphids, red spider mite and whitefly can be a problem under glass. Good ventilation and regular checking prevent most issues.
grow_tips: Pinch out the tip at 30 cm.
harvest: Pick peppers when they are full size and firm. Green peppers can be picked early, but waiting until they turn red, yellow or orange gives a sweeter flavour and more vitamins. Cut the fruit off with scissors or secateurs, leaving a short stalk, as pulling can break branches.

Regular picking encourages more fruit. At the end of the season, before the first frost, pick all remaining fruits. Green ones will ripen indoors on a sunny windowsill, or can be cooked as green peppers.
harvest_tips: Cut with scissors, leaving a short stalk.
Wait for colour for the sweetest taste.
Pick often to prompt more flowers.
use: Eat sweet peppers raw in salads and with dips, stuff and bake them, roast to remove the skins and enhance sweetness, or use in stir-fries, ratatouille, fajitas, sauces and soups. Roasted peppers in oil are delicious on pizza or in sandwiches.

Peppers keep for one to two weeks in the fridge. To freeze, deseed and slice, spread on a tray, freeze, then pack in bags; they will be soft when thawed, so are best used cooked. Roasted peppers can be stored in oil in the fridge for a week, or frozen in portions.
use_tips: Roast and peel for a smoky sweetness.
Stuff and bake the larger fruits.
Store in the fridge’s salad drawer.

care.job: Pot on and harden off before planting in a greenhouse or warm, sheltered spot after the last frost.
Pinch out the first flower to let the plant bulk up, then stake plants as heavy fruit forms.
Water regularly and feed every one to two weeks with a high-potash feed once fruits set.
Leave fruits on the plant to change colour from green to red, yellow or orange for the sweetest flavour.
Pick all remaining fruit before frost.

pests.label: Blossom end rot from irregular watering

preserving.how: Keep whole peppers in the salad drawer.
Slice or dice raw, with seeds removed, and freeze in bags. No blanching needed, and they stay usable for cooking.
Roast, peel and pack into a jar with vinegar, then keep it in the fridge. Do not preserve in oil at room temperature, and use within a week if you cover with oil.
Cook into sweet pepper relish or chutney.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator.

crops.name: Sweet potato
crops.sun_text: Full sun; warm and sheltered, ideally under cover

facts.Type: Tender perennial vine, grown as an annual
facts.Sow: Start slips Mar–Apr; plant out June
facts.Spacing: 40 cm apart in ridges 90 cm apart
facts.Planting depth: Roots buried, slip leaves above ground

info: Sweet potatoes are a tropical crop that will crop in a warm, sunny UK summer, especially in a greenhouse, polytunnel or on a south-facing plot. They need a long, warm season, so they reward gardeners who can provide shelter and plastic mulch.

They are grown from rooted shoots called slips, not tubers. The pretty heart-shaped leaves are edible, and the trailing vines make good ground cover. Choose early varieties bred for short seasons, such as Beauregard or Georgia Jet.
sow: Buy slips in spring, or grow your own by suspending a sprouting sweet potato half-submerged in water on a warm windowsill from February. After 4–6 weeks, shoots form; twist them off with a few roots and pot them up individually in compost at 20°C.

Plant out in early June, once the soil is warm and frost has passed, 40 cm apart on ridges about 20 cm high, covered with black plastic mulch to trap warmth. Plant in a greenhouse border or large 30 cm pots for the most reliable results.
sow_tips: Use a warm windowsill for slips.
Make ridges and warm the soil with black plastic.
Plant out in June, never earlier.
grow: Water regularly while the plants establish, then ease off as tubers swell; overwatering gives lush vines and few roots. Feed lightly with a high-potash fertiliser, since too much nitrogen promotes leaves, not tubers. Keep plants covered with fleece on cold nights.

Vines can be trained up a support or allowed to trail, but do not let them root along the stem, which makes lots of small tubers. Slugs, wireworm and vine weevil are the main pests. Keep plants warm: growth stops below 10°C.
grow_tips: Lift stems that root along the ground.
Protect with fleece on cool nights.
harvest: Dig sweet potatoes in late September or October, before the first frost blackens the vines, or when the leaves yellow. Loosen the soil with a fork well away from the plant, since the skins bruise easily, and lift the tubers carefully.

Cure them for 10 days in a warm (25–30°C), humid place such as an airing cupboard or a greenhouse, which heals skin scratches and sweetens the flesh. Brush off soil rather than washing before storage.
use: Roast sweet potatoes in wedges or whole, bake them like jacket potatoes, mash, or add to curries, soups, stews and traybakes. The flesh is sweet and creamy, and the skin is edible once cooked. The young leaves can be steamed like spinach.
Cured tubers keep for 3–5 months in a dry place at around 13–16°C, never in the fridge, which spoils the flavour. Cooked sweet potato can be frozen mashed or in chunks.

care.job: Plant out slips after the last frost, ideally under cloches or fleece, in a sunny spot with loose, well-drained soil.
Water in dry spells but avoid overwatering, and mulch around the plants to keep roots warm and moist.
Lift the trailing stems occasionally so they do not root along their length, which reduces tuber size.
Lift tubers before the first frost, handling carefully, and cure them in a warm, humid place for about ten days.

preserving.how: Cure at 25–30°C for a week after digging, then keep in a cool, dry place at 12–15°C. Do not refrigerate.
Bake, roast or mash and freeze in portions.
Cook into soup and freeze in tubs.
Slice thinly and dry in a dehydrator for chips.

crops.name: Sweetcorn

facts.Sow: Apr–May indoors; plant out late May–June

varieties: Swift (very early, good for cooler regions)

types.name: Standard sweet
types.when: Sow April to May · Harvest August to September
types.note: Classic taste and the most reliable. Best eaten straight from the plant.

types.name: Super-sweet
types.when: Sow late April to May · Harvest September
types.note: Hold their sugar for longer after picking, but need warm soil. Keep away from standard types.

types.name: Baby corn
types.when: Sow May · Harvest July to August
types.note: Picked young when the silks first show. Good for stir-fries.

info: Homegrown sweetcorn eaten within minutes of picking is far sweeter than anything from a shop, because the sugars begin turning to starch as soon as the cobs are picked. Plants are tall and architectural, and the crop is an enjoyable one for families.

Sweetcorn is wind-pollinated, so plant in a block, not a row, to ensure the cobs are filled. It needs space, sun and warmth, and does best with a good summer, though modern super-sweet F1 varieties are bred for the UK climate.
sow: Sow indoors from mid-April to mid-May, 2.5 cm deep, one seed per 7–9 cm pot (or in loo-roll tubes, as roots dislike disturbance) at 18–21°C. Seedlings appear in a week. Harden off in late May.

Plant out in late May to June, once the frost has gone, in a sunny, sheltered spot with rich soil. Plant in a block of at least 4 by 4 plants, about 35–45 cm apart, so wind can carry pollen between the male tassels and female silks. In warm areas, direct sowing outdoors is possible in mid-May.
sow_tips: Plant in a block, not a row.
Use deep pots or tubes for roots.
Sow direct only if the soil is warm.
grow: Water well during dry spells, particularly when the plants are flowering and the cobs are developing, and mulch to keep the soil moist. Feed with a high-potash fertiliser when the cobs start to swell. Earth up the base of the stems to support them, and stake in exposed sites.

Weed gently, as roots are shallow. Mice, badgers and squirrels can strip the cobs just before harvest. Smut, a fungus that forms grey-white swellings on the cobs, is edible (huitlacoche) but should be removed from the garden after. Do not plant too early, because cold checks growth.
grow_tips: Earth up the base of the stems.
Protect from animals as cobs ripen.
harvest: Cobs are ready from late August to September, when the silks at the tip have turned brown and dry and the husk feels plump. Peel back a small bit of husk and press a kernel with your fingernail: if the juice is milky, it is ready; clear means it is too early, and doughy means too late.
Twist and pull the cob downward to snap it off. Cook and eat immediately, ideally within minutes of picking, for the best sweetness. Pick baby corn when the silks are just showing.
harvest_tips: Check the kernels give milky juice.
Check cobs every few days at harvest time.
use: Boil cobs in unsalted water for 5–8 minutes, or grill or barbecue them in the husk, and serve with butter, salt and pepper. Cut the kernels off for salads, salsas, fritters, soups and chowders. Baby corn is delicious in stir-fries.

Cobs lose sweetness quickly, so eat them on the day. To preserve a glut, blanch cobs for 7–11 minutes depending on size, cool quickly, and freeze whole or cut off the kernels and freeze in bags, which keep for a year.
use_tips: Do not salt the boiling water.

care.job: Harden off and plant in blocks, not rows, 35 to 45 cm apart, because sweetcorn is wind-pollinated.
Water regularly, particularly when the tassels and silks appear and while the cobs fill out.
Earth up around the base of stems to support them and weed carefully, as roots are shallow.
Feed with a high-potash fertiliser once cobs start to swell.
Guard against badgers, birds and squirrels as cobs ripen, and check the silks have turned brown before picking.

pests.label: Poor pollination if grown in a single row

preserving.how: Keep cobs in their husks in the fridge. Sugars convert to starch within a day or so, so eat or freeze quickly.
Blanch whole cobs for 7 minutes (small), 9 (medium) or 11 (large), cool and freeze, or blanch for 4 minutes, cut off the kernels and freeze in bags.
Cook kernels into sweetcorn relish with peppers and vinegar.
Leave cobs of grinding or popping types on the plant until dry and use as cornmeal or popcorn.

crops.name: Swiss chard
crops.latin: Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla var. flavescens

facts.Type: Hardy biennial leaf vegetable, grown as an annual
facts.Spacing: Thin to 30–45 cm apart in rows 45 cm apart

varieties: Fordhook Giant (white stems, large and reliable)

info: Swiss chard is one of the most useful and decorative leaf vegetables, with large glossy leaves and bright coloured stems in red, yellow, orange, pink and white. It is hardy, productive and easy, and a few plants give leaves for months.

Chard is more tolerant of heat and cold than spinach, with less tendency to bolt, so it can be cropped from early summer right into the following spring in mild areas. It suits borders and containers as well as the vegetable bed.
sow: Sow in April to June, 2–3 cm deep, directly into well-prepared, fertile soil in sun or light shade, in rows 45 cm apart. Chard seed is a cluster of several seeds, so each sowing produces several seedlings; thin to the strongest at 30–45 cm apart. You can also start seeds in modules in March and April under cover.

Sow a second batch in July to August for autumn and winter picking, which will crop through the cold months with a cloche or fleece for protection. Soaking the seed overnight speeds germination. Chard also grows happily in large pots at least 30 cm deep.
sow_tips: Thin each cluster to the strongest seedling.
Sow again in July for winter leaf.
Use pots at least 30 cm deep on a balcony.
grow: Keep plants watered during dry spells, and mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. Feed with a general fertiliser once or twice in summer to keep the plants producing. Cut off any flower stems that appear to extend cropping.

Chard is rarely troubled, but leaf miners can tunnel in the leaves, slugs eat young plants and birds may peck seedlings. Pinch off affected leaves and use traps or nets as needed. In cold winters, cover plants with a cloche or fleece to keep the leaves usable.
grow_tips: Pinch off leaves with leaf-miner tracks.
Mulch to keep the soil moist.
Cut flower stems to keep cropping.
harvest: Pick baby leaves from about six weeks, and full-size leaves from eight to twelve weeks. Cut or twist off the outer leaves about 3 cm above the base, leaving the centre to grow more. Take only a few leaves from each plant at a time, so it can keep growing.

Plants keep producing for many months, and overwintered plants give a second flush of leaves in spring before they flower. Pull out the plants once they run to seed and the leaves turn tough. Frost can scorch leaves, but healthy plants will recover.
harvest_tips: Take no more than a third of a plant at once.
Pull plants out once they bolt.
use: Chard is two vegetables in one: the leaves can be cooked like spinach, and the thick colourful stems like asparagus. Strip the stems from the leaves, then cook the stems for about five minutes and the leaves for one or two. Use them in gratins, quiches, pasta, soups and stir-fries.

Unwashed leaves keep for three to four days in the fridge in a bag. For freezing, separate leaves and stalks, blanch for two minutes (leaves) or three minutes (stalks), cool and pack in portions. Raw baby leaves are good in salads.
use_tips: Use baby leaves raw in salads.
Add garlic and lemon to sautéed chard.

care.job: Thin or plant out to 30 cm apart and water well until established, protecting from slugs.
Water in dry spells and feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser to keep leaves growing, and pick leaves from the outside.
Cut off any flower stalks as they appear to keep leaf production going.
Cover plants with a cloche or fleece for winter pickings, and remove damaged leaves.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Blanch leaves for 2 minutes and stems for 3, cool and freeze in portions.
Chard crops for months and survives most winters, so pick little and often.
Make into gratins, soups or fillings and freeze.

facts.Spacing: 20 cm apart (or sow thickly for baby leaf)

info: Tatsoi is a compact, hardy Asian green that forms a flat rosette of dark, spoon-shaped leaves, with a mild mustardy flavour. It tolerates cold, down to about -10°C, so it is a good choice for winter salads and stir-fries.
It grows well in pots, window boxes and cold frames, and it is easy and fast. It is also bolt-resistant when sown in autumn, making it a perfect winter leaf.
sow: Sow from March to April and from August to September, 1 cm deep, either in rows 20–30 cm apart or broadcast thickly for baby leaves. Seeds germinate in 3–5 days. Thin to 20 cm for full heads.
Cover with fine mesh to avoid flea beetle. Autumn sowings can be protected with a cloche or fleece in winter. Sow again every two to three weeks.
sow_tips: Sow in spring and late summer.
Use a cloche for winter crops.
grow: Water regularly, since dry soil makes the leaves bitter and encourages bolting. Weed carefully. No feeding needed in reasonable soil.
Flea beetle and slugs are the main problems. Tatsoi is hardy and survives frost, though protection improves the leaf quality. Rotate with other brassicas.

Tatsoi forms flat rosettes, so keep the soil around it free of slug hiding places and mulch with clean straw to keep the leaves from splashing with mud. The plants are among the hardiest of the Asian greens and are best in the cool months, when they grow slowly but are sweeter and less prone to pests. A cloche on the coldest nights keeps leaves clean.
harvest: Cut baby leaves from three weeks, or harvest the whole rosette at 15–20 cm across, at 6–8 weeks. Cut outer leaves first, or cut the whole plant 2.5 cm above the ground for regrowth.
In winter, pick leaves as needed. The yellow flowers in spring are edible. Pick in the morning.
use: Use baby tatsoi raw in salads, or stir-fry larger leaves with garlic and soy sauce for a minute or two. It is also good in soups, noodle dishes and steamed with sesame oil. The leaves are mild with a hint of mustard.
Fresh leaves keep for 3–4 days in the fridge. It is best eaten fresh. Blanch and freeze for cooking.
use_tips: Keep in a bag in the fridge.

care.job: Water regularly and cover with fine mesh against flea beetles and cabbage white butterflies.
Pick outer leaves or cut whole rosettes when about 15 cm across, leaving the plant to regrow.
Protect with a cloche in winter, as tatsoi is hardy but benefits from shelter and keeps cropping.

preserving.how: Wrap unwashed leaves in damp paper in a bag.
It is hardy, so cut outer leaves through winter.
Blanch for 1 minute, squeeze and freeze for cooked dishes.

facts.Time to harvest: Light picking in year 1; fully from year 2

types.name: Common (cooking) thyme
types.when: Pick all year
types.note: The best all-round flavour for stews, roasts and stuffing.

types.name: Lemon thyme
types.when: Pick all year
types.note: Citrus scent, brilliant with fish, chicken and desserts.

types.name: Creeping thyme
types.when: Flowers June to July
types.note: Low carpets for paths and between paving, which smell lovely underfoot.

info: Thyme is a tough, aromatic evergreen that thrives in poor, dry, sunny places, and it is among the easiest and most useful of the Mediterranean herbs. It lasts for years, is a magnet for bees, and looks good in rockeries, paths and containers.
There are many varieties: common thyme for cooking, lemon thyme for fish and chicken, and creeping thymes for lawn and paths. Poor, free-draining soil produces more flavourful plants than rich soil.
sow: Plant potted thyme from March to October in a sunny position in free-draining, gritty soil. Add plenty of grit or sharp sand on heavy ground, or plant on a raised bed or in a pot with gritty compost. Space plants 30 cm apart.

Thyme can be grown from seed sown in spring on the surface of compost, but it is slow and unpredictable; cuttings or plants are better. Take softwood cuttings in early summer, or layer stems. Water in until established, then leave.
grow: Thyme needs almost no care. Water only in prolonged droughts, and avoid overwatering and feeding. Trim plants lightly after flowering in summer, cutting back to just above the old wood, to keep them compact and prevent legginess. Don’t cut into bare wood, as it won’t regrow.

Replace plants every 4–5 years, when they become woody and sparse. Wet winters are the main killer, so ensure sharp drainage. Aphids and root rot are uncommon problems; grow in pots under cover if your soil is heavy or wet.
harvest: Pick sprigs at any time of year, though the flavour is strongest just before flowering in early summer. Cut the stems with scissors, taking the top few centimetres, and stay in the soft new growth. Light picking in the first year allows the plant to establish.
Cut larger amounts for drying in June, before flowering, in the morning once the dew is off. Flowers are edible and attractive. Plants remain evergreen and can be picked fresh in winter.
use: Add whole sprigs to stews, casseroles, roasts, stuffings, soups and sauces; the leaves strip easily from the stems. Thyme is classic with chicken, lamb, mushrooms, root vegetables and tomatoes. It is part of bouquet garni and herbes de Provence. Lemon thyme is good with fish.

Fresh thyme keeps for a week or two in the fridge, wrapped in damp paper. It dries exceptionally well, keeping its flavour: hang bunches in a warm, airy place, strip the leaves and store in a jar for up to a year. Freezing in oil also works.
use_tips: Strip leaves by running fingers down the stem.

care.job: Trim lightly after winter and feed pots sparingly, as thyme prefers poor, free-draining soil.
Cut back flowering stems to keep plants bushy and productive, and water pots only when the compost is dry.
Clip plants lightly after flowering, but never cut back into old, bare wood, as it will not reshoot.
Keep pots away from waterlogging and protect from prolonged wet, as winter rain is more of a problem than cold.
Divide or replace woody plants every 4 to 5 years, as they become leggy and less productive with age.

preserving.how: Hang bunches in a warm, airy place and strip the leaves into jars. Thyme dries very well.
Freeze sprigs in bags, or chopped in ice cube trays with oil.
Thyme is evergreen, so pick fresh sprigs all year.
Steep sprigs in honey or syrup for coughs and cooking.
preserving.keeps: Honey: 6 months; syrup: 1 month in the fridge

info: Tomatillos produce tangy green fruits wrapped in papery husks, essential for Mexican salsa verde. Plants are vigorous, sprawling relatives of tomatoes, and they crop reliably in a warm UK summer, especially under glass.
They are not self-fertile, so you need to grow at least two plants for pollination. Fruits are ready when they split their husks.
sow: Sow from March to April, 5 mm deep, in pots at 20°C, as for tomatoes. Prick out seedlings into individual pots, and plant out in early June after hardening off, 60–75 cm apart, into rich soil or large pots. Grow at least two.
A sunny, sheltered spot is essential; a greenhouse is more reliable. Provide stakes or cages.
grow: Water regularly and feed with tomato fertiliser every 1–2 weeks once flowering. Pinching out side shoots is unnecessary. Support the sprawling stems.
Pests are as for tomatoes; blight can occur in wet summers. Fruits fall to the ground when ripe; mulch with straw to keep clean.

Tomatillos need sturdy support, as the branches break under the weight of fruit. A tomato cage or three canes with string is ideal. They are thirsty plants, so mulch to help soil moisture. If no fruit sets, check that you have at least two plants and that they are flowering at the same time; pollinators visit the pale yellow flowers freely.
harvest: Pick when the fruit has filled the husk and the husk is beginning to split, usually from August to October. Fruits should be firm and bright green, or slightly yellow if more mature; ripe ones are sweeter.
Pick regularly. Fruit left on the ground is edible if clean. Harvest all before frost.
use: Remove the husk, rinse off the sticky coating and roast or grill the fruits for salsa verde with chillies, coriander and lime. Also good in stews, sauces and chutneys. They are tart and citrusy when cooked.
Store in husks in the fridge for 2–3 weeks. Freeze whole or as salsa for a year.

For classic salsa verde, roast husked tomatillos under a hot grill until blistered, then blend with raw onion, garlic, coriander, a fresh green chilli, lime juice and salt. It keeps for a week in the fridge. Tomatillos also add acidity to stews and chilli sauces.

care.job: Harden off and plant out after the last frost in a sunny, sheltered spot, and stake or cage plants as they grow tall.
Plant at least two for pollination, water regularly and feed every two weeks with a tomato feed once fruit sets.
Pick fruits when the husk is filled and splitting, before the fruit turns yellow, and clear plants after the first frost.

pests.label: Poor pollination if only one plant

preserving.how: Keep fruit in its husk in a cool, dry place, which protects it.
Keep husked fruit in a bag in the fridge.
Roast and blend into salsa verde and freeze in tubs.
Freeze whole husked fruit on a tray, then bag.

crops.name: Tomato
crops.sun_text: Full sun, 6+ hours; a sheltered, south-facing spot

facts.Sow: Feb–Apr indoors; plant out late May–June

types.name: Cordon (indeterminate)
types.when: Sow February to April · Harvest July to October
types.note: Tall single stems tied to a cane, with side shoots pinched out. The longest cropping season, in a greenhouse or sunny spot.

types.name: Bush (determinate)
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest August to September
types.note: Compact, self-limiting plants that need no pinching out. Ideal for pots and outdoors.

types.name: Trailing and basket
types.when: Sow March to April · Harvest July to September
types.note: Cascading cherry types for hanging baskets and window boxes.

info: Tomatoes are the most popular crop in British gardens, and nothing compares with a warm, sun-ripened homegrown fruit. They come in an extraordinary range of colours, shapes and flavours, from tiny cherries and plum types to large beefsteaks, in red, yellow, orange, black and striped.

They grow in a greenhouse, in a sunny spot outdoors, or in pots and hanging baskets on a balcony. Bush and trailing types need no pinching out; cordon (indeterminate) types are trained up a cane and give the longest cropping season.
sow: Sow indoors from late February to April, 5 mm deep in pots or trays of seed compost, at 18–21°C on a bright windowsill or in a heated propagator. Seedlings appear in 7–10 days. When they have two true leaves, pot them individually into 7–9 cm pots, holding them by the leaves, not the stem, and burying the stem up to the first leaves.

Harden plants off for a week or two from mid-May, and plant out after the last frost, usually late May in the south and early June further north. Plant into rich soil, large pots of at least 30 cm, or growing bags, burying the stem to the first leaves to build a strong root system. Space 45–60 cm apart.
sow_tips: Sow in March for outdoor plants.
Bury the stem up to the first leaves when potting on.
Harden off for 10–14 days before planting out.
Wait until the last frost has gone.
grow: Tie cordon types to a tall cane or string as they grow, and pinch out the side shoots that form in the leaf joints. Remove the growing tip when the plant has four to five trusses outdoors, around the beginning of August. Bush types can be left to sprawl, perhaps on straw.

Water regularly and evenly, because irregular watering causes split fruit and blossom end rot. Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato feed once the first flowers have set. Remove lower leaves as the fruit ripen to boost air flow. Blight is the main disease in wet summers; choose resistant varieties such as Crimson Crush, and pick fruit promptly if it appears.
grow_tips: Pinch out side shoots on cordon types.
Feed weekly with tomato feed once flowers set.
harvest: Pick tomatoes when they are fully coloured and slightly soft to the touch, usually from July to the first frosts in October. Pick regularly, as this encourages more fruit. Leave them on the vine as long as possible for the best flavour, but pick before heavy rain, which can split ripe fruit.

Toward the end of the season, remove the growing tip and the lower leaves to help the last trusses ripen. Before the first frost, pick all the fruit, including the green ones. Ripen green tomatoes indoors in a drawer or bowl with a ripe banana, or turn them into chutney.
harvest_tips: Pick regularly to keep fruit coming.
Leave on the vine until fully coloured.
Pick everything before the first frost.
Ripen green fruit with a banana.
use: Eat ripe tomatoes fresh in salads, sandwiches and bruschetta, roast them with olive oil and garlic to concentrate the sweetness, or cook down gluts into rich sauces, soups, passata and chutney. Cherry tomatoes make a good snack, and plum varieties are ideal for sauces and sun-dried tomatoes.

Never store ripe tomatoes in the fridge, because it dulls their flavour and makes them mealy. Keep them at room temperature out of direct sun, and eat them within a few days. Whole, roasted or sauced tomatoes freeze well, and passata can be jarred or frozen in portions.
use_tips: Keep ripe tomatoes out of the fridge.
Roast surplus tomatoes and freeze them.

care.job: Pot seedlings into individual pots once they have their first true leaves, and keep them frost-free and in bright light.
Harden off for 7 to 10 days, then plant out after the last frost, burying the stem up to the first leaves for a stronger root system.
Tie cordon types to a cane or string as they grow and pinch out the side shoots that form in each leaf joint every week.
Water regularly and evenly, preferably in the morning, to avoid split fruit and blossom end rot.
Feed weekly with a high-potash tomato feed once the first flowers have set fruit.
Pinch out the growing tip of cordons at about four or five trusses so the plant puts its energy into ripening.
Watch for blight (brown patches on leaves and fruit) after warm, humid spells and remove affected plants promptly; bin them rather than composting.
Pick remaining green fruit before the first frost and ripen indoors, then clear the plants.

preserving.how: Pick green tomatoes before the first frost, then ripen them on a windowsill or in a drawer with a banana.
Freeze whole, which loosens the skins, or make into sauce and freeze in tubs. Thawed tomatoes are for cooking only.
Halve small tomatoes and dry in a low oven or dehydrator until leathery. Store in jars or the freezer.
Cook down, sieve and freeze, or bottle with added lemon juice or citric acid and process in a water bath.
Use both ripe and green tomatoes, with onions, apples, sugar and vinegar.
Fridge cold dulls flavour, so keep ripe tomatoes on a shelf out of the sun.

images.alt: A truss of ripe red tomatoes growing on the vine

crops.name: Turnip

facts.Type: Hardy annual or biennial root vegetable
facts.Sow: Mar–Apr and Jul–Aug, straight into the soil
facts.Spacing: Thin to 10–15 cm apart in rows 23–30 cm apart

varieties: Purple Top Milan (fast and flat, for early crops)

types.name: Early (summer) turnips
types.when: Sow March to June · Harvest May to August
types.note: Small, sweet, tender roots eaten young.

types.name: Maincrop (autumn) turnips
types.when: Sow July to August · Harvest October to December
types.note: Larger, hardier roots for stores and stews.

info: Turnips are quick, easy roots that can be harvested young as tender, mild, sweet baby turnips, or left to size up for winter. They are among the fastest of the brassicas, and sowings in spring and again in late summer give two main harvest windows.

Both the root and the leaves, known as turnip tops or greens, are edible, and the tops are a useful early spring cut. They like cool, moist weather and bolt or turn woody if they are stressed by drought, so keep them well watered.
sow: For an early crop, sow from March to April under cloches or fleece, choosing a quick, bolt-resistant variety. For autumn and winter roots, sow in July and August, when moisture is steadier and flea beetle is less of a problem. Sow thinly in shallow drills 1–2 cm deep, in rows 23–30 cm apart, then thin as they grow.

Turnips grow best in fertile, moisture-retentive soil that has been well dug and is free of fresh manure. In a small garden, sow a short row every two or three weeks, which gives tender baby turnips from 6–8 weeks. They can also be grown in deep containers for an easy crop on a balcony.
sow_tips: Sow short rows every two to three weeks for baby turnips.
Use fleece in March to protect against cold and flea beetle.
Make a main sowing in July or August for autumn crops.
Water the drill before sowing in dry spells.
grow: Thin seedlings to 10–15 cm apart in two stages, the first when they are 2–3 cm tall. Water regularly: turnips need steady moisture to swell evenly, and drought gives woody, hot-tasting roots. Hoe between rows to keep weeds down, taking care not to disturb the shallow roots.

Flea beetle makes tiny holes in the leaves, particularly in spring, and is best prevented by fine mesh or by keeping plants well watered. Like all brassicas, turnips are prone to clubroot on acid soils, so lime when needed and rotate crops every year, with a gap of at least four years.
grow_tips: Fine insect mesh from sowing is the best flea beetle control.
Water evenly to avoid splitting and woody roots.
Rotate with other brassicas on a four-year plan.
Lime acid soils for clubroot control.
harvest: Baby turnips are ready from about six weeks, at the size of a golf ball, and are at their sweetest and most tender then. Maincrop turnips are best at about 5–7 cm across; larger roots get woody and strong-tasting. Pull or lift with a fork and cut off the tops.

Turnip tops can be cut as greens from about four weeks, picking a few leaves from each plant. Late-sown turnips can stay in the ground through autumn and be lifted as needed, although in colder areas lift them before hard frosts and store.
harvest_tips: Pick small turnips for the best flavour.
Cut the tops as greens while young.
Lift before hard frosts in cold areas.
Pull in the morning and keep roots cool.
use: Young turnips are lovely raw, grated or sliced thin in salads, or lightly steamed and buttered. Larger roots are better roasted, mashed with potatoes, or added to stews and soups. The tops can be sautéed with garlic and chilli, much like spring greens.

Twist off the tops and keep the roots in a bag in the fridge for up to two weeks. For longer storage, keep undamaged roots in a box of dry sand or compost in a cool, frost-free shed for two to three months. Cubed turnips can be blanched for two minutes and frozen.
use_tips: Roast with honey and thyme for sweetness.
Use the tops quickly, like spinach.
Blanch cubes for two minutes before freezing.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 10 to 15 cm apart and water evenly, as dry spells make roots woody and strong-flavoured.
Cover with fine mesh against flea beetles and cabbage root fly.
Lift maincrop turnips before hard frosts and store in boxes of sand or leave in the ground under straw.

preserving.how: Trim leaves and keep roots in a bag in the salad drawer.
Store maincrop turnips in damp sand in a cool, frost-free shed.
Peel, cube, blanch for 2 minutes and freeze.
Pickle sliced turnips in vinegar with a slice of beetroot for colour.
Blanch and freeze the green tops like spring greens.

facts.Sow: Feb–Jun, or Jul–Aug for winter flowers

info: Violas, heartsease and pansies are charming, long-flowering edible flowers in a huge range of colours, from deep purple to yellow, white and bicolours. They provide colour from autumn right through winter and spring, and decorate salads, cakes and desserts.
They are hardy, easy and wonderful in pots and window boxes. Small-flowered violas flower the most, and heartsease (Viola tricolor) self-seeds freely around the garden.
sow: Sow seed on the surface of seed compost, barely covered with vermiculite, from February to June, or July to August for flowers in winter. Keep at 15–18°C. Germination takes 2–3 weeks. Prick out and pot on, planting out when 5 cm tall.
Or buy plug plants in autumn. Plant in sun or part shade in any reasonable soil or in containers, 15–20 cm apart.
sow_tips: Sow in July for winter flowers.
Plant in pots for winter colour.
grow: Deadhead regularly to promote more flowers, which are borne continuously. Water in dry weather and feed fortnightly with a liquid fertiliser in pots. Cut back straggly plants in midsummer to rejuvenate.
Slugs love young plants, and aphids and powdery mildew may appear. Pansies fade in hot summer weather, so replace with fresh plants. Violas tolerate heat better.
harvest: Pick fully open flowers in the morning, by pinching them off just below the flower head. Pick regularly, as this encourages more blooms. Use only flowers grown without pesticides.
Use immediately for the best colour, or candy for longer storage.

Viola flowers wilt quickly, so pick as late as possible before serving, and place them in a small bowl of cold water in the fridge to keep them crisp until needed. Pick flowers only from plants you know have not been sprayed.
use: Scatter flowers over salads, desserts, cakes, soups and canapés, or freeze in ice cubes for drinks. Candy them with egg white and caster sugar for cake decoration, or press them into butter. The flavour is mild and slightly sweet.
Fresh flowers last 2–3 days in the fridge in a sealed box with damp paper. Candied flowers keep for months in an airtight tin.

care.job: Plant out after any hard frosts and water in well, in partial shade for the best flowers.
Deadhead regularly to keep violas flowering, pick flowers for salads and cakes, and feed pots every two weeks.
Cut back leggy plants by half in mid-summer, water and feed to encourage a second flush of flowers.

preserving.how: Brush flowers with egg white, dust with caster sugar and dry on a rack. Use on cakes.
Freeze flowers in ice cubes for drinks.
Press or dry flowers in a dehydrator for decorating cakes.
Steep flowers in a sugar syrup for a pretty, violet-coloured drink.

crops.name: Watercress
crops.sun_text: Full sun to partial shade; needs constantly wet roots
varieties: Land cress (an easier relative for soil)

info: Watercress is a peppery, nutrient-rich salad leaf that can be grown at home in a tray of water, in a bucket, or in a pot standing in a saucer. It needs cool, flowing or frequently-changed water and a partly shaded position.
It is a perennial, but plants are best renewed from cuttings each year. A pot stood in a bowl of fresh water on a patio or windowsill can crop for months.
sow: Sow seed on the surface of damp, peat-free compost in a pot or tray in March to September, pressing in lightly, and stand in a saucer or tray of water 2–3 cm deep. Seeds germinate in about a week at 15–20°C. Keep in partial shade outdoors.
The easiest method is to root supermarket watercress stems in a glass of water, then pot up the rooted cuttings. Keep the water changing every day or two to prevent stagnation.
sow_tips: Stand pots in 2–3 cm of water.
grow: Keep the compost permanently wet, and change the water in the saucer every day or two in summer. Pinch out growing tips to encourage side shoots, and cut flower buds as they appear.

Avoid watercress from stagnant or livestock-affected water, due to liver fluke risk; homegrown plants from clean water are fine. Flea beetle and aphids may appear. Renew plants each year from cuttings.
harvest: Cut stems 5 cm above the base with scissors when they are 10–15 cm long, from 6–8 weeks after sowing. Cut regularly to encourage bushy regrowth, and harvest in the morning.
Plants flower in early summer, after which leaves become bitter. Cut back hard and let it regrow, or take cuttings.

If growing in a pot standing in water, change the water daily in hot weather to avoid stagnation, which can lead to bitter, tough leaves. In winter, plants slow and may die back, so bring pots into a cool greenhouse or cold frame.
use: Eat watercress raw in salads and sandwiches, make it into soup with potato, or wilt it into omelettes and sauces. Its peppery bite pairs with eggs, smoked fish, oranges and potatoes.
Use quickly, since it wilts fast. Keep stems in a glass of water in the fridge for up to 3 days. The soup freezes well.
use_tips: Pair with eggs and smoked fish.

care.job: Keep roots constantly wet by standing the pot in a saucer of water that is changed every day or two, and grow in partial shade.
Pinch out the tips regularly to encourage bushy growth, and cut leaves often, since flowering makes leaves bitter.
Keep plants sheltered over winter or take cuttings in a jar of water on a windowsill to start new plants.

preserving.how: Stand stems in a glass of water in the fridge and cover loosely.
Make watercress soup and freeze in portions. Blanching helps keep the colour.
Blend into a peppery pesto and freeze.
It keeps cropping in cool, wet conditions, so pick fresh and often.

crops.name: Whitecurrant
crops.sun_text: Sun or shade; tolerates a north wall
