info: Whitecurrants are translucent, pearly berries that are sweeter and milder than redcurrants, with a delicate flavour. They are grown exactly like redcurrants, tolerate partial shade, and look beautiful as cordons or standards.
They are a gourmet fruit and excellent for desserts, as they can be eaten raw, and last on the bush for weeks if netted.
sow: Plant bare-root bushes between November and March in moisture-retentive, fertile soil in sun or partial shade. Space bushes 1.2–1.5 m apart, or cordons 40 cm. Plant at the same depth as in the nursery, with a clear leg of 10–15 cm.
Cut stems back by half after planting. Mulch with compost and water in. They also thrive in large pots (30 cm) of loam-based compost.
grow: Water in dry spells, and mulch each spring. Prune in winter, cutting main branches by half of the new growth and side shoots to 2 buds. Cordons are summer-pruned in July.
Net bushes before the fruit ripens. Watch for sawfly caterpillars in spring and currant blister aphid, which causes red blisters on leaves.
harvest: Pick whole trusses in July to August when the berries are translucent and pearly white, sweet to taste. Use scissors, and handle gently. Fruit hangs on the bush for a few weeks, especially if netted.
Pick on a dry day. Berries in shade ripen later, extending the season.

Whitecurrants are tender and delicate, so pick into shallow trays and keep in a cool place. Fruits left hanging on the bush develop sweeter flavour in September. They are particularly good eaten straight from a bush, warm from the sun.
use: Whitecurrants can be eaten raw, sprinkled with sugar, or used in desserts, jellies, sauces and summer puddings. Their pale colour makes pretty jelly. Use as decoration for cakes and cocktails.
Fresh sprigs keep for a week in the fridge. Freeze on stalks on trays and strip with a fork. Whitecurrant jelly keeps a year.

care.job: Prune in late winter, shortening the previous year's growth on side shoots to two buds and removing crossing branches.
Mulch around the base with compost and feed with a potash-rich fertiliser.
Net bushes against birds before the fruit ripens, and water in dry spells.
Check for sawfly caterpillars on the leaf undersides and pick them off promptly.

preserving.how: Freeze on the strig, then pull off with a fork when frozen. Bag and freeze.
Make pale white jelly for meat and cheese.
Keep on the strigs in a covered container.
Simmer into a cordial with a little sugar.
preserving.keeps: About 1 month in the fridge; up to 12 months frozen

crops.name: Wild garlic
crops.sun_text: Shade to partial shade; moist soil

facts.Sow: Plant bulbs Sep–Oct, or ‘in the green’ Mar–Apr

varieties: Wild garlic (Allium ursinum, the only form)
Three-cornered leek (Allium triquetrum, a similar edible relative)

info: Wild garlic, also called ramsons, is a woodland plant with broad, glossy leaves and a pungent aroma, appearing in early spring when little else is available. Its white starry flowers cover the ground in April and May, and the whole plant is edible.
It thrives in damp shade under trees and on north-facing borders, where few crops will grow. It spreads freely, so place it where you are happy for it to colonise, or confine it in a large pot.
sow: Plant bulbs in September and October, 5–8 cm deep and 10–15 cm apart, in moist, humus-rich soil in shade. Alternatively, buy plants ‘in the green’ in spring and plant at the same depth as they were growing. Seed should be sown fresh in autumn and takes up to 18 months to germinate.
Mulch with leaf mould to mimic woodland conditions. Do not dig up wild plants, which is illegal without the landowner’s permission; buy from a reputable nursery.
sow_tips: Buy ‘in the green’ for the quickest results.
grow: Wild garlic needs almost no maintenance once established. Keep the soil moist in spring while leaves are growing; it tolerates dry summer soil, when the leaves die back and the plant goes dormant.
It spreads by seed and bulbs, so remove flower heads before they set seed if it spreads too far. Slugs sometimes eat young leaves. Divide clumps in autumn to extend the patch.
grow_tips: Allow leaves to die back naturally.
harvest: Pick leaves from March to May, before flowering, when they are tender and mild. Take only one or two leaves from each plant so that it can regrow and survive. Flower buds and flowers are also edible, from April.

Seed pods can be picked green in late spring and pickled like capers. Leaves become tough and bitter after flowering. Always positively identify wild garlic and avoid lookalikes such as lily of the valley and lords-and-ladies.
harvest_tips: Take one or two leaves per plant.
use: Use wild garlic leaves in pesto, soups, risotto, omelettes, butters and breads, or wilt like spinach. The flavour is mild and fresh, and best raw or lightly cooked. Whole flowers make a pretty, mild garlicky salad garnish.
Leaves wilt within a day, so use them quickly. Freeze pesto or wild garlic butter in portions, or blanch the leaves and freeze in ice-cube trays. Wild garlic loses flavour on drying.
use_tips: Make pesto in spring and freeze it.

care.job: Mulch with leaf mould after winter and keep the soil moist, as wild garlic thrives in damp, shady spots.
Allow the flowers to appear and set seed so the patch spreads, or pick the buds and flowers for salads.
Leave the leaves to die back naturally in summer, rather than cutting them off, so the bulbs can recover.
Divide dense clumps or scatter fresh seed in a shady, moist spot, as wild garlic spreads freely and can become invasive.

preserving.how: Chop or purée leaves with a little oil and freeze in ice cube trays. Better than drying.
Blend with nuts, cheese and oil, and freeze in portions.
Mix chopped leaves into softened butter and freeze in rolls.
Pickle unopened flower buds in vinegar and salt like capers.
Blend dried leaves with salt for a seasoning.

crops.name: Winter purslane
crops.sun_text: Partial shade to shade; tolerates sun

facts.Type: Hardy annual winter salad (also called miner’s lettuce)
facts.Spacing: Thin to 10 cm, or sow thickly

varieties: Claytonia perfoliata (the usual seed packet type)
Miner’s lettuce (another name for the same plant)
Claytonia sibirica (pink purslane, a pink-flowered relative)

info: Winter purslane, also known as claytonia or miner’s lettuce, is one of the toughest and most useful winter salad plants. The distinctive round, succulent leaves have a mild, fresh, slightly earthy flavour, and the plants thrive in cold, damp, shady conditions where little else will grow.

It is a native of North America, naturalised in some parts of the UK, and it grows happily in pots, cold frames and shady borders. It self-seeds readily, so a single sowing may give you winter salad for years.
sow: Sow from August to October for winter picking, and again from February to April for spring. Scatter seed thinly on the surface of moist, fine soil, or sow in rows 10–15 cm apart, 5 mm deep, and cover very lightly. Germination can be slow in hot weather, so sow in a shaded spot and keep moist.

In pots or trays, use any multipurpose compost and keep in a cold frame, greenhouse or on a bright windowsill. Plants will grow in nearly any soil and are one of the best crops for a shady corner or the dry soil beneath a wall.
sow_tips: Sow in a shady spot to help germination.
Scatter-sow into pots for winter leaves.
Resow in February for spring salads.
grow: Winter purslane is almost carefree. Keep young plants watered until established, and weed carefully by hand. Plants grow slowly through winter, then race away in spring as the days lengthen and the temperature rises, producing small white flowers from March.

Pests rarely trouble it, though slugs may graze the tender leaves and aphids can appear under cover. Plants are hardy to about -10°C or lower. In very cold weather, a layer of fleece keeps the leaves cleaner. Remove flower stems for further leaf production.
grow_tips: Water seedlings through dry autumn spells.
Protect leaves with fleece in heavy frost.
Remove flower shoots to extend picking.
Let some self-seed for next year.
harvest: Start picking baby leaves when they are about 5–8 cm tall, six to eight weeks from sowing, by snipping off leaves and stems with scissors about 2.5 cm above the base. The plants will regrow and can be cut several times. Harvest regularly through winter and spring.

In spring, the flowering stems and flowers are also edible. When plants go to seed in April or May, shake the seed heads over the bed to scatter next year’s crop, then clear the spent plants and replace them with summer crops.
harvest_tips: Cut with scissors and allow to regrow.
Eat the flowers and flower stems.
Shake seed heads over the bed to resow.
use: Eat winter purslane raw in salads, where the juicy, crisp texture and mild flavour is refreshing in winter. The leaves, stems and flowers can all be eaten, and the plant makes an attractive garnish. You can also wilt it lightly, add it to sandwiches or use it like spinach in soups.

Use it as soon as possible after harvesting. Leaves keep for two to three days in the fridge in a bag, but they are best picked fresh from the garden. Winter purslane does not freeze or dry well, but a pot on the kitchen windowsill gives you a continuous supply.
use_tips: Use in salads with citrus and a light dressing.
Use like spinach in a quick stir-fry.

care.job: Thin seedlings to 10 cm apart and keep weeds down, as the plants are small and slow growing.
Pick leaves regularly through winter, and cover with a cloche or fleece in harsh weather, though purslane is very hardy.
Let a few plants flower in spring to self-sow for the following year, or pull up spent plants.

preserving.how: It is hardy, so pick fresh leaves through winter rather than store them.
Wrap leaves in damp paper in a bag.
Wilt into soups and freeze in portions.

recipes.name: Tomato & Basil Salad
steps: Slice tomatoes and arrange on a plate.
Tear basil leaves over the top.
Drizzle with olive oil and season with salt.
Add mozzarella if using, and serve at room temperature.
tips: Use tomatoes that have ripened on the plant and have never been in the fridge, which dulls their flavour and texture.
Tear the basil rather than cutting it so it does not bruise and blacken.
Salt the tomatoes a few minutes before serving to bring out their juices, which also make the dressing.

recipes.name: Garden Salad with Radish & Herb Dressing
steps: Tear the lettuce and place in a bowl.
Add sliced radishes and spring onion.
Whisk oil, lemon juice and chopped mint.
Dress just before serving.

recipes.name: Courgette Fritters
steps: Squeeze grated courgette in a towel to remove moisture.
Mix with onion, eggs, flour, basil, salt and pepper.
Fry spoonfuls in hot oil for 2–3 minutes each side.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve warm.
tips: Squeezing the courgette dry is the key step. If the mixture is still loose, add another spoonful of flour.
Fry in batches without crowding the pan so each fritter crisps rather than steams.
Keep them warm in a low oven. Leftovers reheat well in a hot oven or can be frozen between sheets of baking paper.

recipes.name: Garden Kale & Potato Soup
steps: Fry onion and carrot in oil for 5 minutes.
Add potatoes and stock; simmer for 15 minutes.
Stir in kale and cook for 5 more minutes.
Blend partly for a creamier texture, or serve chunky.

recipes.name: Summer Garden Ratatouille
steps: Fry onion and garlic in oil until soft.
Add courgette and cook 5 minutes.
Stir in tomatoes and simmer 25 minutes until thick.
Finish with torn basil and serve warm or cold.
tips: Cook the vegetables in stages as in the method so each keeps its shape rather than turning to mush.
Taste at the end and add a pinch of salt or a splash of vinegar to lift the flavours. It tastes better the next day.
Freezes well for up to three months. Serve it with rice, crusty bread, or baked with an egg on top.

recipes.name: Runner Bean & Garlic Stir-Fry
steps: Heat oil in a wok until very hot.
Stir-fry beans 3–4 minutes until bright green.
Add onion, garlic and chilli for 1 minute.
Splash in soy sauce and serve with rice.

recipes.name: Strawberry & Mint Yoghurt Bowl
steps: Spoon yoghurt into bowls.
Top with strawberries and chopped mint.
Drizzle with honey and serve.
tips: Use strawberries picked the same day and left at room temperature for the best flavour, because fridge-cold fruit tastes dull.
Thick Greek yoghurt holds the fruit best. Add the strawberries just before serving so they do not bleed into it.
Swap the mint for basil, or crumble over a little granola for crunch.

recipes.name: Crispy Potato & Herb Hash
steps: Parboil potato cubes for 5 minutes and drain.
Fry in hot oil until golden and crisp, about 15 minutes.
Add onion and cook until soft.
Stir in spinach until wilted and season with chilli flakes.
tips: Drain the parboiled potatoes and let them steam dry for a few minutes, because dry potatoes crisp better.
Leave the potatoes undisturbed for a few minutes at a time so a crust forms before you turn them.
Top with a fried egg, or stir in any leftover cooked vegetables.

recipes.name: Fresh Basil Pesto
steps: Blitz basil, garlic and nuts in a food processor.
Slowly add oil while blending.
Stir in parmesan and season.
Store in a jar covered with a layer of oil.
tips: Toast the nuts lightly first for a deeper flavour, and pick basil in the morning before the sun wilts it.
Pulse rather than blitz for a rougher texture, and stir the cheese in by hand so the pesto does not turn bitter.
Keeps for about a week in the fridge under a layer of oil. For longer, freeze it in ice cube trays and bag the cubes.

recipes.name: Asparagus & Chive Omelette

ingredients.label: Asparagus spears, woody ends snapped off

steps: Simmer the asparagus in salted water for 3 minutes until just tender, then drain and cut into short lengths.
Beat the eggs with most of the chives, the parmesan and a pinch of salt and pepper.
Melt half the butter in a non-stick frying pan over a medium heat.
Pour in half the egg, stirring gently with a spatula for 20 seconds, then let it set for a minute.
Scatter half the asparagus over one side, fold the omelette over and slide it onto a plate.
Repeat with the remaining butter, egg and asparagus. Finish with the last of the chives.

recipes.name: Fines Herbes Omelette
steps: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper and two-thirds of the mixed herbs.
Melt the butter in a small non-stick frying pan until foaming but not browned.
Pour in the eggs and stir with a fork for 15 seconds, drawing the set edges into the middle.
When the base is set but the top is still creamy, tilt the pan and roll the omelette onto a warm plate.
Scatter the remaining herbs over the top and eat straight away.

recipes.name: Roast Beetroot, Rocket & Goat's Cheese Salad
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Wrap the beetroot loosely in foil with a splash of water and roast for 45–60 minutes until a knife slides in easily.
Leave to cool slightly, then rub off the skins with kitchen paper (wear gloves if you dislike pink fingers) and cut into wedges.
Whisk the olive oil, vinegar, honey and a pinch of salt for the dressing.
Toss the warm beetroot in half the dressing.
Arrange the rocket on a platter, top with the beetroot, crumbled goat's cheese and walnuts, and drizzle with the rest of the dressing.

recipes.name: Edible Flower Salad
steps: Wash the lamb's lettuce and dry it thoroughly.
Shake the flowers gently to dislodge any insects, but do not wash them as they bruise easily.
Whisk the oil, lemon juice and salt.
Toss the lamb's lettuce lightly in the dressing and pile onto plates.
Scatter the flowers over the top at the last minute. Nasturtium flowers taste peppery, borage tastes of cucumber and violas are mild and sweet.

recipes.name: Winter Leaf Salad with Mustard Dressing
steps: Wash and dry all the leaves, then tear any large ones.
Whisk the oil, mustard, vinegar and honey with a pinch of salt in a large bowl.
Add the leaves and toss gently so everything is lightly coated.
Serve at once alongside soup, cheese or roast meat.

recipes.name: Chicory, Endive & Pear Salad with Walnuts
steps: Arrange the chicory leaves and torn endive on a large plate.
Tuck the pear slices among the leaves.
Whisk the oil, lemon juice, honey and a pinch of salt.
Scatter over the blue cheese and walnuts, then drizzle with the dressing just before serving. The sweetness of the pear softens the bitterness of the leaves.

recipes.name: Crunchy Kohlrabi & Carrot Slaw

ingredients.label: Kohlrabi, peeled and cut into matchsticks

steps: Mix the yoghurt, mayonnaise, lemon juice, mustard and a pinch of salt in a large bowl.
Add the kohlrabi, carrot and most of the parsley.
Toss until coated and leave for 10 minutes so the vegetables soften slightly.
Taste for seasoning and finish with the remaining parsley.

recipes.name: Celeriac Remoulade
steps: Mix the mayonnaise, mustard and lemon juice in a bowl.
Cut the celeriac into fine matchsticks, or grate it coarsely, and drop it straight into the dressing so it does not discolour.
Stir in the parsley and season well.
Chill for 30 minutes before serving with ham, smoked fish or on a sandwich.

recipes.name: Waldorf Salad
steps: Stir the mayonnaise, yoghurt and lemon juice together.
Toss the diced apple in the dressing straight away to stop it browning.
Fold in the celery and most of the walnuts.
Pile onto the lettuce leaves and scatter over the remaining nuts.

recipes.name: Shaved Fennel & Orange Salad

ingredients.label: Fennel bulbs, trimmed and thinly sliced
Oranges, peeled and sliced into rounds

steps: Slice the fennel as thinly as you can, using a mandoline if you have one, and keep the feathery fronds.
Layer the fennel and orange slices on a platter.
Scatter over the olives and the bronze fennel fronds.
Drizzle with olive oil and season with flaky salt and black pepper.

recipes.name: Cucumber & Dill Tzatziki
steps: Grate the cucumber, sprinkle with a pinch of salt and leave for 10 minutes.
Squeeze out as much liquid as you can with your hands or a clean tea towel.
Stir the cucumber into the yoghurt with the garlic, dill, olive oil and lemon juice.
Chill for at least 30 minutes and serve with warm bread, grilled meat or raw vegetables.

recipes.name: Melon, Mint & Feta Salad
steps: Cut the melon into bite-sized cubes and spread on a platter.
Scatter over the feta and mint.
Drizzle with olive oil and lime juice and finish with plenty of black pepper.
Serve cold, as a starter or alongside barbecued food.
tips: Chill the melon well before cutting. The cold fruit against salty feta is what makes the dish.
Dress and season only at the last minute, because the salt draws water out of the melon.
Add thinly sliced red onion or cucumber for crunch, and use any ripe melon you have grown.

recipes.name: French Bean & Shallot Salad
steps: Soak the diced shallot in the vinegar with a pinch of salt for 10 minutes to soften its bite.
Boil the beans for 3–4 minutes until tender but still crisp, then drain and cool under cold water.
Whisk the mustard and oil into the shallots and vinegar.
Toss the beans in the dressing with the tarragon and serve at room temperature.

recipes.name: Leek & Potato Soup
steps: Melt the butter in a large pan and cook the leeks gently with a pinch of salt for 10 minutes without browning.
Add the potatoes and stock and simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is soft.
Blend until smooth, then stir in the milk and reheat gently.
Season to taste and serve scattered with chives.

recipes.name: Fresh Pea & Mint Soup
steps: Soften the onion in the butter for 5 minutes.
Add the stock and bring to the boil, then tip in the peas and simmer for 4 minutes only to keep them bright green.
Add the mint and blend until smooth.
Season, then serve hot or chilled with a swirl of cream.

recipes.name: Watercress Soup
steps: Soften the onion in the butter for 5 minutes, then add the potato and stock and simmer for 12 minutes.
Add the watercress and cook for just 2 minutes so it stays vivid.
Blend until smooth and stir in the cream.
Season with salt and plenty of black pepper and serve with crusty bread.

recipes.name: Lemony Sorrel Soup
steps: Soften the onion in the butter, add the potato and stock and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the sorrel, which collapses within a minute and turns an olive green, and blend until smooth.
Beat the egg yolk with the cream in a bowl, then whisk in a ladleful of the hot soup.
Stir the mixture back into the pan and warm gently without boiling. Serve with a sharp, lemony flavour from the sorrel.

recipes.name: Lovage & Potato Soup
steps: Soften the onion in the butter for 5 minutes.
Add the potatoes and stock and simmer for 15 minutes until soft.
Add the lovage, which has a strong celery flavour so a little goes a long way, and blend until smooth.
Season, stir in the cream if you like and serve hot.

recipes.name: Jerusalem Artichoke Soup
steps: Melt the butter and soften the onion for 5 minutes.
Add the artichokes and thyme and cook for 5 more minutes.
Pour in the stock, bring to the boil and simmer for 20 minutes until completely soft.
Remove the thyme stalks, blend until velvety and stir in the cream.
Season well. Artichokes can cause wind in some people, so serve modest portions at first.

recipes.name: Avocado & Microgreens Toast
steps: Mash the avocado with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Spread thickly on the hot toast.
Pile the microgreens on top and scatter with chilli flakes.
Eat straight away so the toast stays crisp.
tips: Cut microgreens just before serving so they stay crisp, and rinse and pat them dry first.
Use pea shoots for sweetness, radish for a peppery bite or mustard for heat.
Add a poached egg or a few pumpkin seeds to turn it into a fuller meal.

recipes.name: Baked Aubergine Parmigiana
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Brush the aubergine slices with olive oil, lay them on baking trays and roast for 25 minutes, turning once, until golden.
For the sauce, fry the garlic in 1 tbsp oil for 1 minute, add the tomatoes and simmer for 20 minutes until thick. Stir in half the basil and season.
Spread a little sauce in a baking dish, then layer aubergine, sauce, mozzarella and basil, finishing with a layer of sauce.
Scatter over the parmesan and bake for 25–30 minutes until bubbling and golden.
Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

recipes.name: Homemade Pizza Margherita
steps: Mix the flour, yeast and 1 tsp salt, then stir in 160 ml warm water and 1 tbsp oil. Knead for 8 minutes until smooth, cover and leave for 1 hour until doubled.
Meanwhile simmer the tomatoes with the oregano and a pinch of salt for 15 minutes until thick.
Heat the oven to its highest setting with a baking tray inside.
Roll the dough into two thin rounds, spread with the sauce and top with mozzarella.
Slide onto the hot tray and bake for 8–10 minutes until the crust blisters.
Scatter with basil and a drizzle of oil.

recipes.name: Rice-Stuffed Sweet Peppers
steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan).
Fry the onion in the oil for 5 minutes, add the tomatoes and oregano and cook for 5 more minutes.
Stir in the rice and half the feta and season well.
Fill the pepper halves, top with the remaining feta and place in a baking dish with a splash of water.
Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes, then uncover and cook for 15 minutes more until the peppers are soft and lightly charred.

recipes.name: Stuffed Marrow with Tomato & Herbs

ingredients.label: Marrow, halved lengthways and seeds scooped out
Beef or lamb mince (or cooked lentils)

steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan).
Fry the onion in the oil for 5 minutes, add the mince and brown well, then stir in the tomatoes and cook for 10 minutes.
Mix in the parsley, season generously and let the filling cool a little.
Lay the marrow halves in a baking dish, spoon in the filling and sprinkle with breadcrumbs.
Cover with foil and bake for 35 minutes, then uncover and bake for 15 minutes until the marrow is tender and the top is golden.

recipes.name: Roast Patty Pan Squash with Garlic & Thyme

ingredients.label: Patty pan squash, halved or quartered
Garlic cloves, left in their skins

steps: Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan).
Toss the squash with the oil, garlic, thyme and a good pinch of salt on a roasting tray.
Roast for 20–25 minutes, turning once, until tender and caramelised at the edges.
Squeeze the soft garlic out of its skins and mash it over the squash.
Top with shaved parmesan and serve with lemon wedges.

recipes.name: Roast Butternut Squash & Sage Soup
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Roast the squash with 2 tbsp oil and a little salt for 30 minutes until soft and golden.
Soften the onion in a large pan with 1 tbsp oil and half the sage, chopped.
Add the roasted squash and stock and simmer for 10 minutes, then blend until smooth.
Fry the remaining sage leaves in a little oil until crisp.
Serve the soup topped with the crisp sage and a swirl of cream.

recipes.name: Pumpkin & Sage Risotto

ingredients.label: Pumpkin, peeled and cut into small cubes

steps: Melt half the butter in a wide pan and cook the onion for 5 minutes. Add the pumpkin and sage and cook for 5 more minutes.
Stir in the rice for 1 minute, then pour in the wine and let it bubble away.
Add the stock a ladleful at a time, stirring often, waiting until each has been absorbed before adding the next. This takes around 20 minutes.
The pumpkin will break down and make the risotto creamy. When the rice is tender but with a little bite, remove from the heat.
Beat in the remaining butter and the parmesan, cover and rest for 2 minutes, then serve.

recipes.name: Cauliflower Cheese
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Boil the florets for 5 minutes until just tender, then drain very well.
Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook for 1 minute, then add the milk a little at a time, whisking, until you have a smooth sauce.
Simmer for 5 minutes, then stir in the mustard and two-thirds of the cheese until melted. Season.
Put the cauliflower in a baking dish, pour over the sauce and top with the remaining cheese.
Bake for 25 minutes until bubbling and golden.

recipes.name: Roast Romanesco with Lemon & Chilli
steps: Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan).
Toss the florets with 2 tbsp oil and a good pinch of salt and roast for 15 minutes until the tips are browned.
Add the garlic and chilli and roast for 5 more minutes.
Toss with the lemon zest, lemon juice and remaining oil, then scatter with parmesan and serve warm.

recipes.name: Calabrese & Chilli Orecchiette

ingredients.label: Calabrese broccoli, cut into small florets

steps: Cook the pasta in well-salted water, adding the broccoli for the last 4 minutes.
Meanwhile warm the oil with the garlic and chilli over a low heat for 3 minutes, taking care not to brown the garlic.
Drain the pasta and broccoli, keeping a mugful of the cooking water.
Toss everything together in the pan, mashing some of the broccoli against the side to make a rough sauce, adding water to loosen.
Serve topped with parmesan.

recipes.name: Purple Sprouting Broccoli with Garlic & Anchovy
steps: Steam or boil the broccoli for 3–4 minutes until the stems are just tender.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the garlic, anchovies and chilli flakes and stir until the anchovies melt into the oil.
Toss the broccoli in the warm dressing with the lemon juice.
Serve as a side or on toast with a poached egg.

recipes.name: Crispy Roast Brussels Sprouts
steps: Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan) and put a roasting tray in to heat.
Toss the sprouts, shallots and bacon with the oil and a pinch of salt.
Tip onto the hot tray, cut-sides down, and roast for 20–25 minutes until deeply browned and crisp.
Drizzle over the honey and vinegar, toss and return to the oven for 3 minutes.
Serve straight away.

recipes.name: Braised Red Cabbage with Apple
steps: Melt the butter in a large heavy pan and soften the onion for 5 minutes.
Add the cabbage, apple, vinegar, sugar, cinnamon and a good pinch of salt, and stir well.
Cover and cook over a very low heat for about 1 hour, stirring now and then and adding a splash of water if it begins to stick.
Taste and adjust with a little more sugar or vinegar. It keeps for 4 days in the fridge and reheats well.

recipes.name: Quick Chinese Cabbage & Mooli Kimchi

ingredients.label: Chinese cabbage, cut into 4 cm pieces

steps: Toss the cabbage with the salt in a large bowl and leave for 1–2 hours, turning occasionally, until it is soft and has released a lot of liquid.
Rinse it well under cold water three times and squeeze dry.
Mix the garlic, ginger, chilli flakes and fish sauce into a paste.
Combine the cabbage, mooli, spring onions and paste with gloved hands until everything is coated.
Pack tightly into a clean jar, pressing down so the liquid covers the vegetables. Leave an inch of space at the top.
Leave at room temperature for 2–3 days, tasting daily, then refrigerate. It keeps for several weeks.

recipes.name: Oriental Greens Stir-Fry
steps: Heat the oil in a wok until smoking. Add the garlic and ginger and stir for 10 seconds.
Add the pak choi and komatsuna stems first and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add the tatsoi, mizuna and mustard greens with the soy sauce and a splash of water.
Toss for another minute until the leaves have just wilted.
Finish with the sesame oil and serve with rice.

recipes.name: Swiss Chard, Orache & Spinach Gratin

ingredients.label: Swiss chard, stalks and leaves separated

steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan). Chop the chard stalks and simmer for 5 minutes, then add the leaves, orache and spinach for 2 minutes until wilted. Drain, squeeze dry and roughly chop.
Make a white sauce by melting the butter, stirring in the flour, then gradually adding the milk and simmering for 5 minutes.
Add the nutmeg, half the cheese and seasoning.
Mix the greens into the sauce, spoon into a baking dish and top with the rest of the cheese.
Bake for 25 minutes until golden and bubbling.

recipes.name: Honey & Thyme Roast Parsnips
steps: Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan) and heat the oil in a roasting tin.
Parboil the parsnips for 5 minutes, drain and let them steam dry for 2 minutes.
Tip into the hot tin with the thyme and a pinch of salt and roast for 30 minutes, turning once.
Mix the honey and mustard, drizzle over and roast for another 10 minutes until sticky and deep golden.

recipes.name: Buttery Swede & Carrot Mash
steps: Boil the swede and carrots together in salted water for 20 minutes until completely tender.
Drain very well and leave to steam dry for 2 minutes, which keeps the mash from being watery.
Mash with the butter, plenty of black pepper and a pinch of nutmeg until smooth.
Serve with roast meat, sausages or a pie.

recipes.name: Glazed Baby Turnips
steps: Put the turnips in a wide frying pan with the butter, sugar, stock and a pinch of salt.
Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 8 minutes.
Remove the lid and boil away the liquid, shaking the pan, until the turnips are tender and coated in a shiny glaze.
Scatter with parsley and serve.

recipes.name: Salsify & Scorzonera with Brown Butter
steps: Fill a bowl with water and the lemon juice. Peel the roots under running water, cut into 5 cm lengths and drop straight into the lemon water to stop them browning. Wear gloves, as the sap is sticky.
Simmer in salted water for 12–15 minutes until tender, then drain.
Melt the butter in a frying pan and cook until it smells nutty and turns light brown.
Toss the roots in the brown butter and cook for 3 minutes until lightly golden.
Scatter with parsley and serve.

recipes.name: Caramelised Shallot & Thyme Tarte Tatin
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan).
Melt the butter and sugar in an ovenproof frying pan. Add the shallots cut-side down and cook for 8 minutes until caramelised.
Add the vinegar and thyme and cook for 2 minutes until sticky, then take off the heat.
Cut the pastry slightly larger than the pan and lay it over the shallots, tucking in the edges.
Bake for 25 minutes until puffed and golden.
Rest for 5 minutes, then flip onto a plate and top with crumbled goat's cheese.

recipes.name: Charred Sweetcorn with Chilli-Lime Butter
steps: Mash the butter with the chilli, coriander, lime zest and a pinch of salt.
Boil the cobs for 5 minutes, drain and pat dry.
Char on a hot griddle or barbecue for 8–10 minutes, turning, until blackened in places.
Smear generously with the flavoured butter and squeeze over the lime juice.

recipes.name: Spiced Roast Sweet Potato Wedges
steps: Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan).
Toss the wedges with the oil, paprika and 1/2 tsp salt on a large tray, giving them space so they roast rather than steam.
Roast for 30–35 minutes, turning once, until crisp at the edges.
Scatter with the chilli and serve with lime wedges and a bowl of yoghurt for dipping.

recipes.name: Globe Artichokes with Lemon Butter
steps: Snap off the tough outer leaves and cut the stalk flush so the artichokes sit flat. Cut the top third off and rub the cut surfaces with lemon.
Simmer in a large pan of salted, lemony water for 30–40 minutes, weighing them down with a plate, until a leaf pulls out easily.
Drain upside down for 5 minutes.
Warm the butter with the garlic and a squeeze of lemon.
Pull off each leaf, dip the fleshy base in the butter and scrape it off with your teeth. Finish with the heart, discarding the hairy choke first.

recipes.name: Sea Kale with Brown Butter & Lemon
steps: Wash the shoots and steam them for 8–10 minutes until just tender, like asparagus.
Melt the butter in a small pan and cook until nutty and golden.
Add the lemon juice, take off the heat and pour over the sea kale.
Season with black pepper and serve on toast or alongside fish.

recipes.name: Chilli-Garlic Edamame
steps: Boil the pods in salted water for 4–5 minutes and drain.
Heat the oil in a frying pan and fry the garlic and chilli for 30 seconds.
Add the edamame and soy sauce and toss for a minute.
Sprinkle with flaky salt and serve in a bowl, squeezing the beans out of the pods with your teeth.

recipes.name: Broad Bean, Pea & Mint Crostini
steps: Boil the broad beans for 3 minutes, adding the peas for the last minute, then drain and cool in cold water. Slip the larger broad beans out of their grey skins.
Roughly crush the beans and peas with the oil, lemon zest and juice, most of the mint and the parmesan.
Season to taste.
Spoon onto the toasted bread and finish with small mint leaves.

recipes.name: Borlotti Bean & Sage Stew
steps: Warm the oil in a heavy pan with the garlic, sage and savory for 2 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes until they collapse.
Add the beans and stock and simmer gently for 30–40 minutes (10 minutes if using tinned) until the beans are creamy.
Mash a few against the pan to thicken, season and serve with crusty bread and a drizzle of oil.

recipes.name: Garlic Chive & Cabbage Dumplings
steps: Sprinkle the cabbage with salt, leave for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the liquid.
Mix with the pork, garlic chives, ginger and soy sauce.
Place a teaspoon of filling in each wrapper, wet the edges, fold in half and pleat to seal.
Heat the oil in a non-stick pan, add the dumplings flat-side down and fry for 2 minutes until golden.
Add 100 ml water, cover and steam for 5 minutes until the water has gone and the dumplings are cooked through. Serve with soy sauce and chilli oil.

recipes.name: Spring Onion Pancakes
steps: Mix the flour with 180 ml boiling water until it comes together, then knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Divide into 4 balls and roll each out very thinly. Brush with the oil, sprinkle with salt and spring onions and roll into a long sausage, then coil into a spiral.
Roll out again gently to a flat round about 2 mm thick.
Fry in a little oil over a medium heat for 3 minutes each side until golden and flaky. Drizzle with sesame oil, cut into wedges and serve with soy sauce.

recipes.name: Wild Garlic Pesto

ingredients.label: Pine nuts or sunflower seeds, toasted

steps: Blitz the wild garlic, nuts and parmesan in a food processor.
With the motor running, slowly pour in the oil.
Add the lemon juice and season with salt.
Spoon into a clean jar and cover with a thin layer of oil. Keeps in the fridge for a week, or freeze in ice-cube trays for up to 3 months.

recipes.name: Roast Elephant Garlic
steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan). Slice the tops off the bulbs to expose the cloves.
Place on foil, drizzle with oil, add the rosemary and salt and wrap tightly.
Roast for 45–50 minutes until the cloves are soft and golden.
Squeeze the sweet, mild cloves onto warm bread or stir into mash, soup or pasta.

recipes.name: Fresh Horseradish Sauce
steps: Open a window, as freshly grated horseradish is very pungent.
Grate the horseradish finely and stir in the vinegar immediately to stop it going bitter.
Fold into the cream with the mustard, sugar and a pinch of salt.
Chill for an hour and serve with roast beef, smoked mackerel or beetroot. Keeps for 5 days in the fridge.

recipes.name: Home-grown Popcorn (How to Pop It)
steps: Check that the kernels are dry and hard. Pop a small spoonful first as a test, and if more than a handful stay unpopped, dry the rest for another week or two.
Choose a large, heavy-based saucepan with a tight-fitting lid. Add the oil and 3 kernels, cover and heat over a medium-high heat.

When all 3 kernels have popped, the oil is hot enough. Tip in the rest of the kernels in a single layer, put the lid on and take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds so they all reach the same temperature.

Return the pan to the heat. The kernels will begin to pop within a minute. Hold the lid on with a cloth, shake the pan gently every few seconds, and tilt the lid slightly to let the steam escape so the popcorn stays crisp.
When the popping slows to two or three seconds between pops, take the pan off the heat straight away, because popcorn burns quickly. Tip it into a large bowl.
Toss with the salt, and with the melted butter and rosemary if using. Eat while it is warm.
tips: Use an oil that copes with high heat, such as sunflower or rapeseed, not olive oil.
A few unpopped kernels at the bottom are normal. Many unpopped kernels mean the corn was too dry or too moist.
Try smoked paprika, cinnamon sugar or grated Parmesan instead of rosemary.
Popcorn is a choking hazard for babies and toddlers, and the pan and steam are hot, so children should not do the popping themselves.
Popped corn goes stale within a day or two, so keep the kernels and pop a fresh batch each time.

recipes.name: Apple & Blackberry Crumble
steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan).
Toss the apples and blackberries with the caster sugar and tip into a baking dish.
Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like coarse crumbs, then stir in the oats and brown sugar.
Scatter the crumble over the fruit without pressing down.
Bake for 35–40 minutes until golden on top and the fruit is bubbling at the edges. Serve with custard.

recipes.name: Rhubarb, Ginger & Sweet Cicely Crumble

ingredients.label: Rhubarb stalks (never the leaves), cut into 3 cm pieces

steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan).
Mix the rhubarb with the ginger, sweet cicely and caster sugar. The cicely is naturally sweet and aniseedy, so it softens rhubarb's sharpness and lets you use less sugar.
Rub the butter into the flour, stir in the brown sugar and spread over the fruit.
Bake for 35–40 minutes until golden. Serve warm with cream or custard.

recipes.name: Blackcurrant Fool
steps: Simmer the blackcurrants with the sugar and 2 tbsp water for 8 minutes until they burst and become syrupy. Cool completely.
Lightly whip the cream until it just holds its shape, then fold in the yoghurt.
Swirl through most of the blackcurrant compote, leaving ripples.
Spoon into glasses, top with the remaining compote and chill for 1 hour.
tips: Cool the compote completely before folding it in, or it will thin the cream.
Stop whipping the cream while it still holds soft peaks, because over-whipped cream turns grainy.
Gooseberries, raspberries or rhubarb all work in the same way. Make it up to a day ahead and keep it chilled.

recipes.name: Summer Pudding

ingredients.label: Slices of day-old white bread, crusts removed

steps: Heat the currants with the sugar and 2 tbsp water for 3 minutes until the juices run but the fruit still holds its shape. Stir in the raspberries off the heat.
Line a 1 litre pudding basin with cling film, then line it with bread, cutting a round for the base and fitting slices around the sides with no gaps.
Spoon in the fruit with about two-thirds of the juice and cover the top with more bread.
Place a small plate and a weight on top and chill overnight.
Turn out onto a plate and spoon the reserved juice over any pale patches. Serve with cream.

recipes.name: Redcurrant Jelly
steps: Put the currants in a large pan with 200 ml water and simmer gently for 20 minutes until they are completely soft.
Strain through a jelly bag or muslin-lined sieve over a bowl for several hours, without squeezing, so the jelly stays clear.
Measure the juice and add 450 g sugar for every 600 ml.
Warm gently to dissolve the sugar, then boil hard for about 8–10 minutes until it reaches setting point (a drop wrinkles on a cold saucer).
Skim off any scum, pour into sterilised jars and seal. Lovely with lamb, game or cheese.

recipes.name: Blueberry Pancakes

ingredients.label: Butter, melted, plus extra for frying

steps: Whisk the flour, baking powder and sugar together.
Beat the egg with the milk and melted butter, then pour into the dry ingredients and stir until just combined. A few lumps are fine.
Fold in most of the blueberries.
Heat a little butter in a frying pan and cook ladlefuls of batter for 2 minutes until bubbles appear, then flip for 1–2 minutes more.
Stack and serve with the remaining blueberries and maple syrup.

recipes.name: Cherry Clafoutis
steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan) and butter a shallow baking dish.
Scatter the cherries over the base.
Whisk the eggs and sugar until pale, then whisk in the flour and gradually the milk to make a smooth batter.
Pour the batter over the cherries.
Bake for 35–40 minutes until puffed and golden. It will sink as it cools.
Dust with icing sugar and serve warm.

recipes.name: Apricot & Almond Tart
steps: Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan). Line a 23 cm tart tin with the pastry and chill for 15 minutes, then bake blind for 15 minutes.
Beat the butter and sugar until pale, then beat in the egg and ground almonds.
Spread over the pastry base and press the apricot halves cut-side up into the mixture.
Bake for 30–35 minutes until golden and set.
Warm the jam with a splash of water and brush over the tart while it is hot.

recipes.name: Grilled Peaches with Honey Ricotta
steps: Brush the peach halves with the melted butter.
Grill or griddle cut-side down over a medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes until caramelised and softened.
Stir 1 tbsp of the honey into the ricotta.
Spoon the ricotta into the hollow of each peach, drizzle with the remaining honey and scatter with pistachios.
tips: Choose peaches that are ripe but still firm, because very soft ones fall apart on the heat.
Oil the grill or griddle lightly and leave the peaches alone for the first few minutes so they release easily.
Nectarines, plums or figs also work well. Swap the pistachios for toasted almonds or hazelnuts.

recipes.name: Spiced Poached Pears

ingredients.label: Firm pears, peeled with stalks left on

steps: Put the sugar, 600 ml water, lemon zest, cinnamon and vanilla in a pan that will hold the pears snugly. Stir over a low heat until the sugar dissolves.
Add the pears, cover with a circle of baking paper and simmer very gently for 20–30 minutes until a knife slides in easily.
Lift the pears out and boil the syrup for 10 minutes until reduced and glossy.
Serve warm or chilled with the syrup spooned over and ice cream or cream.

recipes.name: Plum & Almond Traybake
steps: Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan) and line a 20 cm square tin.
Beat the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy, then beat in the eggs one at a time.
Fold in the flour, ground almonds and milk and spread in the tin.
Press the plum halves cut-side up into the batter.
Bake for 35–40 minutes until golden and a skewer comes out clean. Cool in the tin and cut into squares.

recipes.name: Gooseberry Fool
steps: Simmer the gooseberries with the sugar and 2 tbsp water for 10 minutes until pulpy. Mash and cool completely.
Whip the cream until it holds soft peaks and fold in the custard.
Gently fold through the gooseberry purée to ripple it.
Spoon into glasses and chill for 1 hour. Taste the fruit first and adjust the sugar, as gooseberries vary a lot in sharpness.

recipes.name: Raspberry & Loganberry Jam
steps: Put the sterilised jars and a few saucers in the freezer.
Gently heat the fruit with the lemon juice until the juices run, crushing the berries lightly.
Add the sugar, stir until dissolved, then boil hard for 5–10 minutes.
Test for set by dropping a little jam on a cold saucer: it should wrinkle when pushed.
Skim, leave to stand for 10 minutes so the fruit distributes, then pour into hot sterilised jars and seal.

recipes.name: Fig, Goat's Cheese & Honey Flatbread
steps: Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan).
Brush the flatbreads with the oil and crumble the goat's cheese over.
Bake for 6–8 minutes until the edges are crisp.
Top with the figs, return to the oven for 2 minutes, then drizzle with honey and scatter over the thyme.

recipes.name: Grape & Rosemary Focaccia
steps: Mix the flour, yeast and 2 tsp fine salt, then stir in 400 ml warm water and 2 tbsp oil to form a sticky dough. Cover and leave for 1 hour until doubled.
Tip into an oiled 30 x 20 cm tin, stretching the dough to fill the corners, and leave for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan). Dimple the dough with oily fingers, press in the grapes and rosemary, and drizzle with the remaining oil and flaky salt.
Bake for 25 minutes until golden. Cool a little before cutting.

recipes.name: Kiwiberry & Yoghurt Parfait
steps: Spoon half the yoghurt into two glasses.
Add a layer of granola and half the kiwiberries.
Top with the remaining yoghurt, kiwiberries and cobnuts.
Drizzle with honey. The skins of hardy kiwi are thin and edible, so there is no need to peel them.

recipes.name: Cobnut & Honey Granola
steps: Heat the oven to 160C (140C fan) and line a large tray.
Warm the honey and oil together and stir into the oats, nuts, seeds and cinnamon with a pinch of salt.
Spread out on the tray and bake for 25–30 minutes, stirring halfway, until golden.
Leave to cool completely without stirring so it forms clusters, then store in a jar for up to 3 weeks.

recipes.name: Elderberry Syrup
steps: Never eat elderberries raw as they can cause stomach upset; they must be cooked.
Put the berries, 500 ml water, cloves and ginger in a pan and simmer for 20–30 minutes until the berries have burst.
Strain through a muslin cloth, pressing gently.
Return the juice to the pan with the sugar and lemon juice and simmer for 5 minutes until syrupy.
Pour into a sterilised bottle. Keep in the fridge for up to 3 weeks and use over pancakes, in drinks or on ice cream.

recipes.name: Quince Paste (Membrillo)

ingredients.label: Quinces, washed, cored and chopped (skin left on)

steps: Simmer the quinces in water for 30–40 minutes until completely soft, then drain and purée in a food processor.
Weigh the purée and return it to a heavy pan with an equal weight of sugar and the lemon juice.
Cook over a low heat, stirring constantly (it spits), for 40–60 minutes until it turns deep orange-red and is thick enough to leave a trail when you drag a spoon through it.
Spread into a lined tin, leave to dry and set overnight, then slice. Serve with manchego or hard cheeses. Keeps for months wrapped in the fridge.

recipes.name: Chocolate-Dipped Physalis

ingredients.label: Physalis (cape gooseberries), papery husks peeled back

steps: Line a tray with baking paper.
Melt the chocolate gently in a bowl set over barely simmering water.
Hold each physalis by its papery husk and dip about two-thirds into the chocolate.
Place on the paper and chill for 15 minutes until set.
tips: Dry the physalis well and keep them at room temperature, as damp fruit makes the chocolate seize.
Take the bowl off the heat as soon as the chocolate has almost melted and stir the rest in, which keeps it glossy.
Store in a cool place and eat within a day or two. Use milk or white chocolate if you prefer something sweeter.

recipes.name: Tomatillo Salsa Verde
steps: Heat the grill to high. Grill the tomatillos, chillies, onion and garlic for 8–10 minutes, turning, until softened and charred in places.
Peel the garlic and tip everything into a blender with the coriander and lime juice.
Blend to a rough purée and season with salt.
Serve warm or cold with tortilla chips, tacos, grilled chicken or eggs.

recipes.name: Fresh Coriander & Mint Chutney
steps: Blitz the coriander, mint, chillies, ginger and lime juice with 2 tbsp water until smooth.
Stir in the yoghurt and season with salt and a pinch of sugar.
Serve with curries, samosas and grilled meats. Keeps for 3 days in the fridge.

recipes.name: Lemongrass & Coconut Chicken Soup

ingredients.label: Lemongrass stalks, bashed and cut in lengths

steps: Simmer the stock, lemongrass, ginger and half the chilli together for 10 minutes to infuse.
Add the coconut milk and chicken and simmer for 8–10 minutes until cooked through.
Stir in the lime juice and fish sauce and adjust to taste.
Fish out the lemongrass pieces, which are fragrant but too tough to eat, and serve topped with coriander and the remaining chilli.

recipes.name: Garden Herbal Tea Blend
steps: Bruise the leaves lightly in your hands to release their oils and place them in a teapot with the chamomile flowers.
Pour over 500 ml of just-boiled water and cover.
Steep for 5–7 minutes.
Strain into cups and sweeten with honey if you like. Chamomile is calming, so this is a good evening drink. Served over ice it makes a refreshing summer cooler.

recipes.name: Lavender Shortbread

ingredients.label: Culinary lavender flowers, dried and finely chopped
Caster sugar, plus extra to sprinkle

steps: Heat the oven to 160C (140C fan) and line a baking tray.
Rub the butter into the flour, cornflour, sugar and lavender until the mixture comes together as a dough. Use lavender sparingly as it can taste soapy.
Press into a 20 cm square and score into 16 fingers, prick with a fork and chill for 15 minutes.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until pale golden.
Sprinkle with sugar and recut while warm, then cool on the tray.

recipes.name: Hyssop & Rosemary Roast Lamb
steps: Take the lamb out of the fridge 1 hour before cooking and heat the oven to 200C (180C fan).
Mash the hyssop, rosemary, lemon zest, oil, 1 tsp salt and plenty of pepper into a paste.
Cut deep slits in the lamb, push in the garlic slices and rub the paste all over.
Roast for 30 minutes, then reduce to 170C (150C fan) and cook for 1 hr 15 min for pink, or a little longer for well done.
Rest, covered, for 20 minutes before carving. Hyssop has a minty, slightly bitter flavour that suits rich meat.

recipes.name: Sage & Marjoram Sausage Patties
steps: Mix the pork, herbs, breadcrumbs, egg and a good pinch of salt and pepper with your hands.
Shape into 8 patties and chill for 15 minutes.
Fry in the oil for 5–6 minutes each side until browned and cooked through.
Serve in a bun with onion chutney or with mash and greens.

recipes.name: Slow-Cooked Beef Stew with Bay & Thyme
steps: Heat the oven to 150C (130C fan). Toss the beef in the flour and brown in batches in the hot oil in a casserole.
Soften the onions, carrots and celery in the same pot for 5 minutes.
Return the beef, add the stock, bay and thyme and bring to a simmer.
Cover and cook in the oven for 2 hr 30 min until the beef is meltingly tender.
Remove the bay and thyme stalks, season and serve with mash.

recipes.name: Quick Pickled Gherkins with Dill
steps: Wash the gherkins and pack them upright into a sterilised jar with the dill and garlic.
Heat the vinegar, 300 ml water, salt, sugar and mustard seeds until the salt dissolves.
Pour the hot brine over the gherkins until completely covered and seal.
Cool, then leave for at least 2 days before eating. Keeps in the fridge for 2 months.

recipes.name: Candied Angelica

ingredients.label: Young angelica stalks, picked in spring

steps: Cut the stalks into 8 cm lengths, sprinkle with salt, cover with boiling water and leave for 10 minutes. Drain, peel off the stringy outer skin and rinse.
Simmer in fresh water for 10 minutes until tender and bright green, then drain.
Weigh the stalks and put in a bowl with an equal weight of sugar. Cover and leave for 2 days to draw out the juice.
Boil the stalks and syrup together for 10 minutes until clear and translucent, then leave for a day.
Drain, roll in sugar and dry on a wire rack in a very low oven (100C) for about 2 hours. Use to decorate cakes and trifles.

recipes.name: Golden Calendula Rice
steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear.
Melt the butter and soften the onion for 5 minutes.
Add the rice and most of the calendula petals and stir for 1 minute, then add the stock and salt.
Cover and simmer very gently for 12 minutes, then rest off the heat for 5 minutes.
Fluff with a fork and scatter over the remaining petals. Calendula gives a golden colour and a mild, peppery flavour, a traditional cheaper substitute for saffron.

recipes.name: Peppery Nasturtium Pesto
steps: Wash and dry the nasturtium leaves and flowers.
Blitz the garlic, seeds and parmesan, then add the leaves and blitz again.
With the motor running pour in the oil, then add the lemon juice and season.
Toss through hot pasta or spread on toast. It has a gentle mustardy heat and keeps for 5 days in the fridge.

recipes.name: Pan-Fried Fish with Parsley & Lemon

ingredients.label: White fish fillets (cod, haddock or hake)

steps: Mix the parsley, lemon balm, garlic and lemon zest to make a fresh gremolata.
Season the fish and fry skin-side down in the oil for 4 minutes until crisp.
Flip, add the butter and cook for 2 minutes, basting.
Squeeze over the lemon, spoon over the gremolata and serve with new potatoes.

recipes.name: Blackcurrant Cordial
steps: Put the blackcurrants in a pan with 500 ml water and simmer for 15 minutes until they have burst and the juice is deep purple.
Strain through a muslin-lined sieve, pressing gently, and measure the juice.
Return to the pan with 300 g sugar for every 500 ml of juice, plus the lemon juice, and heat gently until the sugar dissolves.
Simmer for 2 minutes, skim and pour into sterilised bottles.
Dilute about 1 part cordial to 5 parts water, or use in hot drinks or over ice cream. Keeps in the fridge for 4 weeks, or freeze in tubs for longer.

recipes.name: Rhubarb & Ginger Cordial
steps: Put the rhubarb, ginger, sugar and 600 ml water in a pan and simmer for 15 minutes until the rhubarb has collapsed.
Leave to steep for 30 minutes, then strain through a sieve lined with muslin without pressing hard, so the cordial stays pink and clear.
Stir in the lemon juice and taste, adding more sugar if needed.
Bottle and chill. Dilute with still or sparkling water, or top up prosecco for a pink fizz. Keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge.

recipes.name: Strawberry & Basil Lemonade
steps: Simmer the sugar with 150 ml water until dissolved, add the basil and leave to infuse for 10 minutes.
Blend the strawberries with the lemon juice until smooth, and strain if you prefer it without seeds.
Strain the basil syrup into a jug, add the strawberry mixture and top with the cold water.
Taste, adjust the sweetness and serve over plenty of ice with extra basil leaves.

recipes.name: Mint & Cucumber Cooler
steps: Muddle the mint with the honey and lime juice in a jug, pressing gently to release the oils without tearing the leaves to bits.
Add the cucumber slices and plenty of ice.
Top up with the sparkling water and stir.
Serve immediately, garnished with extra mint.
tips: Press the mint gently, because crushing it hard releases bitter flavours.
Make the mint, honey and lime base ahead and add the sparkling water and ice only when serving.
Add a splash of gin or a few sliced strawberries for a different version.

recipes.name: Lemon Balm Iced Tea

ingredients.label: Lemon balm, leaves and tender stems

steps: Put the lemon balm and mint in a heatproof jug and pour over the boiling water.
Stir in the honey, cover and leave to steep for 15 minutes.
Strain out the leaves and chill for at least 2 hours.
Serve over ice with lemon slices and a few fresh leaves.

recipes.name: Raspberry Vinegar Shrub
steps: Mash the raspberries with the sugar in a bowl, cover and leave for 24 hours so the juices draw out.
Strain through a fine sieve, pressing lightly, and discard the pulp.
Stir in the vinegar until any remaining sugar dissolves and pour into a sterilised bottle.
Leave for a day for the flavours to mellow, then mix 1 part shrub with 4–5 parts sparkling water. Keeps for several months in the fridge.

recipes.name: Lovage Virgin Mary
steps: Blend the tomatoes until smooth and strain through a sieve, or use tomato juice.
Stir in the lemon juice, Worcestershire sauce, black pepper and finely chopped lovage, which tastes like strong celery.
Taste and season with salt.
Pour over ice and serve with celery sticks as stirrers.

recipes.name: Hot Spiced Apple Punch

ingredients.label: Apple juice, ideally pressed from your own apples

steps: Pour the apple juice into a large pan with the cinnamon, cloves and orange slices.
Heat gently until steaming but not boiling, for about 10 minutes.
Add the apple slices and honey if you like and warm through for 5 minutes.
Strain or ladle into mugs, keeping a few fruit slices in each.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in January
what_to_sow.lead: Mostly planning time. Order seed, chit potatoes and start the slowest crops, such as chillies and onions, on a bright windowsill or in a heated propagator.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in February
what_to_sow.lead: Still cold outside, so most sowing is indoors. Prepare beds when the soil is workable and plant bare-root fruit if the ground is not frozen or waterlogged.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in March
what_to_sow.lead: The sowing year starts properly. Soil is still cold, so use cloches or fleece for outdoor sowings and keep tender crops indoors.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in April
what_to_sow.lead: Soil is warming up. Sow hardy crops outside and keep sowing indoors, but protect everything tender from late frosts.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in May
what_to_sow.lead: Frosts fade, and tender crops can go out once the risk has passed in your area. Harden plants off for a week or two first.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in June
what_to_sow.lead: Peak planting for tender crops, plus successional sowings of salads and roots to keep the harvest going.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in July
what_to_sow.lead: Sow quick crops for autumn and winter. Keep watering and feeding, and pick little and often to keep plants cropping.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in August
what_to_sow.lead: A key month for sowing winter salads and hardy greens, and for planting out spring cabbage and overwintering onions.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in September
what_to_sow.lead: Last sowings of hardy crops, then plant garlic and onion sets as the soil is still warm. Clear spent crops and tidy beds.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in October
what_to_sow.lead: Garlic and broad beans can go in, and bare-root fruit planting begins. Protect remaining crops from the first frosts.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in November
what_to_sow.lead: Quiet outdoors. Plant bare-root fruit and garlic if the soil allows, and sow a few crops under cover.

what_to_sow.title: What to sow and plant in December
what_to_sow.lead: Rest and plan. Check stored crops, clean tools and pots, and order seed for next year.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in January
what_to_preserve.lead: Eat or process what you stored in autumn first, and check for soft or sprouting crops. Little is fresh, so this is a time to use the freezer and the larder.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in February
what_to_preserve.lead: Keep checking stored roots, apples and onions. Use the soft ones first and turn the preserves you made last summer into meals.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in March
what_to_preserve.lead: Little to harvest outside, so use the larder. Check stored crops weekly and use up anything starting to sprout.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in April
what_to_preserve.lead: The first spring crops arrive, with rhubarb and the earliest leaves. Freeze or cook rhubarb while it is young and tender.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in May
what_to_preserve.lead: Early crops such as asparagus, radishes and salad leaves are best eaten fresh. Rhubarb and herbs can be frozen or dried.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in June
what_to_preserve.lead: Strawberries, broad beans and peas are ready, and a glut can be frozen, made into jam or cooked and bottled.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in July
what_to_preserve.lead: The busiest month for gluts. Freeze beans, peas and berries within hours of picking, and make jams, chutneys and pickles.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in August
what_to_preserve.lead: Peak harvest, so preserve little and often. Tomatoes, courgettes, beans, plums and soft fruit all store well made into sauces, freezer packs and chutneys.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in September
what_to_preserve.lead: Apples, pears, squash and the main potato and onion crops. Cure and store onions and squash, and make chutneys and juice from windfalls.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in October
what_to_preserve.lead: Final harvests before frost. Lift root crops for store, wrap and store the best apples, and pick green tomatoes to ripen indoors.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in November
what_to_preserve.lead: Check stored crops regularly and pickle or freeze the last of the root and brassica harvest.

what_to_preserve.title: What to preserve and store in December
what_to_preserve.lead: Most of the preserving is done. Use the larder and freezer, and keep an eye on stored fruit and veg.

pests.name: Aphids (greenfly and blackfly)
pests.summary: Small sap-sucking insects that cluster on soft shoot tips and leaf undersides.
pests.spot: Clusters of tiny green, black or grey insects on shoot tips, flower buds and the undersides of leaves. Leaves curl, growth is stunted, and the plant may be sticky with honeydew, which turns black with sooty mould. Ants running up a plant often mean aphids.
prevent: Encourage ladybirds, lacewings and hoverflies with open flowers such as calendula and borage, and leave some wild corners.
Avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which produces the soft growth aphids love.
Check plants weekly from April, as early colonies are easy to deal with.
Grow a sacrificial plant such as nasturtium to draw blackfly away from beans.
control: Squash small colonies with your fingers or wipe them off with a damp cloth.
Blast plants with a jet of water, which knocks aphids off and they rarely return.
Pinch out the infested tips of broad beans and cut off badly hit shoots.
Spray with a soft soap or fatty-acid solution in the evening, away from open flowers, to protect bees.
pests.when: April to September, peaking in warm, dry spells.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.summary: Night feeders that shred seedlings, leaves and tender roots.
pests.spot: Ragged holes in leaves, silvery slime trails and seedlings that vanish overnight. They also hollow out potatoes, strawberries and lettuce hearts.
prevent: Water in the morning rather than the evening so the surface is dry at night.
Clear debris, long grass and old pots where they hide, and keep beds tidy.
Grow seedlings in pots and plant them out when they are tougher.
Encourage frogs, hedgehogs, ground beetles and birds with a pond and log pile.
control: Go out after dark with a torch and pick them off, then move or dispose of them.
Use beer traps sunk into the soil, emptying them often.
Water slug nematodes (a biological control) onto warm, moist soil between March and October.
If you use pellets, choose ferric phosphate ones, which are approved for organic gardening. Metaldehyde pellets are no longer legal in the UK.
Protect seedlings with clear bottle cloches.
pests.when: All year, worst in mild, damp weather and spring.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.summary: Tiny jumping beetles that pepper the leaves of brassicas and salad crops with small holes.
pests.spot: Lots of tiny round "shot holes" in the leaves of radish, rocket, mizuna, kale and other brassicas. The beetles are very small and jump when you disturb the plant. Seedlings suffer most.
prevent: Cover sowings with fine insect mesh (less than 1 mm) straight away.
Keep seedlings watered, as the beetles prefer dry conditions.
Sow in light shade in summer, or sow later in the season.
control: Established plants usually tolerate damage, so wait for them to outgrow it.
Water regularly to speed up growth.
Eat damaged leaves, as the holes are cosmetic.
pests.when: April to September, especially in hot, dry weather.

pests.name: Caterpillars (cabbage whites and others)
pests.summary: Butterfly and moth larvae that chew leaves, especially on brassicas.
pests.spot: Holes in leaves, droppings, and yellow-green caterpillars or clusters of yellow eggs on the underside of brassica leaves. Plants can be stripped to the veins in days.
prevent: Cover brassicas with fine mesh or butterfly netting from planting, with no gaps at the edges.
Check the undersides of leaves weekly from May and squash eggs.
Encourage birds, which feed caterpillars to their young.
control: Pick off caterpillars by hand and squash the eggs.
Remove badly damaged outer leaves and use the rest.
Clear old stalks in autumn, as chrysalises overwinter in debris.
pests.when: May to October, with two or three waves of butterflies.

pests.name: Cabbage root fly
pests.summary: Maggots that eat the roots of brassicas and kill young plants.
pests.spot: Young plants wilt on sunny days, leaves turn blue-grey and growth stops. The roots are tunnelled by small white maggots, and radish and turnip are bored through.
prevent: Fit a collar (a 15 cm square of carpet underlay or cardboard) around the stem of each plant at planting.
Cover the crop with fine mesh from planting, with the edges buried.
Plant larger, stronger transplants, which tolerate attack better.
control: There is no cure, so lift and bin affected plants and do not compost them.
Earth up around stems to encourage extra roots on tall plants.
Rotate brassicas to a new bed each year.
pests.when: Flies are active from April to June and again in August and September.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.summary: Low-flying flies whose maggots tunnel into carrots, parsnips and celery roots.
pests.spot: Reddening or yellowing foliage and rusty-brown tunnels in the roots, with small pale maggots. Parsnip, celery and parsley can be attacked as well as carrots.
prevent: Surround the bed with a 60 cm high barrier of fine mesh or fleece, as the flies fly low.
Cover with fine mesh from sowing.
Sow after mid-May or in late summer to miss the first egg-laying flight.
Thin in the evening, bury the thinnings and avoid bruising foliage, as the smell attracts flies.
Choose resistant varieties such as Flyaway or Resistafly.
control: There is nothing to spray, so prevention is key.
Lift crops early if damage is spotted and cut away the damaged parts of otherwise good roots.
pests.when: May to June and August to September.

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.summary: Maggots that eat the roots and bulbs of onions, leeks and shallots.
pests.spot: Seedlings or young plants turn yellow, flop and wilt. Small white maggots feed inside the bulb or at the base of the stem.
prevent: Cover plants with fine mesh from planting, with the edges buried.
Grow from sets rather than seed, as they are less likely to be hit.
Rotate onion crops each year.
control: Remove and bin affected plants, including the maggots.
Raise new onions in a different bed.
pests.when: May to June, with a second wave in late summer.

pests.name: Leek moth
pests.summary: Small caterpillars that mine the leaves and stems of leeks, onions and garlic.
pests.spot: White, translucent blotches or tunnels in leaves, and caterpillars burrowing into the centre of the plant. Small silky cocoons appear on leaves.
prevent: Cover plants with fine mesh from May to September.
Clear plant debris in autumn.
control: Squash caterpillars and cocoons by hand.
Cut off damaged leaves and use the remaining plant.
pests.when: May to September.

pests.name: Red spider mite
pests.summary: Tiny mites that thrive in hot, dry conditions, especially under cover.
pests.spot: Fine yellow speckling on leaves, bronzing, and fine silky webbing on the undersides and between stems. The mites are barely visible without a magnifying glass.
prevent: Keep greenhouses damp: wet the floor on hot days and ventilate well.
Water regularly, as drought-stressed plants suffer worst.
Clean the greenhouse thoroughly in winter.
control: Introduce the predatory mite Phytoseiulus persimilis as a biological control between March and September.
Spray leaves, undersides especially, with water to raise humidity.
Remove badly infested leaves and use soft soap sprays on smaller outbreaks.
pests.when: June to September, or all year in a heated greenhouse.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.summary: Tiny white flies that suck sap and coat plants with sticky honeydew.
pests.spot: Clouds of tiny white flies rise when you brush the plant. Leaves become sticky and covered in sooty black mould, and growth slows. Common on tomatoes, cucumbers, aubergines and brassicas.
prevent: Keep the greenhouse clean and free of weeds and old plant debris.
Hang yellow sticky traps to monitor and catch adults.
Clear old brassica stalks in winter to remove overwintering whitefly.
control: Release the parasitic wasp Encarsia formosa in a greenhouse from spring.
Remove heavily infested leaves and bin them.
Spray with soft soap, taking care to reach the leaf undersides.
pests.when: Spring to autumn, all year under heat.

pests.name: Leaf miners
pests.summary: Tiny maggots that tunnel between the surfaces of leaves.
pests.spot: Winding pale tunnels or brown blisters in leaves of beetroot, chard, spinach, celery, parsley and alliums. Small maggots or pupae are visible inside the blotches.
prevent: Cover young plants with fine mesh from early spring.
Check regularly and remove the first damaged leaves.
Rotate crops.
control: Squash the maggot by pinching the blister, or cut off the leaf and bin it.
The plant usually carries on growing, so pick off damaged leaves and eat the rest.
pests.when: April to September.

pests.name: Codling moth and plum moth
pests.summary: Moth larvae that burrow into apples, pears and plums, causing "maggoty" fruit.
pests.spot: A small hole near the eye of the fruit with a trail of brown droppings. A pink-white caterpillar lives in the core, and fruit often drops early.
prevent: Hang pheromone traps in the tree from late May to monitor and trap male moths.
Thin clustered fruit, as moths lay eggs where fruits touch.
Put grease bands on trunks in autumn to catch other pests.
control: Wrap corrugated cardboard around trunks in August; larvae hide in it, then remove and destroy it in winter.
Collect and bin windfalls promptly.
Encourage birds, which eat overwintering larvae.
pests.when: Moths fly from June to July, with damage showing in August.

pests.name: Pea moth
pests.summary: Caterpillars that eat the peas inside the pods.
pests.spot: Pods look normal outside, but opening them reveals small cream caterpillars with black heads and chewed peas, mostly on the side of the pod.
prevent: Sow early (March to April) or late (after mid-June) so flowering misses the main moth flight in June and July.
Cover plants with fine mesh from flowering.
Hang pheromone traps to see when moths are active.
control: Discard damaged peas, as there is nothing to treat once the caterpillars are inside.
Check the remaining pods before cooking and pick regularly so damaged pods do not stay on the plant.
pests.when: June to August.

pests.name: Raspberry beetle
pests.summary: Small beetles whose larvae spoil raspberries, loganberries and blackberries.
pests.spot: Dry, shrivelled patches on the fruit, usually at the stalk end, and tiny pale brown maggots when you pick.
prevent: Fork lightly over the soil under canes in winter to expose pupae to birds and frost.
Grow autumn-fruiting raspberries, as they flower after the beetles have gone.
Keep plants well watered and spaced.
control: Pick fruit regularly and check for maggots.
Remove any infested fruit and bin it.
pests.when: June to August.

pests.name: Vine weevil
pests.summary: Beetles and grubs that eat leaves and roots, especially in pots.
pests.spot: Adult beetles notch leaf edges in neat scallops. The plump, white, C-shaped grubs eat roots, so plants in pots suddenly wilt and collapse. The base of the plant pulls away easily.
prevent: Check pot plants in autumn for grubs, and use fresh compost.
Look for adult weevils on warm evenings and remove them by hand.
Water pots with nematodes (Steinernema or Heterorhabditis) as a preventive in late summer.
control: Tip out affected pots and pick out the grubs.
Water the compost with nematodes when soil is warm, between late summer and autumn or spring.
Replant in fresh compost.
pests.when: Adults from April to September, grubs from late summer to spring.

pests.name: Pea and bean weevil
pests.summary: Small beetles that nibble neat notches from the leaf edges of peas and beans.
pests.spot: U-shaped bites around the edges of leaves on young pea and broad bean plants. It looks worse than it is.
prevent: Keep seedlings growing strongly with enough water.
Cover young plants with fine mesh.
control: Established plants tolerate it, so no treatment is needed.
Protect small seedlings until they outgrow the damage.
pests.when: April to June.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.summary: Attractive metallic beetles that eat rosemary, lavender, thyme and sage.
pests.spot: Metallic green and purple striped beetles, and fat grubs, chewing leaves and shoot tips of rosemary and lavender.
prevent: Check plants regularly from late summer to spring.
Keep plants healthy and avoid overwatering.
control: Shake plants over a sheet and remove the beetles and grubs by hand.
Repeat every few days until numbers drop.
pests.when: Mostly from September to April, with a second peak in early summer.

pests.name: Sawfly caterpillars (currant and gooseberry)
pests.summary: Green caterpillars that strip the leaves from gooseberry and currant bushes.
pests.spot: Small holes in leaves in late spring that grow rapidly, until only the veins remain. Pale green caterpillars with black spots feed in the centre of the bush.
prevent: Inspect bushes from April, looking under the leaves near the centre of the bush for the first small holes.
Fork over soil under bushes in winter to expose pupae.
control: Pick off caterpillars by hand, or shake them onto a sheet.
Check every few days from April to August, as there are several generations.
Keep bushes healthy with feeding and watering so they can recover.
pests.when: April to August.

pests.name: Wasps
pests.summary: In late summer wasps damage ripe plums, apples and grapes.
pests.spot: Hollowed-out fruit, often with wasps feeding inside, from August to October. Earlier in the year wasps help by feeding on caterpillars.
prevent: Pick fruit as soon as it is ripe and collect windfalls daily.
Cover ripe bunches or fruit with fine mesh or organza bags.
control: Hang wasp traps (a jam jar with sweet bait) a few metres from fruit, away from where you sit.
Leave nests alone unless they are close to the house, as wasps are beneficial in spring.
pests.when: August to October.

pests.name: Big bud mite
pests.summary: Microscopic mites that live in blackcurrant buds and spread reversion virus.
pests.spot: Round, swollen buds on blackcurrant stems in winter, instead of the usual small, pointed ones. Affected bushes lose vigour and crop poorly.
prevent: Buy certified, mite-free plants and resistant varieties.
Check buds in winter.
control: Pick off swollen buds and bin them.
Remove and replace heavily infested bushes.
pests.when: Easiest to spot between November and March.

pests.name: Powdery mildew
pests.summary: A white powdery coating that appears on leaves and stems in dry, warm weather.
pests.spot: White or grey powdery patches on leaves, stems and sometimes fruit. Leaves yellow, curl and drop. Common on courgettes, cucumbers, peas, apples and gooseberries.
prevent: Water regularly at the base, as dry roots make plants more susceptible.
Space plants for good air circulation and avoid overcrowding.
Mulch to hold moisture in the soil.
Choose resistant varieties.
control: Remove affected leaves as soon as you see them and bin them rather than composting.
Water well in the morning and feed to keep plants vigorous.
Late-season mildew on courgettes and squash is usually harmless once the crop is nearly done.
pests.when: June to October, worst in hot, dry spells with humid nights.

pests.name: Downy mildew
pests.summary: A damp-weather disease with yellow patches above and grey-purple fuzz below the leaf.
pests.spot: Yellow or pale patches on the upper leaf surface, with grey or purple fuzzy growth underneath in humid weather. Leaves turn brown and die. Common on lettuce, spinach, onions, brassicas and basil.
prevent: Space plants and avoid overhead watering.
Water in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
Rotate crops and clear debris at the end of the season.
Choose resistant varieties, especially lettuce.
control: Remove and bin affected leaves, or the whole plant if badly hit.
Improve airflow around crops.
Sow successive crops in different spots, as the disease can build up.
pests.when: Spring and autumn, or any cool, wet spell.

pests.name: Clubroot
pests.summary: A soil-borne disease of brassicas that causes swollen, distorted roots.
pests.spot: Stunted plants with leaves that wilt on hot days, often with a purple tinge. The roots are swollen and knobbly. Spores can live in the soil for up to 20 years.
prevent: Test the soil and lime it to a pH of 7 or above before planting brassicas.
Buy plants from trusted sources, or raise your own in pots.
Plant brassicas as larger pot-raised plants.
Choose clubroot-resistant varieties.
Clean boots, tools and pots to avoid spreading soil from infected beds.
control: There is no cure, so lift and bin affected plants and do not compost them.
If you have clubroot, grow non-brassica crops in that soil or use resistant varieties and raised beds with clean soil.
Remember that radish, swede, turnip, mooli and wallflowers also host it.
pests.when: Spring to autumn, worst in wet, acid soil.

pests.name: Potato and tomato blight
pests.summary: A rapid fungus-like disease that turns potato and tomato foliage brown and rots tubers and fruit.
pests.spot: Dark brown patches on leaves, spreading fast in warm, humid weather, with white fuzz on the undersides. Fruit and tubers develop firm, brown, rotting patches.
