prevent: Grow early potatoes, which are harvested before blight usually strikes.
Choose resistant varieties of potato and tomato.
Grow tomatoes under cover, where leaves stay dry.
Remove any leftover potatoes (volunteers) and use certified seed.
control: If blight hits potatoes, cut off all the foliage and bin it, then leave the tubers for about three weeks before lifting.
Remove infected tomato plants as soon as you see signs and bin them.
Water at the base and keep foliage dry.
pests.when: July to September, in warm, wet spells.

pests.name: Rust
pests.summary: Orange or brown pustules that appear on the leaves of leeks, garlic, beans, mint and chives.
pests.spot: Bright orange, rust-coloured or brown raised pustules on leaves. Leaves yellow and die early. The pustules rub off as orange powder.
prevent: Space plants well and avoid overhead watering.
Do not over-feed with nitrogen.
Rotate crops and clear plant debris.
Choose rust-resistant varieties of leeks and beans where available.
control: Remove affected leaves and bin them.
Harvest garlic and leeks early if the disease is serious.
Cut mint and chives to the ground and bin the cuttings, and the plant will regrow clean.
pests.when: Mid-summer to autumn in humid weather.

pests.name: White blister (white rust)
pests.summary: Raised white blisters on the leaves and stems of brassicas and some salad crops.
pests.spot: White, raised, chalky blisters on leaves and stems, which can distort growth. Common on rocket, radish, mustard and other brassicas.
prevent: Rotate crops and avoid overcrowding.
Clear debris at the end of the season.
control: Remove affected leaves and bin them.
Plants usually continue to grow, and the damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.when: Summer and autumn, especially in damp weather.

pests.name: Onion white rot
pests.summary: A soil fungus that rots the roots and bulbs of onions, garlic and leeks.
pests.spot: Yellowing, wilting leaves and a fluffy white mould at the base of the bulb, with tiny black dots (sclerotia) that can survive in soil for 15 to 20 years.
prevent: Buy clean, certified sets and cloves.
Clean tools and boots to avoid spreading infected soil.
Never move soil or compost from affected beds.
control: Lift and bin infected plants, including all soil around the roots.
Do not grow alliums on infected ground again, and grow them in containers of fresh compost or a new bed instead.
pests.when: Spring to autumn, especially in cool conditions.

pests.name: Honey fungus
pests.summary: A root fungus that kills trees, shrubs and fruit bushes.
pests.spot: Sudden dieback or death of a tree or bush, with white fungus under the bark at the base and black "bootlace" threads in the soil. Honey-coloured toadstools appear in autumn.
prevent: Remove dead stumps and roots from the garden.
Install a barrier of thick plastic sheet buried 45 cm deep to stop threads spreading from neighbouring infected areas.
Choose more resistant plants, such as yew and some fruit species.
control: There is no chemical cure, so dig out the infected plant and as many roots as possible, and bin them.
Replant with resistant species after a year or more.
pests.when: Symptoms show from spring to autumn, with toadstools in autumn.

pests.name: Grey mould (botrytis)
pests.summary: A fluffy grey mould that attacks fruit, flowers and soft stems in damp conditions.
pests.spot: Soft brown rot covered in fuzzy grey mould on strawberries, raspberries, tomatoes, grapes and lettuce, and on dying flowers and leaves.
prevent: Space plants for good airflow and ventilate greenhouses.
Water at the base and avoid overcrowding.
Mulch strawberries with straw to keep fruit off damp soil.
Remove dead flowers and leaves promptly.
control: Pick off affected fruit and bin it straight away.
Cut away infected stems to healthy tissue and remove debris.
Do not compost infected material.
pests.when: Spring to autumn, especially in wet, humid weather.

pests.name: Leaf spot
pests.summary: Brown or black spots on leaves caused by fungi or bacteria.
pests.spot: Round brown, black or purple spots on leaves, sometimes with a yellow halo. Spots merge and leaves drop early. Chocolate spot on broad beans is a related disease.
prevent: Space plants well and avoid wetting the foliage.
Rotate crops and clear fallen leaves at the end of the season.
Avoid working among wet plants.
control: Remove affected leaves and bin them.
Water at the base and mulch to prevent soil splash.
Feed to keep plants vigorous, as healthy plants cope well.
pests.when: Summer and autumn, in warm, wet weather.

pests.name: Brown rot
pests.summary: A fungus that rots apples, pears, plums and cherries on the tree and in store.
pests.spot: Soft brown patches spread across the fruit, with rings of cream-coloured pustules. Infected fruit often shrivels and hangs on the tree over winter.
prevent: Handle fruit carefully, as wounds from birds, wasps and bruising let the fungus in.
Thin fruit so it does not touch.
Remove infected and mummified fruit from the tree and ground.
control: Pick off and bin rotten fruit promptly.
Prune out infected spurs and any shoots with blossom wilt.
Store only sound, unblemished fruit.
pests.when: July to October, and on stored fruit.

pests.name: Bacterial canker and coral spot
pests.summary: Diseases of stone fruit and trees that cause oozing, die-back and dead branches.
pests.spot: Sunken patches on bark that ooze amber gum, shot-hole leaves and dying branches on plums and cherries. Coral spot shows as small pink-orange pustules on dead wood.
prevent: Prune stone fruit only in summer, when the sap is rising and wounds heal quickly.
Clean pruning tools between plants.
Keep trees healthy with feeding, mulching and watering.
control: Cut out affected branches back to healthy wood in summer, and burn or bin them.
Remove dead wood bearing coral spot promptly so it cannot spread to living wood.
pests.when: Symptoms show from spring to summer, with infection in autumn and winter.

pests.name: Silver leaf
pests.summary: A fungus that gives leaves a silvery sheen and kills branches of plums and cherries.
pests.spot: A silvery sheen on the leaves, and a purple or brown stain in the wood when you cut a branch. Branches die back over time.
prevent: Prune plums, cherries and other stone fruit in summer, never in winter.
Clean pruning tools and avoid unnecessary wounds.
control: Cut affected branches back to at least 15 cm beyond any stain, in summer.
Burn or bin the wood, and do not use wound sealants.
Trees can recover if the infection is caught early.
pests.when: Leaf symptoms in summer, with infection through autumn and winter.

pests.name: Peach leaf curl
pests.summary: A fungus that blisters and curls the leaves of peaches, nectarines and almonds.
pests.spot: Red, puckered and blistered leaves in spring, which later turn white and drop. Trees are weakened and crop poorly.
prevent: Cover trees with a clear rain shelter from January to May, leaving the sides open for pollinators.
Never let rain wet the leaves in winter and spring.
Choose resistant varieties.
control: Remove affected leaves and bin them, and do not compost them.
Feed and mulch to help the tree recover and produce new, healthy leaves.
pests.when: January to May.

pests.name: Fireblight
pests.summary: A bacterial disease that scorches blossom and shoots on pears, apples and quinces.
pests.spot: Blossom and young shoots wilt and turn brown as if burned, with shoot tips bent into a "shepherd's crook". Orange-brown ooze may appear on the bark.
prevent: Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces soft growth.
Choose less susceptible varieties.
Clean tools after pruning.
control: Cut out infected shoots at least 60 cm below the visible symptoms and burn them.
Disinfect tools between cuts.
If a whole tree is affected, remove it.
pests.when: May to August.

pests.name: Apple and pear scab
pests.summary: A fungus that causes dark scabby spots on leaves and fruit.
pests.spot: Olive-green or dark brown scabby spots on leaves and fruit, and cracked, misshapen fruit. Blistered shoots can occur on pears.
prevent: Rake up and bin fallen leaves in autumn, where the fungus overwinters.
Prune to create an open tree with good air flow.
Choose scab-resistant varieties.
control: Pick off and bin infected fruit.
Prune out blistered shoots in winter.
Lightly scabby apples are safe to eat, so cut away the blemishes.
pests.when: Spring to autumn, in wet weather.

pests.name: Plant viruses
pests.summary: Viruses that cause mottled, distorted leaves and stunted plants, often spread by aphids.
pests.spot: Yellow and green mottled or mosaic patterns on leaves, puckering, stunting and poor cropping. Common on cucumbers, courgettes, raspberries and strawberries.
prevent: Control aphids, which spread most viruses.
Buy certified virus-free plants, particularly raspberries and strawberries.
Clean knives and secateurs between plants.
Remove weeds that harbour viruses.
control: There is no cure, so dig up and bin infected plants. Do not compost them.
Do not save seed or take cuttings from infected plants.
pests.when: Symptoms appear from late spring to autumn.

pests.name: Damping off
pests.summary: A fungal disease that rots seedlings at the base so they collapse.
pests.spot: Seedlings suddenly collapse at compost level, with a thin, dark, pinched stem. Mould may grow on the compost surface.
prevent: Use clean pots and fresh compost.
Water with tap water rather than from open water butts.
Sow thinly, avoid overwatering and ventilate seed trays.
Start sowing in a warm, bright place so seedlings grow quickly.
control: Remove affected seedlings and the surrounding compost.
Ease off watering and improve ventilation.
Resow in fresh compost if many are lost.
pests.when: Late winter to spring, when seedlings are raised indoors.

pests.name: Root and crown rot
pests.summary: Rot caused by waterlogged soil that kills roots and plants.
pests.spot: Wilting or yellowing leaves despite wet soil. The roots are brown and mushy, and the base of the plant may be soft. Mediterranean herbs suffer first.
prevent: Grow in free-draining soil, raised beds or pots with drainage holes.
Add grit to heavy soil and avoid planting too deeply.
Do not overwater, especially in winter.
control: Lift the plant, cut away rotten roots, and replant in better-drained soil if it can be saved.
Stop watering and let the soil dry out.
Replace affected plants and avoid the same spot until the drainage is improved.
pests.when: Mainly autumn to spring, in wet weather.

pests.name: Birds and pigeons
pests.summary: Birds strip brassicas, peck fruit and pull up seedlings and onion sets.
pests.spot: Brassica leaves stripped to the stalks in winter, berries and cherries stolen as they ripen, seedlings pulled out, and onion sets or garlic cloves lying on the surface.
prevent: Cover brassicas, peas and soft fruit with netting or a fruit cage, held clear of the plants so birds cannot peck through.
Use fine mesh or a cloche on seedlings.
Use small-mesh netting that cannot trap birds, and check it daily.
Change scarers, such as shiny strips or windmills, regularly, as birds soon learn to ignore them.
control: Protect crops physically, as netting is the only fully reliable method.
Firm back any sets or cloves that have been pulled up, and cover them with mesh or fleece until rooted.
Remember that wild birds are protected, and they also eat many pests, so aim to share rather than remove them.
pests.when: Brassicas from autumn to spring; fruit from June to September.

pests.name: Mice, squirrels and badgers
pests.summary: Mammals that dig up seeds, steal nuts and raid sweetcorn.
pests.spot: Pea and bean seeds dug up and eaten, nuts stolen from trees, sweetcorn cobs stripped or flattened, and holes dug in beds.
prevent: Sow peas and beans in pots under cover and plant out seedlings.
Cover seeds in the ground with fine mesh or chicken wire until they have germinated.
Pick nuts and sweetcorn as soon as they are ready.
Use a low electric fence or strong fencing around sweetcorn if badgers are a problem.
control: Set humane traps or snap traps for mice near seed rows, in covered boxes so other animals cannot reach them.
Never interfere with a badger sett, as badgers and their setts are protected by law.
pests.when: Spring sowing, and late summer to autumn for sweetcorn and nuts.

pests.name: Bolting
pests.summary: Plants run to flower and seed too early, so leaves and roots turn tough or bitter.
pests.spot: A tall flowering stem rises from lettuce, spinach, rocket, coriander, beetroot, onions or brassicas. Leaves become bitter and the crop stops growing.
prevent: Choose bolt-resistant varieties and sow at the right time for each crop.
Water regularly and mulch to keep roots cool and moist.
Give leafy crops light shade in hot summer weather.
Avoid sowing too early, as cold snaps trigger bolting in onions and beetroot.
Sow little and often so there is always a fresh batch.
control: Harvest quickly, as bolted crops will not recover.
Cut flower stalks off herbs such as basil, coriander and mint to extend picking.
Let one or two plants flower to feed bees, or to save seed.
pests.when: Mainly May to August, especially during heat and drought.

pests.name: Frost and cold damage
pests.summary: Late frosts and cold snaps blacken tender growth and ruin blossom.
pests.spot: Blackened, limp leaves and shoots after a cold night, brown blossom that fails to set fruit, and soft rot on tender plants.
prevent: Plant tender crops such as tomatoes, courgettes and beans only after the last frost, usually mid-May in most of the UK.
Harden off plants gradually for 7 to 10 days before planting out.
Keep fleece or cloches ready to cover plants on frosty nights.
Avoid planting blossom trees in frost pockets at the bottom of slopes.
control: Leave damaged growth in place until new shoots appear in spring, as it protects lower buds.
Cut back only to healthy new growth.
Cover blossom on small trees and wall-trained fruit with fleece when frost is forecast.
pests.when: March to May, and again from October.

pests.name: Blossom end rot
pests.summary: A black, sunken patch at the base of tomatoes, peppers and courgettes.
pests.spot: A dark, sunken, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit. It is caused by uneven watering, which stops the plant taking up calcium.
prevent: Water evenly and regularly, never letting plants dry out then flooding them.
Mulch to keep soil moisture steady.
Use large pots, as small ones dry out quickly.
Avoid damaging roots by hoeing deeply.
control: Remove affected fruit so the plant puts energy into healthy ones.
Keep watering steadily, and later fruits are usually fine.
Adding lime or calcium will not fix it.
pests.when: July to September.

pests.name: Fruit splitting
pests.summary: Tomatoes, plums, cherries and other fruit crack after a dry spell followed by heavy water.
pests.spot: Skin cracks on tomatoes, cherries, plums, grapes and root crops like carrots, often after rain following a dry period.
prevent: Water evenly and mulch to keep soil moisture steady.
Shelter cherries and plums from heavy rain where possible.
Choose varieties less prone to splitting.
control: Pick split fruit promptly and eat it quickly, as it rots and attracts wasps and flies.
Remove any split fruit from the plant.
pests.when: Summer, particularly after rain following drought.

pests.name: Poor pollination
pests.summary: Flowers appear but little or no fruit sets.
pests.spot: Plenty of flowers but few or no fruit, small or misshapen fruit, or sweetcorn cobs with gaps in the kernels.
prevent: Plant flowers that attract bees and hoverflies near your crops.
Grow sweetcorn in blocks rather than a single row so wind can pollinate it.
Plant compatible pollination partners for fruit trees that need them.
Avoid sprays that harm bees.
control: Hand-pollinate with a soft brush or by transferring pollen from male to female flowers (courgettes, squash, cucumbers and indoor fruit).
Tap the stems of tomatoes and peppers on warm, dry mornings.
Cover blossom with fleece on cold nights but remove it by day so insects can reach the flowers.
pests.when: April to August, especially in cold, wet springs.

pests.name: Wind damage
pests.summary: Strong winds snap stems, shred leaves and dry out plants.
pests.spot: Snapped or bent stems, torn leaves, rocking plants, and scorched, crispy leaf edges.
prevent: Grow tall crops like sweetcorn, brussels sprouts and beans in sheltered spots.
Use a semi-permeable windbreak such as a hedge or windbreak netting, which slows wind better than a solid wall.
Stake tall crops and tie them in securely.
control: Re-firm plants rocked loose by the wind.
Cut away damaged stems and support the plant.
Water after windy weather, as wind dries soil quickly.
pests.when: Autumn to spring.

pests.name: Yellow leaves from high soil pH (chlorosis)
pests.summary: Leaves turn yellow between the veins when plants cannot take up iron.
pests.spot: Yellow leaves with green veins, usually on blueberries, raspberries or other acid-loving plants in alkaline soil or hard-water areas.
prevent: Grow blueberries in pots of ericaceous compost.
Water with rainwater rather than tap water in hard-water areas.
Test your soil pH before choosing plants.
control: Feed with sequestered iron or an ericaceous fertiliser.
Repot into ericaceous compost if the plant is in a container.
Mulch with pine bark or composted bracken.
pests.when: Spring to autumn.

pests.name: Plants that spread and self-seed
pests.summary: Some herbs and vegetables spread by runners, roots or seed and can take over a bed.
pests.spot: Mint, lemon balm, horseradish, Jerusalem artichoke, chives and others pop up all over the bed or garden.
prevent: Grow mint and other runners in a pot, or sink a bottomless bucket into the soil to contain the roots.
Deadhead before seed ripens.
Plant Jerusalem artichokes where they can be left alone, and remove all tubers when lifting.
control: Pull up seedlings when small.
Dig out roots and runners completely, as even small fragments can regrow.
Cut back plants hard if they are getting out of hand.
pests.when: Spring to autumn.

pests.name: Drought and irregular watering
pests.summary: Dry spells cause wilting, flower and fruit drop, bolting and poor crops.
pests.spot: Wilting, scorched leaf edges, flowers and young fruit dropping, small or tough crops, and plants that sulk through dry spells.
prevent: Mulch beds with compost or bark to hold moisture.
Water deeply and less often, rather than a little every day.
Water early in the morning at the base of plants.
Collect rainwater in butts and use a drip hose or seep hose.
control: Prioritise watering seedlings, newly planted crops, fruiting vegetables and container plants.
Shade tender plants in heatwaves.
Give a general feed once the plant recovers.
pests.when: May to September, especially during heatwaves.

adult_helper_notes: Stay close by. Little ones need a grown-up for scissors, hot things, knives and anything with sharp edges.
Wash hands after touching soil, compost or plants, and before eating.
Teach this rule: we only eat plants a grown-up has said are safe. Some plants and berries in gardens are poisonous.
Wash anything you pick before it goes in your mouth.
Use peat-free compost and keep garden chemicals well out of reach.
Check for food allergies before sharing a recipe, and never give honey to babies under 1 year.

projects.title: Cress heads
projects.blurb: Give an eggshell a funny face and grow green “hair” in a week.
need: An empty eggshell (or a clean yoghurt pot)
steps: Wash your hands. Ask a grown-up for a clean, empty eggshell or yoghurt pot.
Draw a funny face on the front with a pen.
Fill it with damp cotton wool. It should be wet but not dripping.
Sprinkle cress seeds on top and gently pat them down. Do not cover them.
Put it on a bright windowsill. Give it a few drops of water every day.
After 4 to 7 days your cress “hair” will be ready. Snip it with scissors and put it in a sandwich!
projects.fact: Cress seeds turn sticky when they get wet. That helps them cling to the cotton wool.
projects.adult_note: If you use an eggshell, use one from a boiled egg and wash hands afterwards. A clean yoghurt pot works just as well.

projects.title: Radish race
projects.blurb: Radishes are the fastest veg in the garden. Who will pull the first one?
need: A pot or a patch of garden
A friend or family member to race
steps: Fill a pot with compost, and leave a gap of 2 cm at the top.
Poke your finger 1 cm into the compost to make little holes in a row.
Drop a seed in each hole and cover it with compost.
Water gently, so you do not wash the seeds away.
Keep the compost damp, like a squeezed-out sponge.
After about 4 weeks, gently pull one. If it is as big as a marble, it is ready. First to pick a radish wins!
projects.fact: Radishes grow really fast, and the bigger they get, the spicier they can taste!
projects.adult_note: Radishes can be sown every couple of weeks, so there is always a new race to run.

projects.title: See a bean grow
projects.blurb: Watch the roots and shoots grow where you can see them.
need: A clear zip-top bag or a glass jar
steps: Fold a sheet of kitchen paper to fit inside the bag and make it damp.
Slide it in, and put the beans between the paper and the plastic, so you can see them.
Close the bag almost all the way, and tape it to a sunny window.
Check every day. Add a splash of water if the paper dries out.
First a white root pokes out, then a green shoot appears. Draw what you see each day!
When the shoot is about 5 cm tall, ask a grown-up to help plant it in a pot of compost with a tall stick to climb.
projects.fact: A bean seed is a plant in a case. The seed has its first food packed inside it.
projects.adult_note: These beans are for growing, not eating. Raw runner beans are not safe to eat.

projects.title: Giant sunflower contest
projects.blurb: Plant a sunflower seed, tie it up as it grows, and measure how tall it gets.
steps: Fill a pot with compost and poke a hole 2 cm deep with your finger.
Drop in one seed, cover it, and water it.
Put it on a sunny windowsill. A shoot should come up in about 1 to 2 weeks.
When it is as tall as your hand, and the weather is warm, move it to a big pot or a sunny spot in the garden.
Tie it loosely to a cane with soft string, as it gets taller.
Measure it every week and write it down. Who has the tallest?
projects.fact: Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun across the sky each day!
projects.adult_note: Plant out after the last frost. Birds will love the seeds when the heads are ripe.

projects.title: Potato treasure bucket
projects.blurb: Plant a potato in a bucket, then tip it out and find your hidden treasure.
need: A big bucket or a potato bag, with holes in the bottom
steps: Ask a grown-up to make some holes in the bottom of the bucket.
Put 10 cm of compost in the bucket.
Sit the potatoes on top with the sprouts pointing up, and cover them with 10 cm of compost.
Water well, and keep it damp. Soon green shoots will pop up!
When the shoots are as tall as your hand, pile more compost around them.
When the plant has flowers, tip out the bucket and hunt for the treasure!
projects.fact: The potato is not a root. It is a swollen underground stem that stores food for the plant.
projects.adult_note: Never let children eat green potatoes, the leaves or the berries. They are poisonous. Check the harvest before cooking.

projects.title: Strawberry pot
projects.blurb: Grow your own sweet treats in a pot or hanging basket.
need: A pot or hanging basket with holes
steps: Fill your pot with compost and make 3 holes, spaced well apart.
Put a plant in each hole. Keep the middle (the crown) level with the compost, and not buried.
Press the compost down gently and water well.
Put the pot in the sunniest place you have, and water whenever the top feels dry.
Flowers come first, and then little green berries. They turn white and then red.
Only pick the berries that are bright red all over, and wash them before you eat them.
projects.fact: A strawberry has about 200 seeds on the outside. Not many fruits wear their seeds on the outside like that!
projects.adult_note: A hanging basket keeps berries away from slugs. Net the pot if birds are a problem.

recipes.title: Cress sandwiches
ingredients: A big handful of snipped cress
steps: Wash your hands.
Spread butter or cream cheese on all 4 slices.
Snip the cress over 2 of the slices, with scissors.
Sprinkle a tiny pinch of salt, if you like.
Press the other slices on top.
👩‍🍳 Cut into fingers or use a cutter to make fun shapes.

recipes.title: Rainbow veg sticks with minty dip
ingredients: A small handful of chives or mint
steps: Wash your hands and all the vegetables.
👩‍🍳 Peel the carrots and cut everything into sticks.
Snip the chives or mint into the yoghurt with scissors.
Add a squeeze of lemon juice and stir it up.
Arrange the sticks in rainbow order on a plate.
Dip and crunch!

recipes.title: Strawberry yoghurt pops
ingredients: 1 to 2 tbsp runny honey or maple syrup (no honey for babies under 1)
Lolly moulds, or small paper cups and lolly sticks
steps: Wash your hands and the strawberries, and remove the green tops.
👩‍🍳 Blend the strawberries, yoghurt and honey until smooth.
Pour the mixture into the moulds or cups.
Push in the sticks, and put them in the freezer for at least 4 hours.
To get them out, hold the mould under the warm tap for a few seconds.

recipes.title: Muffin mini pizzas
ingredients: 4 tbsp tomato passata or pizza sauce
Toppings: cherry tomatoes, sweetcorn, peppers, basil leaves
steps: 👩‍🍳 Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan) and line a tray with baking paper.
Wash your hands, and lay the muffin halves cut-side up on the tray.
Spoon on a little sauce and spread it out with the back of the spoon.
Sprinkle on the cheese, and then add your toppings. Make faces if you like!
👩‍🍳 Bake for 8 to 10 minutes until the cheese is bubbling and golden.
Let them cool for a few minutes. Tear on some fresh basil and eat.

recipes.title: Treasure potato wedges
steps: 👩‍🍳 Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan).
Scrub the potatoes clean, and check for any green bits (a grown-up should cut those off).
👩‍🍳 Cut the potatoes into wedges.
Put the wedges in a big bowl with the oil, paprika and salt, and toss with your hands until covered.
Spread them on a baking tray in a single layer.
👩‍🍳 Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and soft inside.

recipes.title: Sparkly mint lemonade
ingredients: A big handful of mint leaves
steps: Wash the mint, and pick the leaves off the stalks.
Scrunch the leaves in your hands, then put them in a jug with the sugar.
👩‍🍳 Cut the lemons in half, and squeeze the juice into the jug.
Squash the mint and sugar with a wooden spoon until it smells amazing.
Add ice and pour in the fizzy water.
Give it a gentle stir, then pour and enjoy!

jobs.text: Order seeds and seed potatoes, and check what is left from last year before you buy more.
Clean and sort pots, trays and tools. Scrub pots with hot water to stop disease carrying over.
Prune apple and pear trees while they are dormant, removing dead, crossing and rubbing branches.
Dig over empty beds on dry ground, or spread a layer of compost on top and leave it to the worms.
Shake heavy snow off hedges and evergreens, and bring tender pots into shelter before a hard frost.
Top up bird feeders and put out fresh, unfrozen water.
Sow chillies, peppers and aubergines on a warm windowsill or in a heated propagator.
Chit first early potatoes on a cool, bright windowsill with the eyes upwards.
Check stored apples, squash and onions and remove anything soft or mouldy.
Sow tomatoes, chillies, peppers and aubergines indoors with warmth and good light.
Sow onions and leeks in trays under cover.
Prune autumn raspberries to the ground and tidy up gooseberries and currants.
Prune apple and pear trees before buds start to swell. Do not prune plums or cherries now.
Cover a patch of soil with clear polythene or a cloche to warm it for early sowing.
Plant bare-root fruit trees, canes and hedging if the soil is not frozen or waterlogged.
Tackle slug and snail hiding places: clear rubbish and old pots from beds.
Plant shallots and onion sets in the greenhouse or outside on workable soil.
Mark out and build new raised beds while the ground is quiet.
Sow tomatoes, peppers, celeriac, leeks and early brassicas indoors or in the greenhouse.
Sow broad beans, peas, parsnips and spinach outside on warmed, workable soil.
Plant first early potatoes in trenches, ready to earth up when the shoots show.
Plant onion sets and garlic if the garlic did not go in last autumn.
Prepare seedbeds: rake to a fine tilth and remove weeds as soon as they appear.
Feed fruit bushes and trees with a general fertiliser and mulch with compost.
Cover blossom and early shoots with fleece on nights when frost is forecast.
Divide perennials and herbs such as chives and mint while they are just starting to grow.
Start slug patrols after dark with a torch, especially around new seedlings.
Sow courgettes, squash, cucumbers and runner beans in pots indoors, ready to plant out after the last frost.
Sow carrots, beetroot, lettuce, radishes and spring onions outside in short rows every few weeks.
Plant maincrop potatoes and earth up early potato shoots.
Harden off young plants by putting them outside by day and back in at night for a week or two.
Weed little and often. Hoeing on a sunny day kills seedlings quickly.
Keep fleece to hand: April frosts can still kill potato shoots, young beans and blossom.
Plant out strawberry runners and new fruit bushes, and water them in well.
Mow the lawn on a high setting and feed it as growth picks up.
Set up slug control that suits you: beer traps, copper tape, or nematodes watered onto damp soil.
Plant out tomatoes, courgettes, beans and squash once frost risk has passed in your area, usually mid to late May.
Sow French beans, runner beans, sweetcorn and salad crops directly outside.
Earth up potatoes and tie in climbing peas and beans on their supports.
Thin seedlings to the spacing on the packet so the rest can grow properly.
Water new transplants well, and mulch to hold in moisture before the summer.
Cover tender plants with fleece if a late frost is forecast, especially in the north and Scotland.
Pinch out side shoots on cordon tomatoes and feed them weekly once the first truss sets.
Net soft fruit and brassicas against birds and pigeons.
Cut back spring-flowering herbs and take cuttings of mint and rosemary.
Water in the morning or evening, giving a good soak twice a week rather than a sprinkle each day.
Harvest salad leaves, radishes, early potatoes, peas and strawberries regularly to keep plants cropping.
Sow successional crops of lettuce, beetroot, carrots and spring onions for autumn picking.
Tie in tomato plants, remove side shoots and start liquid feeding every week.
Pick and freeze or jam surplus strawberries and early gooseberries.
